content.content:
In our previous update sent in late July, we wrote:

*…. Iron ore fundamentals look weaker than they did a month ago. Steel mill profitability in China has fallen sharply, reaching its lowest level since September 2024, making a reduction in hot metal output very likely. In late 2024, the Cape/Newc market weakened significantly; with iron ore fundamentals now resembling that period, the risk of a similar market development is considerable. Minor bulk shipment growth has followed a similar path to iron ore, as global manufacturing momentum has faded. A stronger US dollar, higher US government bond yields, lower precious and industrial metals prices, and higher energy and grain prices all point to an emerging economic downcycle, suggesting that minor bulk shipment growth will decline going forward. The outlook for grains shipments is also not looking too bright according to the International Grains Council. Coal remains a different story, but seaborne supply remains a constraint, evident by the fact that shipments in the first half of this year were lower than in the first half of 2024. Still, the current energy market situation likely means supply will increase going forward.
Overall, we think the spot market levels in May were the peak of this year. The Cape/Newc and Panamax/Kamsarmax segments seem to be on a “lower highs and lower lows” trajectory since then. The Supra/Ultra market has, over the last few weeks, displayed signs of weakness, and the Handysize market struggled to follow the Supra/Ultra market push in the first weeks of July.*

The market strength in the Cape/Newc segment in the month of August was driven by extremely high **bauxite** shipments, along with typhoon-related logistical delays. In July and August, Guinea Bauxite exports on Capes/Newcs increased by 53% compared to the same period last year. Through July, China’s total bauxite imports increased by 24% year on year, compared with Alumina production growth of 1%. Bauxite inventories have accumulated as a result, which means that, at some point, the pace of imports needs to slow. 
China’s **iron ore** imports increased by 2.6% year on year through August. However, the pace of imports has slowed down in the last few months, as the total between June and August was unchanged on the same period last year. Inventories remain elevated, and consumption remains lower than last year. Global **grains** shipments increased by 7.5% year on year through August. The pace has decreased sharply there in the last months, with July and August shipments down 6% compared to last year. Global **coal** shipments increased by 2% year on year through August. Growth is muted considering the circumstances in energy markets, and moreover, total volumes for the first eight months were lower than in both 2023 and 2024. 
Total **global shipment volumes** (all commodities, all segments) were up 3.2% year on year through August, vs DWT supply growth of 3.3%. Comparing the last three months to the same period last year, volumes increased by just 1.2%. Long-haul flows, along with disruptions to normal operations in the MEG, Red Sea, Black Sea, Panama Canal and the Pacific (typhoons) keep the markets trending sideways at high levels. We don’t see anything that fundamentally changes our view for the outlook going forward.

This page gives brief comments on what the charts on the next page tell us. We have pointed to an increasingly bearish picture being painted for the second half of this year and the next year over the last months. The BDI year-on-year change has rolled over and is expected to continue falling. 

Top left chart:

The BDI year-on-year change has been strongly positive since September last year, as usual, lagging behind increased credit growth in China. 
However, the credit growth rate has tumbled sharply during the last few months, which suggests a negative BDI development going forward. Interest rates and reserve requirement ratio changes do not point to any imminent turnaround in China's liquidity conditions. 

Top right chart:

Except for a decoupling in 2024, the change in bond yields in China and the US has been a good leading indicator for dry bulk demand growth. This year it has so far called the demand growth development perfectly, as growth has tumbled sharply following the peak in Q2. 

Middle left chart:

Lower crude oil prices are bullish for economic growth, and vice versa. The chart displays that since 2017, there has been a tight correlation between lower year-on-year oil prices and a higher year-on-year BDI, with the oil price change leading by 1 year. 
The low oil prices of last year suggest the BDI could remain positive year-on-year throughout 2026. However, the increase in oil prices since late February suggest the market will be lower during the first half of next year. 

Middle right chart:

The OECD diffusion index momentum keeps falling, and suggest the year on year change of the BDI will turn less and less positive over the coming six months. 

Bottom left chart:

The OECD diffusion index correlation with the BDI is very high, as usual. The OECD index reading is comparable to previous cycle peaks. The index seems to be rolling over, as the reading has fallen from 18 between January and April to 16 in July. 

Bottom right chart:

Shipment volume growth has, as usual, tracked the development of the US dollar index (a very good proxy for global liquidity conditions).

The oil and tanker markets remain in a paradoxical equilibrium, where China runs a fine balancing act for crude oil, aided by increased Hormuz flows lately, and tanker rates are supported by extraordinary oil price discrepancies and broad inefficiencies. Given the fragile balance we introduce three market scenarios, with materially different implications for rates going forward - the range of outcomes has rarely been wider. 

The odd environment we are in is (likely) the most bullish possible. Already supported, tanker rates have surged to new highs the last month on re-opened West-East arbitrage, recovering Hormuz transits and CPC volumes, and Red Sea rerouting - again catching fleet positioning wrong-footed. However, as has been the case several times this year, after a rush comes calm, and rates now slide again. With substantial oil price swings, refinery margins at historic highs and crude still undersupplied, there is potential for continued rate strength - possibly boosted further by seasonally higher Americas exports. 

Some demand wild-cards going forward are arbitrages and oil price swings (China has an outsized say in whether crude oil prices remain relatively measured), geopolitics and the broader economy (obviously).  On the supply side there is added complexity from the PGSA's  designation of 45 'Hormuz-shuttle' ships as non-compliant (contagion risk), and added fleet growth from former  shadow VLCCs re-entering the compliant market.

The most sustainably positive scenario for tanker demand. There should be incentives for resolution given increasing economic pressure in both the U.S. (Bessent's financial market interventions suggest an uncomfortable position: after years of unsustainable budget deficits, interventions may run into diminishing marginal returns) and Iran (soaring inflation, lower oil exports and goods shortages). However, fundamental differences persist. In this scenario, tanker tonne-miles may soar on a potential race to the bottom for OPEC (and former +) producers on top of strong non-OPEC growth, and strong refinery margins incentivising high runs. The caveat is that extreme price discrepancies will disappear, allowing less room for freight. In other words, a normal (very) strong market for at least the next 12-18 months.

The most bullish scenario for rates is one in which the status quo persists. With widespread inefficiencies around the major chokepoints and wide oil pricing discrepancies, there is sufficient room for oil producers, traders, refiners and owners to earn healthy profits, which is arguably the main reason why we now see record rates. Although volumes remain substantially lower than pre-war, there is enough distance and time effects so that fleet utilisation remains very high, other perhaps than for a few key actors with partly different business models to the norm. 

However, there will be increasing risk of shortages - there is likely a limit to how long China can balance the oil market. Therefore, this scenario inevitably may turn into the next one...

This one is one of the reasons why the U.S. has stepped off further escalation, and why Bessent this week refrained from directly sanctioning Chinese entities for dealing with Iran. Further escalation and regional hostility, with corresponding upside for energy and commodity prices may ultimately tilt the global economy into serious trouble. Soaring inflation is not needed on top of already increasing long-term bond yields and U.S. policy exhaustion. A meaningful oil demand (and price) drop could lead to sustained oil production shut-ins. Couple this with the highest potential tanker fleet growth since the global financial crisis...  

And you may have almost the same outcome for the tanker market the next few years as in 2010 onwards...

In ebb and flow over the last few months, there has been waves of fixtures in both basins which have caught the fleet either wrongly positioned, or just too tight, like most recently. First it was some re-routing from Yanbu to the north and some Bahri ballasters set to go around Africa, then a combination of a re-opened West-East arb. simultaneously with increased Hormuz transits and high fixture activity for STS off Fujairah and Oman. CPC volumes coming back in full have helped too, and position lists have shrunk substantially. 

Panic? Perhaps that has played in too, piling up more fixtures than normal - which may suggest some more calm to come - this week has been quiet and inevitably put pressure on rates. However, oil pricing and refinery margins suggest there is still incentive for charterers to secure ships at high rates, albeit levels may move up and down in tandem across segments and fixing regions. 

Hormuz transit numbers have been hotly debated by oil market watchers amid U.S. administration claims that the flow is much higher (~10 mbpd) than meets the eye through traditional tracking sources (~6 mbpd). There has been an uptick, and may very well be some more upside when more complete tracking becomes available. Some of that, however, seems to be re-routing of Saudi volumes from Yanbu to the Gulf coast, so that the overall uptick in crude loadings has not been vast. There is still an implied (large) shortage of crude oil globally. 

CPP loadings have picked up too, led by Asia and the U.S. over the last month. With crack spreads at all-time highs every refiner who can is incentivised to run max - however, capacity remains a constraint.

content.content:
Tanker demand measured in tonne-days (to better capture waiting time and longer ballast legs etc. vs. tonne-miles) remains above last years' levels, but has come off meaningfully vs. the highs - led lower by VLCCs. Given a much higher Atlantic fixture count for long-haul voyages recently, however, these figures are expected to pick up again near-term - and reverse some of the demand strength for smaller vs. bigger vessels. 

Although still lagging, product tanker demand has picked up meaningfully, with higher volumes and some long-haul arbitrages re-opening, which may also give further upside near-term. 

Overall, the near-term demand outlook is slightly better for crude vs. products, as key Atlantic producers reduce domestic demand to free up more for exports, and there appears to be a gradual pick-up in volumes out of the MEG too. For products, meanwhile, flows are to a greater extent capped by shut-in capacity.

The key indicator to watch for crude tanker demand near-term will be the West-East arbitrage which has re-opened the last couple of weeks, amid a greater demand pull from Asia. Another, less visible, price dynamic which will also be key is the discount for crude grades from inside Hormuz (Dubai vs. Murban below is an imperfect view but at least indicative of direction). If these narrow there may be downside risk for TD3c, which in itself may not be too interesting for others than the select few parties who can actually participate in that (now) niche trade. However, lower discounts may also lower the willingness to pay for surrounding load areas, which are partly connected. Similarly, if TD34 rates come off, the West-East rates may quickly follow.

Low CPP volumes is a double edged sword - lower product tanker demand is a drag, but at the same time very high crack spreads should give trade possibilities and room for high freight. Over the last month, cracks and MR rates have moved in opposite directions - suggesting room on the upside for rates in areas or periods where tonnage gets tight(er).

content.content: Oil market in some sort of balance

The oil market remains undersupplied, although nowhere near as much as feared as evidenced by onshore inventories having drawn relatively little YTD. The latest estimate for shut-in production in the MEG is at 6 mbpd, so has more than halved since the top, and production elsewhere has risen slightly. Meanwhile, global refinery runs are about 5 mbpd lower than the same time last year. 

Much of the fragile balance hangs on China. If Chinese runs and imports can remain low, the equilibrium that currently exists both in the oil and tanker markets may persist. That also hinges on Hormuz transits remaining at about 50% of pre-war levels. If, however, Hormuz flow increases further, that may allow Chinese runs to recover, leaving upside risk for product tanker volumes. Another key question is whether Chinese buyers return before crude volumes rise - which could have a meaningful impact on crude prices..

Lower refinery runs this year is predominantly due to MEG shut-downs, a sharp reduction in China due to optimisation (and possibly some underlying demand weakness), and Russia due to Ukrainian attacks. Utilisation elsewhere is mostly maxed out, as crack spreads are at historically elevated levels. 

Going into autumn maintenance there may be a greater pull of gasoil/diesel into Europe - with arbitrages open from both the U.S. and MEG/India recently. This may be something that eventually bridges the gap between crack spreads and rates.
Some extra fleet growth - but also some potential for further tightness

Over the last few years we have noted that the shadow fleet was for all intents and purposes phased out from the complaint market, and would only return in an extreme rate scenario - a champagne problem.. Well, what do you know!? At least ten former shadow VLCCs have recently ended up doing Hormuz shuttle, thereby effectively re-joining the compliant market. 

Now, an interesting 'problem' has arrived which is the complete opposite. The PGSA has published a list of 45 ships which have been designated as non-compliant after transiting the Hormuz Strait in breach of Iran's terms. Most of these have been used for 'Hormuz shuttle' and now stand at risk of having to pay fees (which would be sanctionable by the U.S...), or be seized. Ships that are spotted doing STS transfers with these ships also stand at risk of being 'sanctioned'. Should charterers or other owners shy away from these 45 ships, it could create further logistical inefficiencies and market tightness going forward. 

In the resolution and paradoxical equilibrium scenarios even the quite elevated fleet growth over the next 12-18 months should be manageable. Most of this may be absorbed by demand growth potential, inefficiencies and consolidation (only about 17% of the VLCC fleet now controlled by 'independent' owners). From 2028 onwards, however, the huge delivery schedules should start to leave downward pressure.

content.content: On again, off again - none the wiser

Rates have been unseasonably strong this summer, especially given the effectively failed MOU and renewed setback for MEG volumes. The conflict has widened, with more chokepoints and disruptions for tanker flows. Although volumes are down, these inefficiencies have led tanker tonne-day demand to new seasonal all-time-highs, which together with fleet consolidation helps explain continuing rate strength. 

With refinery margins at historical highs and persisting crude oil supply deficits, there should be potential for more long-haul flows when Americas production grows further and seasonal local consumption declines. There may also be a willingness among refiners to absorb elevated freight cost - given current profitability, securing crude oil should be more urgent than it currently appears to be. 

The outlook beyond the near-term depends almost entirely on geopolitics — a range of outcomes too wide to call. Accelerating fleet growth will eventually weigh on the market, though current inefficiencies continue to provide a meaningful buffer.
Source: Baltic, Fearnleys (VLCC changed from TD3c to TD15 from March 2026)
Volumes not quite going anywhere - demand supported by inefficiencies

Following a surge through June and early July amid the U.S./Iran MOU, seaborne crude volumes have again declined in recent weeks as the ceasefire has not held. Hormuz transits remain higher than during the early days of the conflict, but far off the recent peaks. At the same time Americas exports have come off due to seasonally higher domestic consumption and exhausted inventory draws. From September onwards there should be some Americas rebound, whilst the MEG and now also partly Yanbu is rather uncertain. 

There was not a similar uptick for products after the MOU, as MEG refineries remained offline and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have ramped up (freeing up some more crude oil for exports). That has been partly offset by higher U.S. and Asian exports, but volumes have remained some 10-15% below pre-war levels. Thanks to crude market strength, however, there has been strong incentive for LR2s to dirty up again.

A combination of earlier long-haul fixtures and a rush out of the MEG over the last month (our July MEG and surrounding areas VLCC fixture count was nearly back to normal) has led crude tanker tonne-mile demand nearly back to normal recently. However, there is some downside risk near-term due to a lack of a west-east arbitrage and renewed escalation in the Middle East reducing flows. That may be partly offset by Saudi Red Sea exports diverting north rather than going through the Bab-el-Mandeb. 

Product tanker tonne-miles demand remains sluggish due to persistent low volume, although the effect on the market balance has been offset by LR2s dirtying up. Extremely strong refinery margins should ensure maximum runs in the areas where capacity is available (although there is also a risk that this might induce unplanned outages) and that there may be room for high freight wherever arbitrages exist. 

Overall, tanker tonne-miles are down 8% YTD vs. the same period last year, and most recently down more. However, looking at tonne-days, which also accounts for waiting time and other inefficiencies, YTD demand is actually up 2% and recently at a seasonally adjusted all-time-high, which better helps explain rate strength.

Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea crude oil exports the last few months have been about 4 mbpd (about 10% of the global) and 400-500 kbpd of products. The main (crude) ramp-up since March has gone to Asia. After attacks on Saudi owned ships and oil infrastructure, insurance for loading in Yanbu is hard to come by and many owners shy away. A number of cargoes has diverted north so far, rather than risking the Bab-el-Mandeb - another layer of shipping inefficiency. 

There are three (main) possible trajectories: no further escalation and consequently little market impact, Continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports or East-West pipeline pumping stations (bullish oil, bearish freight), or Houthi attacks and an effective closure of the Bab-el-Mandeb for Saudi’s exports (bullish freight). Assuming a full replacement gives a distance effect of 2-2.5x – a significant tonne-mile boost, benefiting VLCCs and Suezmaxes the most. 

For products there is not the same potential market impact as most volumes were already heading north.

content.content: Oil market still undersupplied - crack spreads flying

Going forward volume development will mostly depend on the geopolitical situation, with recent incidents in the Hormuz Strait, Bab-el-Mandeb, CPC and now also Egypt highlighting the risks to global oil supply. The latest production shut-in estimate of slightly less than 8 mbpd is well above the 13 mbpd at most earlier this year, but still implies a shortage vs. resilient oil demand in most areas. 

There may be some upside to (seaborne) flows in the near-term, regardless of geopolitics. Americas crude oil production is expected to increase somewhat further, following meaningful growth in recent months (one new 180 kbpd FPSO online in Brazil in May and solid U.S. shale growth), with overall output expected to be 0.5 mbpd higher in Q3'26 vs. the same quarter last year (at which time output also increased substantially). As driving season ends and refinery runs decline from September, there should be some more crude available for exports in coming months - with the delta likely headed long-haul to Asia (unless CPC outages persist and Europe needs replacement barrels). 

Going into next year there is substantial upside potential IF there is a resolution to the (widening) Middle East conflict, which remains a big IF - a meaningful separate discussion which highlights the wide range of outcomes also for tanker demand and rates next year. On the upside, a full normalisation with potential race to the bottom where all oil producers maximise output to make up for lost volume this year, could lead significant tanker demand tailwinds. On the downside, continued conflict, production shut-ins and high enough oil prices to bring demand destruction could lead to tough headwinds.

content.content:
Refinery margins have again reached historical highs, on constrained global capacity and resilient demand. This incentivises the refiners who can to run at maximum capacity and should underpin product tanker volumes. Any meaningful upside, however, depends more on geopolitics, with little new capacity expected to be added near-term in unaffected areas. 

Therefore, product tanker demand may remain somewhat stagnant near-term, other than at times driven by geographical price discrepancies and arbitrages. 

Given strong profitability it is a bit surprising that (Asian) crude buying appetite is not stronger, indicating some level of complacency still (waiting for another MOU..?) - which is also evident in the futures market which hardly reflects recent attacks on key oil infrastructure. Should MEG outages persist, we would expect the West-East crude arbitrage to reopen - and high freight cost should in theory easily be absorbed considering high refinery margins.
The 'only' known is that fleet growth picks up

During the first half of the year the total tanker fleet grew by 2.6%, nearly as much as the two preceding years combined. Growth has been led by LR2s, Suezmaxes and MRs so far. Another 3% is expected through the remainder of the year, and about 6% next year. At current rates any meaningful phase-out is highly unlikely, although the odd ship has left the fleet also this year. 

The only mitigating factor for fleet growth may be if the Middle East conflict escalates, and the U.S. tightens enforcement of sanctions including seizing or disabling more ships, which may eventually give a need for Iran to renew the shadow fleet. Or similarly vs. Russia. About 18% of the tanker fleet is currently sanctioned, which should offer enough flexibility for the sanctioned trades, but harsh enforcement may necessitate new workarounds.

In our previous update sent in late June, we wrote:

*Since our previous report, oil prices have dropped significantly. Based on the correlation between oil prices and BDI, included, as usual, in the final page of this report, the outlook for the second half of 2027 has thus improved considerably. That said, the volatility in energy markets and the complicated physical fundamental situation are unusual, so leading indicators like the one we use might not be as accurate as previously going forward. Regardless, the point is that low oil prices are good for economic growth, and vice versa. Coal volume growth has increased notably in the last few months. An opening of the Strait of Hormuz is a relief for macro but suppresses the upside potential in coal. Industrial metals prices have fallen over the last month, suggesting that global industrial activity is struggling to maintain upward momentum and may even be declining. That is especially the case in China, where iron ore and steel consumption remain lower than last year, and inventories remain higher. Global credit growth rates continue to fall, as reflected by a strengthening US dollar index. The dollar index correlates tightly with dry bulk volume growth and clearly suggests volume growth will continue to fall in the next few months.* 

Since our last report, oil prices have increased significantly, as a lasting solution between the US/Israel and Iran still seems far off. The recent rise in oil prices has caused the year-on-year change to increase from 0% in June to above 30% in July. The last few years’ correlation between the year-on-year change of oil prices and the BDI thus suggests a negative development through the first half of 2027 (chart as usual shown on the last page of this report). Notwithstanding that negative outlook, Brent oil prices have averaged about 100 dollars per barrel since the Hormuz Strait closed. That price level calculates to an “oil expenditure to GDP ratio” of about 3%, which is the average ratio since 1970. In other words, we are still far from a global energy crisis by that measure, which is positive, relatively speaking. 
Iron ore fundamentals look weaker than they did a month ago. Steel mill profitability in China has fallen sharply, reaching its lowest level since September 2024, making a reduction in hot metal output very likely. In late 2024, the Cape/Newc market weakened significantly; with iron ore fundamentals now resembling that period, the risk of a similar market development is considerable. Minor bulk shipment growth has followed a similar path to iron ore, as global manufacturing momentum has faded. A stronger US dollar, higher US government bond yields, lower precious and industrial metals prices, and higher energy and grain prices all point to an emerging economic downcycle, suggesting that minor bulk shipment growth will decline going forward. The outlook for grains shipments is also not looking too bright according to the International Grains Council. Coal remains a different story, but seaborne supply remains a constraint, evident by the fact that shipments in the first half of this year were lower than in the first half of 2024. Still, the current energy market situation likely means supply will increase going forward.  
Overall, we think the spot market levels in May were the peak of this year. The Cape/Newc and Panamax/Kamsarmax segments seem to be on a “lower highs and lower lows” trajectory since then. The Supra/Ultra market has, over the last few weeks, displayed signs of weakness, and the Handysize market struggled to follow the Supra/Ultra market push in the first weeks of July – which it normally does.

This page gives brief comments on what the charts on the next page tell us. We have pointed to an increasingly bearish picture being painted for the second half of this year and the next year over the last months. Shipment volume growth has tumbled sharply, and the next page's indicators suggest this development will continue.

Top left chart:

The BDI year-on-year change has been strongly positive since September last year, as usual, lagging behind increased credit growth in China. 
However, the credit growth rate has tumbled sharply during the last few months, which suggests a negative BDI development going forward. Interest rates and reserve requirement ratio changes do not point to any imminent turnaround in China's liquidity conditions. 

Top right chart:

Except for a decoupling in 2024, the change in bond yields in China and the US has been a good leading indicator for dry bulk demand growth. This year it has so far called the demand growth development perfectly, as growth has tumbled sharply following the peak in Q2. 

Middle left chart:

Lower crude oil prices are bullish for economic growth, and vice versa. The chart displays that since 2017, there has been a tight correlation between lower year-on-year oil prices and a higher year-on-year BDI, with the oil price change leading by 1 year. 
Lower oil prices suggest the BDI could remain positive year-on-year throughout 2026. However, the increase in oil prices since late February suggest the market will be lower during the first half of next year. 

Middle right chart:

The OECD diffusion index momentum keeps falling, and suggest the year on year change of the BDI will turn less and less positive over the coming six months. 

Bottom left chart:

The OECD diffusion index correlation with the BDI is very high, as usual. The OECD index reading is comparable to previous cycle peaks. The index seems to be tipping over, as the reading has fallen from 18 between January and April to 16 in June. 

Bottom right chart:

Shipment volume growth has, as usual, tracked the development of the US dollar index (a very good proxy for global liquidity conditions).

content.content:
The key takeaway for the LPG shipping market at the end of the second quarter is that global LPG trade did not collapse despite the operational closure of the Strait of Hormuz (SOH). Initial market reactions and expectations were arguably more severe than what ultimately materialized. Once again, the LPG market has demonstrated its remarkable resilience and adaptability during a period of significant disruption.

While the closure of the SOH initially raised concerns about a prolonged supply crisis, the second quarter highlighted the flexibility of the global LPG market. Replacement barrels from North America entered the market rapidly, allowing global VLGC liftings to recover much faster than many market participants had anticipated. With the Middle East accounting for more than 30% of global seaborne LPG exports, a sustained disruption to regional supply was expected to have far-reaching consequences should the closure persist.

At the start, few expected the disruption to last as long as it ultimately has. The market's initial view was that the impact on global energy flows was simply too significant for an extended closure to be feasible. However, three months after the conflict began, the LPG market has performed surprisingly well, demonstrating a level of resilience that exceeded most expectations.

North America, and especially the United States, stepped in to fill part of the supply gap, substantially increasing exports throughout the quarter. Coincidentally, but fortunately for the market, Enterprise's latest export terminal expansion came online in early April, enabling additional volumes to reach international markets at a time when they were most needed. As a result, North America now accounts for nearly 60% of global seaborne LPG exports, while the Middle East's share has declined to approximately 20%.

As illustrated in the chart on the right, China and India have been the countries most affected by the supply shock and have aggressively sourced replacement LPG barrels from North America. During the first half of 2026, North America accounted for 44% of their combined LPG imports, while the Middle East's share fell to 43%, down from 70% in 2025. This represents one of the most significant shifts in global LPG trade patterns observed in recent years.

As expected, global seaborne LPG volumes experienced an initial decline at the start of the second quarter, reflecting the immediate disruption caused by the closure of the SOH. However, as the market increasingly recognized that the supply shock would be more prolonged than first anticipated, the VLGC fleet underwent a large-scale repositioning towards the West, where growing U.S. LPG availability offered an alternative source of supply.

Volumes rebounded towards the end of the quarter, supported by a sharp increase in U.S. exports. In May, U.S. VLGC liftings reached a record 6 million tonnes, highlighting the country's growing importance in the global LPG trade. The quarter ultimately demonstrated that the United States is capable of serving as the market's marginal supplier during major geopolitical disruptions, helping to stabilize global LPG flows when traditional supply sources come under pressure.

Since reaching an all-time high of $728.5 on March 19 following attacks on Middle East Gulf energy infrastructure, the East-West arbitrage gradually narrowed as supply chains adapted and product markets stabilized. Although BLPG1 continued to be assessed by the Baltic Index throughout the quarter, the index remained largely theoretical due to the limited volume of Middle Eastern export activity. In contrast, BLPG3 climbed to a record $325.8 per metric tonne on May 26, driven by exceptional U.S. export volumes and Panama Canal auction fees reaching historic levels once again. On a TCE basis, earnings peaked at $202,340 per day, exceeding the previous high recorded in September 2023 by $50,000 per day. Across the three indexes, the average for the quarter was $139,800 per day - making it the highest on record (though somewhat inflated as the publication of BLPG1 has been turbluent). The quarter demonstrated that freight strength was not solely a result of supply disruptions. Record U.S. exports, longer-haul trading patterns, and increasing inefficiencies all contributed to tightening effective fleet supply. Towards quarter-end, however, falling product prices in both the U.S. and Asia reduced arbitrage economics, resulting in a noticeable narrowing of the spread during June.

The increase in U.S.-Far East trade has significantly boosted tonne-mile demand, effectively absorbing a large portion of available fleet capacity. As pressure on the Panama Canal intensified, a growing share of laden VLGCs opted for the longer voyage via Cape of Good Hope (COGH), further extending voyage durations and reducing effective vessel availability. This tightening of fleet supply has helped support earnings at elevated levels throughout the quarter, despite freight rates moderating from the exceptional peaks recorded earlier in the year. While those peak levels proved difficult to sustain, vessel availability has remained constrained enough to underpin a relatively strong freight market. Nevertheless, the sharp increase in freight costs ultimately weighed on cargo economics, resulting in a number of U.S. cargo cancellations for July liftings.

The share of laden VLGCs opting for the COGH route has increased significantly, rising from an average of 25% in 2025 to 40% so far in 2026. Similarly, the share of vessels ballasting from the Far East back to the US Gulf and East Coast has increased from 25% in 2025 to 46% in 2026.

This development highlights an increasingly important structural feature of the VLGC market: sailing patterns are becoming a key determinant of effective fleet supply. Looking ahead, concerns surrounding Panama Canal transit availability may re-emerge with the anticipated return of El Niño conditions, although the Panama Canal Authority currently expects any material impact to occur no earlier than the beginning of 2027. In addition, the continuation of the Long-Term Slot Allocation (LoTSA) system will consume a large share of available transit capacity. As a result, we expect an increasing proportion of VLGCs to rely on the Cape of Good Hope route, supporting tonne-mile demand and reducing effective fleet availability over the medium term.

As expected, Chinese LPG imports declined sharply in April as a direct consequence of the supply shock. During this period, operating rates at the country's propane dehydrogenation (PDH) plants fell from 62% to 42%, prompting many operators to accelerate planned maintenance amid uncertainty surrounding feedstock availability. As the market gradually adjusted and trade flows from North America increased, import volumes began to recover. Imports rebounded in May, although they remained below historical norms, before strengthening further in June. The recovery was supported by PDH operating rates rising to 66%, alongside lower propane import costs, which improved production economics and encouraged the return of demand. 

Despite the gradual recovery, Chinese LPG imports during the first half of 2026 were still down 27% year-on-year. Looking ahead, we expect imports to continue recovering throughout the second half of the year, albeit at a measured pace. According to SCI, total Chinese LPG imports for 2026 are projected to finish approximately 16% below 2025 levels (landing at approx. 31 million tons).
**As newbuild deliveries are absorbed, ordering momentum continues**

A total of nine VLGC newbuilds were delivered during the second quarter, bringing total deliveries in 2026 to 21 vessels. Another 14 are scheduled for delivery in the second half of the year, mostly in the last quarter. The global VLGC fleet now comprises 433 ships, while the orderbook has expanded to 133 vessels, resulting in an orderbook-to-fleet ratio of 31%. The ration has seen a 6% increase in Q2, as newbuild contracting has continued. Year-to-date, 44 VLGCs have been ordered, compared to 14 vessels during the entirety of 2025, equivalent to a 214% increase.

The resurgence in ordering activity reflects growing confidence in the long-term outlook for the LPG market. Despite the geopolitical disruptions experienced throughout the first half of the year, global LPG trade has once again demonstrated its resilience and ability to adapt to changing market conditions. Continued growth in U.S. production, expanding export infrastructure, and expectations of rising global LPG consumption have reinforced owners' confidence in the sector's long-term fundamentals. However, while these developments support a constructive outlook, the rapidly expanding orderbook also highlights the importance of continued trade growth and tonne-mile demand to absorb the significant fleet additions scheduled from 2027 onwards.

**What could lie ahead in 2H of 2026?**

Perhaps the single most important variable for the second half of the year will be developments surrounding the SOH and ongoing negotiations between the United States and Iran. While the signing of a memorandum of understanding has improved market sentiment and increased expectations of a gradual reopening, a signed agreement should not be confused with an immediate return to normality. The recovery of Middle Eastern LPG trade is likely to be a multi-month process rather than a single event.

Despite increasing optimism, a complete and physical reopening will require owners, charterers and insurers to regain confidence in the region. While Middle East Gulf production and export infrastructure may be capable of returning relatively quickly, the availability of suitable tonnage is likely to remain constrained. A substantial share of the global VLGC fleet has repositioned towards the Atlantic Basin over recent months, while the limited number of vessels currently positioned around the Gulf are primarily Indian-flagged or sanction-exposed ships. Mainstream tonnage is therefore unlikely to return immediately, as market participants will seek evidence of sustained safe passage before fully re-entering the region.

As a result, a reopening of the SOH may initially prove supportive rather than detrimental for freight markets. Limited vessel availability, elevated war-risk insurance premiums and uneven owner participation are likely to keep a firm floor under freight rates during the normalization phase. Although the return of Middle Eastern barrels would be expected to reduce reliance on long-haul U.S. exports and narrow arbitrage economics, a lower arbitrage does not necessarily translate into materially weaker freight markets. The operational inefficiencies that have developed throughout 2026, including longer voyage distances and tighter vessel availability, are unlikely to disappear overnight.

The potential easing of sanctions on Iranian energy exports represents another important variable. A temporary waiver allowing Iranian LPG exports could facilitate a more visible return of Iranian cargoes into mainstream trade flows and add incremental supply to the market. However, the longer-term significance of this development will depend entirely on whether a final agreement is reached and maintained. Until greater clarity emerges, many buyers are likely to remain cautious when committing to Iranian barrels, limiting the immediate impact on global trade patterns.

Consequently, while the market appears to be moving towards a less disruptive environment than the one experienced during the first half of the year, uncertainty remains elevated. The second quarter demonstrated that geopolitical disruptions do not necessarily destroy demand but rather reshape trade flows. As long as U.S. export growth remains strong, Asian demand continues to recover, and voyage inefficiencies persist, the VLGC market should remain well supported through the remainder of 2026. The longer-term challenge, however, will increasingly shift towards the industry's ability to absorb a rapidly expanding fleet from 2027 onwards.

The quarter has been characterised by continued geopolitical tension, with charter rates remaining materially above pre-war levels, although stabilising following the initial peaks. Basin spreads have remained elevated, with two-stroke spot rates in the Atlantic Basin exceeding USD 90k/day throughout the quarter, compared to below USD 80k/day in the Pacific.

Middle Eastern volumes have remained largely constrained, with only limited cargoes from Qatar and the UAE transiting the Hormuz Strait to Asian buyers. Following news of a potential resolution in the third week of June, several vessels began repositioning towards the Middle East. However, within less than a week, renewed attacks on merchant shipping were reported in the area, leading to a halt in LNG carrier transits.

JKM prices ranged from close to USD 20/MMBtu in mid-May to below USD 16/MMBtu during the final two weeks of the quarter.

Fleet utilisation has been significantly impacted by the sharp decline in traded volumes, with increased sailing distances only partially offsetting this effect. US exports to Asia did increase by 80% compared to Q1 (from 15% of US exports to 28% of US exports), while total Asian imports (across all supply regions) were 5 MTPA lower than in Q2 last year. Underutilisation has primarily affected older tonnage, while the two-stroke fleet continues to expand tonne-mile demand broadly in line with fleet growth through newbuild deliveries.

Two vessels were sold for demolition, while we estimate 20 idle vessels off Labuan and eight in the Malacca Strait. A number of vessels linked to Ras Laffan remain positioned in the Pacific, awaiting a restart in production. 

21 vessels were delivered in Q2, which is one more than in Q1. Newbuilding activity halved from nearly 40 orders in Q1, with orders spanning speculative, project-linked, and replacement tonnage.

Two projects reached FID during the quarter: Delfin LNG (4.4 MTPA floating LNG) and Commonwealth LNG (9.5 MTPA). Both are US-based developments targeting first LNG by 2030.
Source: JKM from S&P Global Platts

Spot charter rates remained resilient throughout the quarter, supported by elevated gas prices amid continued disruptions to Middle Eastern export flows. Expectations of softer pricing did not materialise, and while market conditions showed some signs of easing mid-quarter, renewed interruptions to Hormuz transits towards the very end of the period prevented any sustained softening and continued to support charter rates.

Basin spreads remained elevated, with Atlantic rates consistently above Middle East and Pacific benchmarks. This reflects continued pressure on Atlantic tonnage, driven by the routing of flows towards Asia and the resulting increase in tonne-mile demand.

The term market has corrected from a durable contango structure in Q1, when the 1-year rate briefly traded above the 7-year TC. This structure has since normalised, with the 1-year now priced below the 7-year rate, although still above the 3- and 5-year tenors, unlike the pre-war market. Movements in term rates remained broadly flat during the quarter, with overall liquidity continuing to be relatively limited.

content.content:
Fixing activity remained elevated, with the total number of short-term fixtures being only 10 fixtures less than in Q1, which itself was an all-time high. Compared to Q2 last year, the spot fixture count increased by 15%. Despite operating in a high gas price environment, which typically reduces fixture volumes due to limited sublet availability, activity has been supported by increased participation from independent owners. As a result, the usual decline in fixing activity at high gas prices has not materialised. In addition, several sublets have originated from Qatari entities, reflecting their reduced shipping demand.

The share of multi-month fixtures (90–365 days) increased this quarter, accounting for 20% of all short-term fixtures, compared to 9% in the previous quarter. In the 1–2 year segment, six deals were concluded, all but one involving two-stroke vessels. 

Liquidity in the TFDE segment has increased markedly year-to-date. In H1, 100 TFDE spot fixtures were concluded, representing the highest level since 2017. Two-stroke vessels have recorded the same number of spot fixtures as last year, and total activity remains elevated relative to pre-2025 levels. The increase in TFDE fixtures reflect vessel ownership structures: independent owners control a larger share of TFDE tonnage, allowing these vessels to remain available in the spot market, whereas two-stroke availability is more constrained by charterer-controlled portfolios and their strategies in a high gas price environment.

101 MT of LNG was loaded in Q2, which is 3 MT less than in Q2 last year, and 15 MT less than in Q1. May loadings ended at 33.5 MT, which is the lowest monthly level seen since May 2024. 

The biggest change in trade flows has been that originating out of the US. In Q2, 28% of US LNG went to Asia, vs. only 15% in Q1. As a percentage share, this is much lower than the previous peak, Q3 2024, where 42% of US LNG went to Asia. However, looking at the absolute values, this year's Q2 levels actually matched those levels from Q3 2024. 

As maintenance periods start, as well as some unplanned outages, total quarterly loadings, excluding Qatar and UAE, decreased from the record 100.6 MT in Q1 to 99.2 MT in Q2. Projects like LNG Canada and the Corpus Christi expansion have ramped up, reaching record production levels in Q2. The first cargo was loaded from Golden Pass in April, but only one cargo per month was lifted from the plant throughout the quarter, suggesting operating levels much lower than a full train capacity. 

Total European imports are down 13 MT from Q1, and 4 MT compared to Q2 last year. This has left storage levels at 49% full at the end of the quarter, which is 14% lower than the 5-year average for this time of the year. 

The Indian sub-continent is very dependent on Qatar volumes through the Strait of Hormuz, and Pakistan, Bangladesh and India has 99%, 60% and 46% of their total LNG imports from Qatar last year, respectively. Despite this, Indian imports reached 6.7 MT in Q2, which is the highest seen since the 7 MT in Q2 2024. The lost Qatari volumes were compensated for through cargoes from the United States.  Bangladesh was also able to largely compensate for lost Middle Eastern volumes through increased flow from United States and Africa. Pakistan on the other hand only imported eight cargoes in Q2 (0.5 MT), of which all but two were from Qatar. Total imports ended around one third of Q1, with a year-on-year reduction of 75%. 

China was the largest importer in Q2, taking 29 cargoes more than Japan. Reloads from China increased substantially at the end of last quarter, with 17 reloads, but their strategy has since changed, and volumes are being kept domestically. For 1H 2026, Japan is marginally ahead of China as the top LNG importer.

A total of 21 newbuilds were delivered in Q2, while two vessels were sold for demolition, bringing the global LNGC fleet to 758 vessels. The vessels scrapped were 22 and 24 years old, owned by SinoKor and Asyad, respectively. In addition, three vessels have reportedly been sold into the shadow fleet.

Two-stroke vessels now account for approximately half of the fleet (49.6%), with 386 units on the water. Steam turbine vessels remain the second largest segment, with 183 ships still in operation. However, effective utilisation within this segment is materially lower, with at least 30 vessels currently in layup or idling. Tonne-mile demand for steam vessels continues to decline at a significantly faster pace than the rate at which they are removed from the fleet through demolition or repurposing.

Despite the recent rate strength, which has likely delayed scrapping decisions, there is limited evidence of older vessels being reactivated for spot trading. The cost and complexity associated with reactivation require more sustained earnings visibility than a single spot employment.

There are 84 LNGCs above 20 years of age, and 15 LNGCs above 30 years (of which six are currently in layup). In addition, 55 vessels fall within the 120–140k cbm size segment, which is becoming increasingly commercially unattractive for both trading and conversion purposes.

A total of 20 vessels were ordered in Q2, roughly half the level seen in Q1, although still exceeding any quarterly total recorded in 2025. Deliveries remained elevated, with 21 vessels delivered during the quarter, just below the quarterly record of 22 achieved in 2025. This leaves 52 newbuilds scheduled for delivery over the remainder of the year, equivalent to approximately two vessels per week.

Newbuilding prices have remained broadly stable at around USD 250 million depending on specification, while yard capacity is largely filled until H2 2029. The orderbook-to-fleet ratio now stands at 38%.

content.content:
Assuming ongoing negotiations between US and Iran ultimately result in a lasting agreement, we expect the LNG shipping market to revert to the oversupplied conditions that prevailed prior to the conflict, rather than being driven by elevated gas prices and a tight cargo market. That said, developments during the first week following the ceasefire highlighted how fragile the situation remains. Only a limited number of LNG cargoes transited the Hormuz Strait before disruptions resumed and transits halted again. As a result, near-term market visibility remains poor, continuing to support freight rates. At the same time, summer requirements remain relatively limited, suggesting some softening as the seasonal demand lull progresses.

In a scenario where the Strait fully reopens, arbitrage opportunities are likely to narrow, as was observed almost immediately when transits briefly resumed. This would reduce voyage distances and ease shipping demand.

While the market was already expected to remain oversupplied for at least the next two years before the conflict, the outlook has been further weakened by the delay to Qatar's expansion project, with start-up pushed from the second half of 2026 to early 2027. No further updates have been provided since the delay was announced in March, and our analysis continues to assume a first-half 2027 start-up.

Our view remains that late 2028 will mark the transition from an oversupplied market to a more balanced one, with the potential for a fundamentally tight winter market into 2029. By that point, the current orderbook of roughly 50 vessels scheduled for delivery in 2029 is unlikely to be sufficient to meet peak winter demand heading into 2030. This tightening is driven by a combination of substantial LNG supply growth currently under construction, ongoing fleet replacement requirements, and longer average sailing distances as an increasing share of US LNG is directed towards Asia.

Supporting this view, S&P Global forecasts European LNG demand to increase from 127 mt in 2025 to 147 mt in 2029. However, this 20 mt increase is modest compared with the nearly 70 mt increase in US LNG supply expected over the same period. As a result, a significant share of incremental US volumes will likely need to be absorbed by markets further afield than Europe, increasing tonne-mile demand and strengthening the underlying requirement for LNG shipping capacity.

The graph below illustrates our fleet balance forecast. Fleet growth is based on the current orderbook, while vessels are assumed to leave the trading fleet at 20 years of age for steam turbine vessels and 25 years for TFDE tonnage. Under these assumptions, the market appears undersupplied during the winter of 2028/29. We believe this initial tightness can largely be absorbed through increased sailing speeds. By the following winter, however, our analysis suggests that operational adjustments alone will be insufficient. Additional newbuilding orders delivered during the second half of 2029 are likely to be required to accommodate demand growth heading into 2030. 

The timing of this tightening remains highly dependent on LNG project start-up schedules. While our analysis assumes projects commence broadly in line with current guidance, commissioning timelines can change and delays are common across the industry. Historically, vessel deliveries have tended to arrive more reliably than new LNG supply volumes, resulting in periods where fleet growth temporarily outpaces cargo growth. The ongoing delay to Qatar's expansion project is a current example of this dynamic. Consequently, further project delays would likely push the expected market rebalancing beyond our current forecast.
