content.content: Freight Follows Geopolitics, Values Follow Opportunity
LNG Sale & Purchase Review – First Half 2026

The first half of 2026 has been one of the more unusual periods seen in the LNG market almost on par with Fukushima and the Russia-Ukraine energy shock. Freight markets, asset values and shipping fundamentals all appear to be telling different stories.

On the freight side, charter rates remained considerably stronger than most expected entering the year. Atlantic Basin two-stroke vessels spent much of Q2 earning in excess of USD 90,000/day while Pacific employment generally hovered around USD 80,000/day, supported by Middle Eastern disruption, elevated gas prices and a reshuffling of global LNG trade flows. At face value, the market looked remarkably resilient. 

Under the surface, however, we see the fundamentals have become progressively softer. Global LNG loadings declined during Q2, fleet growth remained close to record levels, and visible idle tonnage began to build, particularly among older steam turbine vessels. Twenty-one LNG carriers were delivered during the quarter, bringing the global fleet to approximately 760 vessels, while the orderbook remains around 38% of the existing fleet. Approximately twenty vessels were observed idle off Labuan and a further group around the Malacca Strait, illustrating that utilisation pressure is becoming increasingly visible. 

Ordinarily, a market characterised by declining cargo volumes, rising fleet supply and increasing idle tonnage would be expected to experience significant downward pressure on vessel values.

Yet that has not happened.

Instead, LNG asset values have remained surprisingly resilient, with transaction activity spread across modern DFDE and TFDE tonnage, older steam turbine ships, demolition candidates and infrastructure-linked opportunities. The central conclusion from H1 2026 is therefore that the LNG asset market is no longer being driven primarily by current earnings. Instead, it is increasingly being driven by future opportunity.

Or put differently:
**Freight follows geopolitics. Values follow opportunity.**
Shipping Fundamentals Are Softer Than the Headline Freight Market Suggests

The LNG shipping market began the year expecting oversupply. That view has not fundamentally changed.

Global LNG loadings during Q2 totalled approximately 101 million tonnes, down from Q1 and modestly below the same period last year. Freight rates remained elevated mainly because trade patterns became less efficient rather than because cargo volumes increased. Middle Eastern disruptions altered vessel positioning, increased uncertainty and redirected a greater proportion of Atlantic cargoes towards Asia, supporting tonne-mile demand despite falling volumes.

One of the more important observations from the market during the period was the growing divergence between modern and legacy tonnage. Two-stroke vessels continued capturing the majority of attractive employment opportunities. Modern DFDE vessels also remained highly competitive, benefiting from fuel efficiency and broad commercial acceptance. Older steam turbine ships, meanwhile, increasingly appeared on the wrong side of the moon, where utilisation has evaporated together with the corresponding freight rates. 

This has resulted in an increased focus on what owners need to consider doing with their aging vessels.
The Asset Market Is Looking Beyond Today's Freight Environment

Historically, LNG carrier values tended to move broadly in line with earnings expectations. Strong freight markets supported asset values and weak freight markets results in increased supply of tonnage to the market. 

That relationship appears significantly weaker today.

The LNG market currently possesses several characteristics that would normally undermine second-hand values:
•	Cargo volumes are lower.
•	Fleet growth is substantial.
•	Idle tonnage is growing.
•	The orderbook remains elevated.
•	Steam turbine competitiveness is virtually non-existent.

And yet transaction activity remains healthy.

The explanation lies in optionality.

Buyers are increasingly evaluating LNG carriers not simply as transportation assets but as assets capable of fulfilling multiple future roles. A vessel purchased today may continue trading conventionally (155cbm+), become a floating storage unit or conversion candidate (project-dependent 145-174k cbm), or support regional LNG logistics. These potential outcomes provide a value floor that is less dependent on today's or tomorrow’s freight market.
As a result, the market is increasingly assigning value to possibilities rather than current earnings.
First half of 2026 tells an interesting story about transactions

The transaction list from the first half of 2026 provides a surprisingly clear picture of buyer preferences.

The first half of 2026 has been relatively hectic when looking at the number of transactions reported. Compared to 2025, there are 6 more vessels reported in the 2nd hand market, whilst the recycling space has till now, fallen behind with only 5 concluded sales. The drop in recycling activity just shows how a little hope in the form of higher freight rates gives Owners a (false) outlook for their older ladies.

content.title: S&P transaction volume and YoY trend

content.content: When digging into the details it is most notable that relatively few genuinely modern vessels have changed hands till date. The standout transactions that have been reported in the 2013-2015-built TFDE market seem to have been sold above the USD 110 million mark. These sales highlight the continued appetite for younger, larger and operationally flexible assets. There is also a continued demand for older DFDE and TFDE tonnage destined for specific trade or projects. What is notable is that older tonnage is transacting below the USD 100 million mark, ranging from USD 65-95 million. The range in rate is also a function of vessel age, but the origin of the buyer is also playing a significant role.

At the other end of the spectrum, the market remained remarkably active for ageing steam turbine vessels. It is noticeable that a large number of these units have been sold to unknown buyers, but we will get more into that further on in the report.

Remarkably, many of these transactions involved vessels between 19 and 22 years of age. In most shipping sectors, such vessels would sit firmly within the demolition age profile. Yet LNG continues to be different.

What is particularly interesting is that buyers appear to be focusing on a relatively narrow capacity range. Most of the sales occurred in the 145,000–155,000 cbm segment. This aligns with growing evidence that buyers increasingly value storage capacity and conversion suitability significantly higher than any potential freight earnings.

By contrast, vessels below approximately 140,000 cbm appear to be becoming increasingly difficult to place. Current fleet demographics show around 55 vessels remain in the 120,000–140,000 cbm segment, a size category that appears increasingly unattractive both as trading assets and conversion candidates. This is reflected in the graph below, showing the 5 vessels sold for recycling thus far in 2026.

The steam turbine fleet is approaching a pivotal moment.

The global LNG fleet today contains approximately 183 steam turbine vessels, of which more than 80 are already older than twenty years. Fifteen vessels have surpassed thirty years of age. Under normal market conditions, these demographics would imply a substantial demolition cycle.

Some vessels continue finding buyers. Others remain employed in niche trades. A number appear increasingly likely to move towards infrastructure-linked opportunities. The result is that the fleet is ageing faster than it is disappearing.

The LNG sector therefore faces a situation where vessel competitiveness is deteriorating more quickly than fleet capacity is being removed.

From an S&P perspective, this creates opportunities.

Many ageing steam turbine vessels are no longer being evaluated as conventional shipping assets. They are increasingly being evaluated based on their residual optionality. For some vessels that optionality lies in conversion potential. For others it lies in regional LNG logistics or long-term storage applications. For a growing number, however, the market appears to be concluding that demolition remains the most likely outcome.

One of the less discussed but increasingly important developments of the first six months of 2026 has been the evolution of the buyer universe.

Historically, LNG asset transactions were dominated by a relatively small group of specialist LNG shipowners.

Today, the range of buyers appears considerably broader.

The market now includes:
•	Traditional LNG shipowners.
•	Infrastructure investors.
•	LNG-to-power developers.
•	Conversion-focused buyers.
•	Strategic storage participants.
•	Domestically-linked opportunities
•	Buyers pursuing opportunities linked to future energy infrastructure.

And of course, we cannot ignore the strong presence of buyers linked to **"He-Who-Must-Not-Be-Named."**

Market observers increasingly associate several ageing LNG carrier acquisitions with opaque ownership structures and alternative employment strategies. The pattern is becoming known for this type of transaction, where an unknown entity typically buys the vessel, skips-hops a few intermediaries and flags, and ultimately ends up under sanctioned entities and flags. Whether these vessels ultimately participate in conventional trading, specialised logistics or other activities is less important than the fact that they represent a genuine source of demand.

From an S&P perspective, additional buyer categories almost always support values.
That appears to be prevalent today.
The Optionality Premium Is Becoming Real

One of the most important conclusions so far in 2026 is the emergence of what can legitimately be described as an **optionality premium**.
Vessels are no longer valued solely on projected freight earnings.
Instead, buyers increasingly assess:
•	Trading optionality.
•	Conversion optionality.
•	Infrastructure optionality.
•	Storage optionality.
•	Geographic optionality.

This framework explains many of the apparent contradictions currently visible in the LNG market.
•	It explains why twenty-year-old vessels continue changing hands.
•	It explains why values remain stable to firming, despite weaker utilisation.
•	It explains why buyers remain focused on larger vessels above 145,000 cbm.

Most importantly, it explains why the LNG asset market appears considerably more optimistic than the freight market.

But what it doesn’t take into consideration is, **“Should I try to sell now to get out?”**

We believe that when pairing the S&P paradigm to the general market observations, serious consideration for exiting older tonnage, even below current market levels, may be a strategically strong position to take.

Our base case remains that the shipping market itself remains fundamentally oversupplied through much of 2028. Add the fact that by end 2028 we’ll have another 150+ 2-strokes in the market, STs and DFs alike become even less attractive.

When today’s geopolitical disruptions ease, freight markets could soften relatively quickly. Fleet growth remains substantial, Qatar's expansion delays pushing incremental demand further into the future, and visible utilisation pressure already exists among older tonnage. 

The asset market, however, is clearly focused on a different horizon.

Many buyers appear to be positioning for the next major wave of LNG supply growth expected between 2028 and 2030. Whether they ultimately prove correct remains to be seen.

For now, the first half of 2026 has demonstrated that LNG carriers are increasingly being valued not for what they earn today, but for what they might morph into tomorrow.

We believe that that is the defining investment theme of this cycle.

**Remember, if you are there to sell your assets, come talk to us! **

Close to 100 days into what is now firmly one of the most significant — and least anticipated — LNG supply disruptions on record, we draw the conclusion that **it is supply that is the problem, not demand**. We claim no prize for stating the obvious, but it is reassuring to see the underlying drivers of the FSRU market remaining robust. As we entered the quarter we saw a prompt reaction from ongoing projects to pause activities, but the **prevailing message in our engagement with projects and end-users since is that they need to move now to be ready for 2028–2030**. "That is when the supply wave emerges, now that Middle East start-ups have been pushed out" has been playing on repeat in our discussions.

Despite the near-term uncertainty — or at least the increased risk premium — created by the situation in the Middle East, there has not yet been a sense of urgency around **long-term supply diversification** to the same extent seen in the wake of Russia-Ukraine in 2022. **LNG SPA contracting data reflects relatively muted activity so far in 2026**, with around 30 MTPA contracted year-to-date. We attribute this to a perception that the situation will eventually normalise, as opposed to the view that the disruption of Russian gas flows to Europe would create a permanent structural gap. However, contracts entered into this year appear to be at lower pricing points — whether oil-linked, gas hub or hybrid structures — **suggesting suppliers remain eager to place volumes**. In the context of FSRUs, **a 12%-to-Brent deal is considerably more stimulating than the 14–16%** seen in 2023–2024, and lower-cost SPAs broadly improve project economics in ways that strengthen the case for FSRU-based solutions.

In terms of **project activity**, we see a relatively constant balance between **Asia and LatAm, with Europe rounding off the geographical focus**. Interest from both private developers and public entities remains strong — a signal that demand is being driven by commercial opportunity and energy security in equal measure. What is worth noting is that the **"canary in the coalmine"** we thought we saw earlier — with suppliers looking to push into FSRU and downstream projects — **has not been visible recently**, which we read as a moderately constructive signal for market discipline.

Chartering activity was higher during the quarter, with **one newbuild booked back-to-back with a 20-year project** at what appears to be a **time charter of around US$125,000–130,000/day**, and one contract substitution in **Colombia for a 7-year deal rumoured to be in the range of US$150,000/day**. We expect to see a few further deals — assuming conditions precedent are lifted — in H2 2026 at somewhat lower levels based on conversions, but still at what can only be described as very healthy returns of around **6–8x Capex/EBITDA**.

Based on our assessment of the market, the **near-to-mid-term outlook for FSRUs has improved through the quarter**. Visibility on a number of "may become available" assets looking to extend or relocate has effectively left the market sold out of prompt tonnage — without forward commitments — until the latter part of 2027. Speculative contracting activity across both newbuilds and conversions has slowed, or more precisely, units that were sitting semi-speculatively have now found contracts. **FSRU providers have also developed the discipline to hold off** on committing tonnage until all conditions precedent are lifted, which is currently causing a handful of "ready-to-go" conversions to be delayed.

To summarize: **elevated FSRU rate levels have proven stickier than we anticipated 12 months ago**. While project development timelines still tend to follow a sine curve rather than a straight line, the discipline among FSRU providers around speculative ordering continues — for now — to **hold back the typical supply wave**. With near-term available FSRUs being absorbed into the market, partly at the expense of conversions and newbuilds, **the ingredients are in place for a solid second half of the year.**
Key market developments during the quarter

**APRIL**

Exmar confirms moving ahead with FSRU in Eemshaven. The FSRU will have a capacity of 750MMSCFD and work together with the **EEMSHAVEN LNG** already in place to provide a peak regas capacity of 1,350MMSCFD and a total of 190,000cbm of storage capacity. According to EET, a significant portion of the capacity has been sold through the recent open season(s) process. However, being a semi-public project we would expect the government to backstop any shortfall to ensure project commencing on track.

Colombia has been the hottest (and most chaotic) location for FSRUs over the past 18 months. At present we count four firm projects, but several of them require approvals for governmental licenses relating to mooring or construction of pipelines which is delaying FIDs. With the four new projects on the radar and the existing **HOEGH GRACE** in Cartagena, we consider Colombian demand covered on both coasts.

NFE announced the lease of the TGS terminal in Santa Catarina, Brazil with local Brazilian media indicating Ambar as the lessee for a period of 10 years. AMBAR were one of the major winners in the recent power auction (LRCAP) and has quickly emerged as one of the major power plant owner/operator and developers in Brazil. While **ENERGOS WINTER** was on station for a short period in 2024-2025, it is expected that another FSRU will be required on back of the reported lease agreement.

Poland issued tender for **FSRU #2** in Gdansk asking for a 15yr charter from Owners. While initially open for newbuilds and conversions, the technical spec has subsequently been narrowed to only include newbuilds. The timing for selection of preferred bidder is expected to be before end of 2026. In June Gaz-Systems announced the successful Open Season for capacity with four separate bidders taking a total of 47 slots per year in then period 2030-2039. Orlen and Unimot reported having taken 12 slots each with PGE having taken an estimated 16 slots and Enea taking the remaining 7.

Iraqi efforts to get its first FSRU operational is delayed due to ongoing geopolitical kerfuffle in the Middle East. According to Iraq’s Ministry of Energy the terminal will be completed early-June 2026. While there are additional delays at the terminal stemming from construction aspects, we understand there are also commercial elements pending to reach a point where the terminal facilities can be put in use. Moreover, the **EXCELERATE ACADIA** will remain in Jordan until early 2027 which in itself underlines the lack of realism on timelines in Iraq.

**MAY**

US and Bangladesh announced an MOU to “advance strategic cooperation on energy resources, infrastructure development and long-term energy security”. While covering a broader base than just LNG, we consider this as increasing the likelihood of seeing another **Excelerate FSRU** sooner or later heading to Bangladesh without the need for a full tender process. However, there are talks of other major energy players also vying for a bundled deal in Bangladesh. What is for sure is that RPGCL and Petrobangla has previously targeted a 3rd FSRU in Moheshkali which inevitably will happen - and most likely through a tedious public procurement process.

**Dioriga Gas** is advancing its regulatory procedures for the planned FSRU in Agioi Theodoroi/Corinth including a sea license and 3rd party exemption from regulator RAEWW (Regulatory Authority for Energy, Waste, and Water). Dioriga Gas also announced having teamed up with trader Mercuria on the FSRU venture with Mercuria likely being an offtaker of capacity from the FSRU. Dioriga is one of the more likely and advanced FSRU projects in Greece which may startup in 2028/2029.

Samsung announced the order for a **newbuild FSRU** for MISC at a price of US$ 328m to be chartered to Petronas for their project in Lumut, Perak (Peninsular Malaysia). The FSRU will be 170,000cbm / 3 x 250MMSCFD and (likely) Open Loop with SW/Glycol. The unit is back-to-back with a 20yr TC expected to commence in Q2/29.
MISC with NB deal for Petronas at Lumut, Perak. 20 yr TC. NB to be built by Samsung with startup in Q2/29. 3 x 250MMSCFD, 170,000cbm at price of US$ 328.4m (KRW 484bn)

Transnet has granted permission to **Ukwanda LNG** to build South Africa’s first LNG import terminal in Ngqura/Coega. The port of Coega has (along with many, many other ports in South Africa) been considered a suitable location for an FSRU at the eastern part of the port. However, being far from demand centers has been a stumbling block for other FSRU projects in the same location and with developments in Richards Bay slowly progressing we are keen to see if Ukwanda can reach lift-off.

Karpowership announced a 3-year deal in Yucatan Peninsula where KPS will provide a 250MW powership together with a dedicated FSRU. It is expected that the FSRU deployed will be one of KarMol’s units, either **KARMOL LNGT POWERSHIP EUROPE, ANTARCTICA or AMERICA**.

**JUNE**

Frontera Energy announced the charter of an FSRU for seven years (with upto 8 years of options) commencing in 2027. The FSRU will have a capacity of ~500MMSCFD, but only send out around 300MMSCFD after a two-year rampup from 126MMSCFD. While no announcement has been made, we expect this to be **EXPRESS** as the allocated FSRU.

DET announced the start of operations at their fourth terminal in Stade is due to commence in Sep-26; approximately three years after the planned start-up in late-23. The project has suffered under a conflict between Hanseatic Energy Hub and DET – at the expense of German tax payers. The **ENERGOS FORCE** will depart its 10-month tenure in Aqaba, Jordan and return to Germany where she’ll be operating until the HEH onshore terminal is completed in 2029.

PLN EPI released long-awaited tender for **NUSANTARA REGAS SATU** replacement. The technical specs suggest a large conversion with extra BOG handling and Small-scale LNG loading capability. However, the critical element as always in Indonesia is the requirement of Indonesian Flag. As we read it, this means **NUSANTARA REGAS SATU** will likely have to stay until at least 2030.

Tokyo Gas announced a JDA for Gas Malaysia’s RGT Yan project with VTTI and Gas Malaysia Berhad. The project will include an FSRU (expected to be a conversion of 170,000cbm+ with 3 x 250MMSCFD) at a sheltered location offshore Yan (Peninsular Malaysia) with an expected startup in 2029.

Zululand LNG Terminal in Richards Bay announced having signed up Exxon as their first major international shipper in a HoA following the "mandatory" agreement with Eskom in early June. EOI for EPC contractors on the marine/onshore side has been issued with closing in July, but VOPAK will remain responsible for the 170,000cbm FSU that represents Phase 1. Many hopeful LNG developers have come and gone from Richards Bay, but hopefully this one sticks...

EGAS has been in the market for a short-term  FSU with the usual bumpy process, but has reportedly ended up with **SEAPEAK BAHRAIN** for a short three month period. While it is is an interesting decision to select a vessel for short-term FSU charter - it is is equally interesting to hear that Bahrain is currently on the lookout for an **FSRU as a long-term replacement for the FSU.**

**SUBSEQUENT EVENTS**
BW confirmed their newbuild to be employed at the AKR/JIIPE project in Gresik, Indonesia. The **170,000cbm FSRU** was reported at a price of **US$ 319.69m** and will be delivered in May-29 with COD expected in Q3/29. AKR and BW will have joint ownership in the company that orders the FSRU and while details have yet to emerge we would expect this to be the typical structuring to ensure compliance with Indonesian ownership requirements while the economics go to the FSRU Owners.
Quarterly corporate highlights: Nothing to knock your socks off...or?

**NFEs** restructuring process has gone through the motions in Q2 with press releases generally focused on legal aspects and the approval of the UK restructuring plan. BrazilCo has effectively raised US$ 885m in notes at an interest rate of 12% (or US$ 106m in interest cost annually) with uses being linked to operations/capex and refinancing of bridge loan/existing notes. In light of being in a restructuring process there have been no updates or quarterly releases, but we are hearing talks of their TM2500s being for sale and the other operations (Mexico, FastLNG1 and Puerto Rico) operating relatively steadily.

**Excelerate** reported Q1/26 in early-May with the most prominent news being the **EXCELERATE ACADIA** heading for a 9-month charter for NEPCO in Aqaba, Jordan as NEPCO are still not ready with their onshore solution which was due to start in Q3/26. The indicated EBITDA for the NEPCO-charter is ~US$ 20m in 2026 (which would equate to a bareboat rate of US$ 110,000/day assuming 01st July to 31st Dec 2026). Excelerate are not expecting to generate much income from the Petrobangla supply agreement due to FM from Qatar Energy – a situation all too familiar for many Asian buyers. The upcoming conversion of **EXCELERATE SHENANDOAH** is progressing with LoI signed with Seatrium for the conversion works. While still not allocated to a project, we consider the India-project at Haldia a potentially suitable fit. The most bullish data point from an FSRU perspective was Excelerate’s comment on expecting to redeploy **EXPRESS** at improved economic terms. We now have visibility on this likely being in Colombia to Frontera Energy, which likely justifies the higher charter rate in light of the substantially higher credit risk compared to ADNOC. 

Following the bond issuance in late-2025, **Kinetics** is now also in the public domain with a recent update on the progress for conversion of their three FSRUs. **OCEANIA** has been completed in Q2 with **TÜRKIYE** targeted for completion in Q3/26 before their largest FSRU; **KARADENIZ** arrives in Q4/27. We see the two initial vessels targeted for Karpowership’s fleet of powerships, but the last FSRU has potential to compete in the “standard” FSRU market given a very wide range of operating conditions.

Finally, perhaps the most interesting corporate movement are those that should be considered as “no smoke without fire” which suggest there may be some upcoming transaction in the coming months that could slightly alter the market balance. More about that when/if it happens.
Quarterly focus: Understand FSRU demand to gain the upper hand and execute as planned

So far in 2026, the FSRU market has kept up a decent pace, with six charters concluded already. Locations, durations and assets vary a lot, but there's clearly momentum out there. For this quarter's focus, we dust off our crystal ball and ask: will the second half of 2026 be just as busy – and if so, **where, why, how and for whom**?

**Where?** We've recently **reviewed close to 280 projects**. Of these, around 130 are effectively dead, 70-80 are in recovery mode, leaving 70-80 projects with a genuine lease on life. We'd write off another 30 or so as unlikely to progress, which leaves **40-50 projects with a real shot at reaching FID**. Geographically, South/Southeast Asia, Europe and South America lead the pack – no great surprise, since Asia still has plenty of untapped potential and South America's gas consumption keeps climbing. Europe is a bit of a wildcard, but a handful of solid projects there should materialize in 2029-2030, meaning decisions need to land in 2026-2027.

**Why?** Economics usually take the wheel once a project reaches a certain stage, but the softer, qualitative factors matter just as much for commercial viability. Our research points to regulatory environment and existing infrastructure as the main sticking points – essentially, the need to build mooring/jetties and pipeline onshore, all under tight environmental rules. If you spend your days in FSRU business development, you'll know these as the usual "red flags" – ones that tend to get pushed aside once long-tenor contracts and strategic importance enter the conversation. Around **60% of our likely projects sit in challenging regulatory environments** (translation: plenty of room for external curveballs), yet **80% come with expected contract durations of 10+ years** (translation: a nice cushion against residual risk for the FSRU provider). Striking the right balance between these two forces is really what makes or breaks a project.

**How?** Newbuilds look set to stay in limited demand, reserved for a select 10-15% of projects – usually driven by project-specific quirks (Poland being a good example) or simply over-engineering (looking at you, SLNG). Conversions, thanks to their shorter lead times, lower costs and performance that holds its own against newbuilds, remain the go-to solution across our likely-list. A few projects could still go either way, but these TBC cases also rank low on our likelihood scale, so they don't move the needle much.

**Who?** Some projects in our database already have a likely FSRU provider lined up; others are still very much up for grabs. The "Big Boys" have already secured around 20-25% of our likely projects – a nod to some sharp, forward-leaning BD teams. That said, roughly two-thirds of the list is still open season. Cross-referencing project likelihood against probable provider, it's clear the Big Boys have generally locked in the opportunities most likely to succeed.

The final piece of the puzzle is **WHEN** all this actually comes to fruition and gets awarded – and for that conversation, we'd love to talk it through with you directly.

content.title: FSRU demand: Expected projects by vessel solution
FSRU demand: Expected projects by region

content.content:
After three consecutive quarters of record volumes, **Q2/26 showed a drop in volumes** delivered to FSRUs. However, it is still the **highest Q2 on record** – which is interesting in the context of the supply disruptions witnessed across the wider market. A total of **17.2mt / 280 cargoes** (up 13% Y-o-Y from 15.3mt / 255 cargoes in Q2/25 and down 10% Q-o-Q from 19mt / 303 cargoes in Q1/26. Activity was higher in all regions apart from Middle East and Mediterranean (which means **Turkey took the foot seasonally off the throttle**). In fact, Turkey is – as highlighted before - becoming a substantial swing consumer with imports in Q2/26 at only 0.4mt compared to 3.4 in Q1/26 and 2.3 in Q4/25. European demand remains relatively steady hovering around 7mt during the quarter and has done so for the past year as all FSRUs (almost) implemented on back of Russia-Ukraine in 2022 are operational now. Americas saw a nudge higher as Argentina restarts seasonal imports with the **EXPEDIENT** locked in for another two-year period. However, it will be interesting to see how Argentina handles their LNG imports to serve Buenos Aires when the first FLNG arrives next year. Lastly, **Egypt is relentlessly importing** at a high pace with **3.1mt or some 50 cargoes** for the quarter and no anomalies on the FSRU operating side. A recent requirement for an FSU for 3-months to EGAS suggests maybe their ADPs are a bit more than what they are able to handle on the regas side.

There were no new additions to the FSRU fleet in terms of new operational terminals during the quarter, but we count 46 active terminals of which 44 received cargoes during the quarter; **ALEXANDROUPOLIS** and Abu Dhabi **EXPRESS** being the only “donut”-terminals in Q2. The busiest terminals were Eemshaven (Netherlands) **ENERGOS IGLOO** at 17 cargoes, followed by Cartagena (Colombia) **HOEGH GRACE** at 16 cargoes and Ain Sokhna Sumed (Egypt) **HOEGH GALLEON** at 15 cargoes. An interesting observation in Q2 was that Bangladesh kept the pace despite being FM’ed across the majority of their long-term SPAs with **Petrobangla FSRU** taking 13 cargoes and **Summit FSRU** taking 14 cargoes.

In terms of cargo sizes we note that Europe, Middle East and Mediterranean are taking full cargoes at appx 150,000-160,000cbm lots delivered whereas **Americas is very much a partial discharge destination** with the average size of 113,000cbm for the quarter. Asian cargoes were also this quarter substantially smaller at106,000cbm on average versus the 110,000cbm on average during the preceeding 12 months – however this is partially skewed lower by some smaller FSRUs in the region as the largest cargoes were just shy of 160,000cbm. We take the opportunity yet again to remind the industry that the **170,000+cbm storage requirement may in many cases be a technical perversion rather than an operational requirement**.

There are now nearly no “insurance FSRUs” in the market as most take a cargo every now and then, but Aqaba (Jordan) **ENERGOS FORCE**, Sergipe (Brazil) **ENERGOS NANOOK**, Dortyol (Turkey) **ETUGRUL GAZI**, Acu (Brazil) **BW MAGNA**, Sepetiba (Brazil) **KARMOL ASIA**, Hong Kong **BAUINIA SPIRIT** and Santos (Brazil), **HOEGH GIANT** each only taking one single cargo in the quarter. Hence, 7 units have crews with plenty of time to do maintenance. TGS remains “in service, but out of service” by the lack of an FSRU at the terminal – but this is expected to change with Ambar having announced a lease from NFE.

From a global perspective, **FSRUs delivered an all-time high 17.4% of all LNG volumes imported in Q2/26**. Global LNG imports dropped to 98.6mt in Q2 vs the current record 117.1mt in Q1. As such, the FSRUs were less impacted by the loss of Qatari LNG – which may not come as a surprise in light of the diverse geographical spread of FSRUs and their respective suppliers. We continue to see FSRUs growing in relevance and with the pipeline of projects and the associated expected demand profiles of the projects we’d be confident to expect FSRUs to provide 20% of global LNG imports within 2-3 years.

content.title: Monthly volumes imported through FSRUs by region (2026YTD)

content.content:
**Asia & Middle East**

**Gas Malaysia** is expected to come to the market with an RFP or tender for newbuild/conversion in the second half of the year. Given the involvement of **Petronas, Tokyo Gas and VTTI** it feels like an open field in respect of FSRU providers – the only question is how many will bother to offer into a tender.

**Bangladesh** remains hampered by political inertia to get their **3rd FSRU** under way. Recent talks suggest any direct or bi-lateral proposal will be put in a pile to wait for a full 2008 PPP (Public Procurement Procedure) tender to get underway sometime in H2/26 (or maybe H1/27?).

**Europe & Mediterranean**
**Poland** is targeting to secure its 2nd FSRU following a successful open season. The selection process is underway and the invitees are reportedly only the “big boys” with decisions due towards end-26.

Additional activity is happening in **Greece** and the **Balkans** with also **Montenegro and Albania** gearing up for FSRU projects. We have a higher conviction on Greece than the Balkans, but as per usual protocol the regulatory environment for bona fide (ie no emergency decree or similar) FSRU project developments remains a clamp.

Despite having announced successful offtakers including Equinor and BASF as well as intentions to reinstall the second FSRU at **Mukran** it has been quiet for some time from DRG. The project remains a high quality prospect with substantial demand into a liquid market – just need to get that FSRU lined up to access it.

**Americas & Caribbean**
Activity in **Colombia** has slowed down somewhat following the rush of announcements through the quarter. At this point it feels more like the task at hand is to understand the power dynamics which eventually leads to a few of the announced projects not moving forward.

We are hearing substantial activity in **Brazil** with some of the new kids on the block taking positions. Admittedly, BW, Hoegh, Excelerate and Energos all have existing exposure and as the largest FSRU market in the world it may have room for some new players. 

**Africa & Other**
**South Africa** is moving on several fronts with both **Coega/Ngqura and Richards Bay** having the foot on the accelerator. While Richards Bay is in essence ring fenced to VOPAK we understand the Coega initiative is an open situation.

**New Zealand** continues to push for an FSRU in Port Taranaki with the government having shortlisted two players. As we understand one of the players have access to an FSRU barge sitting in West Africa that has never regassified since delivery in 2020. Hopefully the Kiwi’s have sense to select the other alternative.

**BW MAGNA** departed Acu at two occasions during the quarter with an extended period for nearly a month mid-May to mid-June. While the reason is not clear the disruption clearly has had an impact on GNAs TPPs.

**EXCELERATE ACADIA** has been the FSRU with most sailing time during the quarter departing from South Korea in early-Apr to pick up a cargo in Trinidad before heading to Egypt for discharge into **ENERGOS POWER** in Ain Sokhna and berthing at Aqaba late-June to replace **ENERGOS FORCE**.

**CAPE ANN** (while technically an FSRU) seems to be doing more spot LNGC work having loaded in Bonny and discharged in India and Thailand before heading further East on her latest voyage.

**BW SINGAPORE** departed station a few times during the quarter – likely due to unfavorable weather conditions forcing the vessel to leave as the breakwater is not yet completed.

**HOEGH ESPERANZA** and **EXCELSIOR** both departed their respective jetties in Wilhelmshaven for a few days during April to accommodate the dredging of the sites. This is another beauty of the German FSRU sites including Stade; annual unavailability due to dredging.
Asset values: Newbuildings and conversion candidates

The steady stream of requirements is driving interest in additional tonnage and we currently count **four newbuilds and three firm conversions** in the orderbook. However, adding the units that are expected to firm up upon satisfaction of CPs we can **add another five conversions** – and then another **2-3 semi-speculative units**. Hence, the potential additional supply at present stands at 13-14 units. Putting that in the context of a fleet of just north of 50 units one may argue the early warnings go off for those thinking orderbook as % of fleet. **However, the different specifications, sizes and to a certain extent bespoke units renders the supply risk somewhat lower.**

Looking ahead we expect to see **at least one more newbuild and could easily count north of 10 projects targeting conversions.** Timing on this may not be 2026, but probably over the next 12 months to reach the targeted CODs. This marks an uptick on our numbers from last quarterly update. The **conversion cases** are interesting as they are mainly a **consequence of the availability of existing tonnage being too late** (and some project specific requirements), but we may ultimately find ourselves very long FSRUs in 2032-2034 in the absence of FSRU stickiness.

**Asset values have moved sideways for ST tonnage while DF tonnage is sliding lower** on back of a few concluded transactions. S&P activity during the quarter has mainly been for trading tonnage and not many LNGCs sold with conversion in mind (we count two sales that are likely conversion-linked) and we continue to be amazed how active KYC-challenged Buyers are. Maybe more surprising are those selling to entities that technically qualify, but are only halfway houses to a Russian flag.

**Preference on size is becoming very visible** and anything below 145,000 cbm is completely yesterday – as **project Buyers focus on 150,000+.** The challenge faced by several is whether to go 150,000-153,000 ST in the 30s or take the leap to 155, 160 or 165 DF where the value of larger storage and existing DF engines balance against the higher pricing which runs from US$ 70-80 million all the way up to US$ 140 million. Not to speak about those focusing on modern 170,000+ who may need to shell out additional green.

Delivery times are generally on forward basis with willingness to conclude pricing on the prompt; an element that FSRU/FSU projects offer to Sellers that we think Sellers have not fully appreciated just yet. The ability to secure your residual of an asset that by most hallmarks will be borderline obsolete in two years (when a mild 200+ additional 2-strokes have delivered and squeezed DFs into more niche trades should be welcomed with open arms – not a “we’re sellers US$ 5-10 million above last”. 

On the supplier side we see **engines as becoming the new critical path item**. Not necessarily due to the time it takes to produce, but the **availability of slots**. Regas modules are **still in the range of 14-18 months** (some quote less, but we find it hard to believe without having secured booster pumps speculatively). The consequence is that there are now **two items that are tricky to deal with on the conversion timeline**, but they are fortunately somewhat separate in the overall process. It also speaks in favor of considering DF tonnage instead of STs. **Total conversion time** from FID to redelivery from yard is as far as we read the EPC contractors still in the range of 23-28 months which means around **25-31 months FID to COD**. Capex also largely sits unchanged, but we’ve seen some early indications of a nudge up on costs. For the time being our range from last quarter remains; **US$ 110-140 million for DFs and US$ 140-180 for STs basis 500/750 SW/Glycol Open Loop** without any additional BOG handling, power supply, boilers or other project-specific bells and whistles.  

Lastly, the **FSRU newbuild market** seems to be getting a bit more traction with MISC ordering their Petronas-linked unit at Samsung at a quoted US$328 million and talks of Poland #2 as well as AKR heading down the newbuild route. This is give or take aligned with our most recent quote of US$ 335m for a “standard” newbuild (170-174,000cbm / 3 x 250MMSCFD SW-Glycol Open Loop). There are many benefits to the newbuilds vs conversions – and for those chasing 170,000cbm as an absolute requirement the price differential is marginal considering useful life. However, what still favors conversions is the lead time due to the fact that **newbuilds now can deliver in Q4/29 at the earliest.**

Oil prices are back to pre-war levels and the Brent front month spread has flipped to contango as Hormuz transits surge after the Iran/U.S. MOU was finally signed. The energy agencies expect the market to be flooded with oil next year, which means the market outlook for next year has meaningfully improved vs. earlier expectations. That is, IF there is a lasting Iran/U.S. agreement. 

That, however, is a big IF. Uncertainty persists, and for every two ships exiting Hormuz over the last week, only one has entered. Fresh loadings are limited, and producers seem cautious about restarting production due to the fragile nature of the 60-day MOU. With a shut West-East arbitrage and potentially underwhelming MEG volume we may get a 'normal' summer market. More evidence of production restart and loadings will be key.

Global seaborne volumes have recovered over the past few months, although remain some 2-3 mbpd shy of pre-war levels. Another bump is expected very near-term as MEG inventories are emptied, but beyond that we could see another leg down when U.S. inventory draws (likely) end after July and MEG production is unlikely to properly restart until there is more clarity on progress in Iran/U.S. talks. 

The latest energy agency oil production and forecasts show a gradual ramp-up with global output coming back to pre-war levels into early next year, before reaching new highs more than 2 mbpd higher than the peak late last year going into the second half of next year. A similar trajectory is expected for refinery runs. That should leave potential for global tanker tonne-mile demand to grow by 3-5% vs. the prior peak - potentially more for the compliant fleet if Iran sanctions are sustainably lifted. 

That is still, however, shy of fleet growth of up to 5% this year and 6% next year, although inefficiencies and congestion might ensure that rates can remain relatively elevated also through next year.

content.content: Volumes nearly recovered, but now what?

There has been a sharp rebound in tonne-mile demand, driven by the outsized Atlantic-East fixture counts in recent months and a resurgence of MEG exports. The longevity of this bounce is questionable, however, as Atlantic loadings are set to come down, and loadings inside the Hormuz Strait far lag transits. 

Over the last week twice as many VLCCs have transited Hormuz outbound vs. inbound, signifying that the recent flow is more about draining inventories than production actually starting up. The most up to date estimates still show MEG production shut-ins well above 10 mbpd, and although crude flow through Hormuz has at times almost been back to normal, tracking of new loadings only indicate up to about 5 mbpd. As long as production does not ramp up, and more vessels do not enter, the recent bounce (in volumes and rates) is unlikely to last.

content.content: Oil market - from glut, to shortage, to glut again. Or is there really one?

Both the EIA and IEA have now introduced 2027 forecasts, with global supply expected to reach 110+ mbpd by the end of the year - 2.5-3 mbpd higher than the peak at the end of last year. Neither agency expect a full recovery to pre-war production levels until Q1'27. 

On the IEA's estimates that may leave a nearly 5 mbpd oversupplied oil market next year, while the EIA's more optimistic demand forecast 'only' suggests a 4 mbpd glut. This does beg the question what will OPEC+ and others do about production - as the global inventory draws this year may be quite quickly replenished. Race to the bottom? 

Global inventories have drawn by slightly more than 200 mb YTD through May per the latest IEA estimates, well short of what most had feared. More draws are expected in coming months, possibly close to 100 mb in June alone, but again less than previously feared, and it may not take long before a glut narrative reemerges. If so, there may not be a rush among crude buyers to secure barrels near-term - which is also to an extent reflected in recent oil price development - lower flat prices, lower differentials, Murban and Brent forward curves in contango, etc. 

However, that may be more the results of narrative, financial positioning and complacency, as what crude now flows out of Hormuz is largely also an inventory drawdown. Unless Chinese imports remain abnormally low, and MEG crude oil production meaningfully picks up, and soon, the market may be much shorter than currently meets the eye.

There are some upside risks to global oil production going into next year. If Iran and the U.S. can reach a lasting agreement, there is meaningful upside for production over time - some 0.5-1 mbpd. Similarly, Venezuela can produce more given investment, and has already surpassed most expectations in terms of exports - at times up to 0.5 mbpd more than most had forecast by now. 

The UAE is another source, with estimated production capacity nearly 1 mbpd higher than pre-war production. Officials have, however, stated that production hikes may be measured according to what market conditions warrant.

A significant driver for tanker demand recently has been the U.S. where a combination of resilient production and big stock draws have boosted exports by up to 2 mbpd. Most of this is now likely to reverse. 

U.S. SPR releases are likely coming to an end. In the last tranche, only 500kb were awarded, out of 40 mb offered which suggests very limited appetite (partly due to unfavourable terms and partly oil pricing). With that, about 130 mbd has been awarded, of which about 50 mb remains to be drawn - another 5-6 weeks of draws at recent pace - or another 2-3 weeks of VL fixing. Commercial inventories are also bordering on tight levels, currently sitting at the very low-end of the 2015-26 range - although there is still another 40 mb to go to the 2010-14 average, so there could be some more draws before oil prices would (likely) respond sharply. However, with only marginal backwardation and a lack of arbitrage to Asia, further significant draws may not be likely. Then, the stocks need to be refilled over the next two years, reversing some of the recent flow.

content.content: Iran comeback net neutral impact for the tanker market near-term

The OFAC's waivers on Iranian crude exports may in isolation give a boost to the tanker market, but there are also waivers on the sanctioned ships. Unless Iranian crude exports go to other buyers than Chinese independent refiners and India, which would be the most likely takers, it is unlikely that a lot will go on anything other than the shadow/sanctioned fleet. 

There are 60 VLCCs in the shadow/sanctioned fleet which are 20 years or younger and are therefore likely to be utilised for Iranian exports near term. That should be sufficient to cover most exports. 

Considering the limited time-period, and fragile peace, there may not be a lot of independent owners or buyers going in, unless there is a more sustainable peace and lifting of sanctions. Longer term, however, this may become more of a positive development for the tanker market balance.

content.content:
Global refinery runs remain depressed by shut-ins in the MEG and Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries. That has supported crack spreads which remain much better supported than crude prices. 

Amid these higher prices there may be decent room for freight, but with ample position lists in most areas, the risk of LR2s switching back to clean as Aframax rates have come off, and low volumes as long as Hormuz uncertainty persists, rates may see some headwinds through the summer. Here too, more clarity on a Hormuz reopening is needed.
Fleet growth will ultimately spoil the party

In line with rising rates and secondhand values the orderbook has risen dramatically. Over Q4'25-Q1'26 more orders were placed than over the eight preceding quarters combined (Q2'26 shows orders that have been confirmed so far, and is likely to rise). At the beginning of June the total orderbook to fleet stood at 25%, up more than 6% points since the beginning of the year - that is after the fleet has grown by slightly more than 2% YTD. Including reported and rumoured orders, we would not be surprised if we hit 30% orderbook to fleet soon. 

There is eventually meaningful phase-out potential too, but insufficient the next few years. The VL, Suez, Afra/LR2 and MR orderbook now stands at a combined 155m dwt. The compliant vessels within the same segments which are already or will become 25 years old the next three years (realistic scrap age given long-lived rate strength) amounts to 'only' 21m dwt. 

The mismatch between the orderbook and realistic phase-out candidates the next three years is equal to 20% of the current fleet.

That is too much, although eventually more phase-out will help rebalance the market.

In our previous update sent in late May, we wrote:

*No major changes to the outlook since early April. Demand growth remains above supply growth, but has fallen during the last few months. Global credit growth rates keep falling, primarily due to lower loan growth in China. Iron ore inventories in China have been drawn down but remain high. However, industrial metals prices have rebounded sharply since late March, reflecting that global industrial activity is not in a downturn just yet. However, the surging oil prices are starting to have its usual bearish impact, with cost increases and eroding margins being reported, not only due to direct energy cost increases, but also because freight rates are higher, due to bunker prices. The brewing El Nino could, along with the lower supply of fertilisers, pose a problem for grain crops over the next year. So, we still have the view that a market downturn is likely to begin in Q3, and that 2027 earnings averages will be lower than this year. Increasing coal demand should cushion some of the weakness likely to come from other commodity groups. However, seaborne supply remains an issue. Otherwise, the soon-to-be-announced Guinean Bauxite export curbs will be important for the outlook going forward.
We think there are clear signs that the upcycle is losing momentum. Shipment volume growth has kept trending down, with data through May showing the rate of volume growth had dropped below the rate of supply growth for all segments, except Capesize/Newcastlemax. Ton-time growth is still above supply growth in all segments, which is why the markets remain higher than they were 1 year ago. However, we still expect that to change, as we expect shipment volume growth to continue trending down through the second half of this year.*

Since our previous report, **oil prices** have dropped significantly. Based on the correlation between oil prices and BDI, included, as usual, in the final page of this report, the outlook for the second half of 2027 has thus improved considerably. That said, the volatility in energy markets and the complicated physical fundamental situation are unusual, so leading indicators like the one we use might not be as accurate as previously going forward. Regardless, the point is that low oil prices are good for economic growth, and vice versa. **Coal** volume growth has increased notably in the last few months. An opening of the Strait of Hormuz is a relief for macro but suppress the upside potential in coal. **Industrial metals** prices have fallen over the last month, suggesting that global industrial activity is struggling to maintain upward momentum and may even be declining. That is especially the case in China, where **iron ore** and steel consumption remain lower than last year, and inventories remain higher. Global credit growth rates continue to fall, as reflected by a strengthening **US dollar index**. The dollar index correlates tightly with dry bulk volume growth and clearly suggests volume growth will continue to fall in the next few months. 
In the second half of last year, the Capesize index averaged about 30.000 USD pd, the Kamsarmax index averaged about 16.000 USD pd, the Ultramax index averaged about 17.250 USD pd, and the Handysize index averaged about 14.000 USD pd. The way we see fundamentals now, we find it hard to expect higher averages than that in the second half of this year.

TRADE FLOWS YEAR ON YEAR GROWTH

This page gives brief comments on what the charts on the next page tell us. Overall, an increasingly bearish picture is being painted from the second half of this year and through the first part of 2027. 

Top left chart:

The BDI year-on-year change has been strongly positive since September last year, as usual, lagging behind increased credit growth in China. 
However, the credit growth rate has continued to fall over the last few months and has been negative for the last two months, which gives us a clear bearish indication for late this year and the start of 2027. 

Top right chart:

Except for a decoupling in 2024, the change in bond yields in China and the US has been a good leading indicator for dry bulk demand growth. Strong support for demand growth this year is suggested, but also a potential peak. Demand growth seems to have peaked according to what was suggested by this leading indicator. 

Middle left chart:

Lower crude oil prices are bullish for economic growth, and vice versa. The chart displays that since 2017, there has been a tight correlation between lower year-on-year oil prices and a higher year-on-year BDI, with the oil price change leading by 1 year. 
Lower oil prices suggest the BDI could remain positive year-on-year throughout 2026. However, the increase in oil prices since late February suggest the market will be lower during the first half of next year, but the recent oil price drop suggests the market might recover in the second half of next year. 

Middle right chart:

The OECD diffusion index momentum keeps falling, and suggest the year on year change of the BDI will turn less and less positive over the coming six months. 

Bottom left chart:

The OECD diffusion index correlation with the BDI is very high, as usual. The OECD index reading is comparable to previous cycle peaks. The latest reading in May showed a drop in the index - the first month-on-month drop since the spring of last year. 

Bottom right chart:

The weakening dollar momentum has stalled in the last few months, along with what seems to be peak volume growth rate. Recently, the dollar has started to strengthen, suggesting volume growth will continue falling.

Last week, we wrote *"The gap between demand and supply is very narrow. Volume growth is below supply growth (4.8% vs 5.2%), but ton x time growth is probably still higher, at around 6%. Therefore, the market is likely to hold firm for at least another month, but should volume growth continue to decrease, it will be harder for the market to stay higher than the same period last year."* 

Volume growth was revised up slightly, to 5.1% - still, below supply growth.

In our previous update sent in early April, we wrote:

*A black swan event has occurred, which changes the market outlook for the worse. **Fundamentals are still likely to remain positive through the second quarter, as there is always a lag before higher energy costs start to impact dry bulk markets. However, the risk of a weaker second half of this year than last year has increased substantially.** This eventual weakness is likely to last through the first half of 2027 as well. The upward price moves in crude oil and refined products are such that historical correlations clearly suggest dry bulk markets will be negatively impacted. In this report, under the macro-economic section, we always include a chart displaying the year-on-year change of crude oil prices with a 1-year lead on the year-on-year change of the BDI. Since our previous report in late February, this chart has changed quite dramatically. 

What if the Strait of Hormuz opens up fully? The outlook will be relatively brighter. However, damages to energy infrastructure in the Middle East, along with lingering uncertainty, likely mean energy prices will not quickly fall back to pre-war levels. It is also important to remember that the outlook is not all dependent on the Hormuz situation. Other factors, such as coincident economic indices, average cycle durations, falling global credit growth, weakening momentum of industrial metals prices and high iron ore inventories in China, all suggest that fundamentals are close to peaking.*

**No major changes to the outlook since early April.** Demand growth remains above supply growth, but has fallen during the last few months. Global credit growth rates keep falling, primarily due to lower loan growth in China. Iron ore inventories in China have been drawn down but remain high. However, industrial metals prices have rebounded sharply since late March, reflecting that global industrial activity is not in a downturn just yet. However, the surging oil prices are starting to have its usual bearish impact, with cost increases and eroding margins being reported, not only due to direct energy cost increases, but also because freight rates are higher, due to bunker prices. The brewing El Nino could, along with the lower supply of fertilisers, pose a problem for grain crops over the next year. So, we still have the view that a market downturn is likely to begin in Q3, and that 2027 earnings averages will be lower than this year. Increasing coal demand should cushion some of the weakness likely to come from other commodity groups. However, seaborne supply remains an issue. Otherwise, the soon-to-be-announced Guinean Bauxite export curbs will be important for the outlook going forward.

While we wait... for the on-again, off-again 'imminent' U.S.-Iran deal, it looks like the impact of lower volumes has started to have a greater impact on the tanker market balance and rates, with a steady slide for nearly all segments over the last month. More of the same may be expected until a deal is actually signed. 

However, the crisis has also contributed to materially lifting the tanker demand outlook for the next year(s), with oil supply growth estimates having been revised sharply higher. While perhaps not fully enough to offset higher fleet growth the coming two years, the 2027 tanker market outlook is brighter than earlier feared. 

Unless there is no deal. So we wait some more...

Although 'sources' continuously claim a deal is near, full details and any timeline is still up in the air, and there are renewed attacks. A few more transits recently could be indicative of a step toward reopening. Some observations can be made for what might be expected for the tanker market if or when the Hormuz Strait does indeed open: 

•	This could be very bullish for LRs in the East, after most have moved into dirty and West. 
•	To start, the academic TD3c assessment could drop closer to rates in other areas if the risk premium disappears. However, rates in other areas may strengthen too. 
•	Oil traders etc. are likely to actively source discounted MEG cargoes which may give an initial fixing rush. With a balanced to thin MEG position list, this could again send rates higher. 
•	A MEG risk premium could, however, remain, if Iran retains control of transits. There is also the issue of whether there are still mines in the strait. 
•	Lower oil prices may entice Asian buyers to be active in both basins to shore up inventories. 
•	After an initial fixing rush basis emptying of MEG inventories etc., the fixing pace may slow if production and Hormuz flow take time to normalise. 
•	Later, activity and rates may gradually strengthen as production ramps up, including the UAE at 'free flow', the latest OPEC+ production target increasing, and possibly some catch-up to under-production the last few months. 
•	2027 oil supply growth may  be materially higher than previously anticipated. 
•	Should this open for Iran sanctions to be lifted down the line, it could be a further boost to tanker demand - shifting parts of Iran's 1.5-2 mbpd onto the compliant fleet, and eventually 0.5-1 mbpd of further production ramp-up. 20+ NITC VLCCs are young enough to continue trading, and there are another 30+ sanctioned/shadow VLCCs that can too. These 50+ vessels should be able to continue lifting at least 1.5 mbpd of crude, provided that receivers allow so.

In the wake of the current crisis comes an improved oil supply and by extension tanker demand outlook. While it may take a while for full production in a re-opening scenario to be restored, there are some key triggers to the upside: 
•	Venezuelan output has already increased slightly more than some cautious estimates suggested - with exports up to about 1.2 mbpd in May. 
•	The UAE has stepped out of the OPEC+, allowing for up to 1 mbpd of potential upside. 
•	The OPEC+ keeps unwinding production cuts, and may overproduce after a re-opening to catch up with underproduction in recent months. 
•	U.S. shale activity has increased, and production forecasts have been lifted. 
•	A potential peace agreement between the U.S. and Iran may likely include lifting of sanctions, which could shift some volumes to the compliant fleet - and leave some gradual production upside. 

Based on the latest EIA estimates, oil supply growth next year, assuming gradual Hormuz normalisation after Q2 this year, could be very high, reaching nearly 2.5 mbpd higher than the previous peak in Q4'25 during Q4'27. The latest EIA estimate has been revised 2 mbpd higher than four months ago. However, the same estimates still show Q4'26 nearly 2 mbpd shy of the end of 2025. 

These estimate revisions indicate some 5% or more tonne-mile growth potential by Q4'27 vs. Q4'25 - substantially above previous expectations.

content.content: Source: Fearnleys, Vortexa, EIA, IEA, OPEC
Demand still low, although recovered somewhat. Overweight of Atlantic ballasters

After some recovery on more long-haul fixtures, tonne-mile demand has dipped again most recently for all segments. This has come after a slight decline in loadings, following a brief up-trend just prior. Overall volumes should gradually rise going forward, and tonne-mile demand should remain around recent levels going forward, supported particularly by high Americas export - provided that U.S. inventory draws do not halt.  

VLCC demand remains weakest across the tanker segments, due to the outsized share of MEG exports. The VLCC market has been somewhat balanced by idle/stuck tonnage, but gravity does work eventually. Suez and Afra/LR2 demand has held up relatively better than the other segments, but also here demand is notably lower than at the beginning of the year, as VLCC competition in the Atlantic has taken hold. 

MRs were for some time supported by leftover volume from the LR2s which switched to dirty and ballasted West. However, the incentive to dirty up further is no longer there, so there may instead be some switching back going forward. CPP volumes have declined too, and there are less long-haul arbitrages which together have impacted product tanker and MR demand negatively. Unless the Hormuz Strait or long-haul arbitrages reopen, there could be some continued pressure for clean rates.

There is still an overhang of ballasters in or heading to the Atlantic basin vs. pre-war levels - leaving pressure on rates despite higher cargo volume in the area too. 

The ballaster count in the Pacific, however, is more in line with the pre-war level, and for Afra/LR2 it is quite a bit lower. Hence, should there be a re-opening of the Hormuz Strait relatively soon, with a corresponding fixture rush, rates may spike.

content.content:
There are two major sources contributing to a better balanced oil market than most had feared by now, high U.S. exports and low Chinese imports. There are of course other factors too, including some demand response, particularly in the petrochemical industry, refinery yield optimisation, use of alternative energy sources including coal to liquids in China, etc. 

The world's largest producer, the U.S., has ramped up exports substantially. This is partly due to large inventory draws - both SPR and commercial. The latter could become a concern for tanker demand going forward, as draws at recent pace is unsustainable and should eventually be supportive for WTI pricing. This may in turn be unsupportive for export economics. However, current commercial crude oil inventory levels are still nearly 100 mb above the 2010-14 average - the last time oil prices were around current levels. 

There has now been an uptick in U.S. onshore activity with rig counts picking up the last few weeks, and shale production growth projections have in turn been lifted. However, that is more likely to affect 2027 export volume potential than the near-term. That may be needed, as the SPR releases are structured as loans, to be refilled at 1.2x the current draws over the next two years.  

The U.S. Gulf has become an increasingly important source for European gasoil (and partly jet) demand as availability from the MEG has shrunk and East-West arbitrage only sporadically working. The longer hauls from the U.S. Gulf are no longer as attractive as during the early stages of the war, also as shortages in the East are not as acute as initially feared. This in turn has been partly helped by China.

content.content:
The world's largest importer, China, has reduced crude oil imports materially - May to date has been more than 5 mbpd lower than January and February, which along with Chinese reselling of crude has given some breathing room for crude pricing. The apparently reduced appetite has been partly driven by lower refinery runs, which in April were the lowest since August 2022, and could slide further in May. 

Inventory trackers show that Chinese inventories have hardly moved, but it is open for question whether there have been draws from caverns etc. which are more difficult to track, since the numbers otherwise do not add up (imports are now down 5 mbpd, refinery runs down 2 mbpd and apparent oil products demand down 3 mbpd, including petrochemical). Unless there is a more pronounced demand response, that is unsustainable. 

Therefore, Chinese refiners likely have to either be allowed to materially tap into inventories, or more crude buying should re-emerge. According to Argus, reselling has now stopped, and there has been some renewed buying from Brazil and West Africa for July delivery after differentials eased. However, the pace remains much lower than normal, allowing other Asian buyers to step in and alleviate shortages. Should Chinese buyers step back in, there could be some more competition for Atlantic grades and upside for Atlantic-East flow again. 

Contrary to what earlier product export bans would suggest, there has not been a drastic decline in Chinese products exports the last two months, which may be one of the reasons why Asian product prices have eased, and some long-haul import arbitrages are no longer there.

So far global observed inventories have declined less than feared, due to an oversupplied market going into this, some demand optimisation, slight production increases from other areas and slightly higher flow through the Hormuz Strait than meets the eye. There could however be some slightly bigger draws ahead unless the Hormuz reopens. Otherwise, it is only a few more months before global inventories are closer to operational constraints. 

The biggest (OECD) draws so far have been for products, as underlying consumption has not budged much. This may lend support for product prices going forward, also after a potential reopening, which should be supportive of high refinery runs and in turn product tanker demand in the medium term. 

A stock rebuild over the next few years may be an oil and tanker demand tailwind in coming years.
Fleet growth and orders picking up

The orderbook has also grown in recent months. The relative value proposition for a newbuild vs. secondhand is favourable - although secondhand values are also well justified by all-time-high TC rates. Realistically, with reported but unconfirmed orders, the overall orderbook to fleet is closer to 25%, and closer to 30% for the biggest segments. This means gross fleet growth of 6-8% this and the next two years. 

Unless sanctions are lifted there may still be a time-gap between deliveries of newbuilds (next two years) and the time when a larger share of the compliant fleet comes toward phase-out age. Given high rates any meaningful scrapping is unlikely near-term. The only near-term phase-out of compliant tonnage that may take place is if the U.S. blockade continues, and more arrests are made, so that the shadow fleet needs to be replenished. Thus far, between lower Iranian oil production and the existing sanctioned/shadow fleet there appears to be sufficient tonnage.

content.content:
Tanker tonne-mile demand remains depressed following MEG production shut-ins, with VLCCs most badly affected while Suez/Afra have shown relative resilience and MRs received a boost. Rates remain historically elevated, but a continuous build-up of ballasters across most regions means the likely near-term rate trajectory is softer. 

A reopening, when it comes, may still produce a (short-lived) rate spike due to logistical hurdles and repositioning, though the scale of that spike depends on how quickly production recovers and inventories can be draw, and more so on whether commercial traffic through Hormuz can safely resume. 

Longer term, the conflict has improved the demand outlook with risk on the upside vs. previous oil production forecasts. However, a rapidly growing and historically elevated orderbook remains a structural headwind.

Last month we outlined three reopening scenarios. A swift reopening scnario can now nearly be ruled out, with little apparent progress in talks between the two parties. Similarly, as both parties seem to dread resumption of kinetic action, an escalatory 'tanker-wars' scenario also seems less likely. 

The remaining scenario appears to be the most likely, with a multi-month Hormuz disruption and tanker demand doldrums. So far, rates have held up much better than anticipated under this scenario, mainly due to high USG exports (inventory draws) and the nearly 5% of the fleet which is stuck inside the Hormuz plus another about 5% of the fleet which is idle or held back by either Sinokor or some Asian charterers, who normally do program barrels from the MEG. Still, given the ballaster availability in most areas, the likely trajectory near-term barring a reopening is softer. 

Even if there is a relatively swift reopening there is in theory ample tonnage available for normalised MEG volumes. While onshore inventory draws could in theory come on top of 'normal' exports, the pace at which these can be drawn may be more limited than the pace at which it can be built. Furthermore, it may take months before full production is restored. Then there is the question of how quickly Hormuz traffic can normalise. Are there mines in the strait? If so, this could be like after the 1990-91 Gulf war when it took 2-3 months before regular commercial traffic resumed, and several more months before all mines were cleared and insurance and confidence was back to normal. 

Still, given logistical hurdles, repositioning, risk premiums and likely frantic fixture activity and sentiment, a reopening may boost freight, at least for some time. Then, if it takes months for normal traffic and volumes to recover, these effects could ebb - just as fleet growth starts to bite.

content.content: Low demand with corresponding tonnage build-up

Tanker tonne-mile demand remains in the doldrums following the unprecedented MEG production shut-ins. In time, VLCC demand will be shown to pick up on increased Atlantic-East flow, although that distance effect cannot fully offset the volume loss. 

Suez- and Aframax demand has held up relatively better than the bigger vessels, but here there may be slight downside near term as VLCCs have cannibalised on Atlantic flows. 

Although total product tanker demand has declined, the market balance impact has been more than offset by LR2s switching to dirty trade. The most recent data suggests that 65% of LR2s now trade dirty, up from 53% just two months ago. As a beneficiary, MR tonne-mile demand has increased to new all-time-highs.

content.content:
Due to the lasting Hormuz closure, oil production, refinery runs and by extension tanker volumes remain low. While the effects on oil prices and the global economy (or stock markets..) have so far not relatively limited, some realities start to set in. Visible oil inventories have started to draw, now also onshore (also in the West), and there is (much) more to come. The biggest change to the upside for volumes has been USG exports, driven by SPR releases, and Venezuela. 

Given the scale of production shut-ins, about 1 billion barrels of global supply has effectively already been lost - a figure that may double by August unless the disruption is not fully over by then. 

The biggest inventory draws so far have taken place in the East, and from oil on the water where nearly 200 mb of the 250 mb excess which built last year has now been drawn - mainly compliant and Russian barrels. There is still around 160 mb of Iranian crude oil on the water, giving the regime some leeway.

Oil pricing volatility persists. Amid a strengthening of Brent and WTI, and less acute buying interest from the East (China selling some WAfr barrels, for instance), the West-East arbitrage which ballooned a few weeks ago has narrowed substantially. This has given somewhat fewer long-haul VL fixtures, which corresponds with the build-up of ballasters to the West, and has hence given pressure on West-East rates - not that current levels around $100k/d is low, by any means. 

Similarly, this has led to some support again for Suez- and Aframaxes in the West, with some swing barrels switching back to shorter hauls. However, there is still a tonnage build-up, which means that there could be some renewed pressure on rates near-term. Like for the VLs, rates around $100k/d is not to be sniffed at! 

Another turn of events is a seeming let-up in the acute product shortages in the East, where the West-East demand pull does not seem to be as strong as it was, particularly for gasoline. Should Chinese product exports resume as has been reported, this demand pull could lessen further. While this could leave some pressure on the Atlantic MR market - with more vessels ballasting into the area, there could be some renewed strength in the Pacific.
Better longer term demand outlook, but a correspondingly growing orderbook

The longer-term demand story has improved somewhat on the back of this conflict. Higher oil prices should all else equal stimulate more upstream investment, especially in short-cycle oil. The EIA has lifted its production outlook for the Americas in its most recent updates, although some of that will have to go toward replenishing the U.S. SPR (1.2 barrels for every barrel drawn). The UAE's OPEC exit, along with Venezuela may also lend upside vs. previous oil supply estimates. Although currently (partly) locked in, the UAE's upside potential may be more than 1 mbpd vs. pre-war levels. Another upside scenario is one in which the U.S. and Iran reach a nuclear (and Hormuz...) agreement which includes lifting sanctions. 

That oil production upside may be needed, as the oil demand recovery after a re-opening could be swift - barring perhaps some flight cancellations and other demand optimisation which might persist for some time. On top of that, global inventories need refilling, and in some areas capacity should be expanded . For the tanker market, oil sourcing diversification could add to sailing distances too.

content.title: Sanctioned flows - some upside potential if sanctions are lifted

content.content:
On the flipside, strong rates have resulted in the same as in every market cycle - a much larger orderbook after a rush to the yards YTD. Based on confirmed orders, the orderbook to fleet ratio is now nearly 23%. Based on reported orders too, it is more likely north of 25%. Similarly, the VLCC and Suezmax orderbooks realistically push toward 30%. 

While the bulk of the bigger tanker deliveries are skewed toward 2028, fleet growth has already started to pick up YTD (1.5% in Q1). Phase-out is limited amid strong earnings, and may continue to be so as long as the older part of the fleet trades in the shadows. Should the shadow fleet need replenishing, however, that may partly reduce net fleet growth, as may a sanction lifting scenario.
