content.content:
The past year has been anything but ordinary for the LPG market, and this quarter will go down in the history books as one of the most impactful for shipping to date. January and February were, for the most part, relatively normal, with healthy market conditions and stable export flows from both main regions. Newbuilds were delivered as scheduled, and they were all well-absorbed. 

Following escalation in the U.S./Israel-Iran conflict at the end of February, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) declared the strait of Hormuz operationally closed, putting all AG export in an overnight-chokehold. Since then, each week has brought new challenges and the global energy market has been forced to confront, first-hand, the critical importance of Middle Eastern supply. As the Middle East accounts for over 30% of global LPG supply, total seaborne exports have, as expected, declined; particularly during the month of March. However, recent weeks have seen a record‑high number of liftings out of the U.S. to replace lost MEG volumes. As a result, we expect seaborne volumes to increase in the upcoming quarter.

The countries hit hardest by the disruption in LPG flows from the region have been China and India, which together absorb approximately 85% of all MEG exports. To date, we have observed some replacement of supplies, with both countries increasingly sourcing barrels from North America.

In China, overall PDH plant run rates have declined by 10%, falling from 64% to 56%. In India, the impact has been more pronounced in residential and service-industry consumption, with numerous hotels and restaurants temporarily shutting down as they are no longer able to operate amid LPG scarcity.

The disruption in flows triggered a sharp increase in price volatility, pushing the arbitrage wide open to a record high of $728.5 on March 19. This was largely driven by the FEI reaching a 12-year high of $1,131 (previously peaking at $1,155 in 2013). The market reaction followed critical Iranian attacks on Gulf producers, which caused extensive damage to Qatar’s Ras Laffan production site. QatarEnergy has since confirmed that the fallout from the attack will have long-term consequences for its massive natural gas projects, with approximately 13% of its LPG production capacity expected to be lost.

As if the loss of MEG supplies were not already severe, planned new capacity from Qatar and Saudi Arabia was expected to play a crucial offsetting role. Initially, the region was set to increase export capacity by 20% by 2027, driven by more than 6 MTPA from new natural gas projects in Qatar and an additional 2.5 MTPA from Saudi Arabia’s Jafurah shale gas project. However, the extent to which these new volumes will ultimately come online, now remains uncertain. QatarEnergy has already announced delays to its projects, calling into question the timing and scale of future supply growth. These volumes were highly anticipated by the VLGC fleet, which is scheduled to expand by 85 newbuilds over the same period.

It has now been a year since “Liberation Day” in 2025, an event that fundamentally altered global LPG trade flows, many of which persist today as the “new normal.” U.S. exports to China remain at only 50% of pre–trade war levels. Chinese LPG imports are now more diversified, with new flows emerging from Canada.

Following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a large-scale repositioning of the VLGC fleet commenced, with vessels ballasting toward the United States. This resulted in a surge of West-bound fixtures during March, leaving limited tonnage available. As has historically been the case, increased transit activity triggered a sharp rise in auction fees, with a VLGC reportedly paying up to $4 million to secure canal transit. This matches the previous historical high recorded during the Great Drought in 2023. Increased demand for canal transits has been observed not only from gas carriers, but across other shipping segments as well, further exacerbating upward pressure on auction fees.

With Hormuz closed, market focus shifted heavily toward U.S. supply, raising the critical question of whether the United States could offset the disrupted Middle Eastern volumes. The short answer is no. That said, two major terminal expansions by Enterprise are scheduled to come online in 2026: Neches River Phase 2, adding 11 MTPA of ethane/LPG-flexible capacity in Q2, and the Houston terminal expansion of 9 MTPA in Q4. Combined, these projects will increase total U.S. NGL export capacity by approximately 20 MTPA. Unfortunately, U.S. export barrels remain propane-heavy, in contrast to Middle Eastern barrels, which are more evenly split between propane and butane. The first propane shipment out of the Neches River facility was loaded onto a VLGC this week.

U.S. export terminals have responded rapidly to the surge in demand, with utilization rates climbing close to 100%. This has pushed terminal fees to their highest levels in more than a decade. Compounding the situation, Targa’s Galena Park terminal declared force majeure on March 18 due to mechanical damage, reducing operating capacity to approximately 70%. This further tightened an already strained market, as Galena Park is the third-largest U.S. LPG export terminal, handling nearly 25% of total U.S. exports.

Despite these disruptions, U.S. LPG production has remained consistently strong throughout 2026, resulting in propane inventories ending March at 69% above the five-year average.

One of the most influential drivers of fleet utilization has been sailing patterns for both laden and ballast voyages. Laden VLGCs heading from the U.S. to the Far East typically transit the Panama Canal, which offers a significantly shorter route than the alternative voyage around the Cape of Good Hope. Activity through the Suez Canal remains very limited, with minimal VLGC traffic reported. During Q1, 73% of laden U.S. export voyages transited the Panama Canal, slightly below the 2025 average of 75%. Conversely, 38% of vessels ballasting back from the Far East to the U.S. opted to route via the Cape of Good Hope, up from a 35% average in 2025.

Average daily spot TCE earnings across the three benchmark routes reached $79,800 per day in Q1, driven primarily by extreme market volatility and record-high bunker prices. This contrasts sharply with Q1 of the previous year, when average earnings stood at $36,300 per day, representing a 120% increase year-on-year. **BLPG1 averaged at $76,000 per day and BLPG3 at $71,200.** As all AG-related activity was halted during the final month of the quarter, BLPG1 publications in March were reduced to a weekly frequency, issued each Wednesday (with the exception of March 2nd, 3rd, and 4th). This reduced publication frequency has been accounted for in the averages. In April, the index publication schedule was increased to bi-weekly.

Although 13 VLGCs have successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz during this period, approximately 10 vessels remain trapped within the region. As of April 7, a two-week ceasefire had been agreed upon between the U.S./Israel and Iran, conditional on a “complete, immediate, and safe” reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. It remains unclear how shipowners and insurers will ultimately assess the situation, and it would be surprising if oil and gas producers were to immediately reverse shut-in production against such a fragile backdrop. Even under stable conditions, it would take weeks to reschedule loadings and reposition vessels - not to mention the risk of ships again becoming stranded should negotiations fail to yield a lasting peace agreement.

Looking further ahead, one of the most significant wildcards for the VLGC market lies in Iran’s demand for sanctions relief within ongoing negotiations with the U.S./Israel. Currently, approximately 14% of the global VLGC fleet is engaged in sanctioned trade, transporting LPG from Iran to China - a flow that in 2025 amounted to nearly 10 MTPA, or around 9% of global trade. These roughly 60 vessels could quickly become phase-out candidates should sanctions be lifted as part of a broader peace agreement. Notably, 41% of these ships are over 30 years old and would likely be unable to re-enter the regular-trading market.
**Newbuilds continue to be delivered, while ordering activity has picked up in 2026**

A total of 11 newbuilds were delivered in Q1, leaving 25 vessels scheduled for delivery over the remainder of 2026. The VLGC fleet now stands at 423 ships, with an orderbook of 107 vessels, corresponding to an orderbook-to-fleet ratio of 25%. The majority of the orderbook is characterized by ammonia-ready designs (up to 98% cargo capacity), LPG dual-fuel propulsion, and Panamax dimensions. Following subdued ordering activity in 2025, newbuilding interest has rebounded in early 2026, reflecting a more optimistic long-term outlook for LPG market growth. Newbuilding prices have edged slightly lower but remain within the $115–120 million range, depending on technical specifications. Yard capacity remains tight, with new deliveries now largely scheduled for 2029. Hyundai Heavy Industries in South Korea remains the largest VLGC builder, while approximately one-quarter of newbuildings are currently under construction in China.

**Now, what's next?**
Market focus in the coming weeks will center on developments in negotiations between the U.S./Israel and Iran, and on the potential reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. We expect ballasting vessels approaching the West to result in a relatively long tonnage list upon arrival - however, as the U.S. continues to demonstrate strong production, with inventories remaining well above historical averages heading into the summer season, we could see a continued surge in exports and a more optimistic outlook regarding the replacement of MEG volumes than initially expected. In parallel, an additional 25 newbuilds are scheduled for delivery during the rest of the year. How trade flows evolve from here will ultimately determine tonne-mile demand; however, we expect the inefficiency associated with longer voyage distances to absorb much of the incremental fleet growth - provided sufficient LPG availability to keep vessels employed.

Looking back on Q1, it is difficult to recall developments from the first two-thirds of the quarter, as the period is overwhelmingly defined by the war in the Middle East and the large share of LNG volumes trapped in the Gulf. That said, the first two months were initially characterized by a typical post-winter demand drop and clear shipping oversupply.

This dynamic shifted abruptly following the U.S./Israeli attack on Iran and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which trapped close to one fifth of global LNG volumes. While, in theory, a loss of cargoes should be negative for shipping demand—implying more vessels chasing fewer cargoes—the elevated uncertainty and sharp increase in gas prices tended to support LNG shipping rates. In addition, Middle East LNG predominantly supplies Asian buyers, and expectations that U.S. LNG would need to move to Asia to replace this supply underpinned tonne-mile demand.

Initially, the loss of volumes did not translate into increased vessel availability through sublets, suggesting a “wait-and-see” approach by market participants. Spot rates reacted immediately, rising above USD 250,000/day for modern two-stroke vessels. As it became clearer that the disruption would persist, some vessels earmarked for Middle East loadings were released into the spot market, leading to a correction in rates.

The market took another turn following the direct attack on Ras Laffan. Rates again spiked, although within days spot rates normalized to levels broadly in line with those seen prior to the attack, albeit still elevated. It was subsequently confirmed that two of the 14 trains were damaged and would be offline for several years. It is reasonable to expect that the current situation and infrastructure damage will result in further delays to the North Field Expansion, which is planned to add 66 MTPA of liquefaction capacity over the next five years. Delays to at least 2027 have already been announced.

Separately, Venture Global reached FID on Phase 2 of the CP2 project, adding a further 14 MTPA of liquefaction capacity from 2030 onwards. On the fleet side, 18 LNG carriers were delivered during Q1, while 33 newbuild orders were placed.
Source: JKM from S&P Global Platts

Charter rates began to decline from their winter peak in early December and had by January eased to the high USD 40k/day range for two-stroke vessels. By early February, rates had fallen further into the low USD 20k/day range, where they ultimately bottomed out.

Over the course of February, regional market dynamics diverged. The Far East and Middle East effectively disconnected from the Atlantic basin: cold weather and operational disruptions lifted rates in the West, while competition remained intense in the Pacific. As a result, two-stroke spot charter rates ended February at around USD 40k/day in the Atlantic and USD 27k/day in the Pacific.

February to March saw the largest month-on-month increase in average rates on record, with two-stroke spot earnings surging from USD 28k/day to USD 178k/day. As a result, the quarterly average settled at around USD 80k/day—well above levels seen a year earlier.

Term rates were also lifted by the geopolitical developments. One-year charter rates jumped week-on-week from the low USD 40k/day range to around USD 100k/day. This marked the first time since end-2023 that 1-year rates have traded above 3-year rates, following an extended period of market contango where longer-term coverage commanded a premium. While 1-year rates have since retraced from their initial peak, they remain elevated. Longer-term rates (3–7 years) have edged higher as strengthening near-term fundamentals spill over.

content.title: Two-stroke spot charter rates by region

content.content:
A new record for fixing activity was set in Q1, with 150 spot fixtures concluded. This surpassed the previous record of 126 spot fixtures recorded in Q1 last year, representing a year‑on‑year increase of 19%—well above the 11% growth in the fleet over the same period. In contrast, total fixed days in the Q1 spot market rose by only 6% year on year, indicating materially shorter fixture durations than last year.

Spot activity has trended higher since 2023, driven by increased sublet willingness as gas prices declined and shipping oversupply grew. Similar to the reaction seen during the gas price spikes following the war in Ukraine, sublet willingness again declined as gas prices rose amid the war in Iran. This time, however, fixture activity continued to increase. This can be explained by a shift in market structure: independent owners now control a larger share of the availability list than in recent years and, unlike portfolio players, have limited incentive to withhold tonnage for optionality. In addition, some vessels that would normally trade Middle East cargoes—now disrupted—were made available to the spot market. As a result, despite reduced sublet willingness from portfolio players, overall availability remained high and supported strong fixture activity.

Liquidity in the one‑year market was the strongest since Q1 2022, with seven one‑year fixtures concluded. All but one involved two‑stroke vessels, and all but two were sublets. The majority of these deals were concluded in March, suggesting that heightened uncertainty prompted charterers to secure tonnage ahead of winter, mitigating exposure to potential seasonal peaks in spot rates. At the longer end, one three‑year and one five‑year deal were concluded, both for two‑stroke vessels from independent owners. Reflecting the strong pace of newbuild ordering in Q1, a notable number of long‑term contracts in the 7–15‑year range were also signed during the quarter.

content.title: Short term fixtures by sublet vs independent owners

content.content:
Q4 2025 closed at record‑high traded volumes, followed by another record in January. With several projects scheduled to lift first cargoes in Q1, the outlook initially pointed to yet another quarterly record, despite entering the shoulder‑season months. However, with the loss of roughly one‑fifth of global LNG supply, March loadings fell to their lowest level in four years. Total Q1 loadings reached 117 MT, down 3 MT from 120 MT in Q4.

Qatar naturally saw the largest decline, with exports down 6.8 MT year on year. This was largely offset by the United States, where exports increased by 7.8 MT year on year. Despite cyclone‑related outages toward the end of the quarter, Australian exports rose by nearly 1 MT year on year, supported by a handful of cargoes loaded from the newly commissioned Barossa LNG project (Darwin).

On the demand side, Egypt, Germany and South Korea recorded the largest year‑on‑year import increases, while France, Kuwait and China saw the steepest declines. India and Bangladesh—who last year sourced 46% and 60% of their LNG imports from Qatar, respectively—both increased quarterly imports year on year. In contrast, Pakistan, which sources almost all of its LNG from Qatar, reduced quarterly imports by 0.35 MT, equivalent to a 20% decline. China continued to scale back imports, with volumes down 0.6 MT, or 3.6%, compared with Q1 last year. Actual consumption may have fallen even more, as reload activity from China reached a new record in March, with nine cargoes re‑exported.

Qatar primarily supplies the Asian market, and lost Qatari volumes cannot easily be replaced by other exporters within the region. Despite this structural constraint, flexible volumes from the United States continued to flow to Europe, with 76% of US LNG volumes heading to Europe in March and 77% over the full Q1 period.

Following record‑high loadings in January, Q1 tonne‑miles exceeded levels seen in previous years. On a monthly basis, however, the decline from January into February and March was substantial, driven by both lower volumes and shorter voyage distances. While quarterly tonne‑miles rose by 3% year on year, this was well below the 10% increase in fleet size, leaving the fleet underutilised on a fundamental basis. Idling reached unprecedented levels, with nearly 40 steam turbine and D/TFDE vessels recorded as idle.

Year on year change in Q1 imports by country

content.content:
The live LNG carrier fleet currently stands at 744 vessels. With an orderbook of 296 ships, this implies an orderbook‑to‑fleet ratio of around 40%. Twenty‑two vessels are officially recorded as being in lay‑up, while a number of additional ships have effectively been idle for an extended period. New ordering activity accelerated further in Q1, with 33 vessels contracted—already exceeding the total number of orders placed during the entirety of 2025 (32 vessels).

Newbuild deliveries slowed in Q1, with only 18 LNG carriers delivered, down from a peak of 23 deliveries in Q4 2025. This leaves 74 vessels scheduled for delivery over the remaining quarters of the year, equivalent to almost 25 vessels per quarter.

Four vessels were sold for scrap in Q1: three from MISC and one from Seapeak. All four were built in 2004–2005, implying demolition ages of approximately 21–22 years. This supports the emerging trend toward younger demolitions, as steam turbine vessels below 140 kcbm face increasingly limited charter prospects.

The LNG carrier fleet still contains around 60 vessels in the 120–140 kcbm size segment. All but two of these units are already over 20 years old, underscoring the continued need for structural fleet renewal. While recent market volatility has temporarily lifted earnings for steam turbine tonnage, fundamental conditions remain oversupplied. As a result, the decision to proceed with costly drydockings for smaller steamers has not become a clear “no‑brainer,” despite the recent spike in charter rates.

The LNG shipping market tends to react strongly to periods of uncertainty, even when underlying fundamentals point in a different direction. A clear parallel can be drawn to 2022, when Europe lost Russian pipeline gas and gas prices spiked. This led to increased US‑to‑Europe flows, which ultimately reduced shipping demand from a tonne‑mile perspective. However, elevated cargo values outweighed this effect, as shipping costs represented only a marginal share of total cargo value.

A similar dynamic is playing out today. Cargo values and charter rates have again spiked, while roughly 20% of global LNG supply disappeared almost overnight, significantly lowering underlying shipping demand. This has occurred in parallel with rising vessel supply: the dedicated Qatari fleet is already substantial, and 128 vessels have been ordered by QatarEnergy (for the North Field Expansion and Golden Pass), of which 42 have already been delivered. While some offset from longer US‑to‑Asia voyages was expected, it would require an unrealistically large share of volumes to move eastbound to compensate for the loss of Qatari tonnes. 

If the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz persists and a restart of production takes time, Asia would need to backfill part of the lost volumes from other regions, as fuel switching and demand destruction cannot absorb all the shortfall. This would imply a higher share of US‑to‑Asia flows, and some tightening of the shipping market as it heads into winter. So, the near‑term impact has been bullish for LNG shipping, and trade flow changes may generate incremental demand, the broader fundamentals have, overall, weakened.

The two damaged trains at Ras Laffan, representing 12.8 MTPA of capacity, are not expected to return for 3–5 years, according to QatarEnergy. From a shipping perspective, this is marginal compared with the broader implications of delays to the North Field Expansion, which is scheduled to add 66 MTPA of liquefaction capacity over the next five years. A delay from 2026 to 2027 has already been announced, and further slippage cannot be ruled out. We have previously forecast an oversupplied LNG shipping market in 2026–2027, and that assessment remains unchanged. While tightening had been expected toward late 2028 and into 2029, further delays to the Qatar expansion—combined with project‑linked vessels delivering on schedule and entering the spot market—would likely push any meaningful tightening into the early 2030s.

All eyes are now on the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the return of flows from non‑damaged Qatari trains, as well as further clarity on the start‑up timeline for the North Field Expansion.

content.content:
In our previous update sent in late February, we wrote:
*We don’t see any significant changes to the bullish factors we listed in our previous report in January. Barring any black swans, it is extremely hard to see how March and Q2 markets will turn significantly lower than expected (similar, or lower levels than last year). In this regard, uncertainty is higher in Q3 and Q4, but the longer leading indicators we use strongly suggest 2026 will average higher than 2025 throughout the whole year. We still expect a cycle downturn in 2027.*

A black swan event has occurred, which changes the market outlook for the worse. Fundamentals are still likely to remain positive through the second quarter, as there is always a lag before higher energy costs start to impact dry bulk markets. However, the risk of a weaker second half of this year than last year has increased substantially. This eventual weakness is likely to last through the first half of 2027 as well. The upward price moves in crude oil and refined products are such that historical correlations clearly suggest dry bulk markets will be negatively impacted. In this report, under the macro-economic section, we always include a chart displaying the year-on-year change of crude oil prices with a 1-year lead on the year-on-year change of the BDI. Since our previous report in late February, this chart has changed quite dramatically. 

What if the Strait of Hormuz opens up fully? The outlook will be relatively brighter. However, damages to energy infrastructure in the Middle East, along with lingering uncertainty, likely mean energy prices will not quickly fall back to pre-war levels. It is also important to remember that the outlook is not all dependent on the Hormuz situation. Other factors, such as coincident economic indices, average cycle durations, falling global credit growth, weakening momentum of industrial metals prices and high iron ore inventories in China, all suggest that fundamentals are close to peaking.  

Coal demand will likely increase going forward, though quite surprisingly, there is not much sign of it just yet. The futures curves of Newcastle and Rotterdam benchmark contracts actually increased in contango since the outbreak of the war, suggesting **less** urgency to buy, not more. Through March, seaborne volumes were down slightly on the same period last year, primarily due to relatively high inventories in China and India. Regardless of eventually improving coal demand, we think that over the next year, the problems are that demand for other commodities looks likely to contract, and that seaborne supply of coal is not sufficient to meet a significant increase in demand. The Indonesian government seems intent on using more coal domestically to lower energy costs. Russian supply will not increase as long as the war in Ukraine continues, and Australia does not seem to have  much extra capacity. 

We revise our earnings estimates for this year down for all segments, and make a slight downward adjustment to our estimates for next year.

Iron ore inventory drawing remains a downside risk, as seaborne prices remains higher than portside prices. 
**Top right chart:** Shipment volumes were 6.3% higher than last year through week 14. Atlantic volumes are growing at a higher rate than Pacific volumes (covered in our shipment volume update sent earlier this week). 
**Bottom left chart:** The South Atlantic tightness indicator has dropped significantly over the last week, and is now firmly in toppish territory. 
**Bottom right chart:** VLOC congestion in Brazil has increased significantly in the last few weeks. The current reading has, over the last years, usually resulted in significant market upside. The FSRU market is a long-term market which usually has its eyes on the horizon – requiring long lead times for both projects to develop and assets to be constructed. One may therefore draw the conclusion that long-term fundamentals for LNG and downstream infrastructure remain intact, but it would be **naïve to not recognize the ongoing change** in fundamentals. With the risk of becoming too shortsighted in the face of availability bias it seems clear that the market is pricing in higher cost of energy in general – but for LNG the entire curve towards 2030 has moved up substantially suggesting a far shorter market than previously priced. We only need to rewind towards the end of 2025 to reminisce over a time where *plat do jour* was the impending supply glut that would force shut-ins and LNG into the low single-digits. However, this was considered to be a boon for unlocking LNG demand in both new and developing markets. Now – we have to rethink.

Higher energy costs will translate into lower growth in the short-/medium term – which alone suggests that energy demand may turn out to be subdued. That doesn’t necessarily mean that LNG or natural gas becomes completely uneconomical (although the steep cost inflation on gas turbines has not aided the relative competitiveness of gas-fired power generation). But, we do see it as plausible that the near-term will face a pause in decision-making processes for downstream infrastructure (be it M&A, tenders, security of supply or other) as project developers and governmental agencies go back to their drawing boards/spreadsheets.

That said, turning the script upside down; having access to regas capacity remains a critical element if/when other source of energy becomes unavailable. The only challenge we face is that LNG is the energy source with the largest disappearance at present. So perhaps the *combo order* of FOB supply, a few LNGCs for flexibility and an FSRU should be the set menu for up and coming (and existing for that matter) consumers of LNG?

Regional activity appears to be high across LatAm, Africa and Far East with also Europe running at high revs. A somewhat refreshing perspective is the number of projects requesting to own/operate (usually one) FSRU themselves. The reasoning being high charter rates and desire to have full control of the asset – which we try to balance out against experience of operation and the inherent additional risks absorbed through direct ownership. Even so, we expect several projects to end up owning the FSRU directly with support from 3rd party to operate.  

While the FSRU charter rate environment has not shown any signs of buckling, there have been fewer deals to benchmark off in Q1. What we are seeing is generally FSRUs developed against firm-ish projects (typically with lots of subjects and flexibility) that does not lead to firm FSRU conversion/orders, but a handful of speculative approaches by some. What is interesting is that *a few market participants are starting to ask questions about “when” we’ll see oversupply – **not “if”***.  While the demand side may be the biggest unknown under current circumstances, we do ***not*** see that the combination of assets coming off charter in 2028-2030 coupled with a handful of speculative FSRUs may be sufficient to tip the balance into the favor of charterers just yet.
Key market developments during the quarter

JANUARY
Adverse weather conditions disrupt operations at both the **Ravenna** and **Brunsbüttel** terminals, leaving them without FSRUs for several days. At the same time, construction of the breakwater in Ravenna experiences delays, *reinforcing the case for weather-vaning solutions in more challenging metocean environments*—where feasible.

**Jordan** issues a tender for an FSRU (135,000–160,000 cbm, minimum 480 MMSCFD) covering the period from Q2 2026 to Q4 2026, with an extension option to the end of Q1 2027. This points to delays on the onshore side, and based on market intelligence, further postponements appear likely. At the same time, vessel availability for this window is крайне limited, with **few—if any—suitable units expected to be open**.

Deutsche ReGas (**DRG**) files a lawsuit against Deutsche Energy Terminal (DET), challenging the EUR 4.96 billion grant awarded to DET at the end of 2024, which effectively covers all costs (charter, fuel, and terminal) until the FSRUs roll off charter. This development precedes DRG’s termination of the **ENERGOS POWER**. Based on how the process has unfolded since 2022, Germany’s *implementation of FSRUs appears fundamentally flawed*. While Brunsbüttel and Wilhelmshaven 1 progress on schedule, Wilhelmshaven 2 and Stade emerge as highly problematic projects, representing significant inefficiencies and, at this stage, a questionable use of public funds—partly subsidized by the Egyptian government, which is unlikely to have been the original intention.

**KN Energies** offers additional regasification capacity at Klaipėda for the period **2033–2044**, following limited interest in the September 2023 market test. The proposed fixed tariff is approximately EUR 2.0–2.2/MWh (USD 0.68–0.75/MMBtu). In parallel, the company is exploring an expansion of capacity from the current 240 MMSCFD to 360 MMSCFD.

**Snam** seeks to **extend operations at Piombino** beyond June 2026, as local stakeholders gradually shift their position. The alternative—relocating the vessel offshore to Vado Ligure—would likely reduce overall availability and entail significant additional costs, including the installation of a turret mooring system and modifications to the **ITALIS LNG**.

**Ecopetrol** approves the development of an FSRU at **La Guajira**, effectively the same location as Ballena. This aligns with existing infrastructure, where **HEVI** has secured an agreement with **TGI**, the owner and operator of the critical pipeline connecting Ballena with Barrancabermeja. Internal tensions between TGI and Ecopetrol have been a key factor behind delays in Ecopetrol’s 2025 FSRU tender. The indicated capacity of **250 MMSCFD** suggests a likely deployment of one of Höegh’s Moss-type vessels, configured with either 3 × 100 or 3 × 125 MMSCFD regasification units.

FEBRUARY

**Morocco** postpones its FSRU tender, citing *“new parameters and assumptions.”* These reportedly relate to uncertainty over who will bear the cost of the FSRU and associated infrastructure, as neither the Moroccan equivalent of the Ministry of Finance nor the Ministry of Energy appears willing to take full responsibility. This development serves as a warning signal for what had been one of the most anticipated projects for 2026. The **outlook now remains uncertain**, and FSRU providers are likely to reconsider their appetite for participation in a renewed tender process.

**Ecopetrol** teams up with **Frontera** to develop an FSRU project at Puerto Bahía, near Cartagena. The planned unit is reportedly sized at **126 MMSCFD**, targeting start-up by Q3 2026. Given these specifications and timeline, the pool of suitable candidates is extremely limited, with only one of **Kinetics’ units** likely fitting the requirement—most plausibly either **TÜRKIYE** or **OCEANIA**, both currently undergoing conversion at Seatrium.

**Excelerate** announces in its Q4 2025 results that **EXCELERATE ACADIA** is scheduled to commence operations at Khor Al-Zubair, Iraq, in **Q3 2026**. While demand for both the FSRU and gas supply is not in question, the project’s execution remains uncertain given ongoing geopolitical instability. The vessel is currently set to be deployed to Pakistan, temporarily covering for **EXQUISITE**, which is due for dry docking. Notably, Excelerate remains *one of the few FSRU operators still requiring dry docking during contract periods*, as most modern FSRUs are designed to operate up to 20 years without such interruptions.

**Excelerate** indicates that it expects to secure a higher charter rate for **EXPRESS** compared to its current contract with ADNOC. While this may hold true for shorter-term fixtures, *longer-term charter rates are likely to trend lower on a like-for-like basis*, given the vessel’s specifications relative to newer, larger, and more efficient FSRUs.

**Energos** actively markets up to three available FSRUs: **ENERGOS IGLOO**, **ENERGOS FREEZE**, and **NUSANTARA REGAS SATU**. While IGLOO stands out as a solid and competitive unit with strong operational performance, we have limited expectations regarding the long-term competitiveness of FREEZE and NRS.

Both Excelerate and Energos continue to explore conversion opportunities. Excelerate has acquired **EXCELERATE SHENANDOAH** with conversion in mind, while Energos is rumored to be progressing with a **160,000 cbm ST** vessel earmarked for conversion.

**Hanseatic Energy Hub** (HEH) indicates in early February that its onshore terminal is now expected to be operational in **2029**, representing a delay from the original timeline of 2027—albeit one that had largely been anticipated. This extension allows the long-awaited FSRU from DET to remain in operation for a longer period. The unit is currently scheduled to start up in **Q2 2026**, although this timeline remains uncertain, as **ENERGOS FORCE** is still located in **Aqaba, Jordan** at the time of writing.

MARCH

The long-awaited **Brazil power auction** yields a strong outcome for gas-fired projects, totaling 15.2 GW. As a consequence, it implies an estimated demand for *three FSRUs* (Ceará/Pecém for ENEVA and Suape + TGS for other successful bidders). It remains unclear who will supply ENEVA with the FSRU, but Energos is tipped for the Suape project, while TGS will reportedly be handled by **AMBAR** following the NFE restructuring.

**Delta Offshore Energy** re-emerges with the same plan under a new name, branding its Vietnamese LNG terminal in Bac Lieu the **“Trump LNG Terminal”.** While the project has been delayed for more than five years, it demonstrates solid credentials on the onshore side. The *main challenge lies offshore*, where metocean conditions are less than ideal for a floating solution. However, Vietnam is in urgent need of additional gas-fired power generation, suggesting that DOE’s project may be regaining momentum.

**PGN** plans to invest **USD 220 million in 2026** for the development of gas infrastructure in Indonesia. Activity in the **Indonesian gas market** can be characterized as *highly dynamic*, with several local players acquiring LNGCs in the secondhand market at a rapid pace, targeting participation in tenders from PGN, PLN, and others.

**Turkey’s** energy minister, Alparslan Bayraktar, reiterates the country’s commitment to developing **two new FSRU terminals**. One is reportedly planned between **Gazipaşa and Anamur**, and the other near **Dörtyol** (where BOTAS already operates the **ERTUGRUL GAZI**). It remains unclear how and by whom these FSRUs will be provided, though the responsibility will likely be assigned to local entities.

**Poland’s second FSRU** project moves higher on the agenda as Gaz-System announces in mid-March that it is targeting a final investment decision (**FID**) no later than the **end of July 2026**. Based on the *outlined requirements*, it appears likely that this will involve a *newbuild unit form South Korea*.

**Gas Malaysia** receives approval from the national energy commission to develop an LNG terminal of up to **6 mtpa on the west coast of Peninsular Malaysia**. The indicated cost is USD 770 million, with no confirmed commercial operation date. This development adds to the pipeline of FSRU projects in Malaysia, where a requirement for two to three FSRUs in the medium term is anticipated.
Quarterly corporate highlights: Noteholders Formally Empowered

New Fortress Energy provided the **long-anticipated restructuring plan** in late-March and as largely anticipated the company will be split into two entities; **BrazilCo** and **New NFE**. Most restructurings tend to have a *“good bank/bad bank”* situation, but in the case of NFE it is *not as clear cut in our view*. While the documents (more specifically Exhibit 10.1 and 99.2 of NFEs 8-K issued 17th March 2026) outlines a vast amount of very interesting information; from historical events to operational aspects and incentives to management staying on, there are a few interesting elements from an industrial/FSRU perspective.

BrazilCo (which effectively is owned by its former creditors including Capital Group, Blackrock and mainly US-based funds) includes Barcarena assets, TGS and some legacy Suape opportunities. TGS will eventually get an FSRU, but through Ambar who according to Brazilian press have taken the terminal on long-term lease. Ambar secured a substantial amount of capacity in the recent power auction and will be interesting to follow.

New NFE (of which largely the same creditors in BrazilCo will own around 65% of the new equity) includes Puerto Rico, La Paz (Mexico) and Puerto Sandino (Nicaragua) with an additional 10 x TM2500s generating around ~300MW (in single cycle). PR and La Paz are spoken for in terms of regas, but **Nicaragua** will require an FSRU in the near-term if the **Oct-26** target is to be reached. We struggle to see this timeline being achieved based on current available assets in the market. However, *considering the current LNG market dynamics the most valuable part of New NFE today may ultimately be its gas supply which includes a 2.5mtpa/20yr contract with Venture Global commencing in the period 2027-2029*.

The restructuring process is expected to be completed in mid-26, but we would expect some delays given dates are already being pushed out in time. In our view, it seems likely that there will be more transactions going forward, mainly driven by the new majority holders of both New NFE and BrazilCo being very large funds (who originally owned credit) wanting to recover as much as possible of their capital sooner rather than later. *When the restructuring lawyers are done, the M&A bankers come knocking.*

Elsewhere there has been limited corporate action apart from an amuse-bouche for the special-interest section; **Snam** has retained 100% control over **OLT** after acquiring **Golar LNGs** 2.7% stake for a US$ 3.1m. Snam now own three FSRUs including **ITALIS LNG**, **BW SINGAPORE** and **FSRU TOSCANA** and are the largest Owner as end-user of FSRUs.
Quarterly focus: Is the world investing sufficiently in LNG downstream?

The common market perception has long been that *"global regasification capacity has never been a bottleneck."* The data tells a more nuanced — and increasingly concerning — story.

Three facts worth noting:
The **regas-to-liquefaction capacity ratio** been declining for a decade, falling from **2.7 in 2015** to **2.1 in 2020** before inching higher to 2.4 in 2025. This compression has been driven by a surge in US liquefaction capacity coming onstream alongside limited investment in regasification outside of China.

**Global LNG trade** is simultaneously becoming "**shorter dated**." Long-term offtake contracts are giving way to spot and short-term trading, with LNG increasingly functioning as a swing factor in national energy mixes. This *structural shift* puts additional pressure on **flexible, available regasification capacity**.

With the **base case** being (subject to change considering the ongoing conflict in the Middle East) that **steep growth in liquefaction is locked in through 2031–2032**, with projects already under construction or in commissioning across multiple continents we see the continued compression in liq-to-regas ratio.

Three observations that follow:
By **2035**, the regas-to-liquefaction ratio is on track to reach its **lowest level in recorded history** — approximately 1.75 — eliminating much of the system redundancy that has historically provided a buffer. This excludes proposed/speculative projects on both sides of the equation.

Meanwhile, **investment in regasification outside China** and a handful of other markets **remains minimal**. China, interestingly, may itself be building toward one of the largest regas overcapacities globally, positioning it as a potential LNG re-exporter on back of lower industrial demand and increased access to Russian gas.

*Capital continues to flow into LNG upstream development and shipping* — the world is long ships through at least 2028 – additional non-Middle East supply may get another wind. Yet **downstream investment**, particularly import terminals and regasification, **appears to be a relative blind spot**.

The geopolitical wildcard:
The ongoing conflict in the Middle East introduces significant uncertainty over the future trajectory of global liquefaction. Shipping route disruptions, energy security responses, and shifting geopolitical alignments all have the potential to alter both the pace and geography of new LNG supply additions — and by extension, the future demand for regasification capacity. In a world where energy supply chains are increasingly fragile, the asymmetry between upstream investment and downstream infrastructure deserves serious scrutiny.

*(Avid readers of Fearnley LNG LinkedIn posts may have read this point of view already from our weekly post on 31st March 2026.)*

Q1 clocked in as the *third consecutive quarter* with record-breaking volumes imported through FSRUs. Although a nice all-time high it also shows that *interruptions to FSRUs in March on back of Middle East were limited*. It will be very interesting to see how this changes in Q2 for countries like Bangladesh and Pakistan. A total of **19.4mt / 304 cargoes** (up 37% Y-o-Y from 14.1mt / 232 cargoes in Q1/25 and 2.6% Q-o-Q from 18.9mt / 300 cargoes in Q4/25). Activity across the regions is surprisingly steady except for **Mediterranean** which experienced a continued steep jump to **3.5mt (from 2.3mt in Q4/25)**, solely driven by **Turkey** which really sprung into life with Saros and Dortyol each taking 1.56 and 1.08mt each while Etki was somewhat lower at 0.84mt. Across the *three terminals this accounts for 49 cargoes which is on average a cargo every 5.5 day*. Turkey has a very seasonal demand profile and with the targeted two additional FSRUs we would expect this seasonality to be even more pronounced in the years to come. Another FSRU hotspot is Egypt which saw volumes drop slightly due to **ENERGOS ESKIMO** performing a long-overdue drydock in Jan. Nevertheless, Egypt continues to run at around 3mt per quarter and it will be interesting to see how that changes in April.

There were no new additions to the FSRU fleet in terms of new operational terminals during the quarter, but we count a total of **42 FSRUs receiving cargoes during the quarter**. The busiest terminals in Q1/26 were Dortyol (Turkey) **ERTUGRUL GAZI** with 22 cargoes, followed by Saros (Turkey) **SAROS** and Ain Sokhna Sumed (Egypt) **HOEGH GALLEON** with 16 cargoes each. We continue to monitor cargo sizes and note that the *average cargo size in Q1/26 was just shy of 137,000cbm* with Americas seeing cargoes of around 127,000cbm (which suggest partial cargoes) and Europe receiving cargoes of around 142,000cbm. What is interesting to note is that cargo sizes generally are lower than cargo capacities which suggests that the many discussions around storage/demurrage are lost in the averaging out when reviewing on a regional basis.

For the quarter we only counted *a handful of FSRUs not receiving any cargoes*; **EXPRESS** (Dubai), **EXPEDIENT** (Escobar, Argentina), **KARMOL ASIA** (Sepetiba, Brazil) and **BW BATANGAS** (Batangas, Philippines). Additionally, no cargoes were seen at **TGS** (Brazil), but driven by the lack of FSRU which is expected to change with the recent announcement of AMBAR reportedly taking capacity at the terminal from NFE Brazil following the Mar-26 power auctions. 

On a global scale **FSRUs delivered 16.4% of all LNG volumes imported in Q1/26** – keeping steady over the last couple of quarters. It is also worth nothing that **global LNG imports reached a new record high** in Q1/26 at **117.9mt**. Although we do not foresee the percentage of volumes on FSRUs to change materially in 2026 (or 2027 for that matter) *there is not much excess capacity in the FSRU system globally when accounting for seasonality and maintenance schedules*. It also further underpins our view on underinvestment in regasification capacity as FSRUs should be able to trend towards 20% of global LNG imports.

content.content:
*Asia & Middle East*

**New Zealand** remains in progress with limited news flow since the deadline in late-25. Seems politics, seasonality, feasibility and cost has led to another round of internal deliberations amongst the Kiwis. However, three players have reportedly been shortlisted.

**Malaysia** and **Indonesia** remains relatively active with **PLN** issuing their **Bali FSRU** requirement to no less than 30+ pre-qualified players (we didn’t know there were 30 qualified FSRU players globally…) at a yet to be agreed location. There are also other projects in the motion, but some of the more well-progressed mining-linked projects appear to have hit a snag. We would likely focus more on the projects in Malaysia in the near-term.

*Europe & Mediterranean*

**Poland** is out with a tender for its 2nd FSRU to be located at the same site as the first one which is currently under construction and to be delivered by MOL. Winterization, combined loop, light ice reinforcement and strict age requirements strongly suggest this will be a newbuild – but it is contingent on a successful Open Season which may potentially slow the project down.

**Greece** appears to be moving a bit faster again with a few projects gaining momentum (or at least able to revamp) on the back of US-Greece link and the fact that Greece offers (like Poland) a very interesting access to old Gazprom consumers who are not left high and dry.

*Americas & Caribbean*

The playbook for **Colombia** is not entirely scripted yet it seems and we do see activity on a few projects that continue to push forward despite two announced FSRUs and one FSU.

**Brazil** will see demand for FSRUs on back of the power auction, but these are largely accounted for as players had lined up ahead of the auction.

*Africa & Other*

Activity in **Sierra Leone** may pick up with **World Bank** close to dotting the I’s and crossing the t’s on a local power plant development. SL is notoriously tricky both from a demand and operational stability perspective, but with WB backing it may see some traction.

*We encourage clients with deeper interest in ongoing project developments, tender activity and business development to contact Fearnleys directly; the above is merely to give our readers something to think about.*

**ENERGOS ESKIMO** departed Ain Sokhna on 13th Jan 2026 for drydock in Turkey. The unit was off station for 61 days, but spent only ~28 days in the yard in Turkey.

**CAPE ANN** left Le Havre at the end of 2025, but has been idling in the Mediterranean in anticipation for new business. She recently did a cargo from Fos to Rotterdam and currently signalling to Bonny so appear to be surfing in the spot market for the time being.

**EXPEDIENT** left the terminal in Escobar, Argentina on 02nd April and has yet to return – sitting idle outside Buenos Aires. However, with recent news of high demand we expect her to return to her seasonal duties in Argentina shortly.

**EXPLORER** did a short stint away from DUSUPs berth in Dubai, but now back after completing drydock and seemingly a short voyage out early March which could have been a precautionary measure.

**EXPRESS** also on some “internal business” following the swap to support **EXPLORER** drydock and a cargo at Das Island before returning to Ruwais.

**ETYFA PROMETHEAS** remains idle in Malacca and for orders although the visibility on her next project remains opaque at best.

**EXCELERATE ACADIA** remains alongside in the yard in Ulsan, but should be heading either to Pakistan (short-term) or Iraq. Admittedly, it feels unlikely to see her in Khor Al-Zubair, Iraq in 2026 and maybe Excelerate repositions **EXPRESS** once she comes off charter in Sep-26.
Asset values: Newbuildings and conversion candidates

During the quarter, we’ve seen **movement from testing waters to firming up plans on the conversion front**. There are still a number of semi-speculative positions doing engineering to shave off 2-3 months, but we currently count **five LNGCs firmly contracted for conversion** – of which *three are linked to projects* and *two seemingly speculative*. This adds to two MOL newbuilds already on order – leaving the full **orderbook at 7 units**. The project pipeline and conversion projects *with subjects attached* (subjects ranging from winning auctions to obtaining permits to concluding associated transactions) remains relatively long with a **realistic potential for 3-4 additional firm conversions emerging through the year**. Overall, the *real speculative plays are not coming through yet* – which gives us some confidence in an impending oversupply in 2030 seems less likely.

For the first time in several quarters we’ve seen a flattening out on asset values with a **small uptick on 145k+ STs to high-20s compared to mid-20s in Q4/25** on prompt basis. However, the **TFDE/DFDEs** in the 155k-160k range **appear to be under slight pressure** with 2010-2015 built tonnage anywhere from **mid-70s to 120s** depending on size, age and specifications. Admittedly, the *majority of projects have limited regard for age as focus is on storage capacity*. We see **substantial pricing differentials** on a 137k ST (very limited interest for FSRU conversions) to a 153k ST (the apex of cost/benefit) and even a 160k STs (do they even exist) as the **value of storage directly plays into project economics**. Moreover, the desire from Sellers, who are in growing numbers, to *entertain deferred/forward delivery is limited* and hence **prompt transactions appears more tangible at this point** – leaving Buyers with any cost of layup until conversion. 

Following our engagement with the main EPC contractors/conversion yards, we note **conversion timelines and costs remain largely unchanged**. Timelines are in the range of **23-28 months (from FID to ex-yard redelivery on LSTK basis)** with an additional 2-3 months for mobilization, installation and commissioning leaving the **“end-to-end” timeline at 25-31 months**. Capex is still in the range of **US$ 110-140m (DFDE/TFDE)** and **US$ 140-180m (ST)** excluding contingencies, mobilization and commissioning) for 500/750 SW-Glycol Open Loop. Adding project-specific equipment (usually MSO or Reliq for projects with intermittent send-out or flexible dispatch situations) pushes the costs higher.

The **FSRU newbuild market** remains relatively subdued on the back of **very high ordering activity of LNGCs in Q1 (our tally is at 32)** – and while the newbuild yards do provide indications their interest for LNGCs over slightly more bespoke assets appears clear. However, we would not be surprised to see a newbuild against Poland #2 FSRU and a few other situations where a newbuild emerges as the preferred solution. Our **current quote** for a “standard” newbuild (174,000, 3 x 250 SW-Glycol Open Loop) is in the range of **US$ 335m** – which allows us to reiterate that conversions still give more bang for the BTU.

While discussions between Iran and the U.S. may or may not be ongoing, disruptions to tanker flows are real, and may continue for prolonged periods depending on the trajectory of the conflict. For now, huge oil price swings and acute vessel shortages in some areas produce very high rates. Among the many potential scenarios that can be painted here, three main ones stand out: 

- A swift ceasefire and resolution. This may cause some pent-up demand, with flows returning from the MEG at the same time as more vessels have ballasted to the West, causing logistical issues and firming rates. 
- A multi-month Hormuz disruption causing acute oil shortages, necessitating further SPR releases etc. That may give a lasting oversupply of vessels in all areas, and the harm caused to oil production may give a slower ramp-up if/when a resolution is finally reached. Similarly, SPR releases may smoothen the upside potential in a re-opening phase. The flip side would be high enough oil prices to boost oil production growth in 2027 and 2028. 
- Tanker wars 2.0.... A long-lasting conflict and disruption to seaborne oil (and other commodity) flow, which may have dire consequences for the global economy and tanker market.

Average month to date crude oil and condensate loadings have declined by 8.6 mbpd vs. the February average, while products have declined by 2.2 mbpd. The latest weekly data point to another 4 mbpd downside for crude. Various sources estimate that MEG production shut-ins have reached 10-12 mbpd, including condensates and liquids. As long as the Hormuz remains closed, this gap may persist, and even grow. 

Even if and when there is a reopening, it will take some time for production to fully recover - hence the oil and financial market reaction may be too complacent. Nergy agencies such as the IEA in its last monthly report have assumed a quick ramp-up after March, but this looks increasingly less likely. For instance, KPC's CEO said that it would take 3-4 months for Kuwait to restore full pre-war production. In Iraq and other countries the situation is likely not any better. Hence, even if the war should stop tomorrow, full volumes might not be back until the summer.

Total tanker tonne-mile demand over the last two weeks has on average been 19% lower than at the beginning of this year. The biggest downside is unsurprisingly seen for VLCCs, where demand is down 32%, whereas Suez, Afra and MRs have held up relatively better. There are also regional differences, where Atlantic demand has held up significantly better than East of Suez. 

Eventually, increased West-East shipments can make up for some of the shortfall, as can ships stuck inside the Hormuz and idle ships elsewhere. However, considering the size of the drop in volume it is unlikely that all can be offset.

The VLCCs have been hit the hardest from supply disruptions, considering their weight in the MEG market which has effectively been sidelined. Yanbu diversions is only a partial substitute, as is laden tonnage sitting inside the Hormuz. The latter is, however, oil that will be sought after if and when the Strait reopens. 

For Suez- and Aframax additional volumes in the Atlantic from SPR releases, some longer sailing distances and a very wide WTI-Brent spread has lent support - especially until more ballasting VLCCs come into play from the East - increasingly from next week. 

The LRs are the most exposed among the product tanker segments, with an outsized portion of normal demand being derived from the MEG. More tonnage is now seen ballasting west and/or dirtying up, alleviating some potential pressure. 

MRs have been less directly exposed, although here too some lower refinery runs in the East has taken its toll. In the West, however, volumes run as before, and given outsized product price move, and acute shortages in some areas, we see more long-haul demand for these vessels, resulting in very strong rates.

Outsized oil price moves have contributed to strong rates. A very wide WTI-Brent spread has significantly boosted USG-UKC returns and due to tight positioning in the prompt end, Suezmax lumpsum USG-East is not far from VLs. The USG-East rate is theoretically well supported at very high levels due to a wide WTI-Murban spread. SPR releases and sanction waivers have, however, alleviated some of the pressure on Asian buyers to lock in these high freight rates, but if outages persist that pressure to buy may increase. 

Very high oil products prices have also driven product tanker rates. MRs have benefited the most, especially in the USG where refined product supply is plentiful and arbitrages are open just about everywhere.

content.content:
There are some mitigating factors. Although it may take several months to fully restore oil production after abrupt shut-ins, onshore storage has built up, which can bridge some of the gap to pre-war export levels - for a period. More importantly, fleet dispersion and logistical re-scheduling may cause inefficient shipping, which can help boost rates during a reopening phase. 

On fleet dispersion, 6% of the tanker fleet is now 'stuck' within the MEG, and as much as 9% of the VLCC fleet. Similarly, due to slower than perhaps anticipated re-routing of flows through Yanbu (now about 4 mbpd) and Fujairah (hardly changed vs. before the war), amid what looks like constrained load capacity, there are plenty of idle vessel sitting off ports. 

Increased Atlantic-East flow may also absorb some of the demand shortfall. In recent months Atlantic-East flow has been about 2.5 mbpd lower than at the peak last year. Some upside can possibly be added from Venezuela and SPR releases, but at the same time MEG-Atlantic crude flow has been more than 1.5 mbpd lately, some of which may now come to a halt. Realistically, there may thus be up to about 2 mbpd upside for Atlantic-East flow, which in tonne-mile terms can offset nearly 4 mbpd of lost MEG volumes due to much longer sailing distances.

content.title: Share of the fleet within the Strait of Hormuz

content.content: Meanwhile, there is 1.5% added to the fleet per quarter

In the midst of all the demand uncertainty and fleet reshuffling, more vessels are added to the global fleet. After three very low delivery years, about 1.5% will be added to the fleet every quarter this year. There has been some phase-out lately, mostly shadow tankers, but even this may come to a halt now that waivers have been given to discharge Russian and Iranian crude, even from sanctioned tankers. Given headlines about additional ('creative') measures to address oil pricing from the U.S. administration, further waivers may not be ruled out, and hence some additional employment opportunities can be suspected for shadow tankers near-term. Hence, very little scrapping is expected, and net fleet growth this year may come very close to the 6% scheduled to be delivered.

The most significant medium to longer-term implication of the Iran conflict may be a shift in the perception of energy security. Countries whose vulnerabilities have been exposed, particularly in Asia, may need to expand strategic reserves. This creates a near-term demand impulse that could partially offset any war-related demand destruction. 

A more durable demand implication could come from supply diversification away from the MEG and sanctioned barrels. This could again boost average sailing distances.

Through the conflict, OPEC spare capacity may have taken a hit. The group's effective spare capacity, already thinner than headline figures may suggest, may now be even more constrained. Hasty conflict-related shut-ins are unlikely to reverse quickly and could have some implications for upside potential longer term too. That may remove a ceiling that has historically kept oil prices in check.

Firmer than previously expected oil prices, underpinned by tighter spare capacity and resilient demand, could drive upstream investment. In the current environment, that investment is likely to skew toward short-cycle production: US tight oil, Brazilian pre-salt tiebacks and similar projects. Resurgent Atlantic Basin production could therefore provide demand tailwinds again, likely into 2028 and onwards — a more constructive outlook than appeared plausible just months ago. 

This may come at the same time as a more meaningful portion of the compliant fleet comes up toward historical average phase-out ages - especially for the bigger vessels. If it does, it could very well be the start of a new tanker up-cycle.

In this case, the degree and duration of any eventual market strength will depend on many uncertain factors, like how quickly energy prices rise, and to what degree industrial commodity prices are able to follow the rise in energy prices. Also, how much coal is available at short notice to replace the loss of oil and gas? 
Following previous oil price shocks in 1973/74 and in 1979/80, dry bulk markets eventually dropped sharply, with a lag of 6 to 9 months. 
If the Strait of Hormuz opens quickly, the economic damage will hopefully be limited.

Quite the start to the year! Demand is stronger than the same time last year, providing the underlying conditions, On top of that, market strength has been driven by the supply side and geopolitics. 

Going forward, a return after oil production outages, some growth elsewhere, and a potential shift in Venezuela flows may give continued strong demand for tankers. With West-East arbs closed, demand is strongest for Suez- and Aframaxes, but there could eventually be some more switch toward the biggest vessels. Product tankers can benefit from open long-haul arbitrages and continued incentives to switch to dirty for LRs. 

Oil price diffs could be some cause for concern, although are unlikely to affect the tanker market in the very near term.

TC rates are reported at daily new highs, supported by pick-a-number-spot rates and a well bid FFA curve. The strength from VLCCs has spread to Suezmaxes where cargo splits are in several areas now more economical - as are TCs. 

The most recent TC deals point to large implied upside potential for asset values too. That said, a 1-year VLCC TC rate which is now five standard deviations from the mean is rare, to say the least. Something to lock in..? 

With demand tailwinds set to last and fleet consolidation in full force, it may take longer than we had initially thought before fleet growth may meaningfully eat into the market balance. Hence rates are likely to significantly outperform our bull case in the coming few months, which also means quite some outperformance also for the full year average.

Crude tanker volumes have rebounded slightly in February vs. March, while product flow is a bit lower. Crude tanker volume gains have been led by the MEG and CPC, and there may be slightly more to come with the latter still ramping up after outages, and some suggestion that the OPEC+ may continue to ease production cuts from April (although the real m/m change may be rather small). There are also some signs of Saudi Arabia exporting mo

From the Americas exports have slid recently, most of which is seasonal. Here too, then, there may be some upside in coming months. This can also in part be driven by a ramp-up of Venezuelan exports as flows normalise and find new buyers. 

Most of these volume gains near-term may benefit Suez- and Aframaxes still, unless the West-East arbitrage reopens.

Tonne-miles are also up, overall nearly 5% vs. the same period last year, although for VLCCs and product tankers the development is not so strong due to less long-haul flows. Suez- and Aframax tonne-miles have strengthened the most, to a large extent driven by high Americas exports, a lot of which has remained in the Atlantic basin due to a closed arbitrage to the East.

For the remainder of the year, tonne-mile demand may strengthen due to increased volumes, and partly geopolitics. Added volumes per energy agency expectations could give around 1% tonne-mile growth, with OPEC+ unwind potentially adding up to another percentage point gradually. 

Beyond that, Venezuela stand-alone may add 1-2 percentage points if a meaningful portion of volumes goes East. This could benefit VLCCs the most, whereas it may slightly negatively impact Suez/Afra demand if any corresponding downside to Russia-India volumes (on compliant tankers) shifts to China (on shadow/sanctioned tankers). That said, with Trump's latest tariff setback, could there be a rebound in Indian buying of Russian oil..?

Global refinery runs are expected to rise by 0.8 mbpd this year, mostly in the Middle East and Asia. That may contribute to product tanker tonne-mile growth of 2-3%, depending on how much goes long-haul. Currently, relative pricing suggests some boost.

content.content:
...And not really the way we thought it would be going into this year. While fleet growth is set to accelerate, it has been all about consolidation and delays so far. Sinokor's buying spree and traders' taking in TC ships has significantly tightened vessel availability, especially the number of owners with ships in fixing position in the open market, and as Sinokor (and possibly others) hold back tonnage. Sinokor now controls about 20% of the compliant VLCC fleet, more if you strip out NOCs and others which are to an extent committed to program barrels. 

How many ships will continue to be held back, and for how long has a huge impact on the rate trajectory the next few months. 

Congestion and weather has also had a large impact on the market over the last few months, the former mostly for VLCCs in the Far East, and the latter mostly for Suez/Afra in the Atlantic basin.

content.content:
Eventually, fleet growth should start to ease the tight market balance, with 6% gross fleet growth scheduled for this year and more the next two years. With a plethora of newbuild orders in recent months, the orderbook to fleet is now back to the historical average at 20%, with more to come. Newbuild prices are significantly lower than 2nd hand, which likely means orders are going to keep trickling in, which in turn should eventually lift newbuild prices too. 

There is, however, also plenty of phase-out potential, although more likely in the slightly longer term as scrapping (especially of compliant tonnage) will be miniscule near-term at these rate levels.

In the biggest tanker segments, what would normally be phase-out candidates by now is already semi-phased out by migration to the shadows. Hence, the gross will be very close to the net fleet growth figure this and possibly next year. For the smaller segments, meanwhile, there is a more balanced picture between deliveries and real phase-out potential, which may soften the neet fleet growth outlook somewhat.
Oil may point to some downside risks

Supported by a softer Dollar, strong demand, production outages and geopolitics, oil prices have strengthened YTD. The forward curve remains backwardated too - in contrast with energy agency forecasts which imply significant stock builds. 

These pricing conditions mirror the last few instances where the OPEC+ has unwound production cuts, and it is now widely expected that this unwind may resume from April again into the normally stronger demand season. 

This may be supported by relatively flat development for OECD inventories over the last year. These arguably hold more sway over pricing than does Asian inventories, which have built substantially more - especially China's and offshore storage of sanctioned barrels. If oil prices remain high(er) these inventories can also be drawn..

A challenge the OPEC+ may face is that differentials and crack spreads tell a slightly different story about oil market strength. There are reports of West African crude being offered at sizeable discounts to Brent, still without being lifted. Similarly, a largely closed West-East arb. suggests plentiful supply for Asian buyers. Another production hike from the OPEC+ and more market share into Asia may exacerbate this 'problem' which may eventually lead to bigger OECD inventory builds. High freight does not help in this equation either, so something may at some point have to give - oil prices, refinery margins, pump prices and/or freight. 

That said, refinery margins are still (at least in the West) fairly close to the historical average, which should be supportive of decent run growth this year, benefiting product tanker demand. A slightly weaker price picture in the East is now supportive for more West-East gasoil and jet fuel movement, whereas another change in sailing patterns due to Russia/Venezuela dynamics support longer-haul demand, partly for gasoil from Russia to Brazil, and partly for global Naphtha flows.

In our previous update sent in January, we wrote:

*We still see the same fundamental strength that led us to give the view that this year should be even stronger than in 2024. We think a higher average than 2022 (BDI 1933) is also likely, with the difference this year being higher average earnings for Capes/Newcs but lower for Kamsarmaxes down to Handysizes.*

*Factors on why we are bullish on 2026 market prospects:
-	Global manufacturing is in expansion. This supports all commodity groups. 
-	Industrial Metals prices have surged to the highest level since early 2022. These prices has correlated tightly with 1-year TC rates and second-hand values in the last 10 years. 
-	Coal prices bottomed in April last year and have risen slowly since then. The coal futures curve structure is the most backwardated since the beginning of 2024. 
-	Coal shipment volume growth turned positive at the end of last year after being deeply negative at the start of 2025. 5-year energy cycle repeating?
-	Iron ore shipment volume growth increased significantly during the second half of last year. The three-year cycle suggests strong growth until mid 2026, after which growth might start falling. Iron ore prices, spreads and curve structures look good, but its not “booming”. 
-	Bauxite growth should continue due to continued Alumina smelter capacity additions in China. Growth likely to slow from last year’s pace, however. 
-	Projections for the ECSAM grain season is to see higher volumes than last year. 
-	All the above is likely to be strongly supported through most or all of this year by factors like relatively cheap oil prices, global interest rate cuts, high global credit growth and a weak US Dollar. 
-	Regarding supply, total dwt additions are likely to end slightly lower than 3%. Ships having to go in for special survey this year will reduce the effective supply by between 0.5% and 1.0%.*

The year has started very strongly. The Jan/Feb average for Capes is the highest since 2010, whereas the mid and small-sized segments are averaging the highest since 2022. The mid and small-sized markets have risen through the Chinese New Year, which is highly unusual. Second-hand values have also started the year on a firm note. We see price increases in all segments and across most vintages. 
We don’t see any significant changes to the bullish factors we listed in our previous report in January. Barring any black swans, it is extremely hard to see how March and Q2 markets will turn significantly lower than expected (similar, or lower levels than last year). In this regard, uncertainty is higher in Q3 and Q4, but the longer leading indicators we use strongly suggest 2026 will average higher than 2025 throughout the whole year. We still expect a cycle downturn in 2027.

This page gives brief comments on what the charts on the next page tells us. 

Top left chart:

The BDI year-on-year change has moved into positive territory in the last months. As usual, lagging behind credit growth in China. 
The credit growth rate have dipped noticeably in December and January. Should this continue it will be a bearish signal for 2027 market prospects. 

Top right chart:

Except for a decoupling in 2024, the change in bond yields in China and the US has been a good leading indicator for dry bulk demand growth. Strong support for demand growth in 2026 is suggested, but also a potential peak. 

Middle left chart:

Lower crude oil prices are bullish for economic growth, and vice versa. The chart displays that since 2017, there has been a tight correlation between lower year-on-year oil prices and a higher year-on-year BDI, with the oil price change leading by 1 year. 
Cheaper oil prices suggest the BDI could remain positive year-on-year throughout all of 2026. 

Middle right chart:

Lower global interest rates strongly suggest 1-year TC rates could continue rising from here, and be above last year's levels throughout this year. Tentative signs of a peak in early 2027, however, 

Bottom left chart:

The OECD Diffusion index correlation with the BDI is very high, as usual. The OECD index momentum is strong, which suggest the BDI year on year change will remain positive in the next 6 months. Worth noting is that the current OECD Diffusion index level of 18 is close to the maximum. This could mean the cycle top will be this year. 

Bottom right chart:

The dollar index has weakened in the last months, and as usual, the result is increased dry bulk shipment volume growth, with a few months' lag. The dollar index suggests total dry bulk shipment volume growth will remain around current levels.

In our previous update sent in late November, we wrote:
*We updated our earnings estimates for next year, reflecting that we think 2026 is likely to average a bit higher than in 2024. Commodity price levels (industrial metals, iron ore, coal, oil), manufacturing data, interest rate levels, cycle comparisons, and the supply situation all look comparably stronger than the months before we entered 2024. So, we think it is reasonable to expect the highs in second-hand values and 1-year tc rates seen that year for Kamsarmaxes, Ultras/Supras and Handies to be reached and/or exceeded next year, probably during Q2. For Capes, the story is a bit different in terms of second-hand values, as values have kept climbing despite the market weakness seen between Q4 last year and the first half of this year. Further upside is harder to expect, even with a bullish outlook on fundamentals. 2027 is still premature to call, but tentatively, we expect the markets to average lower than in 2026.*

We still see the same fundamental strength that led us to give the view that this year should be even stronger than in 2024. We think a higher average than 2022 (BDI 1933) is also likely, with the difference this year being higher average earnings for Capes/Newcs but lower for Kamsarmaxes down to Handysizes. 

**Factors on why we are bullish on 2026 market prospects:**
-	Global manufacturing is in expansion. This supports all commodity groups. 
-	Industrial Metals prices have surged to the highest level since early 2022. These prices has correlated tightly with 1-year TC rates and second-hand values in the last 10 years. 
-	Coal prices bottomed in April last year and have risen slowly since then. The coal futures curve structure is the most backwardated since the beginning of 2024. 
-	Coal shipment volume growth turned positive at the end of last year after being deeply negative at the start of 2025. 5-year energy cycle repeating?
-	Iron ore shipment volume growth increased significantly during the second half of last year. The three-year cycle suggests strong growth until mid 2026, after which growth might start falling. Iron ore prices, spreads and curve structures look good, but its not “booming”. 
-	Bauxite growth should continue due to continued Alumina smelter capacity additions in China. Growth likely to slow from last year’s pace, however. 
-	Projections for the ECSAM grain season is to see higher volumes than last year. 
-	All the above is likely to be strongly supported through most or all of this year by factors like relatively cheap oil prices, global interest rate cuts, high global credit growth and a weak US Dollar. 
-	Regarding supply, total dwt additions are likely to end slightly lower than 3%. Ships having to go in for special survey this year will reduce the effective supply by between 0.5% and 1.0%.
