It has been a volatile, but strong start to the year for tanker earnings, boosted again by geopolitics and consolidation. The latter could go far in explaining rate strength for the largest vessels, where tonne-mile demand has fared much worse than rates imply. 

Basis oil supply growth vs. tanker fleet growth expectations, there is meaningful downside risk for rates from here as the tanker market balance should gradually soften. However, given the geopolitical set-up (and possibly one emerging strong force within the VLCC owning community) the earnings outlook has rather tilted toward the bull-case, although it is still too early to tell how everything will play out. Any day now the outlook could change dramatically should the Middle East situation escalate, for instance. 

On the flipside, what happens when winter storms ease, deliveries ramp up, and all ships/owners start fixing regularly..?

content.title: Rates coming off a bit, but remain very volatile

content.content: The basics - the map does not fit the terrain

Sticking to the fundamentals, it is challenging to explain the market strength recently, as it also was to explain the depth of the early-year plunge. While preliminary tonne-mile demand figures suggest a new seasonal all-time high for January, the numbers are well below last year's peaks. 

For the total fleet, preliminary January tonne-mile demand is 5% below last year's peak, while for VLs it is 8.5% lower, driven by slightly lower volumes, and much less Atlantic-East fixture activity as the West-East arbitrage is closed. The latter, in combination with bad weather has contributed to significantly boost Suez- and Aframax earnings in the Atlantic. 

For product tankers, meanwhile, demand holds up better and has grown slightly into the start of the new year, boosted by recovering volumes and better long-haul arbitrages.

Going forward there is not expected to be much growth in demand, apart from returning production from some areas where there have been recent outages. The main supply growth engine over the last decade, the Americas, is expected to see some seasonal downside, and new projects are not expected until the summer. Overall non-OPEC+ production is 'only' expected to increase by about 0.5 mbpd this year. 

The OPEC+ plans to hold production flat through Q1, after which market conditions will decide whether the group may continue to unwind cuts. Global inventories have kept building in recent months, although not by as much as the energy agency balances imply as demand has been strong and supply in some areas curtailed. With that, and some geopolitical events, oil prices have remained resilient and the forward curve remains backwardated. These oil price conditions resemble the last instances the OPEC+ has decided to unwind production. 

That is one upside scenario for tanker demand going forward. Others include Venezuela and Iran - and possibly Sinokor.

content.title: Oil production vs. tanker demand growth

content.content:
Fleet growth now starts to pick up meaningfully after a few low delivery years. This quarter alone, gross fleet growth is scheduled at 1.5%. That is the same as the yearly average net fleet growth the last three years. For both this and next year the delivery schedule is north of 6% which means some more headwinds for the tanker market balance. 

Congestion has been more of a tailwind lately, with bottlenecks partly caused by sanctioned infrastructure in China, and plenty of bad weather. That has, however, now started to ease, although VLCC congestion in the Far East remains relatively elevated vs. the norm. Thus, some more pressure could emerge if and when discharge operations start to run more smoothly. Similarly, bad weather in the Atlantic has slowed down sailing speeds and hampered port operations.
The known unknowns - what could drive market upside

The bullish sentiment YTD has been driven by consolidation and geopolitics. The first, in the form of Sinokor's (and MSC) buying and TC-in spree will further consolidate the VLCC fleet. Whether the recent tally is sufficient to obtain any real pricing power over time remains to be seen, but it is safe to say that so far Sinokor's holding back from open market fixing (an increasing number of ships being delivered) has contributed to driving spot rates higher. The big question then, is what happens when this player starts fixing more of these ships? 

It is likely that a more consolidated fleet, with a much smaller portion now controlled by 'independent' owners, may contribute to increase volatility further this year. The rate development YTD could be an indication of precisely that. Position lists look very different with and without Sinokor's fleet on them.

The U.S. intervention in Venezuela has also contributed to boosting market sentiment, in anticipation of a switch from shadow to compliant tankers. So far, there has been uncertainty how this trade will shape up, and little measurable impact on the tanker market, although a few fixtures to the U.S. and Europe now start to emerge. Chevron is now expected to lift exports to the U.S. to 300 kbpd in March. 

Of Venezuela's nearly 800 kbpd 2025 exports, about 500 kbpd went to China on shadow tankers. The majority of this may now go to the U.S. and Europe on compliant Suez- and Aframaxes, and partly India on VLs. The latter portion, plus possibly some displacement of other heavy grades from the USGC, could contribute to higher tonne-mile demand: up toward 1% added to our base case demand assumption for this year. That is, provided that production and exports rebound from its recent slump, and unless more of that superfluous heavy crude go toward rebuilding the U.S. SPR. It is worth noting that in 2024, when there were waivers for Venezuelan exports to the same regions, this did not materially impact the overall tanker market balance. 

The longer term upside potential from Venezuela could be bigger, if or when production upside can be eked out. That may take some time.

content.content:
The potentially biggest supportive factor that may develop for tanker demand is if the U.S. lifts sanctions on Iran. That could give a shift of the 1.5-2 mbpd that currently goes on the shadow fleet onto the compliant fleet, and there could be 0.5-1 mbpd of upside to volumes within not too long. 

There are some mitigating factors too, however. At least 22 of the NITC VLCCs should continue trading as they are still in normal trading age. Assuming that sanctions are also lifted on other Iran-linked vessels, there may be another 30+ VLCCs that can continue trading. Those 50+ vessels should be able to continue lifting at least 1.5 mbpd of crude from Iran, provided that receivers allow so. Hence, the upside potential for the tanker market is rather around 0.5-1 mbpd within a relatively short time-span. 

Alternative scenarios are military conflicts in Iran, which may escalate to the broader region, and/or a U.S. embargo on Iranian exports. Both could lead to rate spikes through increased risk premiums for the MEG, and potentially higher pricing for MEG crudes which could support the West-East arbitrage.

content.content: A look at the oil market

The oil market appears well supplied, although not nearly as oversupplied as expected by energy agencies. Last year, global observed inventories built by an estimated 475 mb, or 1.3 mbpd. That is far from the IEA's expected 2 mbpd, but still significant. This year builds are expected to accelerate, but have so far been limited by outages in Kazakhstan and now the U.S. among others. 

Meanwhile, the Brent forward curve remains backwardated which contrasts with the observed inventory builds. This is partly explained by strong refinery margins which incentivizes prompt crude injection, and low-ish OECD inventory builds. 

A tighter oil market West of Suez, partly driven by recent outages, contributes to keeping the West-East arbitrage firmly shut, other than for some grades. Until or unless these constraints ease we may not see high Atlantic-East activity. If the OPEC+ continues to unwind cuts after Q1 this may also contribute to reduce West-East potential.

Oil on the water also indicates plentiful supply globally. The build-up seen over the last few months of 2025 has persisted, although eased slightly into this year. The majority of this build-up has been driven by sanctioned barrels, which remain 130 mb above the average of the first half of 2025. For compliant crude the recent number is 'only' 40 mb above, having come down after a lot of the long-haul fixtures from Sep-Nov last year have discharged. 

Floating storage of sanctioned barrels indicate that this oil struggles to clear. Iranian exports have been somewhat reduced in recent months, as has Venezuelan. Russian exports remain stubbornly high, despite reported discounts of Urals vs. Brent of closer to $30/bbl. How long this can be held up remains to be seen.

Global refinery runs are expected to increase by 0.8 mbpd this year, slightly less than last year's 0.9 mbpd growth. Global capacity is expected to expand by slightly more, but a large portion of that in China were new capacity may replace older. 

Global capacity could therefore remain a constraint this year, and remain supportive of refinery margins unless oil demand surprises negatively. Although margins have largely softened lately on more capacity coming back from maintenance and outages, they remain well above historical averages in the West. This has left a demand pull for gasoil and jet fuel into the region, with renewed demand from the MEG and India recently. 

In China, meanwhile, there has been some softness, in line with sluggish reported numbers for implied products demand. This may cause some worry for continued demand for high crude oil imports if sustained.
Newbuild orders are back in fashion

Ordering picked up markedly in the second half of last year, especially for the biggest vessels with 60 VLCCs confirmed and plenty more reported. With that, the orderbook to fleet has likely risen to closer to 19% when all is included - that is in line with the historical average. Based on recent reports, that figure may rise further too, although it could be offset by higher deliveries. 

Phase-out, meanwhile, was still limited although picked up somewhat from recent years. 'Only' 0.5% of the fleet was scrapped, most of it shadow tankers. This is likely to remain the case also this year. High earnings, and most of the phase-out potential having already migrated to the shadows should prevent any meaningful phase-out from the compliant fleet.

Deliveries are now set to pick up, with 6% gross fleet growth scheduled for this year and slightly more next year. The highest growth comes for product tankers with 9% this year 

Although a number of LR2s are expected to continue switching into the dirty market, we should also see Suez- and VLCC newbuilds doing CPP liftings on maiden voyages - correlations work both ways.

Our expectations for a Jan/Feb low season comparable to 2024 have so far been exceeded. An index move like yesterday is extreme, considering we are in January. 
We think the market could still cool off a bit due to the upcoming Chinese New Year, but in general, we expect firm levels. 

**Top left chart:** The share of profitable steel mills in China ticked up last week, and profit margins for hot-rolled coils turned positive for the first time since early October. Hot metal output is 2% higher year on year. 
**Top right chart:** The iron ore price complex is giving mixed signals. Spot prices remain stable, but the 1st month minus 3rd month futures spread has dipped into a slight contango. The price spread between higher-grade Brazilian ore and Australian iron ore is low. The latter is often bullish for freight as it incentivises longer-haul shipments. 
**Bottom left chart:** The price of copper is a good barometer of global industrial activity, and leads asset values with high accuracy. The suggestion is for further upside in values in the next few months. 
**Bottom right chart:** There has been an increase in the share of the active fleet in shipyards since the start of the new year. From 0.9% to 1.4% currently. We will see this rise above 2% frequently this year.

The LNG shipping market in 2025 was defined by continued pressure on rates, with annual average charter levels for two‑stroke vessels falling by around USD 17,000/day compared with 2024. Global LNG trade expanded by nearly 30 million tonnes year on year, but this was not enough to offset the impact of significant fleet growth, as 80 newbuilds entered service. Shipping demand was further softened by shorter average voyage distances, driven by a record share—nearly 70%—of U.S. exports flowing to Europe.

Despite the oversupplied market, a brief winter peak emerged, with two‑stroke spot rates exceeding USD 100,000/day. This was supported by unexpectedly high U.S. Gulf production and a strong preference for modern tonnage. However, by year‑end, rates had resumed their downward trend, reflecting underlying fundamentals.

Vessel retirements reached new highs, with 15 ships sold for demolition and a clear shift toward younger scrapping ages. Delivery delays in 2025 resulted in an orderbook of roughly 100 vessels scheduled for 2026, followed by 88 in 2027 and 72 in 2028. The LNG carrier market is therefore expected to remain oversupplied at least through to 2028, even though long‑term fundamentals remain constructive due to increasing long‑haul trade and fleet‑renewal needs.

Gas and LNG prices trended downward throughout the year. Both JKM and TTF peaked around USD 17/MMBtu in February, but only briefly dipped below USD 10/MMBtu at the end of the year—not for long enough to trigger price‑sensitive demand.

2025 was extraordinary for FIDs: eight projects (some multi‑phase) moved forward, adding more than 80 million tonnes of future liquefaction capacity. Nearly 70% of these new volumes are U.S.‑based.
Source: JKM from S&P Global Platts

The average 2025 spot rate for modern two‑strokes was USD 37,000/day—a record low, even compared with historical TFDE levels. Excluding Q4, the average falls to just USD 27,000/day, underscoring the importance of the brief winter peak. The year began with exceptionally low rates and high vessel availability, which later corrected modestly without any strong fundamental driver. 

A persistent Atlantic premium remained, with modern ships earning on average USD 6,600/day more West of Suez due to stronger demand for large, modern vessels versus older tonnage. TFDEs averaged USD 22,000/day, and 145k steamers averaged USD 6,000/day—both historically low. The rate differentials versus two‑strokes (approximately USD 15k/day for TFDEs and USD 30k/day for steamers) were broadly unchanged from 2024.

In the term market, the decline that began in late 2022 bottomed out early in 2025. One‑year rates reached the low USD 20k/day range in Q1. Five‑year rates remained stable around USD 70,000/day, as charterers maintained appetite for longer coverage despite visible oversupply heading into 2026.

Liquidity was exceptionally high in 2025: more than 450 spot fixtures were concluded—the highest number ever in LNG. The spot fixture count grew 28% year on year, while total fixed days increased 44%, indicating a rise in average fixture duration.

Two‑strokes accounted for 64% of all spot fixtures, consistent with the growing modern fleet. In contrast, steam turbine spot activity collapsed by more than 80%, representing only ~2% of total spot fixtures. Many steamers now lie idle and uncommitted, highlighting a clear market preference for larger and more efficient vessels.

Term activity (1–5 years) remained broadly similar to 2024, though with slightly more volume toward the longer durations. Both 2024 and 2025 saw significantly less term fixing compared with 2021–2023, when energy‑security concerns dominated. Interest in multi‑year (>5 years) terms remained muted, reflected in the low ordering activity of just 33 vessels—far below the recent four‑year average of 97.

content.title: Short term fixtures by sublet vs independent owners

content.content:
Global LNG trade increased by 27 million tonnes, almost entirely driven by U.S. supply growth. U.S. output rose by 21 million tonnes, supported by strong ramp‑up at Plaquemines, which alone loaded 2 million tonnes in December. October–December were all record months for global loadings. Slightly counteracting that growth, several exporters recorded small reductions in volume.

Egypt registered the largest import increase (+6.4 MT), driven by declining domestic production, high summer demand, and reduced pipeline inflows from Israel. Most other demand growth came from Europe, which increased LNG imports by 26 MT to 123 MT—matching 2022 levels following the loss of Russian pipeline gas.

China reduced LNG imports by 8 MT, shifting toward cheaper pipeline gas and domestic production, with geopolitics and tariffs further influencing flows.

Europe sourced 56% of its LNG from the U.S.; a record 66% of U.S. LNG cargoes was absorbed by Europe. Strong TTF pricing consistently diverted flexible cargoes away from Asia. The increased demand is a result of low renewable energy output and lower pipeline flows from Russia (with no flows through Ukraine since start of 2025). High European demand continues into early 2026, supported by lower storage levels and cold weather.

Despite more loadings particularly later in the year, tonne‑miles remained flat year on year due to shorter voyage distances. In 2024, there were significantly more U.S.–Asia cargoes than in 2025, which largely routed the long voyage via the Cape. Qatar flow to Europe, also via Cape, was also higher in 2024. With nearly 80 newbuilds joining the fleet in 2025 and tonne-miles flat, fleet utilization was low. However, with increased segmentation of the fleet, it is important to note that the underutilization largely targets the old, less efficient ships. Steam turbine volumes fell 22% year on year, even though their fleet size shrank only 9%, resulting in sharply lower utilization. Two‑strokes saw steady utilization, with tonne‑mile growth largely matching fleet expansion. Interestingly, TFDEs reduced tonne-miles by 13% globally, but number of loadings in the Atlantic saw a reduction of 20%. This is likely a result of FuelEU Maritime, which includes methane in the emission calculations. This trend is likely to continue, as the EU ETS as of January 2026 also includes methane emissions.

content.title: Yearly exports of top 5 exporting markets

content.content:
The active LNGC fleet now totals 730 vessels, with an additional 25 in layup—up sharply from just 6 a year earlier. These laid‑up vessels average 29 years old. Beyond these, roughly 15 steamers are inactive but not officially laid up; these are younger, averaging 23 years.

Ordering fell significantly to 33 ships in 2025, though half were placed in Q4, and strong early‑2026 activity suggests a new ordering cycle has begun. The temporary slowdown brought slight reductions in newbuild prices, but these have already reversed, with current levels around USD 250 million.

The orderbook to fleet ratio is 39%. Interestingly, the first vessel order was placed in the United States at the Hanwha Philly Shipyard. 70% of the orderbook is in Korea, and 29% in China.

Deliveries in 2025 reached 79 ships—a new record—though slightly below the planned schedule. Qatar’s North Field Expansion accounted for 35% of these. With 102 vessels scheduled for delivery in 2026, followed by significant volumes in 2027 and 2028, the fleet will continue to expand rapidly.

Two‑strokes now represent 46% of the fleet; steam turbines 26%. Ageing is becoming a major theme:
- 37 ships are older than 25 years
- 84 ships are older than 20 years
- 81 steam turbines will turn 20 within the next four years

Given costly drydock requirements and weak employment prospects, many owners face challenging decisions for older vessels. Demolitions reached a record 15 ships, continuing the trend of increasing scrap volumes and declining scrapping age. 15 LNGCs were sold for demolition in 2025; by far a new record. The last few years have seen a trend in increasing number of demolitions, and decreasing age at demolition.

A clear mismatch between LNG supply and vessel availability persists across 2024–27, reflected in sustained rate weakness. While major new liquefaction capacity will tighten the market over time—particularly long‑haul U.S. exports that increase tonne‑miles—the LNGC market is unlikely to become fundamentally tight before late 2028.
Even in a scenario where scrapping age falls to 20 years, vessel supply is expected to exceed demand in both 2026 and 2027. Short‑term fluctuations will continue to be driven by weather, arbitrage, portfolio strategies, and geopolitics.

In 2026, roughly three ships will be added for every new million tonnes of LNG—an elevated ratio given today’s voyage distances. The ratio improves modestly in 2027 and further in 2028, with increasing supply and fewer deliveries. This indicates gradual tightening, but the already present oversupply also needs to be absorbed before we can expect a structurally tight market.

The average daily spot earnings across the three index routes reached $61,500 per day in Q4, a result from a stable market at relatively high levels. Earnings in all three months of the quarter exceeded those of the previous year. The Middle East–Asia route rose by 53%, while the U.S.–Asia route increased by 30%. With Q4 concluded, **2025’s average TCE earnings closed at $55,700 per day**, marking another strong year for VLGCs - a 10% increase compared to 2024.

On a dollar per metric ton basis, BLPG-1 averaged at $67.9 in Q4, BLPG-2 at $62.3 and BLPG-3 at $125.4.

Following a hectic year marked by numerous geopolitical curveballs, the last quarter was defined by a calmer market with fewer abrupt trade disruptions. The spread between West and East cargo premiums narrowed compared to the prior quarter, signaling a more balanced fleet. The abolition of USTR measures and retaliatory port fees on U.S.-linked ships on November 9 allowed the market to regain equilibrium after two volatile quarters. Nevertheless, despite the abrupt cancellation of fees, both owners and charterers remain cautious about potential renewed turmoil.
U.S. Production and Terminal Capacity Expansion

U.S. LPG production continues to rise, with total output increasing 90% from 2015 to 2025. While growth is expected to moderate to approximately 5% over the next three years, export capacity is projected to expand significantly during the same period. Domestic consumption remains stable at around 60%, though household heating demand is forecasted to decline by 2% this winter. Propane production will increase by 2% compared with last winter. Coupled with continuous expansion of export capacity at several major terminals, conditions are aligned for a solid start to 2026.

*Furthermore, production from the Permian Basin is projected to grow at an annual rate of 7% through 2030, outpacing crude oil growth by 4%.*

Propane inventories reached a new peak in the final week of October at 106 million barrels, more than 20% higher than the three-year average. The U.S. exported 67 million tons in 2025, of which VLGCs accounted for 82% (55 million tons) - an increase of 2 million tons from 2024. The majority of volumes were shipped to the Far East, while 15–20% headed to Europe and Africa, representing substantially shorter voyages.

Sailing patterns remain the most influential factor in fleet utilization. In 2025, 75% of laden voyages from the U.S. to the Far East transited via the Panama Canal - down from 82% in 2024. The Panama Canal continues to be a critical bottleneck due to unpredictable operational capacity and VLGCs’ lower transit priority. The Long-Term Slot Allocation (LoTSA) system, fully implemented in 2025, auctioned 40% of Neo-lock slots in advance, leaving limited room for non-booked ships. The PCA has confirmed LoTSA will continue into 2026 with modifications.

Another factor contributing to canal congestion is the emergence of VLECs transporting ethane from the U.S. to China. These voyages almost exclusively transit via the Panama Canal and do not use the COGH route. In 2025, the average number of VLEC transits reached 8 ships per month. U.S. ethane transported to India opt for the COGH route, but this is a small percentage of the live fleet. With continued growth in U.S. exports of both LPG and ethane, this trend is expected to intensify. Additionally, the orderbook for other shipping segments that frequent the canal is vast, set to increase pressure from the global fleet in the coming years.

Total U.S. export capacity is set to increase from 68 to 113 MTPA by 2028 with the completion of ongoing projects. This represents a 66% boost from 2024 to 2028—a substantial jump welcomed by a growing fleet. While actual incremental exports may fall short of full capacity, this move by U.S. energy suppliers further underscores the market's desire to expand and grow.

Both the Nederland and Neches River facilities will offer flexible capacity for LPG and ethane. Given recent growth in U.S. ethane exports and the VLEC orderbook (150% of fleet), a portion of these volumes will likely be allocated to ethane rather than LPG.

Middle East exports surpassed 40 million tons in 2025, a year-on-year increase of only 1%. Key contributors remain Qatar, the UAE, and Iran, each accounting for 22–24% respectively. Notably, 92% of Iranian LPG exports were destined for China, with 96% transported by VLGCs, primarily by the dedicated part of the fleet, which is 14% of the total fleet, 60 ships that are currently sanctioned.

New natural gas developments in Qatar, including the North Field projects, are expected to come online in 2026 and 2027, adding 6.2 MTPA and raising regional export capacity from 46 to 52 MTPA. Saudi Arabia’s shale gas project in Jafurah is set to produce 2.5 MTPA of LPG in 2026, with volumes projected to surpass 10 MTPA by 2030. In 2025, Saudi Arabia accounted for 6% of all VLGC volumes. This incremental supply will help balance a fleet that is growing substantially over the next three years.

In the latter half of the year, Saudi CP was lowered each month, reaching $475/mt for propane and $460/mt for butane in November—the lowest point of 2025 - before readjusting upward toward year-end.

After a period of market instability following “Liberation Day” in April, trade flows are gradually returning to normal. However, U.S.–China LPG trade remains below previous levels, with both countries diversifying supply and demand - a trend expected to continue into 2026. Though imports decreased towards the end of the year, total imports reached 33.82 million tons, up 1% from 2024. This was below expectations, though not surprising given the tensions in trade. Imports are expected to reach 36 MTPA in 2026. With increased demand, the Asian propane price is expected to rise, and with the U.S. set to increase their production and exports, this will likely push the arbitrage wider, supporting the freight environment. 

China’s LPG demand continues to be primarily driven by the petrochemical sector, with ongoing growth in propane dehydrogenation (PDH) capacity. Although Chinese PDH plants are currently facing negative margins, recent improvements in run rates have been observed, currently around 72%.

In November, an Indian one-year tender for 2.2 MTPA of LPG was won by U.S. energy majors. This diversification of supply is a clear effect from the tariff-turmoils in 2025, which has allowed new trade routes to emerge. This requirement is equivalent to more than 40 VLGC cargoes, representing a 190% increase from volumes traded in 2024. Rumors of another market tender is swirling, but nothing is confirmed yet. India is set for further growth in 2026, with their first PDH plant with an annual propane demand of 600,000 tons. The biggest pipeline of its kind, will also come online, which connects India's West Coast terminals to its inland demand centres in the north. The pipeline will be able to transport 8.25 MTPA of LPG.

12 newbuilds were delivered in 2025, with two ships rolling over into 2026 and one scheduled for 2026 delivered early. The fleet now stands at 412 ships, including floating storages. The orderbook consists of 109 ships, resulting in an orderbook-to-fleet ratio of 26%, slightly above the 20-year average of 21%. The fleet is set to grow by 20% through 2026 and 2027, which could lead to an accumulated oversupply.

As the Panama Canal is expected to become increasingly congested in the coming years—driven by rising U.S. exports of ethane and LNG, along with the addition of over 100 VLGCs on the water—there is reason to anticipate that a larger share of the fleet will regularly utilize the Cape of Good Hope (COGH) route. This shift will stretch fleet capacity and reduce overall vessel availability. At the same time, new LPG export capacity is coming online in the U.S., requiring additional transportation. These dynamics suggest a potential need for more ships, as longer sailing distances reduce the number of voyages each vessel can complete annually.

Ordering activity in 2025 remained modest compared to the previous two years, due to high newbuilding prices and the size of the orderbook. Hyundai in South Korea remains the largest builder, while one-quarter of newbuilds are being constructed in China. No significant price differences have emerged between Japanese/Korean and Chinese yards. The last recorded VLAC order was priced at $120.44 million in December - Hyundai building for Benelux, with delivery in Q2 and Q3 2028.

On the ammonia side, market interest and activity has remained limited throughout the year. Smaller ship segments are currently under pressure, although the large orderbook for MGCs is expected to accommodate any incremental volumes entering the market. More critically, the infrastructure investments required to support seaborne ammonia trade via VLACs are not being made. These investments typically involve long lead times, further delaying market readiness. Additionally, the market lacks sufficient project development to generate new ammonia volumes. The first VLAC in the orderbook is scheduled for delivery in June, but as previously noted, these ships are expected to operate as conventional VLGCs for the foreseeable future. We do not differentiate them within the fleet, aside from their technical capability to carry ammonia at 98% capacity, if required.

*Fearnleys expects earnings to remain broadly in line with 2025 levels throughout 2026.*

The coming year will bring additional capacity expansions in the U.S., coupled with a projected supply boost from the Middle East. These developments are anticipated to help offset the impact of fleet growth over the next 12 months, which includes 36 newbuild deliveries in total.

Following a volatile year marked by uncertain trade relations, flows are gradually normalizing, though new trade patterns have emerged. India is set to increase its imports of U.S. LPG, while China will continue sourcing volumes from Canada’s West Coast. This voyage is shorter and it offers greater flexibility by avoiding transit volatility at the Panama Canal, which will maintain its Long-Term Slot Allocation System in 2026, continuing to reduce Neo-lock capacity. Additionally, the substantial orderbook for container vessels and VLECs is likely to absorb canal capacity, as these segments have a higher willingness to pay than VLGCs. Transit availability is expected to tighten further with these newbuild deliveries, likely forcing more VLGCs to sail around the Cape of Good Hope.

Supply will continue to grow for both LPG and VLGCs in the coming year; however, demand from the petrochemical sector remains fragile. PDH margins in China are under pressure despite increasing plant capacity. Traditionally, the LPG market has been considered supply-driven. If this dynamic holds, 2026 could offer a shipping market with relative stability - though underlying demand risks suggest this is not guaranteed. As witnessed in the past year, the geopolitical dice could be thrown in any direction, and markets will have to follow.

The ratio between Capes and Kamsarmaxes remains quite high, which, along with a high laden/ballast vessel ratio suggest the market will trend down in the next weeks. 

**Top left chart:** Hot metal output in China usually lags steel mill profitability by a few weeks. This suggests hot metal output will remain stable around current levels. 
**Top right chart:** Higher backwardation = more urgency to buy, and vice versa. The futures curve suggests tailwinds for Capes through most of Q1, but the curve has recently become less backwardated. 
**Bottom left chart:** The price of copper is a good barometer of global industrial activity, and leads asset values with high accuracy. The suggestion is for further upside in values in the next months. 
**Bottom right chart:** Iron ore prices have risen over the last few weeks, which, along with persistent backwardation, suggests iron ore demand remains firm.

content.content: https://pbrkapp.blob.core.windows.net/report/f1b56dc0-0df6-4717-8893-895ba397a8f2/COPPER PRICE LEAD VS SUPRAMAX 10 YEAR OLD.png

With 2025 in the books, we can conclude that the FSRU market maintains its winning streak – showing continued strength for the fourth consecutive year. Our tracking shows **seven contracts concluded**, of which only **two are for new locations** (Dominican Republic and Iraq) and for relatively short firm periods of 3 to 5 years. **EGAS’ fixing spree** resulted in **four charters** ranging from 5 to 10 years. Rounding out the field is one short-term extension for undisclosed project. Charter rate levels remain highly sensitive to FSRU specifications and duration, but generally in **six-digit range** and not too far from starting with a “2” if shorter durations for the right FSRU. For **longer charters (7-15 years)** the market seems to be ever so carefully pricing in the fact that a number of FSRU conversions are likely to arrive at the same time as a handful of existing units come open. By no means a collapse, but **in the range of US$ 120-140k/day** (subject to specifications and project)

In the context of longer charters; what is worth noting is the absence of concluded charters for new long-term projects with solid fundamentals. The number of projects that should (unfortunately not “will”) secure FSRU capacity to hit their more or less realistic timelines is in double-digits; with attributes that are win-win for both FSRU owners and the projects themselves. Therefore it is **frustrating to see what we can only attribute to mediocre project management, unstructured market processes and politics time and time again washing away timelines drawn in the sand**. The consequence is hard work by FSRU (and FSU for that matter) players to understand which horses to back.

While we acknowledge that Fearnleys cannot work miracles (even though we’d like to think so), it is increasingly clear to us that project owners in particular should seek professional advice to achieve a higher number of successful outcomes; **the lines are open!**

Peering into **2026** we count **more than ten projects that may take FID**, but a closer look reveals that we may see **3-4 new projects**; projects which we by and large see stitched up with a selected FSRU already. **Key focal points** will be power auction in **Brazil** (how much will be gas-fired and need FSRUs?) , developments in **Southeast Asia** (will they stop beating around the bush?) and a handful of **European** projects (will shippers be putting pen to paper in open seasons?). Of course, the FSRU market is never dull and we look forward to what we expect will be **another strong year**.
Key market developments during the quarter

OCTOBER
**Ecopetrol** relaunches/changes tender for 2nd FSRU with “technically and logistically superior site” Coveñas as the new location. Apart from the change of location, the requirement looks the same – and we wonder how Ecopetrol did not identify the improved site earlier. General conversations around Colombia hit topics such as lack of structure, low level of guarantees and unrealistic expectations.

**Excelerate** announced having secured the **Iraq**-project which has developed through the year with multiple G-t-G discussions where it seems Uncle Sam prevailed. Excelerate will supply LNG in addition to the FSRU (initially their newbuild **EXCELERATE ACADIA** and topside equipment for the terminal in **Khor Al-Zubair** (located upriver in shallow waters)

**LNG CROATIA** returned online after periodic drydock and installation of an additional **4th regas train**. Since returning, the unit has taken seven cargoes and sending out full-throttle.

**Snam** and **Hoegh EVI** formally tie up for FSRU in Oristano, Sardinia where Snam will take ownership of the (former) Avenir LNG terminal and install an FSRU to facilitate the methanization of Sardinia. The FSRU replaces previous attempts in Porto Torres and Portovesme.

**Eems Energy Terminal** announced **Exmar** as the supplier of FSRU in Eemshaven once the current contract for **ENERGOS IGLOO** expires in Q3/27. Exmar already operates the **FSRU EEMSHAVEN LNG** and is expected convert a **TFDE**-vessel for the project.

Karpowership’s newly formed FSRU-arm **Kinetics** issued US$ 400m bond with intentions to undertake **three FSRU conversion** projects at Seatrium. Kinetics will take a step into the “big leagues” with one of the conversions being a high pressure/high send-out unit; differing from their existing FSRU portfolio designed to support KPS’ fleet of powerships.

NOVEMBER

**Centrica** signed up “approximately six cargoes per year” for 15 years with Exodus which will form the supply to Genesis’ project in **Puerto Cortes, Honduras**. The FSU allocated to the project is **BILBAO KNUTSEN**. Depending on the cargo size, six cargoes would equate to around 400,000 tons per year which appears to be slightly too much for a 240MW CCGT if this is the sole offtaker. However, positive to see another country include LNG in its energy mix.

**UKs Department for Energy Security and Net Zero** (DESNZ) issued a market consultation for the potential development of **one or more FSRUs** (along with other alternatives). The consultation is expected to close mid-Feb and is a high-level evaluation without specific details of site, timing or specifications. With several FSRU projects with a commercial mindset not gaining traction over the last 15-20 year in UK, maybe government intervention will make it stick.

**Gas Networks Ireland** has reportedly selected **Shannon** as the preferred location for its strategic FSRU. Discussions were mainly between Cork and Shannon. Shannon has for a long time been considered the most progressed location for an FSRU in Ireland and with the approval of Shannon LNGs 600MW power plant (which is a subsidiary of NFE) in Mar-25 we’re hopeful of the next steps by GNI to eventually come to market for an FSRU.

**DET** ended up not allocating any slots for **W’haven 1+2** during the auction for Dec-25, Q1+2+4/26 and Q1/27. A total of 28 slots were offered at a reserve price of **EUR 0.56/MMBtu (~US$ 0.66/MMBtu)**. While the FSRUs in Wilhelmshaven have been busy it is somewhat curious that DET now implements a relatively high reserve price given their decision to sell slots at below-market during earlier auctions.

Total Energies confirmed **CAPE ANN** will be demobilizing from Le Havre after not seeing a cargo since Jun-24. The unit received a total of 10 cargoes between Nov-23 and Jun-24, being one of few “insurance” FSRUs in Europe. While it is not clear when she will depart Le Havre (she is currently in port), it expected that Cape Ann may be subchartered to another project.

DECEMBER

**Morocco** emerged from hiding after the EOI earlier in the year with a **Prequalification of FSRU providers**. The timeline suggests preselection will be done by **end-Feb 2026** with the preferred bidder by **end-Jun 2026**. The six qualification criteria are relatively stringent and will effectively only qualify the major existing FSRU players given the requirement to having owned/operated at least two FSRUs for at least five years within the last fifteen years.

**Snam** acquires stake in **OLT Livorno** at a price of EUR 126m (appx US$ 147m) for 48.2% - implying an asset value of approximately US$ 305m. The price is high and does in our view reflect the cash flows at a very low return rate, not the underlying value of the asset.

**Egypt** and **Israel** agreeing on gas supply agreement. The first phase starting in 2026 will increase gas exports from Israel to Egypt by appx 2BCMA (equivalent to ~1.5million tons of LNG) from 4.7 to 6.7 BCMA before the second phase (targeted for 2029) will increase flows to 12-13BCMA. The incremental volumes (5-6BCMA) in the second phase is equivalent to 3.5-4.5 million tons of LNG. While still early to draw conclusions it may be the **first sign of a fleet of underutilized FSRUs**… 

**Squadron Energy’s** terminal in **Port Kembla (PKET)** took a step closer to confirming startup in 2027 with the appointment of **Reganosa** as **O&M provider** for the terminal. The FSRU allocated to the project is **HOEGH GALLEON** which is currently on a subcharter to EGAS. While considerable uncertainty remains around the various Australian FSRU projects – including the “ready-to-operate” PKET – the long-term requirement for an insurance to the southeastern part of the country seems inevitable.

‘Tis is the season for **Open Seasons** as both **Zeeland Energy Terminal** and **Gaz-System** started consultations for binding volumes. With **DET** failing to sell slots at what we would deem reasonable prices and **Eemshaven Energy Terminal** coming to market in 2026, there is no shortage of future regas capacity being offered – *something to consider for the players very long LNG as a potential sink?*

On the corporate front, **NFE** continues to kick the ball down the road with its creditors which impacts **Energos Infrastructure**. During the quarter, Energos came to market with **US$ 0.5bn+1.5bn credit issuances** to refinance which ultimately turned into a **hung deal**. As we understand, it may still be alive, but as long as visibility on NFE is opaque at best it will remain challenging to refinance in our view. A more successful bond process was **Kinetics** which is Karpowership’’s FSRU outfit trying to break in to mainstream FSRUs. Lastly, **Snam and Igneo** closed the **OLT transaction** at a price that gives *zero reference points as to the value of an FSRU*, but rather good insight in how fixed, long-term cash flow and return on invested capital on **Regulatory Asset Base (RAB)** creates value for sellers.
Quarterly focus: Can FSRUs provide support to absorb LNG as we head into an oversupplied LNG market

While we reflect on 2025 from an FSRU perspective, the last quarter of 2025 brought about an increased focus on what the world will do with all the LNG that is set to come into production over the next decade. Talks about Short Run Marginal Costs (SRMC), JKM in the US$ 5-6/MMBtu-range and projecting US cargo cancellations in 2028-2029 has led the market down a bearish rabbit hole.

In this quarter’s focus piece, we look at the ability of FSRUs to support the demand side from what we deem as three main attributes: time-to-market, project likelihood and throughput.

Starting with time-to-market; a critical limitation to FSRU demand is that they need to support structural demand, not short-term/price-sensitive demand pockets that may emerge on back of lower LNG prices. Despite short-term deals done in 2025 they are generally bridging solutions to long-term requirements (Dom.Rep.) or in anticipation of other sources of natural gas becoming available (Egypt). What the LNG market needs to fundamentally absorb the supply is new markets with strong underlying demand for power generation or industrial use – such as Vietnam, Malaysia, Brazil, Morocco, Indonesia and Bangladesh to mention a few no-brainers. Based on our demand forecast, these six nations alone will add around 30mtpa of imports by 2030 of which the majority is structural. All of it will not be on FSRUs, but they are all FSRU-hot spots. Not to say that the other potential new importers will not support LNG demand, but the magnitude is likely too limited to make a notable dent.

The challenge faced is lead time for FSRUs to commence operations; we continue to estimate 27-30 months from FID to COD for an FSRU project and that excludes the preparatory works to get to an FID. This is where “project likelihood” comes into play; when we evaluate our database/pipeline of prospective projects a key aspect is the underlying real need for an FSRU. Europe showed that things can move quick in the face of adversity, but similarly it could be argued (as an example) that the power sector in Vietnam is facing serious adversity which should have prompted fast-track projects…it has not. There are a number of reasons why (we haven’t even touched credit and bankability), but perhaps this highlights the uncertainty of LNG as a long-term affordable energy source, looking at volatility in LNG prices over the past decade could easily be mirrored into the next one.

The third element we consider is throughput once an FSRU is operational. Every project is unique, but on a generalized basis we would argue 600-700MW-equivalents of gas demand is a minimum for an FSRU to be economically justifiable. On the other end of the spectrum, few FSRUs are able to support more than 3,500-4,000MW-equivalents (3.7-4.2 million tons per year) – at which point regas costs become very competitive. Taking a holistic view on FSRUs, our data shows FSRUs globally average at around 1.2-1.4mtpa (with the extremes being zero on the low-end and closer to 5mtpa in the high-end). Assuming increased utilization of FSRUs by 25% on back of a structural demand for natural gas with visibility on consumers we’d still need 20 FSRUs to handle 30-35mtpa. Or in plain language; around 15% of the incremental supply – which is historically the share of LNG imported on FSRUs.

These are just a few aspects of how FSRUs can impact long-term LNG demand and we most certainly stress the importance of FSRUs as lean and mean way of accessing LNG, but a dose of realism makes us doubtful a potential LNG oversupply will be mitigated in a timely manner by new FSRUs. However, turning it upside down: Without development of a substantial number of FSRU projects in the next five years the world is at risk of having to deal with the oversupply for an extended period of time.

content.title: FSRU "Hot spots": Set to absorb additional 30mtpa by 2030
FSRU Utilization: Global average has been around 1.3mtpa

content.content:
Q4 was another (consecutive) record-breaking quarter for FSRU imports as the global FSRU fleet is now in operation by-and-large. Overall activity at operational FSRUs reached a total of **19.0mt / 300 cargoes** (which is up 42% from **13.4mt / 226 cargoes** in Q4/24, but *only 2%* from **18.6mt / 304 cargoes** in Q3/25). The Y-o-Y increase is driven by-and-large by **Europe, Egypt and Turkey**. Europe reached 7.0mt during the quarter (marginally down from the 7.2 in Q3) while Egypt racked up another 3+ mtpa-quarter at 3.1mtpa. Additionally, Turkey is in full throttle-mode with 2.2mtpa for the quarter across 32 cargoes in typical seasonal pattern. In Europe, there seems to be a more stable environment with no new units added in the quarter, but slightly lower activity across all terminals. Egypt, now have 4+1 FSRUs; Damietta taking its first 6 cargoes and +1 in Aqaba having taken 1 cargo during the quarter.

For the full year of 2025, our tally shows **67.1mt / 1,091 cargoes** were imported through FSRUs compared to **49.6mt / 861 cargoes** in 2024. This is a stunning 3**5% Y-o-Y** growth. Regional development shows higher activity in all regions apart from Americas and Middle East which are notoriously seasonal/insurance-based regions.

As we continue to see FSRUs increase their importance in the global LNG value chain; global LNG imports in 2025 came in at appx 435mt; which now means FSRUs continue to account for **around 16% of global LNG imports**. While we’d prefer to see the relative imports on FSRUs increase – *we do not foresee this increase in 2026 (or 2027)* given the lead-time for new projects.

The busiest terminals in 2025 were Elengy Engro (Pakistan) **EXCELERATE EXQUISITE** with 72 cargoes, closely followed by Eemshaven (Netherlands) **ENERGOS IGLOO/EEMSHAVEN LNG** at 70 and Ain Sokhna Sumed (Egypt) **HOEGH GALLEON** at 64. However, on a volume basis Eemshaven moved more product at 4.8mtpa with Ain Sohhna Sumed at 4.5 and Elengy Engro at 4.4, What is interesting to note is the *wide range in implied cargo size*. Damietta (**ENERGOS WINTER** being a 145,000cbm FSRU) took the larges cargoes at around **158,500**cbm whereas cargoes going into Dakar (**KARMOL LNGT AFRICA**) took partials at appx **72,000**cbm.

Finally, the only FSRU without a cargo in 2025 was CAPE ANN in Le Havre (a reasonably good data point for why she is now departing), but also Terminal Gas Sul in Brazil saw zero cargoes while technically being an operational terminal. (We expect that to change come power auctions in 2026).

content.title: Monthly volumes imported through FSRUs by region (2025)

content.content:
*Asia & Middle East*

**New Zealand** has been developing its project for **Port Taranaki** during the quarter with **TORMAN I** as a hot candidate together with a few other more esoteric solutions. The project remains a political priority, but recent news suggest a slowdown in the process.

**Malaysia** is progressing their **RGT 3 & 4** projects and are expected to come to market in **2026** with FSRU requirements. Several FSRU Owners are already engaged directly, but tender processes are expected to be the most likely route.

*Europe & Mediterranean*
**Poland** is slowly, but surely progressing their **2nd FSRU** in Gdansk. Timing is not defined yet, but the first FSRU is set to reach COD in 2028 and hence the next unit is **probably a 2030+ startup**.

There are rumours of **Lebanon** returning to the FSRU-scene after having been “out of office” since 2018-2019. Talks are linked to **Tripoli** as the site to support the only feasible consumer at **Deir Ammar TPP**.

*Americas & Caribbean*

Continued activity in **Brazil** as the power auction is scheduled for mid-March with startups in **2026-2031** (the earlier likely being brownfields and the later being greenfields). We’re seeing discussions for both near-term FSRUs to support 2026-2027 operations and long-term FSRU/FSU conversions for the later-dated CODs.

**Guatemala** will be closing the technical bids for their 1.4GW auction in **Feb-26**. Thus far *limited talks about FSRUs* to support CCGT, but the outcome will be closely watched.

*Africa & Other*
**South Africa** remains stagnant from an LNG perspective, but talks about FSRUs in new sites in **Mozambique** has prompted renewed interest as the government-allocated sites of **Inhassoro** and **Port of Beira** were announced in November. It is unclear whether this is a genuine project or a way for *Moz to force domestic LNG back to shore*.

*We encourage clients with deeper interest in ongoing project developments, tender activity and business development to contact Fearnleys directly; the above is merely scratching the surface of activity.*

As the FSRU market remains by and large sold out there are limited units moving around (which is in many ways good and reflected in the high volumes).

**EXPRESS** has replaced **EXPLORER** at **DUSUPs** facilities as **EXPLORER** undergoes drydock at Dubai Drydocks. The swap is likely a short-term bridge and **EXPRESS** will return to Ruwais early-26.

**EXCELERATE ACADIA** has been launched and is currently undergoing sea trials in South Korea, The unit should be mobilizing to Iraq once delivered to Owners.

**SAROS** moved a bit around in early-Oct, but seemingly nothing material.

**ETYFA PROMETHEUS** remains in Malacca where works to complete the unit is ongoing still.
Asset values: Newbuildings and conversion candidates

Despite the view that new FSRUs may come up short in saving the day in respect of the impending LNG oversupply, the **activity level remains very high**. The width of the project pipeline remains wide (albeit a bit leaky in terms of project quality) and we maintain that at least 3-4 genuine new projects will reach FID. What was a reserved approach to taking semi-speculative positions on FSRUs has turned during the quarter and **our tally shows 8-10 conversion units** in the works of which **4-5 have a dedicated home/project** already. The remaining are essentially speculative, but we caveat it by the fact that **nobody has gone full blast** on a conversion just yet. The approach is to do pre-engineering and ordering regas module – and for a select few – position with a vessel acquisition.

Asset values have dropped through the quarter with a **145k ST** now in the range of **US$ 23.5m** on prompt basis while **TFDE/DFDEs** in the 160k range are assessed around **US$ 125-130m**. However, for projects wanting to secure a LNGC for conversion with later delivery or with conditions precedent on project award, the prices are generally a notch higher through reservation fees and the likes.

The trend of more focus on larger units remains prevalent as the extra US$ 100m in asset cost will likely yield improvement in LNG price, reduced shipping costs, lower demurrage and potentially longer life span; all adding up.

Conversion costs and timelines remain relatively unaltered with end-to-end (and we continue reiterate this is **FID to COD**) being in the range of **27-30 months for both in-house and LSTK conversions** at a yard. As mentioned in our last update one new player has emerged on the conversion scene with a pitch of doing the job in around 20 months – having raised eyebrows (and interest). Having digested the offering the reception in the market has been relatively muted and met with skepticism. Conversion costs remain in the range of **US$ 130 (TFDE) -170 (ST) million** (excluding contingencies and commissioning) for **500/750 SW/Glycol Open Loop**. Of course, the vanilla FSRU spec indicated may not reflect project specifications which we stress may materially alter the price (such as the “Singapore Unicorn” of MOL at ~US$ 414m).

The FSRU **newbuild market has been quiet**, but there are murmurings of players contemplating this for 2029-deliveries. However, with a steady stream of LNGCs ordered and 2028 effectively sold out it is less tempting for yards to pursue special projects. None of the requirements we see today are specifically requiring a newbuild and we reiterate the view that conversions currently give more bang for the buck.

We still expect a downtrend in the coming weeks due to seasonality, coupled with lower iron ore consumption in China. The most regular seasonal pattern is for the market to drop a bit more into the new year, but then find some stability or even firm up during the first two weeks of January. 

**Top left chart:** Hot metal output in China usually lags steel mill profitability by a few weeks. Output is suggested to continue falling in the coming weeks, with tentative signs that the fall will stop around late January. 
**Top right chart:** Higher backwardation = more urgency to buy, and vice versa. The futures curve suggests tailwinds for Capes through most of Q1, but the curve has recently become less backwardated. 
**Bottom left chart:** The price of copper is a good barometer of global industrial activity, and leads asset values with high accuracy. The suggestion is for further upside in values in the next months. 
**Bottom right chart:** Profit margins at steel mills in China have been trending down since July. There are some signs of stabilisation now, with HRC margins recently turning positive.

A potent set-up near-term, then the newbuilds come

After a strong end to the year, exceeding even our bull case scenario (who would have thought the way things looked a year ago, huh?) we may also be in for a stronger start to 2026 than we had earlier thought. Still, higher fleet growth and lower demand growth likely means a sliding rate trajectory through the year. There are, however, some potential triggers that may keep rates elevated. 

Below we outline three scenarios for next year, where our base case is unchanged as stronger demand going into the year is likely to be gradually offset by higher fleet growth than we had earlier thought too. 

By the end of 2027 the equivalent of more than 12% of the current fleet is scheduled to be delivered. It will take a lot for demand to grow anywhere near that much, and meaningful phase-out may take some time to emerge. Hence, we expect a much softer market in 2027.

Base case: Some continued oil production growth: 0.5-1 mbpd, most of which into the second half, and there is little need for the OPEC+ to further unwind production cuts. An oversupplied oil market can contribute to long-haul demand in the first half as contango supports economics - which could give a short-term spike for rates. However, eventual inventory builds in the West may drag. Fleet growth may rise to 4-5%. Strong start to the year, but a downward rate trajectory thereafter due to building fleet growth. 
 
Bull case: If oil demand surprises materially to the upside the OPEC+ can keep unwinding its production cuts, and U.S. production growth may continue. Further ship sanctions may give more compliant ship exit into the shadow market. Similarly, further sanctions on (Chinese) oil infrastructure or secondary sanctions could give further congestion. The most bullish (yet not very likely) scenario is one where Iran sanctions are lifted. 
 
Bear case: weaker than expected oil demand growth could send oil prices materially lower, so that the OPEC+ may need to cut production again and U.S. production declines. Even in a bear scenario there may initially not be a lot of phase-out, as rates should not plunge too far and alternative employment opportunities persist.
2026+27 forecasts: VLCC basis TD3c, Suez and Afra basis Baltic averages, LR2 basis TC1, LR2 basis TC2 and MR basis average Atlantic and Pacific averages

content.title: Global oil supply growth vs. tanker tonne-mile growth

content.content:
Russia can contribute to both up- and downside risk. If sanctions are more stringently enforced more floating storage of Russian oil may be necessary and buyers may need to replace with barrels from further away, which can give upside risk. Similarly, continued Ukrainian attacks on sanctioned tankers coupled with a potential EU ban on shipping services for Russian oil could give a need to increase the shadow fleet - further reducing the amount of compliant tankers. However, if sanctions are lifted or Russian production is materially cut, that can give downside risk. There are several sub-scenarios and nuances between the various tanker segments. However, experience so far shows there may be little change from the status quo... 

Similarly, China can continue building inventories which could give some incremental demand pull for tankers. After building an estimated 125 mb of new storage capacity this year, another 150 mb is expected to be built next year - nearly 0.5 mbpd of additional import potential.

content.content: Strong tanker demand and congestion is a potent mix for rates

Coupled with congestion and large parts of the fleet still being tied up in long-haul shipments or floating storage at the moment, elevated demand sets the market up for continued volatility at high levels near-term. 

November tonne-miles dipped a bit vs. the all-time-highs in October, on slightly less long-haul flows and slightly lower seaborne (crude) volumes. It remains elevated, however, and is likely to continue to do so although there may be some seasonal downside in coming months. Americas supply typically dips a bit in end-Q4 and Q1, although parts of that may be offset by refinery maintenance toward the end of Q1 which frees up more crude for exports.

One of the primary drivers for the latest and strongest leg up for rates has been congestion. This has in large part been driven by sanctions on terminals and oil infrastructure in China, delaying discharges, as well as bad weather. Average waiting time in the Far East for VLCC has more than doubled over the last months, and waiting time for Suezmaxes globally has nearly doubled since the summer. Additional import quotas for Chinese independent refiners and persistent bad weather may give continued congestion in the Far East near-term, but over the next few months an unwind may eventually become a headwind for tanker rates.
Supportive oil market, but is it enough?

Next year, volumes may grow at a substantially slower pace than this year. Energy agencies expect non-OPEC+ production growth of about 0.5 mbpd (vs. 1.8 mbpd this year) and a significantly oversupplied oil market. Hence, it is questionable whether the OPEC+ will resume production cut unwinds after Q1. Even if it does unwind the rest of the current 1.65 mbpd cut tranche, that may in reality only give about 0.5 mbpd real upside (vs. 2.1 mbpd growth this year). Only Saudi Arabia, Oman and Kuwait have spare capacity and upside to quotas, while others already produce well above targets. Russia does have upside to its target, but potential looks limited near-term - Urals discounts of $20/bbl or more suggests enough of a struggle to clear current production, although sanctions workarounds are likely. 

There are fewer new production projects scheduled to come onstream the next few years, which means that if oil demand keeps growing at recent pace (which may be much stronger than the IEA's estimates), the OPEC's spare capacity may eventually be tested. When that is closer to fully utilised, potentially already in 2027, current storage build-ups may have to be (partly) drawn again.

There are conflicting signs from the oil market about balances. Oil pricing does not indicate oversupply, with the Brent forward curve having been in backwardation nearly all year, apart from a small blip into contango a month and a half ago. That, along with strong refinery margins suggests that oil demand is much stronger than the IEA's forecasts. In the U.S. alone demand looks to be about 150 kbpd stronger than the IEA's estimates imply and there is strength elsewhere too. 

On the other hand, lowered OSPs from Middle Eastern producers and a West-East arbitrage which has now closed again do not imply an urgent demand pull, but rather abundant supply. WTI, as a marginal barrel, is currently not very well priced into either Europe or Asia, which could become a bit of a drag on tanker demand unless the WTI price drops going forward. Similarly, West African crude has struggled to clear, and a build-up of floating storage of sanctioned barrels suggest a glut.

Global inventories have built by about 1.4 mbpd YTD. There are not many periods historically when there have been this meaningful builds - especially if sustained (and more) into next year. A big portion of the YTD build is oil on the water (which ties up tonnage). A lot of that is sanctioned barrels, but also some compliant in long haul shipments from the last few months. Eventually, that is likely to hit either onshore storages or refineries and is real oversupply. 

OECD stocks have built less than the rest of the world. Going forward WTI (and other Atlantic grades) pricing may need to drop, otherwise there could be bigger builds also there, which may to a greater extent affect oil pricing due to greater visibility. If that causes steeper contango, it could support higher tanker demand for a while, although there then usually comes a 'hangover' after. If such a contango scenario coincides with some Q1 demand strength it could give another solid run for rates.

Refinery margins remain well above normal, driven by strong demand, elevated maintenance and some outages. As runs have recovered post maintenance now, and run estimates for next year are revised higher, margins have come off from the peaks, other than in China. 

Global refinery runs are close to maximum utilisation, apart from in China and Russia. The former cannot increase runs materially unless the government allow so, and the latter cannot because Ukrainian attacks do not allow so. 

Next year, about 1 mbpd of new refining capacity is expected, in China, India and the Middle East. That is on paper not enough to absorb the current oversupply of crude, let alone allow for further OPEC+ increases. Thus, the latter is questionable.

The tanker fleet has grown by 2% YTD, with another 0.6% scheduled through the remainder of the year, although most of that may slide into 2026. That means gross scheduled deliveries for 2026 will be about 6%. With elevated rates and most of what would already be phase-out candidates having migrated to the shadow markets, phase-out should remain low. That means net fleet growth could be 4-5% next year. Scheduled deliveries for 2027 are even higher, although by then some more compliant vessels may become eligible for phase-out. 

The orderbook to fleet ratio has grown to 16%, but including reported orders which have not yet been officially confirmed it could be at about 18%, if not more.

While phase-out potential is vast, it may take a while before scrapping materially picks up. Most of what would otherwise be phase-out candidates is already semi-phased out of the compliant market. Sanctions could tilt the picture, depending on what happens next. With the EU considering a ban on maritime services for Russian oil shipments, Ukrainian attacks on sanctioned Suezmaxes, the U.S. seizing a sanctioned VLCC off Venezuela etc. there may be a greater urgency to increase the shadow fleet, which could tighten the compliant fleet.  

In a steady state scenario, however, rates need to soften substantially before there is any meaningful scrapping. From 2027/28 onwards, when more compliant tankers reach historical average scrap ages, there should be some more potential again - which could set the stage for a market recovery.

content.content: Asset values well supported currently, downside risk ahead

With historically elevated spot and TC rates values have recovered across segments over the last few months. This is well supported as TC rates can derisk high values substantially. Near-term, would-be buyers are forced to lift bids to meet an ever increasing ask from sellers. 

Given our market outlook, however, there is downside risk. Newbuild prices may be relatively well supported as order backlogs are comfortable for yards, input prices remain high, and ordering interest in several shipping segments is strong. For secondhand, which is priced 10-20% above the depreciated newbuild price curve, even more so for very modern VLCCs and Suezmaxes, there is bigger downside risk down the line.

The Jan/Feb low season is approaching, so the spot market will continue falling in the coming weeks. We think a Q1 average similar to 2024 (24kpd) is more likely than 2023 (9kpd) or 2025 (13kpd). 

**Top left chart:** Hot metal output in China usually lags steel mill profitability by a few weeks. We pointed to this as a downside risk for the market, but falling output has been counteracted by inventory building. Output is suggested to continue falling in the coming weeks. 
**Top right chart:** Higher backwardation = more urgency to buy, and vice versa. The iron ore futures curve suggested headwinds for Capes in Q4. Why these headwinds did not impact the market negatively is due to the mentioned inventory building, along with Bauxite and Coal volumes. The futures curve is now suggesting tailwinds for Capes in Q1, however, as it is suggesting iron ore consumption could rise again. 
**Bottom left chart:** The price of copper is a good barometer of global industrial activity, and leads asset values with high accuracy. The suggestion is for further upside in values in the next months. 
**Bottom right chart:** The iron ore spot price served as a very good leading indicator of the market direction for a few years - until the middle of this year. Why did the market rally this summer even as the iron ore spot price lead suggested it would continue to be weak? The futures curve lead was backwardated during the same period, along with a preference for higher grades of iron ore, supporting ton-miles.

In our previous monthly update in October, we wrote:
*As the first month of Q4 is about to end, the bearish seasonality seems to repeat itself, as spot markets are down from the peak levels in September/October. For a few months, increased contango in the iron ore futures curve warned that iron ore demand could slow down in Q4, which is now seen in China’s consumption data, as daily import demand has fallen from slightly above 3.01 mtpd to 2.96 mtpd. Otherwise, contango in the coal futures curve has increased,  and China is well-stocked on Soybeans. On the other hand, prices of industrial metals keep rising, reflecting firm underlying demand for minor bulks. So we do not expect any major weakness for the remainder of Q4, but a lower average than Q3 still seems likely. 
Regarding Q1 next year, the mentioned iron ore futures curve is already suggesting rising iron ore demand, the coal futures curve is much less in contango than earlier this year, with improving global manufacturing conditions and various climate factors like a weak polar vortex, potentially weak la nina and above average snow cover in Siberia suggesting the upcoming winter could be colder than usual in the northern hemisphere, supporting the demand for coal. Brazil’s planting area for Soybeans and Corn is larger than last season, so if conditions turn out right, there could be more agriprods shipped next year than this year. So although Q1, as usual, is likely to be lower than Q4, we do not expect the kind of Q1 where there is an extended "opex market". 
For 2026 in full, we expect earnings to average similar to those in 2024. As of now, we believe a slightly higher average than 2024 is more likely than a slightly lower one.*

As November draws to a close, the BDI has averaged 3.5% higher so far in Q4 than in Q3. Falling iron ore consumption in China has not negatively affected Capes, as this has been counteracted by inventory building, the onset of the bauxite shipment season, and improved coal volumes. The improvement in coal fundamentals has also benefited the other segments, most notably Panamaxes, where Indonesian RVs keep making year-to-date highs. Otherwise, minor bulks demand growth remains strong, although momentum could be at a near-term peak, going by the correction in industrial metals prices since late October, which in turn signals that Handies and Supras/Ultras spot markets will not climb above the peak seen in late October before year-end. 
We updated our earnings estimates for next year, reflecting that we think 2026 is likely to average a bit higher than in 2024. Commodity price levels (industrial metals, iron ore, coal, oil), manufacturing data, interest rate levels, cycle comparisons, and the supply situation all look comparably stronger than the months before we entered 2024. So, we think it is reasonable to expect the highs in second-hand values and 1-year tc rates seen that year for Kamsarmaxes, Ultras/Supras and Handies to be reached and/or exceeded next year, probably during Q2. For Capes, the story is a bit different in terms of second-hand values, as values have kept climbing despite the market weakness seen between Q4 last year and the first half of this year. Further upside is harder to expect, even with a bullish outlook on fundamentals. 2027 is still premature to call, but tentatively, we expect the markets to average lower than in 2026.

content.content: TRADE FLOWS YEAR ON YEAR GROWTH

This page gives brief comments on what the charts on the next page tells us. 

Top left chart:

The BDI year-on-year change have moved into positive territory in the last months, a few months before the 12-month lead of China's credit growth suggested. The credit growth rate suggests the positive trend will continue through next year. This is further supported by the positive year-on-year change of truck and excavator sales in China. 

Top right chart:

The relative improvement in China's economic growth continues, with October data showing 0% year on year, meaning China is no longer in contraction, for the first time since January 2024. 
Direction-wise, the correlation of China's growth with global dry bulk volume growth holds, but as written in our previous monthly report, as a growth *driver*, China is becoming less relevant. Emerging economies, primarily in the Indian Ocean region and Southeast Asia, are becoming more relevant. 

Middle left chart:

Lower crude oil prices are bullish for economic growth, and vice versa. The chart displays that since 2017, there has been a tight correlation between lower year-on-year oil prices and a higher year-on-year BDI, with the oil price change leading by 1 year. 
Cheaper oil prices suggest the BDI could remain positive year-on-year throughout next year. 

Middle right chart:

Lower global interest rates strongly suggest 1-year TC rates will continue rising from here, and be above this year's levels throughout next year. Tentative signs of a peak in early 2027, however, 

Bottom left chart:

Direction-wise, the correlation between the OECD G20 Diffusion index and the BDI year-on-year change has held up as usual, but the OECD index has outperformed over the last year, as services growth (primarily driven by the AI boom) stayed high despite the downturn in manufacturing. The OECD diffusion index level looks set for a push higher to peak cycle levels (the index is still below the peaks seen in 2021, 2017, etc..) next year, along with a surge of the BDI year on year change. 

Bottom right chart:

The dollar index has weakened in the last months, and as usual, the result is increased dry bulk shipment volume growth with a few months' lag. The dollar index suggests total dry bulk shipment volume growth will rise to an average of 4%-5% on a six-month moving average basis.

In our previous monthly update in September, we wrote:
*As we are about to enter Q4, it is worth noting that over the last 10 years, the BDI has averaged lower in Q4 than in Q3 eight out of ten years. Apart from seasonal factors, the surge in demand growth seen for Panamax, Supra, and Handy in July and August was so strong that a temporary exhaustion would be natural. The year-on-year growth in total shipment volumes for those segments has averaged 6% in the last three months, with the previous seven similar demand surges seen in the last 10 years leading to at best sideways over the following months. For the dry bulk segment in total, a similar comparison can be made, as the 7% year-on-year growth in July and August exceeds the 5% average seen during upcycles. The CAGR for total dry bulk shipment volumes was 2.4% between 2017-2024 (a close match with global GDP growth). So, demand downcycles usually bottom around 0% growth, like in the first half of this year, and demand upcycles usually peak around 5% growth. In April this year, Trump’s trade policies posed a severe risk of the global growth baseline declining significantly from the 2017-2024 average, but fortunately, he went back on most of those policies, though, of course, there is a lingering risk in that regard. 
Regarding 2026, the bullish factors are stacking up, so our view that 26 would average higher than 25, held since September last year, still looks likely. The main risk, as we see it, is the potential for a US recession, but this also depends on what type of US recession it is. If Trump’s tariffs is the factor that causes it, then it will likely go along with higher inflation, which in turn could lead to a reversal in US monetary policy, causing the Dollar to strengthen and forcing the World ex-US to raise interest rates. The US dollar is an important driver of dry bulk demand (shown on the last page of this report), so it bears close watching.* 

As the first month of Q4 is about to end, the bearish seasonality seems to repeat itself, as spot markets are down from the peak levels in September/October. For a few months, increased contango in the iron ore futures curve warned that iron ore demand could slow down in Q4, which is now seen in China’s consumption data, as daily import demand has fallen from slightly above 3.01 mtpd to 2.96 mtpd. Otherwise, contango in the coal futures curve has increased,  and China is well-stocked on Soybeans. On the other hand, prices of industrial metals keep rising, reflecting firm underlying demand for minor bulks. So we do not expect any major weakness for the remainder of Q4, but a lower average than Q3 still seems likely. 
Regarding Q1 next year, the mentioned iron ore futures curve is already suggesting rising iron ore demand, the coal futures curve is much less in contango than earlier this year, with improving global manufacturing conditions and various climate factors like a weak polar vortex, potentially weak la nina and above average snow cover in Siberia suggesting the upcoming winter could be colder than usual in the northern hemisphere, supporting the demand for coal. Brazil’s planting area for Soybeans and Corn is larger than last season, so if conditions turn out right, there could be more agriprods shipped next year than this year. So although Q1, as usual, is likely to be lower than Q4, we do not expect the kind of Q1 where there is an extended "opex market". 
For 2026 in full, we expect earnings to average similar to those in 2024. As of now, we believe a slightly higher average than 2024 is more likely than a slightly lower one.
