content.content: TRADE FLOWS YEAR ON YEAR GROWTH

This page gives brief comments on what the charts on the next page tells us. 

Top left chart:

China's credit growth remains relatively high, with the last three months' average at 15% - the highest since early 2021. A positive BDI year on year change is suggested from the start of next year. 

Top right chart:

China's economic growth index has seen a relative improvement over the last months, with growth in September at -1.3%, up from a low of -6.5% in February. 
The average growth rate for the year is -4.0%, compared to -3.3% in 2024. The average growth rate since 2020 is +0.4%, clearly displaying that China is peaking, which can also be seen from crude steel production. 
Emerging economies are becoming more relevant, which is why dry bulk demand growth has started to decouple from China's economic growth in the last 2 years. 

Middle left chart:

Lower crude oil prices are bullish for economic growth, and vice versa. The chart displays that since 2017, there has been a tight correlation between lower year-on-year oil prices and a higher year-on-year BDI, with the oil price change leading by 1 year. 
This indicator suggests the BDI year-on-year change is past the low point, and that it will trend upwards over the next year. Should one trust the indicator 100%, there will be a dip in the BDI year-on-year change in the coming months, however. 

Middle right chart:

Global interest rate cuts suggest 1-year TC rates will be higher during the second half of 2026 than what it was through the first half of this year. That implies at least the mid-teens for Kamsarmaxes. Further, it implies 1-year TC rates could be higher than what it is now in the first part of 2027. There are early signs of a cycle top at the start of 2027, as the rate of interest rate cuts has fallen slightly from the peak. 

Bottom left chart:

The OECD G-20 Diffusion index and the BDI year on year change have correlated tightly for decades. However, over the last year, there has been a decoupling, as the Diffusion index suggests the global economy is at peak cycle, whereas the BDI year-on-year change have been in downcycle territory since Q4 last year. The main reason for this decoupling is that the services sector has driven most of global economic growth over the last year, whereas manufacturing has been weak. However, manufacturing is in the early innings of an upswing, signalled by JP Morgan's Global Manufacturing PMI, which remained strong in September, with a reading of 50.8, a slight decline from the 14-month high reading in August. 

Bottom right chart:

The dollar index has weakened in the last months, and as usual, the result is increased dry bulk shipment volume growth with a few months' lag. The dollar index suggests total dry bulk shipment volume growth will rise to an average of 4%-5% on a six-month moving average basis.

content.content: FRED, OECD, S&P Global, MySteel, AxsMarine, Baltic Exchange

Over the last month there have been quite a few events including U.S. sanctions on tankers and Chinese oil infrastructure companies, China's Special Port Fees in response to the USTR 301, the EU's 19th Russia sanctions package, U.S. sanctions on Rosneft and Lukoil, and now a U.S.-China trade truce. And then there are typhoons and hurricanes. It seems every time oil pricing and tankers rates start to take a breather, some event happens to boost sentiment. In an already tight underlying market that can produce very high rates. 

This stands in stark contrast to the first half of the year, when the fundamentals were not that much weaker than now, yet there is a big a difference for rates. More volatility is expected through the remainder of the year, with a rate trajectory more in line with our bull case - for which most factors have played out. 

This also likely means a firmer trajectory into next year than earlier expected in our base case, which possibly means some upside risks for next year's forecasts due to a strong Q1. During the remainder of the year, however, with fleet growth picking up and demand growth slowing, we expect limited changes to our outlook. Similarly, the trajectory into 2027 also looks somewhat softer - although not as much as in previous market downturns. 

In the longer term more investment in fleet renewal will be needed. For now, most phase-out candidates have found employment in the shadow market, and are thus already phased out of normal trade. The next 'wave' of compliant phase-out may come in 2028-30 when more compliant vessels come up toward historical phase-out ages.

After September's Atlantic fixing rush preliminary October tonne-miles have soared, especially for crude tankers. This is driven by higher production both in the Americas and from the OPEC+ and by the big supply push West-East in September amid a wide open arbitrage. Since then, however, the West-East arb. has eased, apart from the most recent Russia sanctions induced (short-term) spike. 

Americas exports typically ease somewhat in Q4 due to higher local demand and some production maintenance in Brazil - partly offset by rising MEG production. Hence, tonne-mile demand may soften slightly from the recent peak. Still, global volumes remain high, as should tanker demand be through the remainder of the year and into next year.

Loadings in October to date have eased slightly from the highs in September, but remain near all-time seasonal highs for crude tankers. Product flows have slid somewhat more on extended refinery maintenance and Russian outages.

content.content:
In coming months there may be slight downside to seaborne flows. One thing is refineries coming back out of maintenance, which could give some less crude oil export potential from the likes of the U.S. Another is that the biggest growth engine of global supply over the last years, the Americas, may see some downside. The EIA expects a 450 kbpd Q/Q decline in Q4 vs. Q3 2025 production (mainly in Brazil), and another 560 kbpd quarterly drop (mainly Canada and partly U.S.) in the first quarter of next year. The latter may be offset by refinery maintenance and higher seasonal U.S. exports, and hinges on the EIA being right that U.S. crude production will decline by about 100 kbpd per quarter after year-end. 

The OPEC+ may offset some of the downside, assuming that the group will continue its gradual monthly unwinds of production cuts. However, all producers but Saudi Arabia, Oman and Russia already exceed their production targets, and hence upside is somewhat limited vs. the headline numbers - especially as Russian output may come under some further pressure. 

Both the EIA and IEA currently expect global oil supply growth of about 0.5 mbpd next year. If the OPEC+ fully unwinds the current tranche of cuts, that likely means another about 0.5 mbpd. Assuming all of that hits the water it means about 2% seaborne volume growth potential.

content.title: Global oil supply vs. VLCC demand growth

content.content: Source: EIA, IEA, OPEC, Fearnleys, Vortexa

Not that more production is necessarily needed for the oil market balance near-term, as most expect a growing oversupply of oil going forward. The IEA's oversupply estimates are likely vastly exaggerated, but some more build-up in the coming few quarters is likely as global oil supply in Q4 is estimated to be 2-3 mbpd higher than in Q2, depending on which energy agency you look at. Demand is likely higher than the IEA estimates, but not by that much, hence some bigger inventory builds are likely. 

YTD through the first three quarters global inventories have built by 1.3 mbpd, far less than the IEA's implied balance of nearly 2 mbpd. Most of that build has been in non-OECD, but OECD inventories have also built by nearly 0.4 mbpd. Hence, unless oil demand or supply dramatically surprise there could be further pressure on oil prices and in turn production going forward - although that is partly baked into energy agency forecasts.

A part of what has been driving the oversupply is sanctioned flows. YTD these are on average about 250 kbpd higher than last year (when they were also up 250 kbpd). Over the last two months, however, exports are 700 kbpd higher y/y. Due to a combination of sanctions/inefficiencies and exhausted crude import quotas for independent Chinese refiners, a lot of this has ended up as oil in transit - explaining most of the surge in this figure which has been widely reported by media the last few weeks. These are in other words (delayed) floating inventories waiting to discharge. 

Assuming Russian exports will not be greatly affected by Trump's latest sanctions, buyers of sanctioned flows may not be in great rush to replace, although there has been some initial scrambling. The wording in the sanctions on Rosneft and Lukoil provide flexibility with regards to enforcement - possibly in order to avoid too big a reaction in oil prices. There have already been reports of cargoes offered from other sellers than Rosneft and Lukoil and that the discount for Urals has widened by about $5/bbl to lure Chinese and Indian buyers back in. With Murban and Dubai prices quickly giving up most of the premium gained after the sanctions, it would seem the 'market' is relatively undaunted. There are reports that Indian refiners now have big tenders for Atlantic crude, but at first glance these are not vastly higher than Indian imports from the basin has been in the past.

Refinery margins have generally been stronger than most expected this year, still runs are only estimated to be 0.6 mbpd higher vs. last year, and for next year the IEA forecasts less than 0.5 mbpd growth. This is more a function of limited spare capacity than economics, other than in areas where it is curbed (China) or incapacitated (Russia). There has also been unplanned outages and extensive maintenance contributing. 

Crack spreads are currently the strongest for gasoil in Europe, propped up by the Russian outages, refinery shutdowns over time, a lighter crude slate and other outages. The latest hit to supply is the Al Zour fire - a key supplier of winter grade gasoil for Europe. This should be supportive of arbitrages into Europe, but has not really been. Gasoil has also been boosted globally by Russia supply related fears - to the point where MEG gasoil has been better priced into Asia than Europe, for instance. Similarly, U.S. gasoil has been better priced into South America than Europe - partly on very high freight. Jet, however, is somewhat better priced to move East-West (particularly USWC), although also works to Asia. 

The normal TC2 gasoline arb. however, is negatively affected by (abnormally) low gasoline cracks in the U.S. which skews the Atlantic MR picture these days - although ever returning Dangote outages gives a home for European gasoline into West Africa.
Plenty of ships, for a while

Fleet growth YTD through the beginning of October had been 1.7%, with another 1% scheduled to be delivered through year-end. The orderbook to fleet ratio has crept up to 15%, which is not scary in a historical context, especially considering that 15.5% of the fleet is already 20+ years old. 

Some more (old) vessels have been sold at suspiciously strong prices to undisclosed or questionable buyers, suggesting that they have or probably will leave the compliant market. Hence, effective fleet growth for the compliant market is probably closer to zero YTD. 

The next couple of years, however, fleet growth may pick up to closer to 5%, depending on phase-out.

What would normally be phase-out candidates have in recent years ventured into the shadow markets, and hence are already phased out of the compliant market. Some more older vessels might follow in coming years, depending on sanctions enforcement. Still, this also means that it is not until 2028-30 that the next 'wave' of phase-out candidates will reach normal phase-out age, so unless rates plunge it is unlikely that scrapping will pick up meaningfully near-term.

Ordering has continued, with nearly 19m dwt ordered YTD, and some more to come with a few reported orders in recent weeks. 15% of the YTD reported orders are scheduled for delivery next year, 46% in 2027 and 28% in 2028. The YTD tally is thus already higher than the historical average of 15.8m dwt, but just about half of last year's. 

Demolition remains low, as the 1.9m dwt YTD is still far below the historical average of 7.5m dwt, albeit much higher than the last two years. The 24 tankers demolished YTD were on average 25 years old.

With an FSRU market that is all but sold out and only a handful units (maybe) available, the inevitable smell of “fast” profits is attracting people to the sector. The “Big 5” FSRU players are moving in cautious pace with our count of semi-speculative positions being 3-4 depending on how one counts. Those players long conversion tonnage appear to have taken position on regas modules while those short tonnage have secured/are working to secure tonnage before moving to long-lead items.

Based on our conversations running up to Gastech in September, the landscape seems to be widening with more (both known and unknown) names considering to throw their hat in the ring. Admittedly, a segment where 10yr deals can be done with payback of 5.5-7.5 years should generate attention in board rooms whether owning an LNGC or not. As always, capital may be perceived as a barrier to entry and not everyone can afford to take lottery tickets at US$ 250m a ticket. But history has clearly shown that capital will flow to segments of high return, irrespective of the understanding of the odds of the game. As we see more names positioning, we highlight the importance of operations in the world of FSRUs. While possible to use 3rd party managers, the real moat for FSRU players lies in knowing their assets and the needs of their clients (as the clients every now and then don’t understand it themselves).

It may perhaps be superfluous to say that we remain positive to the FSRU market, but underlying fundamentals continue to point in the right direction with limited firm orders/news of conversions. However, they are happening under the radar and we expect to see the news surface over the next 6 months. The demand side is still “on fire”…but as usual the fuse is a little longer. Based on our assessment, we see 4-8 new (credible-ish) projects likely to come to market in 2026 for tonnage – keeping the rate environment elevated.
Key market developments during the quarter

JULY

DET sold capacity at **W’haven 1** (2026 slots) and **W’haven 2** (2025+2026 slots) in July with all slots sold. **W’haven 1** secured prices around EUR 0.26 for Obligation to Deliver (OTD) and EUR 0.40 for No-OTD (NOTD). W’haven 2 slots came in at EUR 0.29/EUR 0.36 (OTD/NOTD) for 2025 and a flat EUR 0.22 (OTD & NOTD) for 2026. The low-ish pricing seem to reflect DETs public subsidy package (~EUR 5bn) announed late-24 which effectively means they can give away capacity at the expense of German tax-payers. It is worth highlighting the prices does not include Gas-in-kind which is reported at around 1% during summer (0.7% / 1.3%) and 2.2% during winter.

DET confirmed **ENERGOS FORCE** on a short-term lease to EGAS with the FSRU to be berthed in Jordan at the Aqaba-terminal. The FSRU is expected to be back in Germany late-25/early-26 as the German government has urged DET and HEH to find a solution to the fallout around Stade. The FSRU will likely be in place until Stade onshore commences operations in late-27/early-28, leaving ~5 year of firm charter period.

EGAS concluded its FSRU chartering spree with **ENERGOS WINTER** heading for Damietta under a 5-yr charter. The TC rate is rumoured to be in the USD 115k-130k/day range – a very healthy rate considering the size and specifications of the unit.

TGS in Brazil is now a “plug-and-play” ready terminal after **ENERGOS WINTER** departed for planned drydock and subsequent charter to EGAS. We expect to see interest in TGS for the upcoming power auctions.

Squadron Energy confirms their intention to commence operations at Port Kembla with **HOEGH GALLEON** in 2027. While the demand picture in Australia remains murky at best, driven by political undercurrents – it would be good to see the FSRU head to her allocated destination after finishing intermediate operations in Egypt.

**Petronet** receives approval for a 5mtpa onshore terminal, replacing former plans of a 4mtpa FSRU. The project was on our list of likely to materialize with a project score of 62 (out of 100) and the decision to go onshore is another note to buy a big scissor when doing FSRU projects in India (to be able to cut through all the red tape).

AUGUST

**AG&P LNG** announces completion of the acquisition of Venice Energy’s Outer Harbour project and targets FID by end-25. While it remains unclear which until will be used, the storyline remains consistent with a 145,000cbm unit with ~250-300MMSCFD nominal capacity. Timing for startup is not entirely clear, but has been talks of 2028 which would make sense given nothing firm has been seen on the FSRU conversion.

Seatrium and **Karpowerships** cement their relationship following the latest FSRU conversion – adding three more FSRUs to the “todo”-list for Seatrium. While all Karadeniz FSRUs to-date are low pressure/low send-out there have been talks of adding one high pressure/high send-out unit for conversion. Seatrium and Karpower also agreed on Seatrium doing integration on 4+2 powerships, which is technically a bigger deal than three FSRU conversions in our view.

DETs latest addition to the FSRU front – W’haven 2 (**EXCELSIOR**) – commenced commercial operations late-Aug. Following an extensive delay to the project, the FSRU is the third operational unit in Germany which will only operate until 2028 as the original deal was 5 years (of which 2.5 has already passed with zero send-out).

**LNGCROATIA** went offline as she departed for Turkey for a planned 5-year drydock and installation of the fourth regas train (212MMSCFD) which will increase capacity to a peak of 596MMSCFD. 

After a lot of back and forth which according to rumours had both **ENERGOS FORCE** and **ENERGOS WINTER** heading for Iraq, it was announced that there were two remaining players for the FSRU to be located at Khor Al-Zubair. The two remaining players were Breeze Investments (reportedly working with ADNOC) and Excelerate Energy. On 1st October, **Excelerate** announced having won the project and while it is not clear which FSRUs have been offered, we expect it to be a subset of Excelerate FSRUs, including the newbuild **EXCELERATE ACADIA**. In any case, the deal is expected to include supply of LNG and FSRU on what is likely a G-t-G initiative.

SEPTEMBER

Polish **Gaz-System** is testing interest for another FSRU in Gdansk Bay. The first FSRU is a newbuild currently under construction for MOL who won a tender reportedly in close contest with BW LNG. The **second FSRU** has no timing, but depending on market interest and open seasons we would expect startup in the early-2030s. 

**BOTAS** effectively confirmed their demand for FSRUs for the next three years at least with a total of 4.5BCMA (3.25mtpa) of deals with **BP, ENI and Shell**. While BOTAS has a seasonal profile on their gas demand, the deals announced would suggest BOTAS will have a more steady send-out as they target to distribute gas to European markets in addition to serving domestic demand.

The **ALEXANDROUPOLIS** has had a rocky start since commencing commercial operations a year ago – and was expected to be at full capacity after a lengthy shut-down. In August, Gastrade stated the terminal would be at full capacity from start of the gas-year (October). However, mid-September it was announced that the terminal would be at 75% for some time before full capacity is reached. No cargo has been delivered since Jan-25.

**Excelerate** made local headlines when receiving a 30-yr license for FSRU at **Haldia, Kolkata (India)**. The license holds a capacity of 1.5mtpa expandable to 3.0mtpa and will according to plan start in H2/27. The project will connect to GAILs JHBDPL-pipeline which is close to finished. While it is not the first time we see projects in Kolkata, this could be a fresh start and maybe kick off natural gas from an FSRU to India.

**Seapeak and VOPAK** formalized the (well-known) tie up in Australia for the Port Philip Bay in Victoria, Australia. While no specifics of the selected FSRU have been announced, we lean towards the older **165,000cbm DFDE/TFDEs**. The project is targeted for start-up in 2029.
Quarterly focus: Walking on sunshine – the impact of growth in solar PV generation on FSRU demand

There has been limited activity on the corporate front also in Q3/25 although Q4/25 may bring some interesting perspectives with interest payment due on NFEs bonds in November.

As with previous editions of this quarterly, we take the opportunity to reflect on topics that have underlying impact on the FSRU market. This time we scratch the surface of one of the FSRUs semi-distant cousins; the PV market. PV (Photo Voltaic) is one of the fastest growing parts of the global energy mix having recorded a growth of 720% in the past decade and 150% in the past five years according to BPs Statistical Energy Review – totalling 1.9TW of installed capacity at the end of 2024. The growth is staggering; 26% CAGR since 2015! This contrasts LNG, the most rapidly growing fossil fuel, at a measly 5.2%. The beauty of PV (and wind for that matter) is the need for large-scale, reliable, flexible, rapid ramp-up and cost efficient thermal power generation; natural-gas fired power plants. To manage the inherent shifts in peak demand driven by daytime PV generation to evenings (the duck curve for all the power market geeks out there); a large capacity reserve in the form of gas-turbine power generation is needed.

Brazil is a wonderful example of how FSRUs provide a solution to multiple challenges; starting out as a source of gas to balance reduced production from hydropower in the early part of the millennium (GOLAR SPIRIT, GOLAR WINTER and VT3) to enabling capacity reserve solutions today (ENERGOS NANOOK). Brazil had 53GW of PV installed in 2024, up from 8GW in 2020 – and the upcoming power auctions (to which numerous FSRU projects are being developed for) are by and large generation capacity to balance the market on back of PV growth. This is one of the key reasons for why we are long-term bullish on FSRUs in Brazil.

Now, one would be prone to look for alternative rapidly growing markets with similar characteristics on PV (or wind). Asian markets such as Vietnam, Malaysia and Philippines are earlier in the growth curve compared to Brazil, but they are coming – and the heavy dependence on coal-fired power generation mixes (no pun intended) badly with PV. While slow and bureaucratic these markets will eventually need FSRUs to unlock the relentless market forces of PV as one of the lowest cost sources of electricity on a levelized basis (LCOE – another one for the power geeks). Of course, efficient auctions, subsidies and other factors come into play, but PV is in fact one of the biggest supporters of FSRUs. So, while FSRU players may already feel like they are “walking on sunshine” given the current market environment; put on shades because the future is bright!

Q3 was another (consecutive) record-breaking quarter for FSRU imports as the announced charters earlier in the year are starting to operate. Overall activity at operational FSRUs reached a total of **18.8mt / 306 cargoes in Q3/25** (which is up 43% from 13.1mt / 223 cargoes in Q3/24 – and 22% from 15.4mt / 255 cargoes in Q2/25). The Y-o-Y increase is driven by-and-large by **Europe and Egypt**. Europe hit a high of 7.3mt during the quarter while Egypt racked up a whopping 3.5mt in Q3/25 (1.3mt in Q1/25). In Europe, the full quarter effect of W’haven 2 and Ravenna added together with a breakneck pace at Eemshaven. In Egypt, we see three FSRUs now fully operational after start of **ENERGOS ESKIMO** and **ENERGOS POWER** in July-25. Global LNG imports in Q3/25 came in at 108mt; which now means **FSRUs account for 16% of global LNG receipts**. 

The prize for most busy terminal goes for the second quarter in a row to Eemshaven with a total of 26 cargoes (a cargo every 3.5 days which is extremely demanding operationally. We again give a BIG UP for the crews onboard **ENERGOS IGLOO** and **EEMSHAVEN LNG**. While the number of terminals not regasifying has dropped substantially the last year, there are a few crews that get a lot of R&R. **ENERGOS NANOOK**, **BW BATANGAS**, **CAPE ANN** and **SAROS** all counted doughnuts in Q3/25.

The pace at which FSRUs are gathering operational momentum may be lost on the general population, but it is without doubt underpinning the fact that FSRUs are both rapidly deployable and can quickly add to the energy mix for those in need. Put an FSRU up against a land-based terminal and the FSRU will outcompete on cost and time every time. In light of the wave of LNG supply the world will experience over the coming years we continue to stress the point that FSRUs offer the fastest way to open new markets – and expand existing ones.

content.title: Monthly volumes imported through FSRUs by region (2025)

content.content:
*Asia & Middle East*

**Petrovietnam** requirement for FSRU in Ba Ria, Vung Tau issued in Q1 continues to move slow. Initially targeted for the 2026-2029 period, the timing remains slippery as the end-user EVN appears to not know what it wants. 

**Australia** is moving ahead on several fronts with VOPAK formally announcing Seapeak as their partner for the project in Victoria. Viva is also in parallel working to get Geelong off the ground.

*Europe & Mediterreanean*

**Ireland** continues to grind through its seemingly endless bureaucratic process of getting an FSRU in place. FSRU providers have been approached, but timing (and location) remains uncertain.

**Italian** FSRU activity may pick up with Snam having been mandated to set up an FSRU in Oristano (and potentially in Porto Torres) on Sardinia.

*Americas & Caribbean*

**Colombia’s Ecopetrol** and the Ballena LNG project is a hot potato as “everyone” has tried with limited luck. The lack of near-term availability is causing issues locally which we do not see resolved with anything but a reset of timelines and a conversion FSRU. 

We see more activity in **Brazil** as the disappointment of the cancellation of power auction earlier in the year is starting to transition into positioning for the next auction. The long timelines for A-4 or A-5 fit well with development of conversion FSRUs.

**Guatemala** issued a 1.4GW tender earlier in the year with one (of many) alternatives is to do a LNG-to-Power project with a dedicated FSRU.

*Africa & Other*

**Morocco** has received feedback on its EOI with deadline in Jul-25. The initial EOI was in plain language a “tell me what you want to do or can do” and the feedback seems to be clear that it will be an unbundled process with FSRU being offered separately. 

**Ivory Coast** is back on the FSRU-track with reports of an FSRU being sourced for Abidjan. The project would be the second or third project after CI-GNL failed some years back. Godspeed.

*We encourage clients with deeper interest in ongoing project developments, tender activity and business development to contact Fearnleys directly; the above is merely scratching the surface of activity.*

As the FSRU market is by and large sold out there are limited units moving around (which is in many ways good).

The most notable movement for an FSRU during the quarter has been **ENERGOS FREEZE** reaching Dominican Republic late-Aug/early-Sep to start operations for Energia 2000 on a 3-year charter.

Additionally, the **ENERGOS WINTER** arrived at Damietta, Egypt late-Sep and is expected to add to Egypt’s already sky-rocketing regas capacity.

**LNG CROATIA** is currently undergoing periodic drydock and installation of its 4th regas train at Kuzey Star in Turkey.

**ETYFA PROMETHEUS** remains in Malacca where works to complete the unit is ongoing still.

**BAUHINIA SPIRIT** has according to her vessel movements departed station three times during the quarter – likely as a precaution for adverse weather conditions. She is at present back at site close to Hong Kong.
Asset values: Newbuildings and conversion candidates

The FSRU market remains virtually sold out and we continue to see 2026 as a very active year for project developers and FSRU players alike. The width of type of projects (national security, private initiatives and a healthy mix of grid and power) suggests a decent part of the pipeline will materialize. The skepticism and conservativism of the FSRU providers appears to show a few slight cracks – benefitting the supply/demand balance. We hear a few speculative regas positions and pre-engineering in the works to shorten lead times. We also see more S&P transactions as conversion candidates needs to be secured. Prices for donor vessels have not stopped the drop and discussions on STs (138k-145k) are ranging between low-20s and high-30s while larger DFDE/TFDEs (160k-174k) are a much wider range. While some projects only need the “cheap and cheerful” FSRU, there has been a notable trend shift towards larger and more modern conversion candidates in our discussions.

Conversion costs/timelines remains relatively static with end-to-end delivery of a conversion being in the range of 27-30 months (from FID to COD) based on both in-house managed and lumpsum-turnkey conversions at Asian yards. We’ve seen one newcomer offering complete conversions in 18-20 months (ex-yard) which has definitely opened eyes, but the comfort level on this timeline is still limited. Costs remain in the range of US$130-170 million (excluding contingencies and commissioning) for 500/750 SW/Glycol Open Loop – the difference being primarily related to the type of donor vessel and installed power.

The FSRU newbuild market has been dead quiet over the quarter – and with high tendering activity for LNGCs and yard slots in that space now being marketed for Q3/28-deliveryes – we find newbuilds to be driven by project-specific situations rather than economic considerations.

The average daily spot earnings across the three index routes reached $75,000 per day in Q3, driven by a tighter market environment. This elevated the year-to-date average to $54,000 per day, marking a $10,000 increase from the post-Q2 figure—a 4.8% quarterly rise and a 45.6% year-on-year gain.

Q3 was largely defined by efforts to establish a new "normal" following the significant disruptions triggered by "Liberation Day" in April. The quarter was notably impacted by the widening spread between West and East cargo premiums, *as can be seen on above graph.* This shift was primarily driven by uncertainty surrounding the USTR and its pending rulings, which created confusion and concern as the fixing window approached the October 14th implementation date.

At the time of writing, operational clarity remains elusive, though consensus suggests the system will take effect next week as scheduled. The U.S. Customs and Border Protection has posted payment details for the fees, and they emphasize that it is entirely up to the Operator to determine whether the ship is due to pay. The fees are intended to target U.S. imports—specifically laden arrivals, which do not typically include VLGCs. However, ships that are Chinese-owned and/or operated will be subject to the fees regardless of arrival mode or country of build.

This regulatory uncertainty had a tangible impact on freight rates in September. Affected ships began repositioning toward the Middle East, and a notable premium emerged for West cargoes. At its peak, the premium reached $16,500 per day, with the monthly average settling at $11,300 per day. Nevertheless, if the premium becomes sufficiently attractive, even affected ships may resume lifting in the U.S., which could help rebalance the market and restore equilibrium.
U.S. Production and Terminal Capacity Expansion

U.S. LPG production continues to rise, with total output increasing by 75% over the past ten years. While growth is expected to moderate to approximately 5% over the next three years, export capacity is projected to expand significantly during the same period. Domestic consumption remains stable, as do export levels, which consistently hover around 60%. All residual volumes of LPG that is not domestically consumed, will be priced to clear out - enabling flexible exports. Furthermore, production from the Permian Basin is projected to grow at an annual rate of 7% through 2030, outpacing crude oil growth by 4%.

Propane inventories in the U.S. are now at the highest point its been in the past five years, with 2015 being the previous year recording these levels of builds. This could give guidance that a price correction is ahead, resulting in increased exports available. 

VLGCs account for 82% of all seaborne LPG exports from the U.S., totaling 52 million tons in 2024 and 41.25 million tons year-to-date in 2025—a 6.4% increase year-on-year. The majority of the volumes go to the Far East, though 15-20% head to Europe & Africa, which is a substantially shorter voyage.

The most influential factor in fleet utilization is the sailing patterns chosen for both laden and ballast voyages. Most laden ships heading to the Far East  from the U.S. typically transit via the Panama Canal, which offers a significantly shorter route compared to the alternative around the Cape of Good Hope. Activity in the Suez Canal remains very limited, with very little VLGC traffic recorded. Year-to-date, 77% of laden voyages have passed through the Panama Canal, down 3% from the 2024 average of 80%. Conversely, 23% of ballasting ships returning to the U.S. from the East have opted for the Cape of Good Hope route—up from 20% in 2024, reflecting a 3% increase.

The Panama Canal remains a critical bottleneck in the VLGC market due to its unpredictable operational capacity and volatility. In Q3, congestion levels typically seen during peak winter months emerged unexpectedly, catching the market off guard. Auction fees surged to nearly $1 million, significantly tightening capacity. As a result, the share of ballasting ships returning to the U.S. via the Cape of Good Hope (COGH) rose from 22% in August to 40% in September.

This congestion was primarily driven by above-average ship arrivals, and since VLGCs hold lower transit priority, they are particularly vulnerable to delays. In 2025, the Long-Term Slot Allocation (LoTSA) system has been fully operational, meaning a substantial portion of transit slots in the Neo-locks were auctioned off the year prior. This has led to full canal utilization, leaving limited room for non-booked ships. Additionally, high demand for Neo-slots is consuming both time and navigational channel capacity, reducing availability at the Panamax locks. The full utilization of Neo-locks has created a leapfrog effect, forcing non-booked ships to idle while waiting for transit opportunities. The Panama Canal Authority (PCA) has announced the continuation of the LoTSA system into 2026, albeit with some modifications.

Another factor contributing to canal congestion is the emergence of VLECs transporting ethane from the U.S. to China. These voyages exclusively transit via the Panama Canal and do not use the COGH route. In 2025, the average number of VLEC transits has reached nine ships per month. With continued growth in U.S. exports of both LPG and ethane, this trend is expected to intensify.

Total U.S. export capacity is set to increase from 68 to 113 MTPA by 2028 with the completion of these projects. This would boost export capacity by 66% from 2024 to 2028—a substantial jump that is warmly welcomed by a growing fleet. What will materialize as the *actual* incremental exports is yet to be seen; however, it will likely be less than the full capacity numbers. Nevertheless, this move by U.S. energy suppliers further underscores the market's desire to expand and grow.

It should be noted that both the Nederland and Neches River facilities will offer flexible capacity for LPG and ethane. Given the recent growth in U.S. ethane exports as well as the VLEC orderbook (170% to fleet), it is expected that a portion of these volumes will be allocated to ethane rather than LPG.

The ongoing trade tensions between the U.S. and China, has caused disruptions in cargo flows, solidifying LPG exports from the Middle East, which have surpassed 30 million tons year-to-date. Key contributors include Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Iran. Notably, 90% of Iranian LPG exports are destined for China, with 96% of these volumes transported by VLGCs, primarily by the dedicated fleet segment.

New natural gas developments in Qatar, including the North Field projects, are expected to come online in 2026 and 2027, bringing incremental LPG volumes. An accumulated 6.2 million tons per annum (MTPA) is anticipated, which would raise the region’s export capacity from 46 to 52 MTPA. 

In parallel, the reversal of OPEC+’s two-year production cut is projected to increase output, potentially adding the equivalent of 4–5 additional cargoes per month from the Middle East. If these volumes translate directly into VLGC loadings, it would represent a 5% increase in exports. Looking even further ahead, Saudi Arabia plans to boost natural gas production by 60% between 2021 and 2030, primarily from the Jafurah Field. Year-to-date, Saudi Arabia accounts for 7% of all VLGC liftings. The anticipation of future incremental volumes is 5-10 MTPA.

In July, the U.S. and Indonesia signed a trade agreement under which Indonesia will increase its purchases of U.S. petroleum products by $13 billion, in exchange for reduced tariffs on Indonesian exports to the U.S. Indonesia currently sources 60% of its LPG imports from the U.S., and under the new agreement, it will shift its remaining demand—equivalent to 2–3 MTPA—away from the Middle East. This shift could increase Middle East tonne-miles, as displaced volumes may now be redirected to the Far East if not India, depending on trade dynamics.

The LPG product market took an unexpected turn as Saudi Aramco lowered its October Contract Prices (CPs) to $495/mt for propane (down 3.1%) and $475/mt for butane (down 4.8%). These levels came in well below market expectations, which had anticipated propane CPs above $540/mt.
This sharp adjustment appears to be a strategic move aimed at stimulating term buying interest and enhancing Saudi competitiveness against rising U.S. exports, which are being supported by ongoing terminal expansions.
The price cut could unlock new arbitrage opportunities and boost demand from Asian buyers, particularly in price-sensitive markets. There is therefore potential for increased liftings from Ras Tanura and Yanbu.
In parallel, if Asian buyers shift preference toward Saudi-origin cargoes, this could displace long-haul U.S. barrels heading East, potentially reducing overall tonne-mile demand and reshaping trade flows.

Following “Liberation Day” in April, cargo flows have been reshuffled, underscoring the high flexibility of the LPG market—though this adaptability comes at the cost of increased logistics expenses. Compared to the same period last year, Chinese VLGC imports remain steady at 25.95 million tons.

The most notable trade shifts include increased U.S. LPG imports into Japan and South Korea, while Chinese imports from the U.S. declined sharply. In response, the UAE and Kuwait have stepped up, replacing much of the lost U.S. volumes.

Starting October 14th, Chinese-owned and/or operated VLGCs calling at U.S. ports will be subject to new fees. This affects 46 live ships (11% of the fleet) and 11 newbuilds (10% of the orderbook). Including ships under Chinese leasing arrangements, the impact is slightly larger. However, the overall effect on the market is expected to be moderate. These ships are now favoring Middle East loadings over U.S., which is increasing competition within the available fleet.

China’s LPG demand continues to be primarily driven by the petrochemical sector, with ongoing growth in propane dehydrogenation (PDH) capacity. Although Chinese PDH plants are currently facing negative margins, recent improvements in run rates have been observed, currently at 70%. 
However, the sector’s planned expansions have been heavily reliant on U.S. LPG supply. Should China reduce or phase out sourcing from the U.S., it would have significant implications for both the petrochemical and shipping markets. If propane becomes either too expensive or unavailable, PDH operators may be forced to scale back expansion plans or switch feedstock.

The current tariffs have been imposed by the same U.S. administration that originally introduced them in 2018, suggesting a more resilient and prolonged stance this time around. This could imply that trade disruptions may persist longer than previously anticipated. However, China’s dependency on U.S. LPG supply is now five times greater than it was in 2018, potentially giving China greater leverage in negotiations. China currently accounts for over $10 billion in annual U.S. energy export value, underscoring a strong mutual dependency between the two nations.

The rapid expansion of China’s PDH capacity in recent years means that significant assets are at risk should supply disruptions occur. Conversely, the U.S. could face a surge in stranded LPG exports if China were to halt imports entirely. While alternative buyers exist, an oversupply of product would likely exert downward pressure on U.S. LPG prices. The situation is complex, and while developments are hoped for in the near term, current expectations point to an extension of the existing tariffs. The U.S. administration appears to be focused on other pressing issues, which may delay any resolution on trade policy.

As we close in on the last quarter of the year, 10 newbuilds have been delivered, and 3 are remaining, giving a total of 13 newbuilds. The fleet now stands at 410 ships, including floating storages. The orderbook consists of 107 ships, resulting in an orderbook-fleet ratio of 26%, which is slightly above the 20-year average of 21%. Nonetheless, the fleet is set to grow by 19.4% through 2026 and 2027 in total, which could have an accumulated effect by offsetting the fleet balance in to a surplus. 

As the Panama Canal is expected to become increasingly congested in the coming years—driven by rising U.S. exports of ethane and LNG, along with the addition of over 100 VLGCs on the water—there is reason to anticipate that a larger share of the fleet will regularly utilize the Cape of Good Hope (COGH) route. This shift will stretch fleet capacity and reduce overall vessel availability. At the same time, new LPG export capacity is coming online in the U.S., requiring additional transportation. These dynamics suggest a potential need for more ships, as longer sailing distances reduce the number of voyages each vessel can complete annually.

Ordering activity in 2025 has been extremely modest compared to the 2 previous years, as both the current newbuilding prices as well as the size of the orderbook has put a damper on ordering interest. 

Hyundai in South Korea remains the largest builder of newbuilds, while one quarter of the newbuilds are being constructed in China. We have not yet seen any difference occurring in asking price for from Japanese/Korean vs. Chinese, and the last price recorded for a VLAC-order was at $125M in June – Hyundai building for Sahara, with delivery in mid-2028. 

On the ammonia side, market interest and activity has remained limited throughout the year. Smaller ship segments are currently under pressure, although the large orderbook for MGCs is expected to accommodate any incremental volumes entering the market. More critically, the infrastructure investments required to support seaborne ammonia trade via VLACs are not being made. These investments typically involve long lead times, further delaying market readiness. Additionally, the market lacks sufficient project development to generate new ammonia volumes. The first VLAC in the orderbook is scheduled for delivery in June, but as previously noted, these ships are expected to operate as conventional VLGCs for the foreseeable future. We do not differentiate them within the fleet, aside from their technical capability to carry ammonia at 98% capacity, if required.

In line with elevated earning levels, asset values for LPG carriers have risen sharply over the past few years. At the end of 2022, a VLGC was priced at $80 million—a figure now equivalent to the cost of a 40,000 cbm MGC. Prices increased by 50% to $120 million as ordering activity surged, reaching record highs for two consecutive years. The peak was recorded in April 2024, when VLGCs were priced at $127 million. Although ordering activity has slowed in 2025, leading to a softening in newbuilding prices, shipyards continue to maintain relatively high price levels due to long backlogs from other shipping segments. This price softening reflects current market sentiment, which is shaped by a larger orderbook.

The graph above outlines the specifications of a conventional VLGC. Since 2021, nearly all newbuilds have been ordered with LPG dual-fuel capability, reflecting a shift toward cleaner propulsion technologies. From 2023 onward, the VLAC specification has dominated the orderbook. This includes an additional cost of approximately $2 million for ammonia cargo-handling capability, and a further $2.5 million for conversion to ammonia dual-fuel engines, assuming the ship's piping and tank systems are pre-configured.

In the short term, earnings are expected to remain stable and at similar levels, for the remainder of the year.

Looking ahead to 2026, additional capacity expansions in the U.S., coupled with a projected supply boost from the Middle East, are anticipated to help offset the impact of fleet growth over the next 12 months. Notably, 35 newbuilds are scheduled for delivery next year. 

Trade relations between the world’s largest LPG importer and exporter remain fluid. However, China is expected to continue diversifying its supply sources to reduce dependency on the U.S.

Transit capacity in the Panama Canal remains constrained under the Long-Term Slot Allocation (LoTSA) system, which the Panama Canal Authority (PCA) has confirmed will continue into 2026. The updated framework includes a reduction in daily transit slots from four to three, and a shortened commitment period from 12 months to two six-month cycles, beginning in January and July. Auctions for these slot packages will commence at the end of October.
This system continues to favor Panamax ships, which benefit from twice as many daily transit slots in the old locks compared to Neo locks. However, with half of the current orderbook consisting of Panamaxes, this dynamic is expected to evolve as fleet composition shifts.

The cautious optimism seen in Q2 faded into Q3, as spot rates hovered sideways through the quarter, reminding us that the LNG shipping market has a few hurdles to get past before Owners can comfortably lean back. In this flat freight environment, it is impossible not to draw comparison to the seasonality in past years (and historically), as the market typically tracks rapidly higher at this time of the year. This can be explained partly by the overhang of tonnage and partly by lack of trading inter-basin arbitrages.

For shipping, the bright spot of the quarter was another barrage of FIDs announced including CP2 (14mtpa), Port Arthur Phase 2 (12mtpa) and Rio Grande T4 (5.4mtpa). FLNGs were also in the spotlight, with Golar firming up their MkII FLNG unit for Argentina at 3.5mtpa and Coral North also reaching FID in early October. The total FID’ed liquefaction capacity in 2025 now stands at just shy of 80mtpa, which will start production in the 2027-2030 period. The combination of FIDs and SPAs is shaping up to result in a new wave of ordering activity, especially as charterers combine volume expansion with fleet replacements. We expect to see an increase in tendering activity on back of these FIDs, as the offtakers will need to act in 2026 to secure shipping capacity with timely delivery for their volumes towards the end of the decade.

While no new projects formally started up in Q3, we did see additional volumes out of Calcasieu Pass and Corpus Christi as well as Greater Tortue volumes continuing to ramp up together with LNG Canada. However, the most interesting “start-up” is Arctic LNG 2 which exported a total of 0.5mtpa during the quarter – heading for China in what appears to become a steady trade (based on the seven cargoes in Q3 and another one scheduled for delivery around mid-October). On the demand side, the most active buyers were Europe (Netherlands, France, Germany and Italy were notable at 30-60% Y-o-Y increases) and MENA (Egypt), while on the opposite side we see China and India breaking their growth trends seen for years. With 75% of the year in the books, China is down 16% to 48mt while India is down 7% to 19mt. 

LNG prices across regions and between basins began the quarter with a tiny arbitrage potential, yet prices compressed in Aug-Sep with spreads between US-Asia in the US$ 0.4-0.8/MMBtu-range and US-Europe in the US$ 0.2-0.4/MMBtu range. More high-level; JKM traded in the range of US$11-13/MMBtu while Europe traded around US$ 11-12.5/MMBtu, not leaving much for Owners and traders alike. For the winter, it seems we’ll need to rely on the weatherman to get some relief. European storage levels hit 82% at the end of the quarter, compared to 94-96% at the same time in 2022-2024, due to less stringent requirements for filling levels, so there is cautious optimism for LNG into Europe as withdrawals are starting to kick in. The continued focus on phasing out Russian LNG in Europe is additionally creating some potential for shipping demand if Yamal volumes were to start heading East, especially having to go Southwest around the Cape of Good Hope or through the Suez Canal.

Fixture activity in Q3 was a little subdued compared to the record-breaking first half of 2025 at just shy of 90 spot fixtures concluded. This is not caused by less volume or fewer ships on the water, but perhaps with thin trading margins some of the portfolio players and traders with excess tonnage have been more active in cargo purchases themselves. Multi-month activity was also lower Q-o-Q, as Owners and Charterers alike assess the near-term outlook and their resulting fixing strategies. On the positive side, we are seeing activity for long-term business, including for tonnage to cover the coming years as well as beyond the end of the decade, although pricing for the prompt years is challenging. 

At the end of September, we counted 52 vessels delivered since the start of the year, suggesting 19 delivered in the quarter. The reality is that there are still another 48 to clear out the century of ships scheduled to hit the water in 2025. We see this as unrealistic to achieve and as such we expect 20-30 vessels to slip into 2026, both from a yard logistics perspective and delayed start-up of volumes and hence charters. Although ordering activity is still subdued at 15 vessels ordered to date, we did see an uptick in activity in Q3 with several European Owners lining up vessels for delivery in 2028-2029. The most notable order placed during the quarter was the Hanwha Shipping announcement of an order for the first pair of LNGCs to be built in the US since the 1970s at Philly Shipyard. It remains to be seen how much construction actually takes place within the US or, perhaps more accurately, what finishing touches can be applied in Philly for the vessels to qualify as “US-built”? Recycling activity is trucking along nicely, albeit at a slower pace than many market participants may have expected or preferred to see. A total of 12 vessels have been scrapped YTD at an average age of 25 years and an average capacity of 138,000 cubic meters. Sellers have been predominantly Asian Owners with ships coming off long-term charters and a good understanding of what stop-loss means. While the number of ships sold for recycling ought to have been higher, we continue to see many steam turbine vessels marketed for sale with keen sellers. The challenge remains in finding buyers with a clear future for the vessel in question. The fleet now stands at 728 vessels with an estimated 26 vessels formally in layup; however, judging by sailing speeds and limited variations in draft, we count just north of 40 vessels effectively in a form of layup including a handful of TFDEs.

content.title: "FID me, baby, one more time!": Liquefaction FIDs hit historical highs in 2025

content.content:
The average spot rate for a two-stroke in Q3 ended at US$ 34k/day, only marginally higher than Q2’s US$ 30k/day, yet still reflective of the weakening trend that has defined the market through 2025. After starting the quarter on relatively firm footing at around US$ 43k/day in early July, rates steadily eroded, closing the quarter in the mid-US$ 20ks/day range by late September, which is often when rates are surging upwards. A narrow East-West rate differential reappeared, with Pacific two-strokes averaging roughly US$ 35k/day against US$ 33k/day in the Atlantic, but this was more a reflection of relative weakness in the West than genuine strength in the East. Q3 emphasized the same imbalance that has plagued the market all year: too many ships chasing too few cargoes, with arbitrage economics and floating storage incentives largely absent.

The abundance of idle tonnage and a slowdown in spot fixtures highlight the structural oversupply that continues to weigh on sentiment. With the forward market signaling little movement through the winter, any meaningful rebound before mid-2026 appears increasingly unlikely without a material shift in global LNG trade dynamics. The situation was even more discouraging for TFDE carriers, where average earnings dropped to around US$ 20k/day, leaving many owners operating on a thin margin. Spot levels in both basins fell through the US$ 20k/day threshold by late September, with some fixtures dipping to US$ 12–14k/day, the lowest since early 2025. Steam turbine units remained effectively out of play, with the few reported fixtures struggling to achieve even US$ 4k/day.

In the term market, activity was confined mainly to short-term employment (<90 days), as uncertainty over future demand and the plentiful spot market kept both sides cautious. A handful of one-year charters for two-stroke were reported in the high-US$ 40ks/day, a modest uptick from levels earlier in the year but already softening toward the end of the quarter; a clear sign that the view on winter seasonality shifted down as the months progressed. The longer end of the curve remains illiquid, though the implied forward rates continue to hover around high-US$ 60ks/day for years 2–3 and low-US$ 80ks/day for years 6–7, suggesting that charterers still view today’s weakness as an opportunity to lock in tonnage at discounted levels.

On the cost side, implied freight economics from the US Gulf Coast to Northwest Europe averaged between US$ 0.41–0.50/MMBtu, while deliveries to Northeast Asia (JKM) via the Panama or Cape routes were in the US$ 1.12–1.29/MMBtu range. Floating storage remained uneconomical as weak rates and narrow spreads offered no incentive to hold cargoes at sea.

Although 2025 remains on track to break records for the number of fixtures, Q3 marked a softer phase in LNGC chartering activity, continuing the gradual slowdown observed since early in the year. The number of short-term fixtures (<90 days) declined to 88, down from Q2’s near-record 108, yet broadly in line with the 85 fixtures recorded in Q3 2024. The average spot fixture duration slipped to 18 days in Q3 2025, down from 20 days a year earlier, signaling slightly faster vessel turnover and reduced voyage commitment amid softer market conditions.

Multi-month (<365 days) activity also eased, with only eight fixtures concluded in Q3 marking a clear slowdown from earlier in the year, and the 1–3 year segment also remained subdued. Thin trading margins and an abundance of spot vessels allowed some leeway for charterers that may previously have taken winter tonnage so the market was constrained by wide bid-offer spread and limited forward visibility for trading. The average duration of multi-month charters shortened to around six months, down from just over seven months in Q3 2024, indicating that even longer-period deals are being structured with greater flexibility. This continued tilt toward shorter commitments highlights charterers’ cautious approach amid uncertain winter demand and narrowing LNG price spreads.

From a structural perspective, independent fixtures accounted for just below 30% of total activity, with the rest driven by sublet deals – a pattern consistent across the past four quarters. The dominance of sublets illustrates the strong secondary market presence of portfolio players, who continue to reoptimize fleet allocation rather than commit to new long-term charters.

Global LNG loadings totalled 110 MT in Q3 2025, slightly above Q2 and up roughly 9 MT year-on-year, emphasizing continued strength in global supply despite regional maintenance outages. The United States, Qatar and Australia remained the top three exporters, collectively accounting for nearly two-thirds of global exports. U.S. volumes held firm at 27.6 MT, supported by sustained feed gas deliveries and incremental capacity at Calcasieu Pass and Plaquemines, while Qatar exported 20.5 MT, maintaining high utilization across its North Field operations. Australia’s output stabilized near 20 MT, with expectations of renewed growth ahead of Darwin LNG’s restart in October. Smaller but consistent contributions came from Russia, Malaysia, and Nigeria, with Canada’s LNG Canada project shipping its first cargo in June marking a new milestone for North American supply diversification.

On the import side, Asia continued to dominate global LNG demand, taking in 70 MT during the quarter, followed by Europe at 26 MT, with the Americas and Middle East & North Africa regions absorbing smaller but growing shares. Among individual buyers, China imported 17.9 MT, showing its first year-on-year growth since early 2024 as industrial restarts, extreme weather and expanding storage drove incremental demand. Japan and South Korea maintained strong intake levels of 15.8 MT and 12.3 MT respectively, underpinned by gas-for-coal switching and new contract deliveries. India’s imports remained steady at 6.3 MT, reflecting a balance between high spot prices earlier in the year and strong monsoon-driven demand recovery. In Europe, Poland and Turkey stood out. Poland’s volumes rose 34% year-on-year, while Turkey expanded its LNG portfolio through new SPAs and short-term contracts ahead of expiring Russian pipeline deals.

From a trade flow perspective, the share of U.S. LNG bound for Asia picked up modestly as long-haul shipments around the Cape of Good Hope increased, adding to tonne-mile demand, though the share remains below the highs seen in 2024. The Panama Canal continues to see limited LNG transits due to congestion and high tolls, reinforcing longer-haul patterns. Meanwhile, Qatar’s flows to Asia stayed elevated, contributing to stable regional balances but limiting tonne-mile expansion globally. Two-stroke carriers continued to dominate long-haul loadings, extending their lead over TFDE and steam turbine tonnage as charterers prioritize efficiency and carbon compliance. The propulsion mix remains heavily skewed toward modern XDF/MEGI units, reflecting the ongoing fleet renewal cycle.

content.title: Average fleet speed by propulsion (speeds > 6 knots)

content.content:
The global LNGC fleet continued its expansion through Q3 2025. The fleet now counts 728 vessels on the water, of which 702 remain active and 26 are in layup. The surge of newbuilds has ensured that 2025 remains on track to become the most delivery-heavy year in LNG shipping history. With 52 vessels already delivered year-to-date, the momentum shows little sign of easing although as noted, we do not expect all the vessels scheduled to delivery this year will actually hit the water. The growing dominance of modern two-stroke propulsion reflects a decisive industry pivot toward efficiency and emissions compliance; XDF and ME-GA designs now account for almost 90% of the active orderbook.

The orderbook itself stands at 289 vessels, or about 41% of the active fleet. However, ordering enthusiasm has cooled sharply, with only a few contracts placed this year and most of these connected to QatarEnergy’s QC-Max program that now spans 24 vessels for delivery between 2028 and 2031. Outside this umbrella, owners have been wary of speculative orders amid high yard prices, tight slot availability, and prolonged freight weakness.

China has entrenched its position as a global shipbuilding powerhouse, with Hudong-Zhonghua, Dalian and China Merchants Jiangsu accounting for roughly one-third of all active LNGC orders. South Korean yards – Hanwha Ocean, Samsung, and Hyundai – continue to lead in technical sophistication, but full backlogs mean new contracts are being pushed into late-decade delivery windows. A notable development came from the United States, where Hanwha Ocean and Philly Shipyard announced the country’s first LNG carrier order in nearly 50 years, signaling a potential revival of domestic shipbuilding capacity under the potential for U.S.-flag requirements.

While deliveries surge, the other end of the age curve is accelerating as well. Recycling activity has gained pace with 12 vessels sold for scrapping year-to-date, particularly among aging steam turbine and early DFDE tonnage, as market conditions are challenging for them. For many Owners, the decision is no longer about timing the market – it is about cutting losses. Average LNG carrier speeds edged lower in Q3 2025, settling at 14.3 knots, down from 14.5 knots a year earlier. The slowdown reflects both weaker market conditions and widespread adoption of eco-speed operations. Two-stroke vessels remained the fastest at about 14.8 knots, while TFDE and steam turbine units averaged 14.1 and 13 knots, underscoring their increasingly limited trading use. In today’s oversupplied market, speed has become an economic choice, not a performance metric.

S&P activity in 2025 continues to be dominated by transactions involving older steam turbine tonnage, either for captive trades or players acquiring FSRU conversion candidates. Unfortunately, there are all too often reports of failed processes in which predominantly the buyers have been unable to come up with agreed elements of contract.

Asset values remain under pressure in the current market environment, but there is a sense of sliding lower rather than dropping fast. Older (20-yr range) steam turbine tonnage is assessed in the US$ 20-30m range whereas 10yr old TFDEs hover around US$ 120-140m, but with more sensitivity on size and age. In the modern tonnage segment, there are limited transactions to point to and hence values become more of a theoretical exercise.

Newbuild pricing has flattened out just shy of US$ 250m with yards seemingly positive on order intake for the coming year. There are reports of Q2/28 deliveries being pushed to Q3/28 upon quote refresh, and at the moment marketed slots are prone to be H2/28 unless an Owner has options or other strong access with a particular yard.

Our crystal ball still suggests that the LNG shipping market will remain under pressure until 2027, with 2026 flat-ish compared to 2025. While there is a lot of new liquefaction capacity arriving at high-pace over the next three years, so are new vessels. However, we are forming a more positive view on the medium-term given the plethora of FIDs concluded and more expected. The question then becomes whether Owners are willing to entertain Charterers alluring calls for newbuilds, and often the temptation of “just one more vessel” results in new orders. In the interim, Q3 is a good example of how a somewhat-static market leads to muted shipping, but as we have seen in the past we only need a little cold (or warm) weather or seasonality to shift trade flows and lift shipping. Add to this the continued uncertainty on geopolitical issues and it may well be that volatility is a closer friend than one would imagine.

The market is already getting some help from fleet phase out and recycling, but the pace and magnitude must pick up to make a real impact. Drydocking schedules in 2026 and 2027 will most certainly play a role here and with some 30 vessels heading for their 4th SS/DD over the next 12 months, Owners are facing decision time. We see that “25 is the new 35” when it comes to scrapping age, but given the earnings potential in spot and term for the steam turbine fleet it is not unreasonable to potentially see a further drop in age when vessels sail their last voyage. 

High FID-activity in 2025 should be a long-term boon for the shipping market, and it should not be forgotten that the pace of supply of LNG is expected to lead to a decline in cost as an energy source, and thus make LNG increasingly competitive relative to other fuels. More – and cheaper – LNG will inevitably unlock end-user demand which in turn means tonne-miles. Through the past years of high (to very high) LNG prices, price-sensitivity has become highly apparent and with lower prices on the horizon this is a trend we should see turning into increased purchases. This demand is very likely to be most prevalent in India, the Indian subcontinent and Asia – far from the liquefaction FIDs – supporting shipping demand with increase inter-basin trade.

Fearnley LNG currently quotes 10-year charters in the mid-/high-80s range. Although this is expensive against the anticipated market conditions in the prompt years, further out these should be attractive levels for Charterers that are long cargo and who will want to secure shipping capacity before the market tightens. Although the cargo length may only appear in 2028-2030, some will see the timing to act as now prior to this freight market rebalancing starts to take effect.

While our outlook, as for the previous quarters, is reflective of a challenging “tomorrow” we maintain a clear position that “next week” will be better. The simple fact is that we see a very positive long-term structural role for LNG in the energy mix, and traded LNG could grow more than 50% by 2030 with the potential for even higher tonne-mile growth.

Last week we wrote "*The market is correcting, in line with usual seasonal developments. The share of profitable steel mills suggests that iron ore consumption in China is peaking, as it has fallen from close to 70% to about 58% over the last month. However, significant drops in consumption usually do not happen unless the share of profitable mills falls below 50%.
Regarding the BHP story, there could be fewer cargoes than usual for a short period, but China buys approximately 250 million tons of BHP iron ore annually, out of a total of 1.2 billion tons. For that reason, the iron ore markets have not been spooked by the temporary ban, as China is dependant on BHP supply..."*

No data from China last week due to holidays. The key datapoint to follow is imported iron ore consumption, which has been stable at around 3 million tons per day since the start of May. Total iron ore inventories have barely changed since May as well. Prices have seen more significant swings, but as long as volumes are not impacted, it will not mean much for the Capesize market. The narrowing spread of near-month iron ore futures is something we have pointed to for a while that might lead to a weaker Q4 than Q3 (top right chart). Interestingly, the futures curve has turned more backwardated since the BHP news broke, so that indicator is now suggesting Q1 market strength following a weaker Q4. Otherwise there has been an unusual development in price spreads between various iron ore grades. Australian iron ore has weakened compared to lower grades (usually a bearish sign), but higher-grade Brazilian ores have increased in price relative to Australian ores. 

Otherwise, the seasonal ramp-up in Bauxite shipments seems to have started (bottom left chart), which is bullish, but the share of the fleet in shipyards have decreased by over 1% over the last month, which could weigh on market levels.
