content.content:
Given the recent rate rally it is timely to revisit our bull case scenario for this year. Arguably, rates have lagged fundamentals, hence the recent month has been a proper catch-up. 

However, some of the factors which have contributed to the recent spike are now reversing, which may mean some normalisation of rates in coming weks and months although there may still be some upside risk to our base case rate forecast for the rest of the year: 
- More dry dock vessels redeliver 
- Dubai and Murban prices have plunged so that the West-East arbitrage has closed
- Western refineries will soon come back from maintenance which may end the recent Atlantic crude oil supply push
- If the Brent forward curve flips into contango Western inventory builds could limit long-haul trade 
  
There are also some risks to the upside from: 
- Stronger oil demand than the IEA estimates
- Continued OPEC+ cut reversal - the tide lifts all boats 
- Continued Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure (and/or secondary sanctions) which might aid the West-East arbitrage.  

Going into next year we see directionally lower rates due to rising fleet growth and slowing oil production growth. How much lower may depend on the continued developments of some of the above risks.

content.title: Rates catching up closer to our forecast

content.content: Most of the bull case has played out, but rates not fully so until now

Going into this year we outlined a bear, base and bull case, where the bear case was quickly ruled out due to broad sanctions. Although tanker demand was strong during the first half, rates never really caught up as they perhaps should have, but sentiment has now thoroughly changed to reflect the tighter underlying picture. At the end of last year we wrote the following: 

"Bull case: Non-OPEC+ producers may live up to strong growth expectations and a harder clamp-down on Iran by the Trump administration may give more volumes to the normal market, potentially boosted further through the OPEC+ reversing some cuts to offset any Iranian supply losses - especially if (Chinese) oil demand surpasses current estimates".

So, a lot of this has played out. Underlying Chinese oil demand has not been that strong, but this has been countered by inventory builds (we did also point to Chinese plans to build 125 mb of new storage capacity this and 100 mb next year - which tends to be filled rather quickly). Although the Trump administration has been more hawkish on Iran, this has not led to a change in flows, other than more shadow tankers added to the sanctions list. In sum, developments this year have been more bullish than rates have suggested - but then the recent rally has caught up to that, and then some.

content.title: Global oil supply growth vs. tanker demand

content.content: Much of the upside may already have been taken out

OECD inventories have built by nearly 50 mb over the first eight months of this year, while non-OECD has built by 170 mb, mainly in the East.  This stockpiling, especially in China, has boosted oil and tanker demand, which could continue for some more time. Based on the Chinese oil storage capacity build-out, one can infer that this stockbuilding is about half way done, ie. could last into the start of next year. 

Going forward, however, more may be sourced from the MEG vs. the Atlantic basin, which means the recent extraordinary demand support could ease somewhat. Potential further OPEC+ cut unwind, which is likely as long as oil prices and structure holds like it has, could further contribute to keeping the West-East arb. shut.

The West-East arb. has narrowed recently to the point where it is now closed. It was for a while supported by the very strong Dubai/Murban prices, which have now fallen. Given increasing output from Middle Eastern producers and less ramp-up in the Atlantic going forward, this should all else equal not be supportive of a wide open arbitrage. 

A risk to the downside is if or when the Brent forward curve flips into contango, which could lead to Western inventory builds. According to the EIA and Euroilstock U.S. and European inventories have drawn recently, which has also been supportive for West-East flows. If this reverses that extra demand leg for the biggest ships could turn. On the flipside, this means more Transatlantic flow for Suez- and Aframax.

content.title: USG-West arbitrage narrowing - WTI better priced into Europe

content.content:
With most of the new FPSOs coming on in Brazil and Guyana having started the last few months, the biggest volume ramp-up from the Atlantic basin has already happened. Although there may be some more in it, the EIA forecasts a Q/Q decline of 120 kbpd in 4Q'25 and another 340 kbpd in Q1'26.  

Near term there may also be some export decline due to increasing refinery runs in the Atlantic from the end of October until year-end - so just beyond the current Atlantic-East fixing window. A total Atlantic refinery run swing of more than 2 mbpd may reduce the West-East potential - something that in recent years has contributed to dampen Q4 seasonality.

content.title: Key Atlantic producers q/q supply growth

content.content:
What may lend upside support, however, is intensified Ukrainian attacks on Russian infrastructure and/or secondary sanctions if such are implemented. Trump's recent change in tune and green light for the Ukrainians to carry out long-range attacks into Russia could give greater implications for export capacity. 

So far there has not been any meaningful change in Russian crude oil exports, but products exports are in the lower end of the range, and with domestic gasoline and diesel shortages there may be more export downside going forward. There are also observations of increased crude oil storage at refineries, suggesting broader outages. 

There has not been any great change in the fleet composition of Western crude oil exports either. YTD nearly half of the volume from the Baltic and Black Sea has been lifted by non-sanctioned tankers. While some 'usual suspects' have shied away from the trade, there has been sufficient other non-sanctioned tonnage to take the rest. This still means tonne-mile support for (compliant) Suez- and Aframaxes, and so far there is little reason for the elevated MEG crude pricing if fear of Russian crude outages is the supposed culprit. 

If, however, crude oil installations are hit and exports curbed, this could lend support to the West/East arbitrage again, and therefore also VLCCs, but be a drag on Suez- and Aframax tonne-miles.

content.title: Russia West crude oil exports by ship type

content.content:
Run-rate tonne-miles for September to date are much higher than the same time last year, supported by increased production from the Atlantic basin and a smaller than normal decline in MEG exports due to production cut unwind (and this year there is no Libya outage). Still, tonne-mile demand remains below the peaks of March this year when there was more West-East movement. 

It is likely that these tonne-mile figures lag a bit and that the full month data and October will be somewhat higher. Rising volumes should help too, although the recent West-East push is likely past the peak now which means flatter development into year-end.

Next year global oil supply growth slows substantially to 'only' 0.5 mbpd per the IEA's estimates (4Q to 4Q) vs. this year's massive estimated 3.9 mbpd. Production growth might get a bit higher considering OPEC+ cut unwind, but even if the current 1.6 mbpd cut tranche is fully unwound the actual effect should be little more than 0.6-0.7 mbpd. In other words, 'maximum' 2.5% tanker volume growth if all these volumes are shipped by sea - and a likely lower tonne-mile effect as sailing distances are likely to be shorter on average. 

That is, if the oil market can accommodate extra OPEC+ barrels. Energy agency balances still point to significant inventory builds through the remainder of this and next year (although demand is probably stronger than the IEA's estimates suggest). While it is not reflected in the forward curve, global observed inventories show meaningful builds YTD. With limited upside to refinery capacity (excluding China, India and the MEG) and the recent ramp-up in production, there should be bigger builds ahead. This in turn begs the question for how long the OPEC+ will keep unwinding unless there are disruptions elsewhere.

Next year global refinery runs are estimated by the IEA to increase by about 0.5 mbpd, down from 0.6 mbpd this year. Refinery capacity may increase by about 1.1 mbpd, which indicates the potential for some more crude oil production to be absorbed. 

Out of that 1.1 mbpd about 250 kbpd is expected to come in each of China and the MEG. The caveat with these is that the MEG additions means less crude exports, and in China the expansion will likely come at the expense of less efficient capacity - at least if export quotas are not materially lifted or underlying demand picks up. Most of the remaining added capacity is expected to come in India. Unless all of these source crude oil from the Atlantic basin, that means shorter than average crude-hauls, while it may also mean some longer-haul products flows. 

Current refinery margins are stronger in the West than the East, partly supported by maintenance and partly by Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. That gives a demand pull, especially for gasoil, which in turn should be a positive for product tanker demand and is part of the reason why product tonne-miles are at seasonal all-time-highs.

Deliveries are about to pick up, first and foremost for product tankers, but increasingly also for crude tankers. From a low of 1% gross deliveries last year, this year is set to come to 3.1% and next year 5.8%. In dwt terms only three years historically have seen higher deliveries than next year's schedule. 

It starts the coming quarter, but this is likely to be more than offset by rising volumes. The next two years could have been 'saved' by the massive phase-out potential, but much of what are phase-out candidates are already out of the compliant market.

Below is an overview of the oldest part of the various fleets: For instance, all VLCCs built 2000 and earlier are either sanctioned or operate in the shadow market. 87% of VLCCs built 2001-2005 are either sanctioned or shadow, while 'only' 21% of VLCCs built 2006-2010 are. In other words, we may not see any phase-out near-term, as almost all vessels which would otherwise be phase-out candidates are already phased out of the compliant market. For 2027-30, however, there could be more meaningful phase-out, especially if rates come off.. 

For Suezmaxes, 93% of the vessels built 2000 or earlier are sanctioned/shadow, as are 56% of 2001-05 and 23% of 2006-10. For Afra/LR2 66% of the 2000 or earlier built vessels are sanctioned/shadow, as are 68% of 2001-05 and 44% of 2006-10. For MRs, 32% of 2000 or earlier are sanctioned/shadow, as are 32% of 2001-05 and 7% of 2006-10.

Compared to the last two years phase-out has picked up significantly and ordering slowed quite a bit YTD. However, on a run-rate basis, phase-out is still only on pace to come to 0.4% of the fleet this year, a third of the the historical average in dwt terms, while ordering may come to 3.7%, 50% more than the historical average in dwt terms.

content.title: Ordering YTD slower, but still elevated

content.content:
As we are about to enter Q4, it is worth noting that over the last 10 years, the BDI has averaged lower in Q4 than in Q3 seven out of ten years. Apart from seasonal factors, the surge in demand growth seen for Panamax, Supra, and Handy in July and August was so strong that a temporary exhaustion would be natural. The year-on-year growth in total shipment volumes for those segments has averaged 6% in the last three months, with the previous seven similar demand surges seen in the last 10 years leading to at best sideways over the following months. For the dry bulk segment in total, a similar comparison can be made, as the 7% year-on-year growth in July and August exceeds the 5% average seen during upcycles. The CAGR for total dry bulk shipment volumes was 2.4% between 2017-2024 (a close match with global GDP growth). So, demand downcycles usually bottom around 0% growth, like in the first half of this year, and demand upcycles usually peak around 5% growth. In April this year, Trump’s trade policies posed a severe risk of the global growth baseline declining significantly from the 2017-2024 average, but fortunately, he went back on most of those policies, though, of course, there is a lingering risk in that regard. 
Regarding 2026, the bullish factors are stacking up, so our view that 26 would average higher than 25, held since September last year, still looks likely. The main risk, as we see it, is the potential for a US recession, but this also depends on what type of US recession it is. If Trump’s tariffs is the factor that causes it, then it will likely go along with higher inflation, which in turn could lead to a reversal in US monetary policy, causing the Dollar to strengthen and forcing the World ex-US to raise interest rates. The US dollar is an important driver of dry bulk demand (shown on the last page of this report), so it bears close watching. 

**Commodity groups outlook for 2026**

**Iron Ore:** Credit stimulus and increased domestic construction activity in China, lower interest rates, and energy costs in the World ex-China to support demand. Simandou and Vale’s S11D will increase long-haul seaborne supply. A risk still remains that iron ore inventories in China have not yet been fully drawn down (inventories were lower in late 2023 than now, for example). Anti-dumping cases against China’s steel exports have the potential to change the dynamics somewhat. This would weigh down China’s iron ore import demand but increase the World ex-China’s import demand. Otherwise, a decline in steel exports pose a downside risk to the Supra/Ultra segment. **Coal:** Global seaborne coal growth has been similarly weak in 2025 to 2020 and 2016. Meanwhile, global consumption keeps rising, so a cycle upturn in 2026 for seaborne coal seems likely. Increased focus on cracking down on domestic overproduction in China and improving global macro could support seaborne demand. Seaborne supply could remain an issue, as of the major exporters, it is only Indonesia that has managed to increase exports significantly  in recent years. **Grains:** As always, weather-driven, so it remains to be seen how crops develop. The first estimate for the 25/26 Brazilian soybean season by CONAB showed they expect even higher exports than this year, as the planting area will increase by 3.6%. The CAGR of global grain exports was 2.5% between 2017-2024. **Bauxite:** Lower growth than this year is likely, as the pace of coastal alumina smelter additions in China will fall in both 2026 and 2027. Chalco recently stated additions will grow by “single digits” the next two years.

content.content: TRADE FLOWS YEAR ON YEAR GROWTH

This page gives brief comments on what the charts on the next page tells us. 

Top left chart:

China's credit growth remains relatively high, with the last three months' average at 15% - the highest since early 2021. A positive BDI year on year change is suggested from the start of next year. 

Top right chart:

Through the first seven months of this year, China's economic growth index has averaged -4.7%, compared to -2.1% for all of 2024. For comparison, China's total dry bulk imports were down 3.3% on last year through August. Next year, we expect China's bulk imports to grow, as inventories of coal and iron have been drawn down this year and as stimulus measures have been increased. 

Middle left chart:

Lower crude oil prices are bullish for economic growth, and vice versa. The chart displays that since 2017, there has been a tight correlation between lower year-on-year oil prices and a higher year-on-year BDI, with the oil price change leading by 1 year. 
This indicator is suggesting the BDI year-on-year change is past the low point, and that it will trend upwards over the next year. Should one trust the indicator 100%, there will be a dip in the BDI year-on-year change in the coming months, however. 

Middle right chart:

Global interest rate cuts suggest 1-year TC rates will be higher during the second half of 2026 than what it was through the first half of this year. That implies at least the mid-teens for Kamsarmaxes. Further, it implies 1-year TC rates could be higher than what it is now in the first part of 2027. Interestingly, the 18-month change of 1-year TC rates continues to trend down despite the last month's rally. We are still in a "downcycle" by that definition. 

Bottom left chart:

The OECD G-20 Diffusion index and the BDI year on year change have correlated tightly for decades. However, over the last year, there has been a decoupling, as the Diffusion index suggests the global economy is at peak cycle, whereas the BDI year-on-year change have been in downcycle territory since Q4 last year. The main reason for this decoupling is that the services sector has driven most of global economic growth over the last year, whereas manufacturing has been weak. JP Morgan's Global Manufacturing PMI had its highest reading in September in over a year. 

Bottom right chart:

The dollar index has weakened in the last months, and as usual, the result is increased dry bulk shipment volume growth with a few months' lag. The dollar index suggests total dry bulk shipment volume growth will rise to an average of 4%-5% on a six-month moving average basis.

Last week, we wrote: *Data from last week's production curbs in China is now visible, and it was quite a drop, with imported iron ore consumption and hot metal output falling to the lowest level since January.
A V-shaped recovery back up to pre-production curbs is likely, given that the share of profitable steel mills has not changed much, but it remains to be seen (bottom left chart). 
The iron ore futures curve has for some time suggested weakening demand, and surely some of that was because of these production curbs, but probably not the only reason. The Capesize index's 60-day rolling average appears to be peaking now, as indicated by the lead shown in the top right chart. 
China's Golden Week is three weeks away. Since 2018, the market has peaked that week every year, except for 2023.*

There was a V-shaped recovery in China's hot metal output and imported iron ore consumption last week. Both are back to the high range seen since the beginning of May. The share of profitable steel mills in China remains above 60%, indicating no imminent risk of a significant deterioration in fundamentals (bottom left chart). 
The most recurring seasonal pattern is for the market to rise into the Golden Week, followed by a correction. The ballaster/laden vessel ratio is now at a similar level to mid-July, which suggests the seasonal pattern could repeat this year (top left chart, a lower ratio correlates with market tops and vice versa).

content.content: Some unanswered questions will determine market strength

While volumes and tonne-miles have moved sideways over the last months, rates have strengthened. This can be partly ascribed to a change in sentiment, and tighter position lists - on dry dockings and congestion. Arguably, rates are ahead of observed fundamentals. So, is this an early start of the seasonal upturn, the start of a fundamentally stronger shift, or a flash in the pan? 

We will explore a few key questions about the oil and tanker market, which may decide whether the coming winter market will be a decent or a strong one: 
- Oil market balance: vast production hikes are likely to give well oversupplied oil market - what is the next OPEC+ move?
- What happens to Russian (and Indian) flows? 
- What implications does the above have for West-East flows? 

Beyond the winter, with fleet growth surging and crude oil production growth slowing, there will likely be softening rates over the next two years.

Volumes have remained flattish the last couple of months, contrary to the normal seasonal downturn. This has been helped by OPEC+ production cut unwind which offsets the increased direct burn in the MEG this time of year. In coming months, MEG exports may rise by up to 1 mbpd on the back of these production hikes, while non-OPEC+ may add another about 0.5 mbpd, which is a bullish backdrop for tanker demand. 

Next year, however, even assuming that the OPEC+ maintains production at current targets, there may be very little production growth. The IEA expects only 0.2 mbpd more to come from non-OPEC+.
Recent demand does not match current rate strength

Compliant tonne-miles YTD including run-rate for August are slightly lower y/y, and quite a bit lower than at the peak in March/April. In other words still good for this time of the year, with upside potential when OPEC+ unwind starts hitting the water, as does new volumes in South America. Where these Atlantic volumes end up will have a meaningful impact on whether earnings will be good this winter or great. 

In the last few weeks amid the Russia-Ukraine uncertainty and Trump's added tariffs on India, there has been some more Asian buying of Atlantic barrels - probably as a precaution. However, the only tangible reports thus far suggest India will 'only' lower imports from Russia by about 200 kbpd - there are even reports that buying for September loading may increase again after a slower August. This means the recent rush to buy spot barrels from elsewhere could lead to less buying going forward. With the solid bump in MEG availability, there is at least on paper a risk that we may not see a (continued) increase in Atlantic- Asia flow. Dubai and Murban prices have surged recently, which has supported the West-East arb. but may be overdone. 

Position lists have been wanting lately, which combined with the recent uptick in Atlantic-East has produced higher rates. However, some of the tightness is a result of elevated dockings - for instance we currently count 27 VLCCs in drydock. At some point in coming weeks, these will exit...

Atlantic-East flows have been relatively low the last few months, with an unattractive arbitrage over the summer. This has changed during the last few weeks, however, and we see a noticable tick-up in September USG VLCC fixtures, supporting VLCC tonne-miles and rates. On the flipside, this means less volume available for Suez- and Aframax in September vs. August. 

Whether this will be sustained hinges on the strength of seasonal demand upturn in Asia, whether Indian refiners will continue to shy away from Russian crude oil, and whether U.S. inventories will contiue to draw to support strong domestic demand AND continued high exports. 

There is now a contango in the first three weeks of the Brent CFD structure. If this builds further into the futures curve, it could be supportive for long-haul freight - with the caveat that it may also lead inventories in Europe and the U.S. to start building.

content.title: WTI/Brent-Dubai spread, adj. for 2-1 month fwd. spread

content.content: Judging from energy agency forecasts there will be a massive oversupply building going forward. Observed global inventories have built by 190 mb in the first half of the year, or about 1 mbpd - slightly shy of the IEA's implied balance for the first half. For the second half the agency expects 2.3 mbpd oversupply, building to 3 mbpd next year. Now, although the IEA may be a bit too optimistic on supply and too pessimistic on demand, something might have to give, as this still implies much lower oil prices which will likely take its toll on supply (although potentially boosting demand). An important question is how much lower oil prices the OPEC+ will tolerate. And for how long. There is a non zero chance that the group may cut into next year unless demand materially picks up.

content.title: IEA implied oil market balance suggest huge builds
Global oil inventories have built by 190 mb YTD

content.content: Can Asian demand pull in more crude?

Another important question is how strong will Asian demand be toward year-end. There is a large divergence between the energy agencies, where the IEA expects that oil demand will rise by 0.7 mbpd from September to December, while the EIA expects 2.2 mbpd. 

So far this year, Asian demand has underwhelmed vs. expectations, with the IEA's latest 1H'25 estimate being 0.5 mbpd lower than it was at the beginning of the year. Hence, the IEA's trajectory for the remainder of the year might look more realistic unless activity drastically picks up. If the IEA is right, there is plenty of available crude oil to meet incremental demand from the Middle East given the OPEC+ cut unwind, which suggests less potential for long-haul trade than in the EIA trajectory.

Chinese demand has disappointed vs. expectations YTD. After a brief recovery in June, Chinese apparent main oil products demand declined in July, and was marginally lower than the same month one year ago (nearly 6% lower than 2023). The YTD average is 4.4% lower than the same period last year. Refinery runs are up 1.8% on average, and crude oil imports up 1.7%. Crude oil inventories have built by nearly 100 mb from the January low, and products exports have started to increase recently. This is all in line with recent Chinese oil company statements suggesting sluggish domestic demand. 

A recovery may be needed soon for import demand to remain high - the recent apparent demand level is on par with the second half of last year which was considered very disappointing and one of the reasons for a lacklustre second half for the tanker market... Further SPR builds may add some support.

content.title: China apparent main oil products demand

content.content: Indian oil demand YTD has fared somewhat better than China's, but 1% growth y/y is hardly what most had expected at the beginning of this year. The July dip could be a one-off, and/or frontrunning of the usual July/August dip, but unless the underlying picture drastically picks up, there may not be that big a need for Indian refiners to keep bidding up spot cargoes from other than 'normal' sources.
Will Atlantic barrels go East or remain in the region?

On the other hand, U.S. (and European) oil demand has held up better than expected YTD, and the U.S. hovers in the very high end of the historical range. As a result, also of declining shale production growth, U.S. inventories have kept drawing, albeit in line with the seasonal norm. This strong demand has also kept some Atlantic basin crude oil prodution growth consumed within the basin. 

A risk for exports going forward is that if the WTI foward curve flips to contango, which it very well might considering expected oil market balances, more crude may be kept for domestic inventory builds, as these are normally more directly linked to the shape of the forward curve.

content.content:
Russian seaborne exports have declined slightly YTD, but remain an important source of tanker tonne-miles - mainly due to India's uptake of the barrels which previously went to Europe. Given Trump's added tariffs on India there has been some market turmoil and speculation about what this may lead to. So far, commentary from India suggest there will be little change in crude sourcing, although those few more Atlantic cargoes have been secured short-term. 

This may not move the needle other than giving a short boost to tonne-miles. If sustained, and especially if a shift is more pronounced, there could be some effects, but still it is not entirely clear which direction it will affect the market. A few key questions: 
- How much less Russian oil may India take? (probably maximum 1 mbpd less considering long term agreements etc). 
- How much will find alternative buyers? (China seems the main alternative taker, but it does not seem there is demand for a full 1 mbpd more - unless extremely cheap). 
- How much will find its way to China on compliant tankers (so far, China's imports of Russian crude has to a greater extent used sanctioned tankers than has India's). 
- How much less crude will China source from other areas (if they take up to 1 mbpd extra, inventories would be filled within a few months...) and where? (mostly shorter distance to India) 
- Where will India source additional crude? (there is 1 mbdp extra coming from the MEG going forward - from which India used to purchase nearly 2/3rds of its crude oil - now only 45%)
- How much may Russia have to reduce exports by? (it is not like they can refine more considering Ukraine's recent attacks - although near-term exports are expected to rise following these attacks).   

From this, it is not entirely clear that any shift away from Russia will be a positive for (compliant) tanker tonne-miles - it could more likely end up being a drag.

content.title: Crude flow shift to India driven tonne-miles

content.content:
Have sanctions so far materially affected flows? Meh. Iranian exports are up more than 100 kbpd on average this year vs. last year, and the growth trend for Iran, Venezuela and Russia is intact, despite more than 15% of the tanker fleet having been sanctioned by the OFAC, EU and UK.  The flow of Iranian and Venezuelan crude on OFAC listed tankers has hardly changed, but where there is a bigger impact is out of Russia. 

That means a greater share of Russian exports is carried by (semi) compliant tankers - only about one third of Russian Western exports is carried by sanctioned tankers, mainly those sanctioned by the EU and UK, whereas from Eastern Russia (to China) the use of sanctioned tonnage is much more common. 

What if sanctions on Russia are eventually lifted, will a lot of tankers be scrapped to offset the decline in tonne-miles that may come from this? Maybe, but mainly if rates drop significantly... Otherwise, only about 3% of the fleet is sanctioned by the OFAC in relation to Russia, and 'only' 60% of these were built in 2007 or earlier and may thus be phase-out candidates. Otherwise, most should find some alternative employment.
Source: Fearnleys, Vortexa, OFAC, EU, UK
Refinery margin strength boosts product tankers, again

In its most recent report the IEA lifted its 2025 (and 2026) refinery run estimates by 240 kbpd driven by solid demand and refinery margins. The latter has also partly been supported by some outages in key areas, and a lighter crude slate in Europe. There is still expectations for a decent slump in runs over the next few months, which should give a shoulder season also for product tankers, but the outlook for the winter could again be strong - depending a bit how well crack spreads and some key arbs hold up. For now, the product tanker market is again well supported by high cracks and open long-haul arbitrages.
Deliveries about to accelerate, can all this be absorbed?

After two years of very low tanker fleet growth, deliveries are about to accelerate in coming months and years. From last year's negligible 0.8% net fleet growth, this year has already seen 1.2%, with another 1.5% scheduled to be delivered by year end - possibly more as many yards seem able to deliver ahead of schedule. This is still not a lot combined, but next year's scheduled 5.8% is - especially as rates are much too high to expect any meaningful phase-out. That will be followed by 5.1% scheduled deliveries in 2027 - again possibly more as there are a number of reported and rumoured orders which have not been finally confirmed yet. 

Quite a lot of fleet growth then - starting with 35% of this year's scheduled deliveries in the fourth quarter. Sure, oil supply additions will absorb some of this fleet growth near term, but then what..?

Although the orderbook to fleet ratio has risen to close to 15%, orders keep piling in, with more to come. And, that may still be needed, due to the vast phase-out potential. The orderbook in dwt is matched by tonnage at or near historical phase-out age, but due to high earnings and alternative employment there has not been any meaningful phase-out. We do not foresee any meaningful phase-out the next year or two, unless earnings drop and/or there are some meaningful changes to sanctions. Eventually, however, phase-out will happen and fleet renewal is needed so the medium to longer term outlook is still relatively strong - meaning some limit to the downside potential. 

Owners seem to have taken note, and the YTD order intake still runs at an annualised level above the historical average. Demolition runs well below.

So, there are a few clear downside risks in the coming months, but on the other hand, imported iron ore consumption in China is still high at close to 3.0 million tons per day, and Bauxite shipments is at the seasonal low point.

content.content:
From our previous report in early June:

*Our view remains that this year will see lower earnings averages than in 2023. Market fundamentals remain sluggish, with shipment volume growth now comparable to years like 2016, 2020, and 2022. We do not expect growth to increase this year, as too many factors weigh heavily.*

The question to ask now is whether the market strength seen over the last month and a half is temporary, or whether we have assessed the fundamental picture incorrectly, in the sense  that the upcycle we expected to start next year is already here? Most market indicators we use suggest the former, which, along with temporary factors like heatwaves causing a surge in coal demand, a strong ECSAM grain season, and front-running Trump’s tariffs, could mean the markets will end this year on a weaker note. The shipment volume development in July was extreme, with the year-on-year growth increasing from an average of around 0% for the first 6 months of the year to 11% in in that month - the fourth highest month-on-month change in growth seen through our data going back to the year 2000. Another comparison is that in the last ten years, the only month that compares to July’s year-on-year growth rate was April 2021. July’s growth rate is not likely to be sustainable, but it is still possible that developments since the panic in April have kicked the global economy into an upcycle, which in our assessment means shipment volume growth could average about 4% over the next year and a half. How so? Disregarding reports of front-running, which, anyway, so far only shows up clearly in US economic statistics and not much elsewhere, the US dollar has weakened considerably since April. This is a reflection of looser financial conditions, and it allows Central Banks to cut interest rates more as they worry less about currency imbalances and inflation. Along with that,  oil prices have been low this year, which is a leading indicator of higher economic activity (chart on the last page of this report). Finally, the PBOC has printed money at the highest rate ever this year, another leading indicator of higher economic activity to come. Some data is already showing that construction activity domestically in China is picking up markedly, which is usually followed by higher import growth. These factors we had already pointed to in the previous months, but usually there is a longer lag before it impacts dry bulk markets. Our conclusion from our previous report in early June:

*We still expect fundamentals to improve in 2026. A lot of factors are moving in the right direction in that respect. Seaborne iron ore fundamentals are likely to bottom in Q4 this year, whereas coal and minor bulks fundamentals are not likely to bottom before Q1 next year, or maybe even Q2. That means there could be a slow start to the next upcycle, then an acceleration during 2H 2026, with fundamentals subsequently remaining strong through 2027 and probably during parts of 2028.*

There is a possibility that we have to change our outlook, with the new timeline being that an upcycle has already begun and that this will last through 2026, then perhaps start fading in 2027. However, we are sceptical that the current market strength is sustainable, and need another month or so to see how shipment volume data, economic data, and the markets develop before making any change.

The spread between second-hand values and period rates remains higher than average, although it has narrowed over the last two months. 

**Capesize:** 

To bring the average spread down to the last 15 years' average, 1-year TC rates would have to rise to the high twenties, or the 10-year-old value would have to fall below 35 million USD. 

**Kamsarmax:**

The spread is just slightly higher than the average of the last 15 years. A small rise in period rates or a small drop in values would bring the spread "back to normal". 

**Supramax:**

To bring the spread down to the last 15 years' average, the value of a 10-year-old would have to drop to 17 million USD, or the 1-year TC rate would have to rise to 14.500-15.000 USD pd. 

**Handysize:**

To bring the spread down to the last 15 years' average, the value of a 10-year old would have to drop to around 15 million USD, or the 1-year TC rate would have to rise to around 14.000 USD pd.

This page gives brief comments on what the charts on the next page tells us. 

Top left chart:

China's credit growth keeps increasing. By the measure we use, credit growth in June was the highest since March 2021. A positive year-on-year change of the BDI from March 2026 onwards is suggested basis a 12 months lead. 

Top right chart:

Through the first six months of this year, China's economic growth index has averaged -2.8%, compared to -2.1% for all of 2024. 
So, thus far there is not much evidence of the PBOCs stimulus measures reviving the country's economic growth. Concerning dry bulk specifically, steel production is reported to be down 1.1% by WorldSteel, whereas imported iron ore consumption is reported to be up by 4.6%, indicating that it is reduced EAF production that is causing the fall in total steel production. Despite higher imported iron ore consumption, China's iron ore imports are down 2.3% on last year through July, as inventory drawing have subtracted from the demand for imports. 

Middle left chart:

Lower crude oil prices are bullish for economic growth, and vice versa. The chart displays that since 2017, there has been a tight correlation between lower year-on-year oil prices and a higher year-on-year BDI, with the oil price change leading by 1 year. 
This indicator is suggesting the BDI year-on-year change is past the low point, and that it will trend upwards over the next year. 

Middle right chart:

Global interest rate cuts suggest 1 year TC rates will be higher during the second half of 2026 than what it was through the first half of this year. That implies at least the mid-teens for Kamsarmaxes. 

Bottom left chart:

The OECD G-20 Diffusion index and the BDI year on year change have correlated tightly for decades. However, over the last year there has been a decoupling, as the Diffusion index suggest the global economy has started to decelerate from a cycle peak, whereas the BDI year-on-year change have been in downcycle territory since Q4 last year. The main reason for this decoupling is that the services sector has driven most of global economic growth over the last year, whereas manufacturing has been weak. That, in turn, is probably an after-effect of the manufacturing boom/services depression seen through the lockdown period of 2020-2022.

Bottom right chart:

The dollar index has weakened in the last months, and as usual, the result is increased dry bulk shipment volume growth with a few months' lag. The dollar index suggests total dry bulk shipment volume growth is past the cycle bottom.

The LNG S&P market is undergoing a notable transformation this year. Initial expectations for a robust second-hand market have been tempered by constant changes stemming from the United States, which have created a complex and sometimes unpredictable environment—a veritable "old-fashioned stew." This mix of ingredients—from decisions on recycling and refinancing to new KYC requirements and volatile interest rates—has created some truly interesting market "tastes."

Since our last report, these dynamics have been demonstrated by several key developments. We have seen discussions surrounding a modern vessel being refinanced through a Japanese Leasing structure, the confirmation of four additional vessels sold for recycling (bringing the total to ten), and multiple instances of vessels being placed on and off "subs." In these cases, buyers have shown a looser interpretation of MOAs than their formal terms, with cultural nuances and ultimate beneficial ownership often emerging as common denominators.

While it remains challenging to determine conclusive transaction levels in the current climate, it is increasingly clear that Steam Turbine vessels are destined for a bifurcated future: either bespoke projects (Steamer Nirvana) or recycling (Steamer Samsara). Similarly, DFDE/TFDE vessels are facing market struggles, though their outlook is somewhat more favorable due to their size and potential for UFS impact in tailormade projects. It is particularly noteworthy that inquiries for alternative uses for STs and DFDE/TDFEs are currently more prevalent than those seeking a cyclical shipping play with 2-stroke vessels.

Amid a renewed focus on building LNG carriers with US participation, Hanwa Philly Shipyards has secured an order for one firm and one optional vessel. The final price for this order will be a point of considerable interest, as historical comparisons with less complex shipbuilding segments suggest this will be a high-cost endeavor for the owner. 
Shipyards, however, are still holding relatively firm on their pricing, and we do not anticipate a significant change as of now.

We can also confirm that Purus, a subject of rumors earlier this year, has officially entered the newbuilding LNG market. This is a welcome development that introduces a new entrant into the sector. The key question now is the extent of their appetite for additional vessels in the remaining months of the year.

Tanker rates in the first half of this year were mostly in line with our forecast, apart from VLCCs which still relatively lag smaller vessels. Going forward we had thought that the growing surplus of crude oil that energy agencies forecast in the Atlantic basin would give solid tanker tonne-mile demand growth. We had also thought that harsher sanctions would give continued replacement need for the buyers of sanctioned barrels. 

However, neither condition seems to hold. Fleet growth has also picked up with more to come. Hence, we now see risk to the downside for rates vs. our base case forecast, especially for VLCCs. The set-up going forward may be quite similar to last year's 2H trajectory, albeit at a higher base rate level due to some tonne-mile growth on increasing volumes. 

VLCC rates are now likely to end up between our base- and bear case, while for the remining segments rates are expected to end up close to, but potentially somewhat below our base case.

So far this year crude tanker tonne-mile demand, excluding OFAC listed vessels, is in line with the same period last year. Last year, extraordinarily high USG export and geopolitics were the main drivers, while this year it was (fear of) sanctions. Fleet growth has picked up slightly, and has been higher than demand growth. Rates are therefore lower YTD, only slightly for VLCCs but more meaningfully for Suez- and Aframax.  The latter two still outperform VLCCs on a relative basis. 

Product tanker tonne-mile demand YTD is nearly 5% lower vs. the same period last year, and rates have followed, although have remained quite strong in a historical context. Tonne-mile demand has been driven lower by more regional products trade, after the extraordinary trade shifts of the last few years have settled a bit. There has especially been less East-West trade. Higher fleet growth has also contributed to rate downside. 

Going into the second half of the year, demand should fare somewhat better than in the second half of last year, but some caution is warranted. This, coupled with increasing fleet growth could mean a softer rate trajectory than some may hope for and than we have earlier expected.

content.content:
For the biggest vessels, there was a decent demand surge earlier in the year when Chinese buyers of sanctioned barrels took a step back, and sought compliant barrels instead. In the last two months, however, West-East flows have come off, and the West-East arbitrage has largely been closed, as it also is now. 

This arbitrage may be unlikely to re-open anytime soon, due to a combination of factors: 
- Iranian exports are back to the highs, and Chinese buyers have resumed, especially after Trump seemingly gave the green light on social media. Recent sanctions announcements contradict this, but little actual change is observable.  
- The OPEC+ output hikes, which may start to show in seaborne exports from August/September, should gain market share in Asia. 
- Chinese apparent oil demand is down 6% YTD while inventories have built by nearly 100 mb since January. 
- Red Sea attacks have resumed, leaving crude oil trade split between the two basins. 
- Oil demand in the West has been resilient, oil supply has grown less than expected, inventories are low, and refinery margins strong. This all suggests that (much of) the additional barrels coming from Brazil and Guyana may find a home within the Atlantic.

content.content:
In its recent Oil 2025 report, the IEA largely held its total oil demand and supply forecasts unchanged, but meaningfully changed their composition to reflect the recent trend: Oil demand growth 2024-2030 West of Suez was lifted by 1.3 mbpd while supply was lowered by 1.2 mbpd. At the same time demand growth East of Suez was lowered by 1.2 mbpd while supply was lifted by 2.5 mbpd. 

For the tanker market, this means that while volumes may continue to grow, sailing distances may shorten as oil demand/supply balances between the West and East are more closely aligned. This is likely to give much lower tonne-mile demand growth than earlier expected..

content.content:
The IEA's monthly reports have followed a similar trend: Since the beginning of this year, the agency has lowered its 2025 OECD demand forecast for by 0.2 mbpd, and non-OPEC+ supply growth by 0.1 mbpd - relatively in line. For non-OECD demand has been lowered by 0.2 mbpd, while OPEC+ supply has been revised up by 0.7 mbpd - in (very) simple math 0.9 mbpd less Atlantic-East potential.  

The OPEC+ 8 will unwind voluntary production cuts by 548 kbpd in August, up from 411 mbpd the last few months. This takes the total target unwind since April to 1.9 Mbpd (the actual unwind is nearly 0.7 mbpd) and leaves 547 kbpd (before the next tranche of voluntary cuts of 1.66 mbpd - planned to be in place through 2026). Adjusting for overproduction, this likely means a 340 kbpd hike vs. July, of which Russia’s 100 kbpd is uncertain, meaning about 240 kbpd extra from the Middle East. The August targets are actually 440 kbpd BELOW June production (a bit technical due to Saudi shifting production as a precaution during the Israel/Iran 12-day war). Realistically, stripping out the countries which have perpetually 'cheated' the upside is about 200 kbpd from the MEG in August vs. last month. 

More importantly, as seasonal demand subsides from September, MEG exports are set to rise further, by about 2-300 kbpd per month from September. While it leaves growing tanker volumes, this also means that Asian buyers will be in no rush to look to the Atlantic for those long-haul barrels. For instance, Saudi allocations to Chinese buyers in August are about 10 mb higher than at the beginning of this year.

content.title: Q/Q production increase, key Atlantic producers

content.content:
The oil market has this year not been nearly as oversupplied as energy agencies have feared. The IEA's estimates imply a 1.8 mbpd oversupplied market in the first half of this year, whereas its own estimates show global inventories have 'only' risen by about 1 mbpd, mainly in China and floating storage. While global stocks appear low vs. the 5-year range, remember this was a historically high period, hence stocks are plentiful. 

The nearly 100 mb by which China's inventories have built YTD nearly matches the 125 mb of new capacity planned to be built this year. Hence, further builds could hinge on attractive pricing. 

The Brent forward curve has remained backwardated, reflecting a much tighter oil market balance than the IEA's estimates imply. Given OPEC+ production cut unwind and new projects coming online in South America, going into shoulder season for demand, there should be a surplus of oil going forward. In the West, some of that may contribute to refilling inventories.

content.content: Refinery margins and runs have held up quite well recently, boosting product tanker flows and rates. Especially in Europe, gasoil margins are firm, leading to a demand pull from other regions. This is likely to eventually pass, and going into shoulder season when product tanker volumes slip is also when deliveries are set to pick up. Hence, we expect a gradual weakening of the product tanker market balance after the next couple of months.

YTD the product tanker market has been much less supported by long-haul East-West CPP flow than in recent years. East-of-Suez to Europe flow has declined by 16.5% YTD. In tonne-mile terms that equates to a near 2 percentage point drop in product tanker demand. 

Little wonder then, that there has been a continued trend for LR2s to dirty up, although over the last months some vessels have started to switch back. There has also been a tick-up in Suezmaxes taking CPP cargoes again - increasingly on newbuilds. The latter may continue to be a threat to CPP demand going forward, as deliveries of Suezmaxes nearly double in the second vs. first half of the year, and VLCC deliveries start piling up into next year. 

Strong gasoil margins in Europe currently offer some support for long-haul product tanker demand, but that may be temporary due to higher seasonal demand and a heatwave - which affects both demand (up) and runs (down).

content.content: Little fleet growth YTD, set to incrementally pick up

Overall tanker fleet growth YTD has still been relatively low, at 0.9% during the first half. That is, however, already more than all of last year, and the the delivery schedule is skewed to the second half with another 2.1% (gross) to come. This means slightly higher fleet growth than we had expected at the beginning of the year, due to less phase-out and earlier deliveries. Some vessels have, however, left the compliant fleet for the shadow markets too. 

The orderbook to fleet ratio has crept up to 14.6%, a more meaningful level, although with 20+ years old vessels amounting to 15.7% of the fleet there is plenty of phase-out potential. Still, most of these ageing vessels are employed in the sanctioned trades, and are therefore already out of the compliant fleet. 

Unless phase-out meaningfully picks up, net fleet growth this year may end up at 2-2.5% and the next two years at 4-5%.  Due to the ever increasing part of the fleet which are trading in the shadows, net deliveries vs. the compliant fleet will be  higher than the gross numbers suggest..

content.content:
Ordering interest has slowed substantially YTD vs. the last two years, but remains in line with the historical average. The run rate order intake points to a 2.5 percentage point hike in the OB/Fleet. Beyond 2027 more orders may be needed, but over the next two years fleet growth looks plentiful. 

Tanker demolition has also picked up to double that of the last two years. However, that remains miniscule, with the run-rate pointing to 0.3% phase-out. There are also a few vessels which have been converted etc. so that total phase-out run-rate may end up at around 1%. Some more vessels have also left the compliant fleet, to offset most of this year's fleet growth.

Given a potentially softer outlook, TC rates which have softened since hitting a peak early in the year and unsupportive FFAs, there could be some (more) risk to the downside for asset values going forward. 

Secondhand values (for modern vessels) have weakened 5-10% on average YTD, other than for VLCCs where there have been few good sales candidates vs. a few keen buyers. For the smaller segments the end of the extraordinary earnings and returns on offer the past couple of years inevitably led to some selling pressure - and there appears to be more sales candidates around. Newbuild prices, meanwhile, have held relatively steady. 

The latter may be the next shoe to drop - as order intake at yards has dropped YTD, and prospective buyers appear to be in no rush - for most shipping segments. So, despite healthy backlogs, yards may need to drop prices going forward, for which there should be some room as some costs have eased and there appears to be decent profitability at current pricing. 

At our rate forecasts for next year, there is in theory 15-20% downside risk for modern asset values implied from the historical correlation between asset values and rates. Given many cash rich owners sitting on the sidelines waiting for an opportunity to pounce on lower asset values, however, we doubt values will decline that much - a bit like for dry bulk over the past two years.

We do not see much chance of this changing over the next 6 months, and therefore expect market levels to remain below that of last year.

As long as energy costs remain at current levels (or drop further), global industry will receive a boost next year and in 2027. Coal prices probably have further room to fall, and oil markets are likely to be well supplied going forward, as IEA says, *"Barring big disruptions, global oil markets are set to be well supplied over the next 5 years, with production capacity growth far exceeding the increase in demand".*
The bottom right chart displays that usually, lower yoy oil prices suggest the BDI will be higher yoy (and vice versa), with a 1-year lead.* 

We expected the Supra/Ultra market to continue treading sideways. content.content:
During the second quarter of the year, average daily spot earnings across the three index routes reached $50,500 per day. This brought the year-to-date average up from $36,000 to $43,000 per day—still 24.5% lower than the same period last year.

The quarter began on a turbulent note, marked by the U.S. President’s “Liberation Day” announcement on April 2nd, which introduced a broad package of import duties, significantly impacting trade relations with China. In response, China imposed retaliatory tariffs, triggering a sharp market reaction and a steep decline in earnings around April 11th. Although the situation worsened briefly, trading patterns soon adjusted, and rates rebounded.

Later in the quarter, geopolitical tensions escalated between Israel and Iran, culminating in missile attacks and a near war-like environment. In June, Iran threatened to close the Strait of Hormuz—a critical chokepoint for LPG exports. A closure would effectively block the UAE, Qatar, and Kuwait from their export routes. These three countries collectively account for 60% of the region’s LPG exports, or approximately 28 million tons, which would need to be sourced elsewhere. This development severely constrained regional exports, while heightened security risks discouraged Owners from fixing new cargoes. As a result of this scarcity of Middle Eastern cargoes, BLPG-1 maintained a significant premium over BLPG-3, as illustrated in the graph above.
U.S. Production and Terminal Capacity Expansion

U.S. LPG production continues to rise, with total output increasing by 27.25% over the past five years. While growth is expected to slow to approximately 5% over the next three years, export capacity is projected to expand significantly during the same period. Domestic consumption remains stable, as do export levels, which continue to hover around 60%.

VLGCs account for 82% of all seaborne LPG exports from the U.S., totaling 52 million tons in 2024, and 29.5 million tons so far in 2025.

Regarding routing patterns, the majority of laden vessels heading east from the U.S. opt for the Panama Canal. Year-to-date data shows that 83% of these voyages have taken this route rather than sailing around the Cape of Good Hope. In contrast, approximately 35% of ballasting vessels returning to the U.S. from the East choose the Cape of Good Hope route.

The announced capacity expansions from several U.S. terminals have boosted market confidence going forward, as this incremental supply is likely to fulfill the expanding fleet's needs better than previously anticipated. *See an overview of the announced capacity increases below.*

It should be noted that both the Nederland and Neches River facilities will offer flexible capacity for LPG and ethane volumes. Given the recent growth in U.S. ethane exports, it is expected that a portion of these volumes will be allocated to ethane rather than LPG. Now that U.S. ethane suppliers are granted permission to discharge in China, as normal, we expect this trade to continue growing in line with its large orderbook (216% to fleet).

Total U.S. export capacity is set to increase from 68 to 111 MTPA by 2028 with the completion of these projects. This would boost export capacity by 65% from 2024 to 2028—a substantial jump that is warmly welcomed by a growing fleet.

What will materialize as the *actual* incremental exports is yet to be seen; however, it will likely be less than the full capacity numbers. Nevertheless, this move by U.S. energy suppliers further underscores the market's desire to expand and grow.

LPG exports from the Middle East has been strong in the first half of the year, with total volumes surpassing 21 million tons. The long-awaited natural gas projects in Qatar will come online (North Field East) next year, which is expected to bring with it incremental LPG volumes. Additionally, in 2027 (North Field South), will further support the increased exports. Approximately 4.2 MTPA is expected in 2026, and another 2 MTPA in 2027, which would increase the regions export capacity from 46 to 52 MTPA. This additional supply of LPG will be beneficial to the fleet expansion that will occur at the same time.

As a natural repsonse to the tensions that have occurred between the two power nations, Chinese imports decreased slightly during Q2, compared to Q1. They imported a total 8.24 million tons this past quarter, and 19.9 million tons on a year-to-date basis.

The majority of this demand is still driven by the petrochemical sector and continuous increased PDH (propane dehydrogenation) capacity coming online. Chinese PDH plants are still struggling with negative margins, however, their run rates have recently improved slightly in line with the flat price decline. The incremental capacity planned to come online in the following quarter, is likely to be pushed back into Q4, or 2026.

After a trade war escalating with increased tariffs on each country, the final verdict was reached in May, where China ended up with a 10% tariff on U.S. LPG. This creates an economic equation where U.S. LPG is still the most attractive, and they have yet again regained their competitive advantage, compared to the Middle East. In terms of the USTR and their attempt to impose port call fees on Chinese-built and/or -operated ships, the impact on VLGCs appear to be small. For Chinese-built ships, they are exempted as they are always arriving in ballast, not laden. Although, for Chinese-controlled/owned ships, there will be fees, starting from October 2025.

Newbuilding activity has been low in the first half of 2025, with 3 ships delivered in Q1 and another 3 in Q2. There is another 4 expected in Q3 and Q4, as well. The remaining number of deliveries for the year is 8, giving a total of 13 newbuilds. The fleet now stands at 406 ships, including floating storage. The orderbook consists of 108 ships, resulting in an orderbook-fleet ratio of 26%, which is slightly above the 20-year average of 21%. Nonetheless, the fleet is set to grow by 19.4% through 2026 and 2027 in total, which could set of the fleet balance in a surplus.

Hyundai in South Korea remains the largest builder of newbuilds, while one quarter of the newbuilds are being constructed in China (bars shown in light blue in chart above). The proposed port call fees by the USTR, on Chinese-built and/or -operated ships, has been clarified as only applicable for laden ships calling U.S. ports. This is rarely the case for VLGCs, thus we can exclude this possibility.

After two consecutive years of record-number orders placed for VLGC newbuilds, only a couple of ships has been ordered in 2025. Even though overall yard capacity remains tight, due to strong activity from other segments, the current price for a VLGC newbuild is around $118 million. Due to the many uncertainties in the geopolitical sphere, all markets have experienced a lack of investments the past quarter.

Following a quarter marked by exceptional uncertainty, the market has now stabilized into a “new normal,” with earnings rebounding sharply to a year-to-date average of $43,500 per day. We anticipate that earnings will remain within the $50,000–$60,000 per day range for the remainder of the year.

The upcoming increase in U.S. export capacity, expected to come online in Q3, is likely to support earnings further. Looking ahead to 2026, additional capacity expansions in the U.S., combined with a projected supply boost from the Middle East, are expected to help offset the impact of fleet growth. Notably, 34 newbuild VLGCs are scheduled for delivery next year, and the added supply should help balance the market.

The fleet will continue to grow, and whether this additional tonnage will be absorbed depends on the realized increases in exports from both the U.S. and the Middle East. Additionally, the sailing pattern of the fleet remains volatile, where each voyage's choice between the Panama Canal or the Cape of Good Hope impacts the fleet's availability and capacity. The first of many VLACs (Very Large Ammonia Carriers) will be delivered next year; however, we do not separate these ships from VLGCs in the fleet, as the only difference is that they can carry ammonia at 98% capacity. They will likely trade LPG as regular VLGCs for the coming years, as the infrastructure to load and discharge ammonia on such large ships is not yet developed.

The Panama Canal has now started the Long Term Slot Allocation System, which takes up 40% of the capacity in the Neo-panamax locks. Panamaxes will therefore likely have an advantage in order to transit. However, half of the orderbook consists of Panamaxes, so this capacity is also going to change going forward.

To say that the shipping market is on a recovering path may be premature, but rates have seen a steady upwards – albeit bumpy - trend through the quarter. It is the first time since 2016 (excluding the market disruption in 2022 caused by the Russia/Ukraine conflict) that rates in Q2 have been higher than in Q1. However, that is more a testament as to how depressed Q1 really was. Moving into Q2, steady spot activityarose from a growth in LNG demand in the Atlantic/Mediterranean (Argentina, Egypt), tonnage being pulled from the spot market in advance of project startups (Canada LNG), the long-awaited commercial production from following Calcasieu Pass and Plaquemines towards end of Q1, and buyers reacting to a higher level of geopolitical uncertainty all combine to a slightly more optimistic near-term sentiment. That said, the fundamentals remain challenging and a reminder that freight should remain attractive for the coming year(s). Newbuild deliveries continues and based on the mismatching of pending start-ups and delivery schedules, we should not be surprised to see an erratic freight market through the next 12 months.

LNG prices in Europe and Asia largely traded in tandem throughout the quarter together with uncle crude, fluctuating between US$ 10-15/MMBtu. Initially dropping as crude fell on news of excess OPEC supply, there was a sharp turnaround on the geopolitical uncertainty erupting as the Israel-Iran conflict escalated. With no major regional events impacting product pricing, the arbitrage has been largely shut during the quarter. It is peculiar though that refilling of European gas storage is only at 58.9% as of 30th June; some 10% below the 5-year average and 18% below the 2024-level at the same time. Add to the mix a desire by the EU to phase out Russian LNG (which continues to flow into European countries), we should be in for an interesting second half of 2025.

The spot market has continued to see high activity, with the second consecutive quarter seeing 100+ spot fixtures (<90 days) concluded. While it keeps Owners, Charterers and brokers alike busy, it also highlights how the growth in volumes and ships on the water will drive the market to more short-term business activity. Another relevant observation during Q2 was the steep increase in short-term (<3 years) fixtures concluded by Owners as opposed to sublets, at 39% compared to Q1 at 26%. This suggests that Charterers are redelivering vessels as opposed to declaring what are likely out-of-the-money options.

We count 17 vessels delivered during the quarter, on par with the 16 delivered in Q1…leaving another 66 to go for the year according to our orderbook (of which nine are for Arctic LNG-2). To put that in context, it would imply an LNG carrier delivering every three days for the remainder of the year. Realistically, we do expect slippage of 2025-tonnage into 2026, with the driver being Owners delaying delivery to match better against delivery to charterers/projects. Although shipyards have been busy delivering ships, the new orders have been sparse with five vessels reported ordered during the quarter – taking the YTD tally to only eight. On the recycling side, four vessels were sold for their final voyage and the average age of vessels scrapped in 2025 is just shy of 25 years. There is no shortage of older vessels being circulated for sale, but with real/qualified buyers scarce on the ground we maintain the view that scrapping will become increasingly relevant for Owners with steam turbine tonnage coming off long-term charters, as prompt business for these ladies to continue trading is minimal. The fleet now stands at 718 vessels with 25 in layup and 298 still in the orderbooks. We note that our layup count has increased by seven over the course of the second quarter and expect this trend to continue – coinciding with our view on scrapping activity.

Despite the uncertainty created around US LNG export projects from an overzealous USTR, there were three FIDs during the quarter – two in the US breaking the drought: Woodside with Louisiana LNG (16.5mtpa with first LNG in 2029) and Cheniere announcing T8-9 at Corpus Christi (3mtpa with first LNG in 2028), which also includes debottlenecking on back of three firm offtake agreements. Golar also announced FID on their 2.4mtpa Hilli FLNG unit to Argentina starting 2027.

The average spot rate for a two-stroke in Q2 came in at US$ 30k/day; down 47% compared to Q2 2024. Rates hit a low of around US$ 20k/day in late-April before staging a comeback heading into July at US$ 46k/day. A clear premium on West developed over the quarter, reversing the marginal premium seen in the East during Q1and for much of 2024. Two-stroke tonnage in the West averaged US$ 34k/day vs US$ 25k/day in East. We are back to a level where Owners are not just covering OPEX (Q1 2025 average was US$17k), but there remains little left for contributions to equity. Although the fundamentals suggest a tough market ahead for Owners, we highlight the price sensitivity to end-users and the uncertainty of trade flows into H2 2025 potentially pointing to some risk to the upside on rates.

While it is rough sailing to be an owner of a two-stroke, its even rougher for those with TFDES as Q2 2025 average came in at US$ 16k/day – essentially covering OPEX. For steam turbines the reported average was US$ 3k/day, if managing to secure employment.

We see an increasing divergence between two-strokes and TFDE/DFDE/STs where Charterers have ample modern, fuel-efficient tonnage to chose from, and older propulsion types regularly get cut out of the equation in tenders. The frustration amongst Owners of TFDE/DFDE/ST is fully understandable and acknowledged, but sometimes a stop-loss can be a way to avoid the risk of long-term pain.

In the term market, 1-year deals for two-strokes are currently fixed in the US$ high-40s/day, up from US$ mid-30s/day at end of Q1. Liquidity in Q2 was predominantly centered around short-term (<90 days), as the bid-offer spread is a little wide for 3-yrs and 5-yrs. An interesting perspective here though is the implied curve, suggesting years 2 and 3 at around US$ high-60ss/day and years 4 and 5 at around US$ mid-80s/day. Hence, doing a 5-yr deal today taking us into mid-2030 should be an attractive position for Charterers. The flipside of that is Owners potentially looking to take some short-term pain over giving away upside and optionality in the medium-term.

The quarterly number of spot fixtures was close to the all-time high (on record) with 106 short-term fixtures concluded. This is marginally below the 118 recorded in Q1. Looking at days fixed on spot, the average duration is flat Q-o-Q at around 21 days, which is still up on the average duration of <90-day charters for the past two years.

On multi-month, we recorded 15 fixtures in Q2 with the average duration being just short of 6 months – suggesting Owners may be more interested in having the vessel back ahead of the winter period. For up-to-3yr deals the quarter was weak at only 5 fixtures identified, albeit for longer periods (around 1.5 yrs on average) compared to what was done in Q1 and throughout 2024.

We are seeing more Charterers looking for longer term deals, potentially as their high-priced charters done a few years back are coming to an end, and they are incentivized to redeliver rather than declaring out-of-the-money options. There is also an increase in tender activity which we expect to materialize in H2 2025 and result in medium-/long-term charters.

content.content:
A total of 107MT of LNG was loaded in Q2 2025, a touch down from the all-time high of 110MT in Q1, but up 7MT Y-o-Y (vs Q2 2024). Continued ramp-up of Plaquemines together with restored production from Nigeria, full production from Freeport, start-up of Gimi FLNG at Greater Tortue and Calcasieu Pass ramp-up were the largest contributors from Q1. On the other side of the spectrum, maintenance at Malaysia LNG, Hammerfest and Qatar LNG as well as lower volumes out of Sabine Pass and Cameron drove volumes down from the highs. US production was at 27MT for the quarter, representing 25% of global LNG supply and expected to continue growing. With Canada joining the list of LNG exporting countries and first cargo leaving LNG Canada at the very end of the quarter, we expect to finally see monthly loadings cross the 40MT mark by year-end.

On the receiving end, Chinese imports have dropped 3.5MT Y-o-Y with also Japan, Thailand and India pulling back, while European buyers including France, Belgium and Italy are growing imports. Egypt is also back in the mix of active buyers and expected to become even more active with a small armada of FSRUs getting ready to operate.

In terms of trade flows, more US LNG is heading towards Asia, with 18% of US volumes passing the Cape of Good Hope and adding to tonne-miles. Alas, it is still substantially below the 35% seen in Q2 2024 and the lack of recovery in US-Asia volumes is clearly a negative for the shipping market. One positive is that the Panama Canal is largely unutilized, so anything going East from US does the long-haul. Qatari volumes to Asia also reached the highest level on record in June with 85% - also not helping voyage distances in the overall tonne-mile demand.

It is becoming increasingly clear that two-strokes are favored for the long-hauls as 65% (51% in Q2 2024) of all Atlantic loadings go onboard the MEGI/MEGA/XDF-fleet. TFDEs account for 20% (27% in Q2 2024) while STs take the remaining 15% (22% in Q2 2024). The Y-o-Y development highlights both how the influx of new vessels and unit freight cost displaces less efficient tonnage.

content.content:
The 17 LNGCs delivered in Q2 brings the total fleet on the water to 718 vessels. However, with 25 vessels in layup, the “live” fleet stands at 693 – less if the idling vessels are considered. The slow-down in new orders and reasonably rapid deliveries has brought the orderbook-to-fleet ratio further down, to 43%. Orders for a total of five vessels were placed during the quarter with one back-to-back with charter and four seemingly speculative but likely positioning for upcoming tenders.

66 vessels are still scheduled for delivery in 2025, of which nine are Arc-7s originally intended for the Arctic LNG-2, and whose delivery is continuously pushed. With 32 delivered thus far, we could reach mid-80s vessels added to the fleet over the course of the year. In some way we hope (and expect) there will be deferral of deliveries towards year-end, but 2025 will inevitably be the busiest year in terms of vessel delivery in history.

89 ships are currently on order in China, or 30% of the orderbook, with 55 at Hudong-Zhonghua. From our latest data, 26 ships in the orderbook are without charters, of which two deliver this year, 11 in 2026 and 13 in 2027. Although yards are happy with the backlog still, available slots will be for Q2 2028 delivery, and from there on - there is plenty of capacity. While we do not anticipate a full-on rush to yards from Owners, the number of potential tenders for both project and replacement programs suggests we will see more activity in H2 2025.

On the recycling front, another four vessels were sold for scrap during the quarter and with seven vessels now done for the year, 2025 will likely not only be a record for deliveries – but also for scrapping. It’s a pity we’re prone to see around 80 vessels delivered and far less scrapped. That said, we expect to see a shift in mentality with Owners in possession of steam turbines as they are marginalized in the freight market and the pace and magnitude of FSRU/FSU projects is not able to soak up all open tonnage. Scrapping age will most certainly remain well below the 35-40yr average seen in the past decade.

The S&P market has been relatively subdued thus far in 2025 with the majority of transactions involving older tonnage with variable quality of buyers as KYC remains a focus. Asset values have come off further during the quarter across steam turbine, TDFE and two-strokes, but the gap between willing buyers and willing sellers needs to narrow.

Acquiring entities (that do pass KYC) tends to be focused on tonnage for project work on both steam turbines and TFDEs – which makes sense given the activity seen in the FSRU/FSU market. For two-strokes the discussions are fewer and further between.

The multi-billion dollar question we get asked (several times) daily is: when could the market tighten? Based on our supply/demand balance (with all the caveats that come with forecasting), the fundamentals show a broadly soft market through into 2027, and finally a real tightening materializing in 2028. This is the base case from Fearnleys, and as always trade volumes and flows can have material impacts on the market tightness. A widening of arbitrages absorbing more tonnage on US-Asia could be enough for rates to nudge higher – at least for a period of time. Another factor is whether the ships ordered to serve Qatar North Field Expansion, and Qatar Energy's share in Golden Pass, will be made available in the market when vessel deliveries occur earlier than volume start-ups. There are talks of some of these vessels being deferred for delivery which would help the market balance.

Another major question mark is how the vintage vessel fleet phase out will play out? While we take the view that “25 is the new 35” in terms of scrapping age, the inertia of LNGCs being sold to the breakers has historically been high. Owners of LNGCs seem at times to misprice the option cost of keeping technologically obsolete tonnage on the books. If the scrapping age drops to 20 years (which is a major step for owners, scrap yards and accounting teams alike) that would contribute to materially reduce fleet capacity. However, it should be clear that the transportation work done by the steam turbine fleet is diminishing – our forecasting is based on an “all vessels are created equal” in terms of utilization – which may itself offer some relief through layups which never return to market.

New FIDs will inevitably play a vital role for future shipping demand, and US FIDs are especially important. Seeing Japanese players ink up on major long-term SPAs underpins our view of continued growth in sailing distances and shipping requirements. Although Chinese demand growth is expected to continue, we see an increasing share of future LNG demand to be absorbed by emerging Asian markets. This adds, if nothing else, to the distance part of the tonne-mile equation.

However, our intelligence suggests a good flow of tender activity from a broad range of market participants, which will keep yards busy. For the time being, yards are pricing newbuilds at relatively high levels which underpin long-term charter deals in the US$ mid-/high-80s/day – deterring some Owners as returns are not sufficiently attractive. Fast-forward 12 months with limited order intake and yards may have a slightly softer stance which may entice Owners to fill the late-2028 and 2029 slots – potentially extending the time of a fundamental market recovery.

While our outlook may be a sobering one, it is important to keep in mind that LNG is the fastest growing fossil fuel and that the growth in supply is set to grow by a whopping 50% by 2030 (vs 2024) according to S&P Platts. That is the equivalent of some 200+MT of LNG which must be moved. The near-term pain will drive older tonnage out of the market as scrapping is a function of a bad market (and not a catalyst for boom times), which means that Owners need to hold on tight, focus on keeping OPEX in check and maintain a strong relationship with the banks. Charterers on their side should be positioned to pick up attractive deals – after having paid the price a few years back.
