content.content: Market reflections: Running out of tonnage

The anticipation and run-up of prospective activity in the FSRU market during the first quarter came to fruition during the second quarter of the year with a flurry of fixtures (to the extent one can use such a characterization for the FSRU market). EGAS led the charge with two firm deals and one seasonal structure concluded at very solid rate levels which we consider a reflection of an end-user having scoured the market for months finally putting pen to paper; well-played to the involved Owners. However, what looked like a transformation of the market to focus on sublets and near-term availability now appears to be returning to somewhat more normalized project processes. The caveat being a further tightening of prompt-ish tonnage availability and those units left all coming with some form of baggage. The quarter also puts in perspective (and potentially in question) Germanys ambitions on the FSRU front with two out of five governmental units now relet for long/short periods.

While the FSRU market tends to act like chaotic pendulum at times (hard to tell what the next motion will be) our read is that we’re poised for high activity in the next 9-18 months – an activity level which should favor conversions over newbuilds over existing tonnage. We’ve revisited our bottom-up analysis during the quarter and continue to view 2-4 new projects annually as realistic with a form of wall-of-projects slated for 2028 start-up coming to market through H2/25 and in 2026. Thus far in 2025 we count three new projects (2 x Dominican Republic + 1 x Egypt) together with potentially three existing projects (1 x Egypt + 2 x Undisclosed) extending contracts or relocating.
Key market developments during the quarter

APRIL

Viva Energy re-emerges with requirement for Geelong project following long hiatus. Requirement is for **160,000-180,000cbm with upto 750MMSCFD** capacity. FID is targeted towards end-2025 with Viva aiming for startup in 2028. Timing and sizing suggest TFDE-conversions will be offered primarily with those having larger (170+kcbm) units to offer likely in pole position.

Deutsche Regas announces capacity sold-out through 2025 with a total of 5BCM sold to shippers. The company also indicated further capacity bookings available through 2043 to be concluded by end of summer. Deutsche Regas redelivered the **ENERGOS POWER** in Feb-25, but has announced intentions to install a replacement FSRU in Mukran to work alongside **NEPTUNE** presently in operation.

Snam completes commissioning of **BW SINGAPORE** at Ravenna with commercial operations commencing in May. Capacity is expected to be limited until the facility has the new breakwater installed.

**EXCELSIOR** finally arrives at Wilhelmshaven 2 after a long holiday at Ferrol S.Y. The unit formally went on-hire in Q1/23 for a five-year charter and has cost the German taxpayers an estimated US$ 55m annually (in charter hire only). The unit was connected in May and is undergoing commissioning over summer with commercial operations expected in August.

**ALEXANDROUPOLIS** start-up pushed back to Aug-25 following a complete shutdown in Jan-25 due to technical issues and damages to booster pumps. While there has been limited news since mid-May, it remains uncertain as to whether the unit will resume full production in 2025.

MAY

After a lot of rumours, **ENERGOS POWER** reported chartered out for appx 8.3 years from BMWK (German government) to EGAS for around US$ 155k/day. Charter duration is back-to-back with remaining original period between Energos and BMWK. Charter to commence prompt and unit expected to be located at Sonker jetty in Ain Sokhna following compatibility modifications. 

Hoegh EVI announces having secured a 10-year charter for **HOEGH GANDRIA** to EGAS with delivery in Q4/26 following conversion to FSRU at Seatrium. Rate is rumoured to be north of US$ 160k/day. The unit will replace **HOEGH GALLEON** which has been extended from its original charter ending Feb-26.  

New Fortress Energy announces having secured a 3-year charter for **ENERGOS FREEZE** to Energia 2000 in Dominican Republic starting Sep-25. The rate is rumoured to be in the range of US$ 110l-120k/day. The unit is expected to be replaced by an FSRU+FSU configuration provided to Manzanillo Gas & Power in 2028 from a separate FSRU provider.

**ENERGOS WINTER** entered drydock in Besiktas S.Y., Turkey and is expected to be available for charter early-/mid-Q3/25. It is not clear whether unit will be returning to TGS in Brazil.

The low-pressure/low send-out FSRU **KARMOL LNGT POWERSHIP AFRICA** stationed in Dakar, Senegal received first cargo in four years as KPS powership in Dakar switches to LNG. Additional cargoes are potentially in the pipeline as supplier has reportedly put options on a strip of cargoes.

JUNE

**ENERGOS FORCE** rumoured to be chartered out for 6-9 months despite HEH/Stade confirming terminal will be ready for winter season. The unit is reportedly heading for Jordan to serve as an interim FSRU in Aqaba. While the saga continues between DET and HEH as to whether the FSRU will ever regasify in Germany, it highlights the need for existing infrastructure to take advantage of any short-term relet opportunities.

Excelerate rumoured as buyers of **METHANE ALISON VICTORIA** after talking about buying conversion candidate since 2023. While the price is rumoured in the mid-/low-20s it is a well-suited candidate for both conversion to FSRU and as a piece of supporting infrastructure to Excelerate’s Caribbean business.

**ENERGOS ESKIMO** completing 10 years of service in Aqaba, Jordan before departing early-June for next charter in Egypt. Unit currently alongside in Ain Sokhna for compatibility modifications before being stationed at Sumed #2 jetty. Jordan will receive **BW FSU (TBN)** in H2/26 as replacement (with onshore regas provided by AG&P) in a 10-year BOOT deal .

DET postpones 2026 auction for Brunsbuttel (**HOEGH GANNET**) scheduled for 26th-27th June due to “unresolved questions reqarding the approval of the new jetty”. If such issues remain in place it would be the second site where DET have encountered challenges as the facilities in Stade remains without an FSRU. Auctions for 2026 capacity in W’haven 1 (**HOEGH ESPERANZA**) and W’haven 2 (**EXCELSIOR**) are expected to proceed as planned.

In a subsequent event (July); **Torman I+II** is being marketed for charter or sale underpinning the tightness of the market as the particular FRU+FSU solution has proven challenging to put into operation for a few years. If it can't find a home now; will it ever?
Quarterly focus: The gas turbine crunch?

It has been quiet on the corporate front during the quarter with public names such as Excelerate Energy seemingly digesting their newly acquired Jamaica business and New Fortress Energy continuing its fight to realigning the balance sheet and get into a more favorable financial situation.

However, using this quarterly to reflect on wider market-related topics there was one interesting piece of information emerging from the power sector; the steep rise in cost and lead time of CCGTs. Steep growth in demand for power related to data centers (effectively the continued surge in AI) has driven up costs for CCGTs in the US market from around US$ 1,000/kW in 2022 to just shy of US$ 2,500/kW in 2025 according to data from Rystad Energy (sourced from GE Vernova). Additionally, orders have surpassed sales for five straight quarters which has led to increased lead times. The combination of higher costs and longer lead times for CCGTs could be a risk to underlying gas demand and deferral of FSRU demand.

Our analysis and discussions with industry players on this topic suggests that the cost/time-issue is prevalent mainly for 60Hz markets and that 50Hz markets are not seeing the same trend. The vast majority of markets where FSRUs are required are 50Hz markets and as a consequence the working hypothesis on gas-to-power as both provider of base load and balancing against renewables remains intact for the time being.

content.content:
Q2 was a record quarter for FSRU imports on back of most FSRUs now employed and operating. Overall activity at operational FSRUs has been firm during Q2 with total quarterly imports at 15.7mt / 251 cargoes  (which is up 31% from 12.0mt / 211 cargoes in Q2/25). The Y-o-Y increase is driven primarily by Europe this quarter as volumes have shot up to 6.8mt for the quarter vs 4.6mt in Q2/24. The increase was predominantly in Mukran, but also Ravenna starting up together with W’haven 2. Global LNG imports in Q2/25 came in at 105mt; which means around 15% of global LNG volumes are delivered to FSRUs. Asian volumes also rose from 2.7mt to 3.4mt, primarily driven by the Summit FSRU back in operation and Hong Kong taking two cargoes per month compared to one cargo last year. 

The busiest terminal during the quarter was Eemshaven with a total of 22 cargoes – or one cargo every ~4 days. Shoutout to the crews onboard **ENERGOS IGLOO** and **EEMSHAVEN LNG**. On the other side of the spectrum, Brazil has seen no cargoes to **EXCELERATE SEQUOIA**, **ENERGOS NANOOK**, **KARMOL LNGT POWERSHIP ASIA**, **HOEGH GIANT** and **ENERGOS WINTER** during the quarter with only **ENERGOS CELSIUS** receiving two cargoes for Barcarena. 

From a fundamental perspective, we' re also encouraged to see the percentage of LNG going to FSRUs increasing - adding support to more FSRUs needed as global LNG supply enters the next growth spurt in the coming years.

**Petrovietnam** requirement for FSRU in Ba Ria, Vung Tau issued in Q1 moving slow. Initially targeted for the 2026-2029 period, the timing has slipped reportedly on back of lack of visibility for demand from EVN.

Requirement in **Iraq** remains real (3-5 years firm potentially with options), but lack of availability and geopolitical uncertainty is keeping a near-term solution from concluding. Our take is that Iraq should refocus efforts on a conversion for delivery in 27 instead of chasing its own tail.

Both projects in **Netherlands** seem to be moving slow with no sign of activity for open season for **Eemshaven Energy Terminal** and Vlissingen (**Zeeland Energy Terminal**) announcing start of permitting process in May. Eemshaven is still targeting to extend its operations beyond Q3/27 while the Zeeland timeline is now for “commence operations by 2028/2029.

**Colombia’s** Ecopetrol and the Ballena LNG project remains open with the requirement being an FSRU to be connected to an existing gas pipeline running from an offshore platform to landfall point in La Guajira.

*We encourage clients with deeper interest in ongoing project developments, tender activity and business development to contact Fearnleys directly; the above is merely scratching the surface of activity.*

As the FSRU market is by and large sold out there are limited units moving around (which is in many ways good).

The most notable movements for FSRU during the quarter has been Energos Power reaching Egypt while the sister vessel Energos Force has over the past week sailed from Skaw to Gibraltar and expected to enter Med on her way to **Jordan**.

Excelsior departed Ferrol S.Y. and connected to her destination site in Wilhelmshaven with reports of gas now flowing. Excelsior finally connected in Wilhelmshaven with gas flowing.

Energos Winter reached Turkey after departing TGS in March.

ETYFA Prometheus remains in Malacca where works to complete the unit is ongoing still.
Asset values: Conversions increasingly competitive, NBs trending lower

The FSRU market is tighter than it was at the end of Q1 and we reiterate our view that H2/25 and 2026 should be a busy 18-month period with a broad palette of projects in the pipeline. The only announced conversion unit (**HOEGH GANDRIA**) is now fixed and we expect to see more news on conversions over the next quarter based on both S&P discussions and conversations with equipment providers. Prices for donor vessels continue to drop – applicable for Steam Turbines and DFDE/TFDE alike – which is lowering the bar for prospective conversion players to take a position. However, the risk appetite amongst FSRU players appear to be in stark contrast to the rate levels as matching of project FID and vessel acquisitions remains an issue. We see a growing interest from projects for larger tonnage (moving out of the “cheap and cheerful” 138,000-145,000cbm range) as lower vessel prices and no need for new power module together with larger storage is attractive to end-users.

We see no material change to conversion costs/timelines with end-to-end delivery of a conversion being in the range of 30 months (from FID to COD) based on conversion at Asian yards. We note Hoegh’s decision to convert at Seatrium with engineering commencing in May-25 and completion in 18 months (Oct/Nov-26) which supports the “risk adjusted”-approach of placing orders for Long Lead Items as a more prudent balance sheet exercise than a fully-fledged speculative conversion. No cost has been announced, but our estimated conversion costs (excluding site team/project team, mobilization and commissioning) remains in the range of US$120-160 million for 500/750 SW/Glycol Open Loop.

The FSRU newbuild market has been relatively quiet over the quarter, but with LNGC price indications creeping lower and some project requirements being very specific we would not be surprised to see an uptick in activity towards 2026.

content.content:
Our view remains that this year will see lower earnings averages than in 2023. Market fundamentals remain sluggish, with shipment volume growth now comparable to years like 2016, 2020, and 2022. We do not expect growth to increase this year, as too many factors weigh heavily. 
Coal is where fundamentals are weakest, as record-high inventories in China, along with increasing power generation from other energy sources like renewables, continue to suppress seaborne demand. Using coal prices as a guide for where we are in the coal market cycle, there could still be a way to go before the bottom is in, as price levels remain above the lows of 2020, 2016, and 2009. 
Seaborne iron ore demand is lower than last year, though it is far from as bad as coal. The two main factors suppressing demand are inventory levels in China and weak fundamentals in Europe, Japan, and Korea. Regarding China, underlying fundamentals are actually better than last year, as imported iron ore consumption has averaged 2.9 million tons per day year-to-date vs 2.75 million tons per day through the same period in 2024. Should iron ore inventories in China be drawn down to the lows of 2023, another 40 million tons remain at ports plus steel mills before the inventory cycle has bottomed. 
Minor bulks demand has been strong in the last year, driven primarily by Bauxite and steel exports from China. Economic growth indices published by the OECD have shown a significant upturn in growth since the middle of 2024. Most of that has been due to the service sector, which, according to the latest PMI reports, has started to weaken. The indices provided by the OECD are at levels comparable to 2021 and 2017, which were both cycle peaks. Although Bauxite demand is likely to remain strong, growth in other minor bulk shipments could decrease over the next year, should the global economy be at a cycle top. 
Grains shipments have been slightly lower this year than last year, as very low volumes from the Black Sea have offset higher volumes from Brazil and the US. The higher volumes from Brazil and the US mean grains ton-miles are up on last year, though. The autumn Soybean shipment season from the US is the main uncertainty going forward. Trump (or rather his advisors?) fortunately came to his senses and at least went back on his embargo policies. However, everything could still happen in that regard, as shown by his recent threat of imposing a 50% tariff on the EU (which he also went back on). The way things stand at the time of writing, the effect of Trump’s policies is probably a slight negative for dry bulk markets due to the ‘uncertainty’ it causes, although that factor is impossible to measure. 
We still expect fundamentals to improve in 2026. A lot of factors are moving in the right direction in that respect. Seaborne iron ore fundamentals are likely to bottom in Q4 this year, whereas coal and minor bulks fundamentals are not likely to bottom before Q1 next year, or maybe even Q2. That means there could be a slow start to the next upcycle, then an acceleration during 2H 2026, with fundamentals subsequently remaining strong through 2027 and probably during parts of 2028.

Tanker rates have broadly weakened over the last month, mostly for Suez- and Aframax. Volumes remain flattish, but tonne-miles have dipped due to less West-East movement. 

In coming months we expect downside risk vs. YTD rates and our forecast curve, but still that rising output from the OPEC+ and Brazil/Guyana will support rates relative to the normal summer season. 

Relative oil pricing is likely to be a key trigger for when rates may recover. 

While the outlook for the second half of this year remains strong, there are some more risks to the downside into 2026, although possibly more toward the second half.

Volumes and tonne-miles have tapered in May to date vs. the preceding two months and current fixing pace for June indicates only small changes. Crude tanker volumes are fairly in line with the same time last year, whilst products have declined slightly. OPEC+ cut unwind and eventually more South American volumes may in coming months offset (some of) the normal seasonal downside. Two out of five new Brazil/GuyanaFPSOs this year have started production, with a combined capacity of 405 kbpd. The remaining three will add another 650 kbpd. Once ramped up, that will be a key trigger for (big) tanker rates to recover again.

The main reason for a slightly weaker (crude) tanker market in recent weeks has been the lack of a West-East arbitrage and as a result lower tonne-miles due to shorter sailing distances. Asian buyers seem to find sufficient supply from the MEG for the time being, which may also be aided by the cut unwind from the OPEC+ near-term. 

Once new production fully ramps up in Brazil and Guyana, however, that should support improved relative oil pricing for West-East movement. Look to the forward curve for clues, as this could very well coincide with a flip from backwardation to contango.

content.content:
The IEA's oil market balance forecasts still point to meaningful inventory builds of 0.7 mbpd this year. In the most recent report, the latest OPEC+ production increase is 'magically' offset by a baseline demand revision for the Middle East and Africa of a combined 3-400 kbpd. This revision also explains why oil inventories have consistently built less than the IEA's estimates have pointed to the last year(s). 

However, observed inventory movement still suggest a tighter market than the IEA has predicted, so further demand revisions may come. Judging from oil and forward prices, the oil market can so far absorb the announced OPEC+ cut unwinds, including another accelerated hike in July which is widely expected. 

When peak summer demand has passed and volumes ramp up also in South America, it remains to be seen how well oil demand can absorb this - a flip of the forward curve into contango is highly possible. 

Per the IEA's latest estimates, including the likely 411 kbpd OPEC 8 hike in July, global crude oil supply growth may be 1.7 mbpd this year, up from 0.7 mbpd in 2024. In 2026 growth is set to slow to 0.9 mbpd again, assuming flat OPEC+ production. That leaves a 1.2 mbpd oversupplied oil market in 2026 - so unless demand picks up more than the IEA's forecast (better hope tariffs are off the table then..), there is downside risk for tanker demand growth next year - especially in the second half of the year.

content.content: Some of what has been missing for tanker demand is USG crude oil exports, which are down 225 kbpd YTD vs. the same period last year - despite supposedly increasing U.S. shale production. The main reason for that is most likely the (re)shuffling of flows of Canadian crude through the TransMountain pipeline, where exports are up 370 kbpd y/y.

Refinery margins have broadly strengthened recently, amid resilient demand and expectations for the summer, although are now at more normalised levels vs. the super profits seen over the past few years. A recent naphtha pull, partly on the back of the U.S./China trade spat as helped boost LR rates, although given the preliminary truce this may prove short-lived.

Still, margins are sufficient for refinery run expectations for the summer season to rise above last year's levels, to new records, where several refineres have lifted run-rate plans for coming months. While that may keep a lid on refinery margins and by extension the potential upside for product tanker rates, higher volumes should help support rate resilience near term - in line with our forecasts.

Fleet growth YTD has been relatively low at 0.6%, although the delivery pace has picked up somewhat vs. the historical lows of the last couple of years. Deliveries are set to pick up somewhat more in the second half of the year, especially for product tankers, although for the full year the scheduled deliveries are still relatively low in a historical context, at 2.9% gross growth. 

There is more phase-out potential, although the majority of candidates are or have been engaged in shadow trades - many of them sanctioned too, which makes scrapping difficult.

While ordering has slowed this year compared to the last two years, scrapping has picked up somewhat. Already, nearly as much has been scrapped YTD as the two previous years combined, more vessels are reported for sale and some have been converted. That said, the absolute level remains low in a historical context as (some) older ladies find alternative employment in the shadow markets. 

Ordering stands below the historical norm, and interest appears limited due to the uncertain geopolitical outlook, lower secondhand prices and somewhat lower rates. Unless rates and secondhand values pick up meaningfully, we expect ordering interest to remain relatively low for the remainder of the year too.

After the latest announcements, a total 14.5% of the tanker fleet is now sanctioned by either the OFAC, EU or UK. While the latter two do not carry the same weight as the OFAC, it does hamper trade opportunities and utilisation. Loadings on sanctioned tonnage, and especially the OFAC sanctioned vessels, have declined significantly YTD which indicates this does impact shipping - although there are still workarounds for exports. 

A renewal of the shadow fleet seems to be ongoing. Over the last few months, since sanctions started ramping up, about 25 'new' VLCCs have been added to the shadow markets, mostly 2004-08 built. This likely relates to sanctions on Chinese teapots, traders, storage and port companies etc. which has made quite a few players more cautious about dealing with OFAC listed tonnage. If there were waivers for scrapping of OFAC listed tonnage, we probably could have seen more scrapping - nearly three quarters of the shadow/OFAC VLCCs is 20+ years old... 

In any case, the compliant VLCC fleet is now shrinking.
Loadings on OFAC, EU and UK listed vessels have steadily declined over the last couple of years, with a steeper decline in recent months after additional vessels have been added to the lists.

The credit markets have been highly volatile since our last report as the fallout of "Liberation Day" drove yields higher with the US 10-year jumping 50bps to 4.5% in the aftermath. Since then investors have been on free soloing on changes in tariffs hitting the headlines leading to some interesting moves. While the story a few months back was lower interest rates on back of diminishing growth prospects it is now turned upside down. With Moody's as the last rating agency to cut US AAA-rating (S&P and Fitch already at AA-level) the cost of borrowing in USD will likely nudge higher. Sure enough, the President seems to have a disagreement with the Fed as to when to cut rates, but overall expectations are of several cuts in 2025 still.
It is interesting to note that ECB are down in the low-2s with talks of another cut at the next meeting - potentially an opportunity for borrowers to think about EUR-denominated financing?

content.content: Choppier macro picture, tankers ride the waves

In last month's report we questioned what was going to give, as fundamentals appeared stronger than rates suggested. Crude tanker rates have firmed in April, to the highest for VL, Suez and Aframax on average since January last year. Going forward, the normal seasonal downside into the summer may be counterweighed by increasing volumes from South America and OPEC+ and rates overall should remain strong for the season. 

The volatile geopolitical and macroeconomic landscape is, however, cause for concern, and gives downside risks. Although this is mostly into next year, it could also affect proceedings nearer term as greater uncertainty may deter longer-haul shipments etc.

While volumes overall have risen further in April, tonne-miles have indicatively declined slightly on less Atlantic-East movements for the biggest vessels especially. Some of that has been due to the trade wars and general uncertainty, and most recently also a narrower arbitrage. A declining Dubai physical premium suggests there may be something to the 'sources' saying that the OPEC+ will further unwind cuts in June, which will lift tanker volumes, but may reduce the West-East flow somewhat. 

Judging from crude oil in transit, there may be some more upside potential for rates, especially if volumes rise further in coming months, although a rebound for Atlantic-East trade may be needed. Product tanker rates have YTD been well supported by resilient refinery margins and relatively strong global refinery runs.

content.content: Source: Vortexa, Fearnleys, Baltic Exchange, Bloomberg

Seaborne volumes have remained healthy over the last month, and there should be more to come. The OPEC+ will unwind cuts quicker than expected in May, and potentially also opt for a bigger hike in June according to 'sources'. However, between some potential compensation cuts (although, why should the over-producers all of a sudden start to comply now..?) and higher domestic consumption going forward, exports upside may be relatively small. For tanker demand, the timing and size of production increases from Brazil and Guyana will set the pace. Combined, OPEC+ increases and higher Americas production are likely to (at least partly) offset the normal seasonal downturn into the summer this year.

While oil prices remain under some pressure, the physical market still looks relatively tight, with inventories flattish YTD and the forward curve still in backwardation. This contrasts with the IEA's expected 0.7 mbpd oversupplied market this year - also in Q1, and could be part of the reason why the OPEC+ is emboldened to ease cuts somewhat near-term. Next year the IEA expects the oil market to be nearly 1 mbpd oversupplied, which does not really leave room for any cut easing, suggesting other motives may be behind. 

At current prices, U.S. shale is unlikely to continue growing. Some downside is probably more likely, which could mean there is some downside risk to the IEA's estimates. However, that may also be counterweighed by negative impact on demand from U.S. tariffs unless these are walked back on or sorted in other ways. Hence, there may be downside risk to tanker volume growth next year too.

Irrespective of OPEC, there is sufficient crude oil supply growth this year to support solid tanker demand growth. As has been the trend for a number of years already, oil supply grows in the West, while demand grows in the East. This year, the vast majority of Americas oil production growth is likely to come offshore, and most of it in Brazil and Guyana where four out of five shceduled FPSOs are now on field. This suggests export volumes should start to pick up within the next few months.

A big part of the recent Suez- and Aframax outperformance vs. VLCCs has been driven by sanctions, where the OFAC listed fleet is no longer active in Russia, and alternatives have had to be found. Urals trade well below the G7 price cap, and as a result more compliant tonnage has entered into the Russia trade to enjoy high rates. 

On top of that, more CPC exports on Suezmaxes has been shipped to Asia, boosting tonne-miles substantially. As long as these two factors hold, rate outperformance may also hold.

While deliveries are set to pick up this year, the overall delivery tally is still relatively low in a historical context. Next year fleet growth will pick up further, which coupled with lower demand growth potential means a gradually softening tanker market balance.

Ordering has picked up slightly, or the reporting of orders has, so that the annualised ordering pace YTD is slightly above the historical average. It does seem like ordering interest is much lower than over the last couple of years, so unless yards meaningfully drop prices, there should not be another wave this year. Given relatively long backlogs, however, there should not be an urgency for yards to do that.. 

Scrapping has also picked up somewhat vs. the last couple of years, and given reports of plenty more vessels sold or offered for scrap there should be more to come, despite continued strong rates. The real decider for scrapping pace this year will likely be whether waivers are given for sanctioned vessels to be scrapped... It is at least interesting to note the relatively high interest for 2005-10 built VLCCs and Suezmaxes from 'undisclosed buyers,' which may suggest a renewal of the shadow fleet may be in the cards.

Looking further ahead, the market could soften in June as the VLOCs will be back to take Brazil cargoes. Further, there are indications that China's iron ore consumption will drop over the next few months as we are in the peak season, and as Trump's trade war has hurt sentiment and the export sector.*

content.content:
Adding Trump's trade war to other factors, this year looks more bearish than before. Potentially much more bearish. 

At the time of writing this, there is a de facto trade embargo between the two most important economies in the world. 
The countries that had not been so rude as to retaliate against Trump have now been "rewarded" with a less severe punishment, and invited to come and crawl before him over a 90-day period. The behavior is more like that of a feudal King than an American President. 
It is highly doubtful whether, over this 90-day period, there will be an orderly, fair, and intellectual negotiating process between the USA and the other trading partners. 
The premise Trump has put behind the negotiations is that all other countries are cheating against the USA. Baked into the initial tariffs he slapped on everybody was an assumption that apart from the actual tariffs, sinister currency manipulations, export subsidies, and other unfair practices have taken place over decades. No documentation was provided to prove that these manipulations were going on. All economists we have seen comment on it say that even if these manipulations were going on, it would be extremely hard, if not impossible, to quantify the effects of it. Further, Trump seems to want a trade surplus with every other country, which is impossible, and displays complete economic illiteracy. 
How will negotiations go with that considered?

What has been the real reason why the USA has had massive trade deficits for decades? The status of the US dollar as the global reserve currency. Since the US dollar became the global reserve currency, there has been strong demand to accumulate dollar reserves, more specifically, risk-free US government bonds. The US could thus finance its deficits by issuing currency, an advantage that already decades ago was dubbed by some an "exorbitant privilege" (exorbitant meaning unfairly large or disproportionate). 
This privilege was probably deserved, as it was the USA that, in large part, built the modern economic structures we have. This of course included the last decades push to lower global trade barriers, which have contributed to bringing billions of people out of poverty. 
The ability of the United States to fund deficits by issuing reserve currency is, in a sense, a financial imbalance, and this financial imbalance has probably to some degree contributed to a physical imbalance. There could indeed be relatively less manufacturing going on in the United States compared to what it would have been had the United States not had the reserve currency. 
However, putting up massive trade barriers as the solution to this imbalance is catastrophic considering that the world economy is entirely globalized. 
Under Trump's proposed policies, all Americans will get poorer either through higher costs of imported goods and a crashing stock market. Further, Trump will for sure not get the CAPEX investments he is seeking under the degree of uncertainty he is creating. A few days ago, US tariffs on imported goods from the EU was 30%, then a few days after, it was 10% - what will it be in 2 weeks? Nobody can plan long-term investments under such circumstances. 

Concerning dry bulk markets, cyclical indicators like energy costs, interest rates, and a Chinese stimulus will likely be pointing even more towards a bullish 2026 and 2027 than before. However, it is of the **utmost importance** that the trade wars end for that to happen. Why? Because pushing the same old stimulus buttons that one has become used to will have a different effect than before, should Trump's new trade regime be put into place permanently. If more money chases fewer goods, inflation will move up rapidly and put a quick end to an eventual upturn in demand, eventually leaving you worse off than before. 

Regarding estimates for earnings averages, we previously held the view that this year looked weaker than 2023. One could cling to the hope that the "direct effect" on dry bulk volumes is not too significant (USA exports made up 6% of the global total last year). But this is meaningless in a highly interconnected World economy. 

The outlook remains bearish until there is an end to the trade war. We hope for a swift resolution of ongoing events.

content.content:
As the first quarter of 2025 concludes, activity in the market has been reasonable but has not yet reached anticipated levels. Of the reported transactions, approximately one-quarter were for recycling, fifty percent were allocated to storage projects or regional distribution, and the remaining quarter is still under negotiation. Additionally, there are emerging reports suggesting that some previously expected deals may now be uncertain, making future developments worth monitoring.
Our assessment remains that older ST vessels within the fleet are more inclined towards recycling than second-hand trading. Nevertheless, it this level of activity continues, that would bring 2025 to a new record in terms of scrap sales. There is a large pool of vessels idling, and it is anticipated that a significant number of these vessels may undergo extended layups, driven by the hope of more favorable market conditions and a subsequent return to operation. Previous instances have highlighted the risk of placing vessels in layup with the expectation of a market upturn, only to realize six months later that recycling is the more viable option, often resulting in a lower realized price compared to a direct sale to a recycling facility.

While the order book for conventional LNG carriers remains quiet, the small-scale and bunkering sectors have seen significant activity. So far in 2025, we have recorded only three new conventional vessel orders, compared to nearly double-digit orders in the smaller segment. Despite this disparity, prices appear stable with little indication of weakening. Given the current global market volatility, speculative ordering is expected to remain limited.

If there is interest in the SSLNG and LNGBV business, please reach out and we will ensure that you start receiving our reports on this segment as well.

The continued disruption to the markets on the back of the 47th president of the United States very different view on the world is continuing to disrupt world order and creating increased unpredictability. 
One interesting development is that we are now seeing the implications of increase in trade barriers and uncertain geopolitical environment challenging the fundamental outlook on global growth, which we have previously indicated would have an impact on interest rates, which we are now seeing. 
While global financial markets are being rattled on back of tariffs and what can only be seen as a potential trade war, reference interest rates have slid lower. The US 10yr is down around 50bps to just shy of 4%. It would have been great if the drop in interest rates were driven by lower inflation and a form of normalization as per the playbook laid out by the FED, but the reality is that dimmer growth prospects is what has been draging down rates.

The level of uncertainty on a macro level is at its highest since COVID - and albeit for a completely different reason - resulting in the risk premium widening despite underlying rates contracting. As such, it is tricky to see a scenario where capital gets cheaper in the near-term, rather the opposite.

content.content:
The year was off to a smooth start, with earnings levels fluctuating in rather small waves. **The quarterly average ended at $36,000 p.d.** across the three indexes. See detailed overview in the charts below. This is 32% lower than the quarterly average in 2024.

U.S. exports have been growing at a quicker pace than production, resulting in rather large draws in propane inventories. This has further increased the Mt. Belvieu price, narrowing the arbitrage possibilities, which in turn takes a toll on freight rates, as seen below. It appears that all eyes are on the U.S. these days, both in terms of their newly appointed President and his political strategies, as well as the announced terminal capacity expansions expected to come online and boost the market.
Panama or Cape of Good Hope?

Total transits through the Panama Canal was down 20% in 2024, due to a larger portion of the world fleet choosing to sail longer routes, in order to avoid potential and familiar congestion at the canal.  This opened up more capacity, both beneficial to, and utilized by the VLGCs, where total transits were up by 220. This compared to 2023, when a lager share of the fleet chose to sail around COGH instead.

The general cost for a VLGC to transit the canal, saw a big jump on Jan. 1st of 2025, a total increase of 36.8%. This might be an indication of the canal’s bullishness for this year, where they have incorporated their Long Term Slot Allocation system, where several packages of slots was pre-auctioned away in 2024. These slots make up 40% of transit capacity in the Neo-panamax locks, which are the ones most utilized by VLGCs, as 88% of the fleet are Neo-panamaxes. This causes further concern that a portion of the fleet is likely to continue to utilize the COGH route, as capacity is set to be tighter. This will especially be the case for ballasting legs going back to the West. *Chart below is of U.S. laden voyages going East.*
U.S. Production and Terminal Capacity Expansion

U.S. LPG production continues to increase, with total production up 27.25% over the past five years. Only 5% growth is expected in the next three years; however, export capacity is set to increase substantially during the same period. Domestic consumption remains stable, as do export levels, which hover around 60%. VLGCs account for 82% of all seaborne exports, which amounted to 52 million tons in 2024.

Announced capacity expansions from several U.S. terminals have boosted market confidence going forward, as this incremental supply is likely to fulfill the expanding fleet's needs better than previously anticipated. *See an overview of the announced capacity increases below.*

It should be noted that both the Nederland and Neches River capacities will be LPG/ethane flexible volumes. Total U.S. export capacity is set to increase from 68 to 111 MTPA by 2028 with the completion of these projects. This would boost export capacity by 65% from 2024 to 2028—a substantial jump that is warmly welcomed by a growing fleet.

What will materialize as the *actual* incremental exports is yet to be seen; however, it will likely be less than the full capacity numbers. Nevertheless, this move by U.S. energy suppliers further underscores the market's desire to expand and grow.

So far this year, supplied exports from the Middle East have been stable, with about 2 million tons provided from each country. We are not expecting to see much growth from the region in 2025, however, in 2026, long-awaited natural gas projects in Qatar will finally come online (North Field East). Additionally, in 2027 (North Field South), which will result in some incremental LPG output. Approximately 4.2 MTPA in 2026, and another 2 MTPA in 2027, increasing the regions export capacity from 46 to 52 MTPA. This additional supply of LPG will be beneficial to the fleet expansion that will occur at the same time.

Strong import demand from China has continued into 2025. In Q1, they imported 8.5 million tons via VLGCs, up 700,000 tons compared to Q1 2024. Their demand is still driven by the petrochemical sector and increasing PDH (propane dehydrogenation) capacity coming online. This capacity is set to grow further during the rest of the year.

During February and March, Chinese PDH margins turned positive after being negative throughout the second half of 2024. However, at the end of March, they went negative again.

There is currently much uncertainty in China regarding the imposed tariffs, and possible fees suggested by the President of the United States and the USTR. As 50% of all imported LPG in 2025 came from the U.S., it could have significant consequences for trade. It remains to be seen how China will respond to the import tariffs and whether the port call fees will be imposed. This sets the stage for an already interesting second quarter of the year.

During the first quarter of 2025, three newbuilds were delivered—one in January and two in March. All three ships are capable of lifting ammonia at 85% capacity. The remaining number of deliveries for the year is nine, giving a total of 12 newbuilds. The fleet now stands at 404 ships, including floating storage. The orderbook consists of 100 ships, resulting in an orderbook-fleet ratio of 24.75%, which is just above the 20-year average of 21%. However, during 2026 and 2027, the fleet will grow by 19.4% in total, potentially causing more substantial disruptions to the fleet balance.

The trading fleet is aging, with 61 ships now over 20 years old, equaling 15% of the fleet. These ships are likely to enter the sanctioned part of the fleet (some already have) or become scrapping candidates. This could help relieve some of the fleet growth expected in the next two to three years. The number of ships scheduled for their 5-year special survey is high in the next years; 75 in 2025 and 82 in 2026.

Hyundai remains the largest builder of newbuilds, while one quarter of the newbuilds are being constructed in China. Normally, this would not be of much interest to the masses; however, in light of the recent proposed port call fees for Chinese-built ships, it could have an impact, going forward.

There are currently 50 live VLGCs that are Chinese-built, with an additional 23 on order. Combined, this equals 12.4% of the live fleet and 23% of the orderbook.

The situation could turn more sour for the VLECs (Very Large Ethane Carriers), where 37% of the live fleet is Chinese-built, and 73% of the orderbook is going to be Chinese-built. The VLEC trade route is a one-way trade from the U.S. to Far East Asia. For this market, it would cause a massive impact on the delivered cost of ethane, which has gained its competitiveness largely from being a cheaper feedstock compared to alternatives. A higher delivered cost would minimize the competitive advantage of U.S. ethane, resulting in a negative outcome for both countries.

After two consecutive years of record-number orders placed for VLGC newbuilds, contracting has eased in Q1, with no orders placed year-to-date. Even though overall yard capacity remains tight, due to strong activity from other segments, the current price for a VLGC newbuild is around $118 million.

We expect earnings to remain in the $40,000 p.d. range for the remainder of the year. Increased export capacity in the U.S. coming online in Q3 will likely have a positive effect on earnings. For 2026, further capacity will come online in the U.S., in addition to the expected supply boost from the Middle East. We expect this supply to ease the effect of a growing fleet when another 30 newbuilds come onto the water next year.

The fleet will continue to grow, and whether this additional tonnage will be absorbed depends on the realized increases in exports from both the U.S. and the Middle East. Additionally, the sailing pattern of the fleet remains volatile, where each voyage's choice between the Panama Canal or the Cape of Good Hope impacts the fleet's availability and capacity. The first of many VLACs (Very Large Ammonia Carriers) will be delivered next year; however, we do not separate these ships from VLGCs in the fleet, as the only difference is that they can carry ammonia at 98% capacity. They will likely trade LPG as regular VLGCs for the coming years, as the infrastructure to load and discharge ammonia on such large ships is not yet developed.

The Panama Canal has now started the Long Term Slot Allocation System, which takes up 40% of the capacity in the Neo-panamax locks. Panamaxes will therefore likely have an advantage in order to transit. However, half of the orderbook consists of Panamaxes, so this capacity is also going to change going forward.

The FSRU market has been increasingly active through the quarter. Morphing from a market that historically has been focused on long-term charters and long-lead project developments into a more prompt requirement situation. High activity for prompt requirements in North Africa and Middle East of the "We need an FSRU yesterday"-type are driving out underutilized FSRUs to a sublet-market that is uncommon to see. Although the limitation on rapid-fire FSRU projects tend to be on the onshore-side, the most visible requirements come from countries with available jetty/pipeline connections and hence the demand should be considered real.

Looking beyond the near-term, we see a relatively high activity of projects at early/medium-stage development with potential to materialize over the next 12-18 months. That said, the quality, bankability and structuring of these projects may need additional massaging and/or guidance to arrive at a point where they can reach lift-off. Our bottom-up analysis on a project-by-project basis lends credibility to 2-4 new projects (or extensions) reaching FID in 2025 and as such we see the fundamentals of the FSRU market pointing to a continued firm rate environment.
Key market developments during the quarter

JANUARY

DET auctions Q1 regas slots for Wilhelmshaven 1 (**Hoegh Esperanza**) and Brunsbuttel (**Hoegh Gannet**). Reportedly sold OTD (Obligation-to-Deliver) slots sufficient to keep 2 x FSRUs cold. Price reported was an average of EUR 0.11/MMBtu – well below regas tariffs seen elsewhere in Europe.

Uncertainty arises on startup of DETs two FSRUs at W’haven 2 and Stade. Reporting delays into Q2/25, but market talks of further delays. Stade FSRU (**Energos Force**) removed to perform dredging at terminal.

Gastrade FSRU (**Alexandroupolis**) goes offline two times during month. FSRU has effectively been offline for majority of Q1 and recent Urgent Market Message from Gastrade annoncing that the unit will be out of service until at least 15th May 2025. The extended outage has lead to speculations around the cause which at present appear to be focused around the regasification system.

Hoegh Evi announces partnership with SEFE on green hydrogen from FSRUs. Information is scarce, but the announcement highlights the need for LNG infrastructure supporting the energy transition in European countries.

FEBRUARY

DET auctions remaining 2025 slots (Q2-Q4) at W’haven and B’buttel at an average price of EUR 0.30/Mmbtu.

BOTAS rumoured to have chartered out FSRU (**Saros** (ex-Vasant 1) or **Etugrul Gazi**)  for May/Jun-Nov 2025 to EGAS at around US$ 250,000/day. Deal reported to have subsequently failed.

Deutsche Regas terminates **Energos Power** with BWMK. FSRU idling offshore Mukran terminal. Unit marketed for alternative use with reportedly high interest from multiple parties.

Snam’s second FSRU **BW Singapore** arrives at Petra offshore terminal in Ravenna following minor works at Fincantieri Palermo and GU/CD with heel cargo in Spain. Commercial operations likely to commence in Q2/25.

Gastrade indicates targeting FID on second FSRU to be located close to Thrace, Greece in early-26.

Tokyo Gas acquires 20% of FGEN LNG Corp, the charterer of **BW Batangas** following previous JDA for project.

MARCH

Deutsche Regas reiterates position to restore regas capacity at Mukran to level (13.5 BCMA/~1,350MMSCFD) prior to terminating **Energos Power**. 

Ireland announces plans to secure FSRU for development of **“state-led strategic gas emergency reserve”**. Location, timing and process is not defined, but expectations are of an FSRU with 170,000cbm cargo capacity and what appears to be an MSO as BOG management.

**Energos Power** is being discussed for charters with a number of parties following termination by Deutsche Regas. EGAS (Egypt) emerges as  most likely taker, but also hearing talks of Iraqi interests targeting the FSRU. Rate and term unclear, but remaining charter to BMWK is ~8 years with rumoured TC of ~US$ 150,000/day.

**ETYFA Prometheus** idles offshore Malacca. Terminal at Vasillikos bay expected ready towards end-25. Unit no longer being marketed for short-term business.

Jordan emerges with requirement for FSRU in period Jun-Sep 25 to Sep-26 when **BW FSU** is set to arrive. We see limited availability for this requirement with any FSRU likely to come at a premium.

Hanseatic Energy Hub terminates contract with DET for connection between FSRU and terminal in Stade. **Energos Force** is intended for Stade, but the recent news may suggest also Energos Force could become a relet candidate along with sister vessel Energos Power.

Excelerate Energy and New Fortress Energy made headlines on the corporate side with a late-quarter announcement of Excelerate acquiring NFEs Jamaica assets in a transaction valued at US$ 1.055bn - or ~9x EBITDA (2025est). NFEs assets had been rumoured for sale for some time with prospective buyers reportedly ranging from traders to infrastructure funds - and hence a relatively wide valuation range. Emerging as the successful bidder, Excelerate is taking over Montego Bay and Old Harbour LNG terminals as well as the 100MW Clarendon CHP plant together with small-scale distribution to a number of local clients. With a total of appx 30 TBtu of annual demand, the Jamaica business fits well with Excelerate's 0.7mtpa (~35TBtu/yr) contract from Venture Global. While it is not clear whether the Hoegh Gallant will remain in service at Old Harbour (or Excelerate would prefer to use one of their own FSRUs), there is clearly upside to Jamaican LNG demand both from onshore consumers (power generation/industrial) and LNG bunkering. The transaction will definitely be a step-change for Excelerate as it strengthens its position in the Atlantic - and we wait eagerly for the organic growth to trickle through next.

Overall activity at operational FSRUs has been firm during Q1 with average monthly imports at 4.85mt / 232 cargoes (which is up 24% from 3.90mt / 200 cargoes in Q1/24). The Y-o-Y increase is driven primarily by Egypt coming into the play from mid-24. Global LNG imports in Q1/25 came in at 109; which means around 13% of global LNG volumes are delivered to FSRUs. European volumes declined slightly from Q1/24 to 4.2mt from 4.5mt with a big jump in Asia from 2.1mt to 2.9mt, primarily driven by the Summit FSRU back in operation. The last notable change in flows was a solid increase in Turkish imports who took 2.8mt in Q1/25 - up from 1.7mt in Q1/24.

While the absolute levels for each region may not provide a whole lot of information, our read is that the end users seem relatively unphased from changes in commodity prices as the likes of price-sensitive buyers such as Pakistan, Bangladesh and Turkey are steadily importing volumes. From a fundamental perspective, we' re also encouraged to see the percentage of LNG going to FSRUs remaining steady/increasing slightly - adding support to more FSRUs needed as global LNG supply enters the next growth spurt in the coming years.

content.title: Monthly volumes imported through FSRUs by region (2025)

content.content:
*Asia & Middle East*

H-Energy emerged with an RFQ for FSRU for Jaigarh terminal in **India**, targeting 145,000-160,000cbm FSRU for short-term (2-3 years) and/or long-term (15 years) charter. Start-up planned late-25/early-26.

Rumours of **Bangladesh** set to issue tender for FSRU to “restart”/”test” market ahead of elections expected this year. Unclear as to when requirement will be out, but likely to coincide with more political visibility.

**Petrovietnam** emerging with a requirement for FSRU in Ba Ria, Vung Tau. Targeted period is 2026-2029 with capacity of 135,000-174,000cbm and 500/750MMSCFD. No formal documentation released as of yet.

**Iraq** has been approaching market for upto two FSRU commencing operations in H2/25 for minimum 5 yrs firm. 

**Jordan** issues RFQ for appx 12 month requirement (Jun-Sep 25 until Sep 26) to bridge gap between departure of Energos Eskimo and arrival of BW FSU. Requirement is 135,000-160,000cbm with 500/715MMSCFD.


*Europe & Mediterreanean*

In **Netherlands**, Eemshaven Energy Terminal announces non-binding EoI (Open Season) for regasification capacity for a duration of 8 years starting Sep-27. Indicating FID in Q3/Q4 2025.

**Ireland** announcing charter or purchase of FSRU (170,000cbm) for strategic gas emergency reserve. No startup time provided. Location remains undecided, but previously mentioned FSRU locations in Ireland include Cork and Shannon and Strategic reserve “is likely to be refilled up to 6 times per year” – suggesting an average daily send-out of appx 60MMSCFD and as such looks to be a seasonal or insurance measure.

**Egypt** is pursuing additional FSRU capacity with talks of up to four FSRUs (3 in south / 1 in north). EGAS have been rumoured discussing widely with market, but no firm transactions disclosed yet.

*Americas & Caribbean*

**Colombia's** EcoPetrol issues RFQ for “LNG Ballena” project, targeting FSRU for connection to existing offshore infrastructure/pipeline appx 17km offshore. Targeting FSRU with 400MMSCFD nominal capacity and startup in Q1/27, but no indication on cargo capacity or preferred contract duration.

Talks of several movements in **Brazil** in preparation for upcoming power auctions. Current auction structure and short dispatch notices are driving interest on FSU and FSRU as storage capacity is becoming critical.

**Dominican Republic** tender reported awarded to Singapore-based player.


*Africa & Other*

Talks of FSU + Onshore regas solution in Dakar, **Senegal** through Elton Oil. Revamp of project first surfacing in 2021. Timing unclear, but expected in 2025 or 2026.

Talks about FSU in Freetown, **Sierra Leone** reemerging. Contractual structure not confirmed, but expected to be supplying RLNG to power plant and LNG to trucking/distribution

**Morocco** project has started to move again after grinding to a halt towards the end of 2024. Now talking about three LNG terminals in Nador West Med, Dakhla and Mohammedia/Jorf Lasfar. Startup indicated around 2027.

The most notable movements for FSRUs during the quarter has been **Energos Power** and her sister **Energos Force**. **Energos Power** was moved from Mukran terminal following termination of the contract and subsequently sailed to Skaw, Denmark for orders. **Energos Force** had been idling in the German Bight for an extended period of time in anticipation of connecting to Stade terminal, but also she has been sent to Skaw for orders.

Germany's third FSRU-in-waiting is **Excelsior** which has been in Ferrol S.Y. for a long time. It is not entirely clear the reason, but Wilhelmshaven 2 is reportedly close to completion which should mean **Excelsior** will soon be on the move.

**BW Singapore** has hooked up at Ravenna following works at Fincantieri Palermo and a GU/CD in Spain.

**Energos Freeze** continues to remain alongside in Ferrol S.Y. (next to **Excelsior**) and there are no tangible reports of her next job for the time being.

**Energos Winter** departed late March from TGS terminal in Santa Catarina, Brazil and is currently for orders in Rio de Janeiro. She is likely heading for a drydock as she has been in service in Brazil for close to 16 years at this point.
Asset values: Newbuildings and Conversion candidates

With an FSRU market that is expected to remain tight in the near- to medium-term, the number of players looking at adding capacity is in no shortage. However, deciding to move from window shopping and planning to pulling out the credit card remains a challenge for most as many market participants prefer to take a back-to-back approach as opposed to a speculative position. This strategy has thus far proven wise in light of declining secondhand values for conversion candidates. The list of prospective sales candidates in the ST segment with 138,000-155,000 cargo capacity is getting longer by the day, allowing those looking for FSRU (and FSU) conversion candidates to be selective. Pricewise the situation is the same for TFDE with arrows pointing lower, but the number of candidates is fewer and further between although we would not be surprised to see the list grow into summer.

Conversion costs and timelines have not changed materially during Q1. Indications on conversion timeline for end-to-end projects is in the range of 30 months based on conversion works at Asian repair yards. Costs are highly dependent on the specification and project requirements - but for plain vanilla FSRUs indicative costs are in the range of US $120-160 million.

Limited interest and activity in the newbuild market with yards still seeing a solid backlog of LNGC and hence limited reason to drop prices notably.

The year began with a steady descent as usual at the start of the year, although somewhat unusually this market softening came after a relatively flat winter. This resulted in historically low rates, which have since recovered slightly. There hasn't really been a significant change in the fundamentals to support the uptick, and it is clear that the rate floor was an undershoot which was not sustainable in the longer term despite the oversupply of tonnage and additional newbuild deliveries. The main drive for the recovery has instead been a shift in shipping portfolio management and sublet availability, mainly due to the start-up of long-term volumes from Calcasieu Pass. This, in combination which a very quick ramp-up of volumes from the newly commissioned Plaquemines project, has driven some demand for two-stroke ships while reducing sublet availability, but newbuilds have continued to deliver at a pace greater than the market's ability to absorb the increased demand. In addition to Plaquemines, Corpus Christi Stage 3 has also started commissioning and, with limited outages, March saw a new record in loaded LNG, with nearly 39 MT lifted. 

Cargo values increased at the start of the quarter, with JKM reaching 17 $/MMBtu  in the beginning of February. This was a result of strong bidding competition from the Asian market, and significant gas withdrawals from European storage due to cold weather. The arbitrage has largely been shut, with European storage levels well below the 5-year average and ending the quarter 25% less full than same time last year. 

Liquidity has continued to be high, with well over 100 spot fixtures concluded. This is the highest in our records, and shows both a large fleet to play with and high availability and sublet willingness, coupled with a long list of requirements. 72% of short-term fixtures were sublets, which is about the same level as the previous quarter. 

16 LNGCs were delivered in Q1, slightly less than originally planned, and down from the 20 delivered in Q4 last year. That leaves another 79 for the remainder of the year given current schedules (of which nine are for Arctic LNG-2). The LNGC fleet on the water has exceeded 700 ships, with 685 live and 19 in layup (a big increase from the 6 in layup at the start of the year). Three orders were placed, and three vessels were sold for demolition. Interestingly, the two latest vessels sold for demolition were delivered in 2002 and 2004, meaning they were 23 and 21 years old, respectively. This shows the increasing difficulty for smaller steam turbine ships to find employment after their long-term charters end, and that owners increasingly choose to avoid the high layup costs and potential 25-year drydock costs when the prospects for future business are limited.

Despite the new administration in the United States greenlighting several projects throughout the quarter, there haven't been any project FIDs. This proves that there is more to an FID than just approvals for exports, and SPAs play a major role here. With the big demand growth forecasted from China over the next 10 years, the tariff on US LNG is not a supporting factor for the considerable number of US projects hoping to reach FID in the near term.
Source: JKM for S&P Global Platts

The average spot rate for a two-stroke in Q1 ended at 17k $/day, which is a mere 26% of the same measure in Q1 last year. The year started with average rates in January at 17k $/day and ended at a monthly average of 23k $/day in March, inverting the normal trend for which this period typically sees rates on a downward slide. While we believe the undershoot at the start of the year was "too low" to be sustainable, from a fundamental perspective there are not many factors that would support a continued increase in rates as we head into the shoulder season. The situation was worse for TFDEs, with Q1 rates averaging at 8.7k $/day, only 18% of the year before and including close to zero in February, driven by extremely low demand. There have been a handful of TFDEs idling at the start of the year, rumoured to be heading to layup. However, these vessels are trading again now, and there is no doubt that while the preference for two-strokes increases, the TFDEs are still needed. 

1-year term charter rates are currently in the low-mid 30ks $/day range for a two-stroke, indicating that the market expects the current oversupply to continue near term. Looking longer term, it is still the case that charters giving coverage for 2028+ are at a premium, with 3-year rates around 50k and higher for longer periods out to the end of the decade. However, liquidity in this segment remains low. With close to no newbuilds ordered, the long-term market also remains very illiquid although a slight softening of newbuild prices may encourage more activity.

The quarterly number of spot fixtures was the highest in our records, with almost 120 fixtures concluded. The spot fixture count increased by 18% from Q1 last year, and the number of fixed days (spot only) increased by 43%.  Comparing to the previous quarter (Q4, 2024), the number of fixtures increased by 33%, while fixed days increased by 111%. It is therefore clear that fixture durations for spot fixtures so far this year have been higher than in 2024. 

Multi-month fixing has been about the same as the previous quarter, but less than Q1 in previous years. The story is the same for other short term fixtures up to 3 years, with only a handful of deals concluded. The share of fixtures involving independent owners compared to sublets has gradually increased since the start of 2024, and in Q1 73% were sublets (about the same as in Q4).

The number of 3-5 year deals concluded has been on a decreasing trend since end of 2023, likely as a result of the low spot charter rates and a lot of charterers being long shipping. It is also difficult to bridge the bid-offer gap as charter periods extend into the anticipated stronger years. Few long-term requirements and low ordering activity has meant no long-term deals have been concluded.

content.title: Short term fixtures by sublet vs independent owners

content.content:
109 MT of LNG was loaded in Q1; the highest ever. This has been strongly supported by commissioning of the Plaquemines liquefaction plant in the United States, which has loaded 29 cargoes throughout the quarter. A total of 39 MT was loaded in March, which is also a new monthly record. The United States continues to be the largest exporter, and at 26 MT they closed the quarter 4.4 MT higher than the next highest exporter, Qatar. Japan was the top importer, taking 18 MT which is almost 3 MT more than China. European imports reached a new record, with 37 MT discharged, which was almost 10 MT more than Q1 last year. 

Red Sea transits remain largely off-limits for LNGCs, only one ship doing the full transit. That means that number of voyages around the Cape of Good Hope remain high, especially as the share of Qatar cargoes heading to Europe increased from 12% in January, to almost 15% in March. Of the 51 cargoes that went from the US to Asia in Q1, only 5 transited the Panama Canal, and 4 transits were registered on the ballast voyage. 

Europe started the year by importing 69% of all US cargoes, and in March that had increased to a share of 83%. Thus, the arbitrage has been far from open, and Europe has won the fight for cargoes despite the low additional shipping cost to go to Asia. Distances have therefore been decreasing throughout the quarter, but the high levels of traded LNG have kept tonne-miles slightly above last year's levels. Speeds have been the lowest seen in years, and February saw a significant number of vessels idling, so tonne-time has also increased slightly. Looking at speeds by propulsion though, it is clear that the steamers are the main contributor the the average fleet speed reductions, and 2-stroke speeds are very much in line with last year's levels. 

Looking at tonne-miles by propulsion, it is only the 2-strokes that are doing more work than in Q1 last year (naturally, as this is the only segment of the fleet that is growing). However, the steam turbine fleet did 23% less tonne-mile work this year than last year, while scrap activity only reduced the fleet size by 8%. For 2-strokes, the fleet was 31% larger in in cargo carrying capacity (in cbm) at the end of March compared to last year, and tonne-mile grew around the same amount, 30%. This does indicate an underutilized fleet, with the fleet growing quicker than the tonne-mile demand, especially for older tonnage. This should, and has, triggered layup activity.

The 16 LNGCs delivered in Q1 brings the total fleet on the water to 704 ships. However, with the 18 in layup, the "live" fleet stands at 686. The slow-down in ordering and quick deliveries has brought the orderbook-to-fleet ratio down to 45%. Only three orders were placed. 

78 vessels are still scheduled to be delivered in 2025, of which nine are Arc-7s originally intended for Arctic LNG-2, and whose delivery is continuously pushed. Excluding those, the delivery schedule is currently 20, 23 and 26 ships respectively for each remaining quarter of the year, bringing the yearly total to 85. 

91 ships are currently on order in China, almost 30% of the orderbook and spread across six yards (although more than 60% are at Hudong-Zhongua). 27 ships in the orderbook are charter-free, with three delivering this year, 11 in 2026 and 13 in 2027. 14 LNGCs ordered for Qatar Energy (North Field Expansion and Golden Pass) have already been delivered, leaving an orderbook of 114 (36% of the total orderbook), to be delivered between now and 2031.

The yards are now full until the end of 2027, and 2028 is now the earliest slot available for LNGC delivery. The orderbook for 2028 would currently add 41 vessel; less than half of the year before. There are therefore still numerous slots available for delivery 2028, but for a rebalanced shipping market the orderbook should not fill to 2025-2027 levels. 

Three vessels were sold for recycling in Q1, and if this pace continues, that could bring the yearly total to a record high. It is interesting to see that younger ships are sold for scrap, with the latest being 2004-built. Historically, LNGCs have been scrapped at 35-40 years old. As selling for scrap is a big step, we have also seen the oversupplied market result in increasing idling and layup activity. We foresee that some ships from this pool of vessels will also be sold for recycling in the near term, as layup costs continue to run and the question of expensive drydocks comes up. There are unfortunately not enough projects for all the underutilized vessels right now.

content.title: Fleet growth and fleet average ship size (considering current orderbook and phase-out at 25 years)

content.content:
While there is little doubt that, near term, the orderbook is more than enough to cover growth in demand coming from new projects, the questions to ask are what could tighten the market? As always, trade flows matter, and an open arbitrage and more long-haul trade from the US Gulf to Asia would be a significant tightening factor; however, if Europe's gas storage refilling targets remain then European demand this refilling season will be high. Another factor is whether the ships ordered to serve Qatar North Field Expansion, and Qatar Energy's share in Golden Pass, will be made available in the market when vessel deliveries occur earlier than volume start-ups. 14 vessels have been delivered, with 21 additional ships expected this year, while volumes from Golden Pass and Qatar are expected from early next year. If, instead of adding to global fleet availability, these vessels idle or replace old vessels serving Ras Laffan (which then proceed to idle/layup/scrap), that would help the rebalancing of the shipping market. However, the effect of this is mainly in 2025, before the volumes from Golden Pass and North Field Expansion come online. 

Another question arises around the age at which LNGCs will be scrapped? We believe the days of scrapping at 35 years are over, and anticipate 25 years as being a new realistic normal, due to factors such as size, environmental regulations, drydock schedule and age restrictions at terminals. However, if this age comes down to 20 years, that would significantly reduce the fleet capacity, as there are nearly 90 ships that are already 20 years old or more, and there are 40 ships turning 20 in 2025 and 2026. While it is unrealistic to be a new normal for all LNGCs, a quick look at the list of idle/laid up ships and their ages, yields an average of around 20 years. 

Looking further ahead, FIDs will play an important role. While the new administration in the US has greenlighted several projects, it has yet to result in FIDs. Looking at LNG demand forecasts for 2030, there is a gap and more FIDs will be needed. However, adding up the capacity of projects previously considered realistic candidates for FID in the near term by far exceeds the demand gap in 2030. It will also be interesting to see whether Chinese players, whose demand is forecast to increase massively over the next 15 years, choose to sign SPAs with non-US projects to avoid the 15% tariff on US LNG, which looks like it just increased to 34%. 

Speaking of tariffs, if the US go through with the proposed regulations that introduces fees on all ships entering US ports if the vessel is built in China, or is operated by a company who has ships built or on order in China, the effect on the LNGC fleet could be material. It is unclear how this regulation would define “operator”. There are many LNGC shipowners who don’t have any LNGCs built or on order in China, but a lot of the major owners have vessels in other segments, where Chinese-built ships are more common. Assuming owners will be considered across all segments, the effect would be huge and the number of LNGCs able to trade tariff-free from the US would be small.

Looking at the supply/demand balance, our conclusion remains that there is shipping oversupply in the next 3 years given the current project and orderbook schedules. 2026 should see some tightening, due to the high number of projects scheduled to come online. It is not until end-2028 that additional ships will be needed to avoid undersupply. Worth noting though, is that both additional volumes through new FIDs and additional vessel deliveries are possible by end of 2028. We forecast that average shipping distances will continue to increase, as more US volumes come online. While European demand looks high in the near term, European demand growth is expected to be slower than the growth in US volumes over the next few years. This means more US-to-Asia voyages, which likely add significant voyage distances as the Panama Canal remains under-utilised. In short: tonne-mile demand through volume growth and longer distances will drive the need for a continued growth in the LNGC fleet, despite the near term oversupply.

Last week, we wrote the following: *Average seasonality suggests the market could be close to peaking. However, the second wave of the ECSAM Soybean season is incoming, and the ballaster list looks thin. The Pacific also looks firm for the time being. So even though the market could be near a peak, we do not expect much, if any, downside from current levels in the next month.*
Last year, the "second wave" of the ECSAM grain season started on the 25th of March (defined as the bottom in the count of Pmx/Kmx sailing towards Brazil basis AIS). In 2023, the second wave started on the 5th of April. So it should be imminent now, and it will provide market support. Apart from ECSAM grains, coal shipments in the Pacific remain lower y-o-y, the US grain season will wind down, and the general macro-economic picture is not bullish. So, notwithstanding potential YTD spot market highs driven by ECSAM, the lower y-o-y market is likely to continue.

content.content: Risks skew to the upside - what's going to give?

Rates have strengthened for all segments over the last month, with Suezmax, Aframax and LR2 gaining the most. With crude oil production and refinery runs slated to pick up in coming months there should be further upside for rates too, although with the constantly changing newsflow and geopolitical picture there are plenty of potential scenarios. There are a few key bullish and bearish factors which may influence the trajectory for this year, skewed to the upside: 

Bull factors: 
- Sanctions driving a need to replenish the shadow markets and/or replace flows with compliant barrels 
- Higher crude oil production in the Americas, most of which needs to be shipped by sea
- Lower global oil inventories which may need to be replenished 
- Rebounding refinery margins which suggests relatively healthy oil demand
- Limited fleet growth, especially for crude tankers 

Bear factors: 
- Trade wars may negatively impact demand 
- Conflict resolution and/or easing of sanctions
- Charterers accepting older vessels 
- Charterers controlling more vessels than before

Crude tanker flows excluding Iranian oil have in March to date recovered and is slightly above the same month last year. Products lag a bit, but is still among the highest historically for this time of the year. Both are expected to rise in coming months with higher crude production in both hemispheres, though mostly in the West as the OPEC+ cut reversal is relatively small, and with refineries gradually coming out of the maintenance period. 

Contrary to our expectations, Suez- and Aframaxes and to some extent product tankers again ouperform VLCCs. Some of that may be explained by sentiment and psychology which appear to keep a lid on VLCC rates. There is also a factor of uncertainty, where the threat of tariffs and potential port fees for Chinese (built) ships in the U.S. have disincentivised charterers and traders to lock in freight ahead in time, hence the VLCC fixture count from the USG in April for instance, lags where it ought to be. We are now starting to see more USG exports materialise in Suez and Afra cargoes relative to the last couple of months again. 

This comes at the same time as the Urals price has dropped well below the G7 price cap, which has lured more uncompromised tonnage into the Russia trade, absorbing vessel availability from the Suez- and Aframax market. CPC exports have also been very strong, and a larger than normal portion is headed East on Suezmaxes, further stretching the fleet.

Arguably, rates lag fundamentals, where oil in transit is among the very highest in the past few years, surpassed only by Covid and the immediate aftermath of the Russia-Ukraine conflict and related sanctions. At the same time, vessel availability is and has for a few weeks and months been among the lowest over the past few years. At previous times when oil in transit has been this high and/or vessel availability has been this low, rates have been substantially higher than now, especially for VLCCs. 

What is going to give?
