content.content:
What lacked through most of H2'24 was Atlantic-East movement. So far this year that has rebounded as (some) Eastern buyers replace (some) flows from Iran and Russia. There should be more to come too, on higher crude oil production from the Americas predominantly, but also some other Atlantic sources. According to the EIA, Q2 should see more than 0.5 mbpd q/q production growth (0.6 mbpd y/y) from the Americas, led by the U.S. and Brazil, with another 0.7 mbpd hike in Q3 (0.9 mbpd y/y). 

The U.S. growth figure is questionable considering low activity and real-time indications suggesting that YTD development has been flat, and lower than energy agencies have expected. The latest Dallas Fed survey suggests the average price needed to profitably drill new shale wells is $65/bbl - just about where the forward price for next year is. Still, even adjusting for that downside risk there should be around 1 mbpd of additional Atlantic crude which is likely to be shipped by sea over the next six months, greatly contributing to tanker tonne-miles. 

Three out of four FPSOs scheduled to start up in Brazil this year (total capacity of 800 kbpd) are now on field, and one of them has started production. The 250 kbpd FPSO destined for Guyana has recently sailed from Singapore. Within about half a year most of these should be operational.

content.title: Crude oil production change by quarter

content.content:
Partly driving the Suezmax outperformance recently has been the prices for Russian crude oil dropping well below the G7 price cap after sanctions have hindered the ability to lift effectively on the shadow fleet. Loadings from Russia on OFAC listed vessels have dropped by nearly 1.3 mbpd vs. the 2024 average, and most have been replaced by compliant tonnage. By now, 10.6% of the tanker fleet has been sanctioned by OFAC, 13.2% of the crude fleet and 4.3% of the product fleet. 

Loadings on OFAC listed vessels from Iran have dropped by 'only' 350 kbpd, and discharges into China have risen this month vs. the January low, which shows there are still ways around sanctions and will continue to be. The latest U.S. 'threat' of a 25% tariff on countries which buy oil from Venezuela may be a veiled threat, also in regards to Iran. That adds to pressure from the sanctioning of a Chinese teapot refinery (Luqing) and an import/storage terminal (Huaying). Still, Iranian exports are 'only' down by about 200 kbpd YTD vs. the same period last year, and Shandong keeps importing also on sanctioned tankers despite statements suggesting otherwise... 

There are, however, reports of Iranian, Russian and Venezuelan cargoes being denied entry into China and India, and according to Argus Chinese state-owned firms fear that the upped sanctions push will drive independent refiners to again turn to the MEG and Atlantic basin for spot cargoes to replace sanctioned barrels, although there are few signs of this just yet. There has been a turn to more Russian crude, albeit more on compliant tonnage, but that is in competition with other Chinese buyers. Delivered price in China for both Iranian light and ESPO are now among the highest in years, hence compliant grades look increasingly competitive. As this happens at the same time as OPEC will start to unwind production cuts, that may again start to support the West-East arb.

Hence, we may see another boost for long-haul tanker demand, akin to the one we say in December and January amid the big sanction push then. 

Chinese crude oil imports have declined YTD, which is driven by a drop in imports of sanctioned crudes. Imports excluding Iranian, Russian and Venezuelan crude have risen, and should rise further this and next month too as long-haul cargoes arrive. Still, crude oil inventories have drawn YTD, as refinery runs hit all-time highs for the January-February period. 

An x-factor this year will be whether new storage capacity will be filled. 125 mb of new capaity is planned this year, up from 33 mb last year and 65 mb in 2023. This may not happen if the oil price curves remain backwardated, and will be a function of price. Hence, price and structure will be key to watch.

content.title: China available crude oil vs. refinery runs

content.content: With refinery margins largely strengthening YTD and oil demand expectations having been revised slightly higher, refinery run expectations have also been revised slightly higher. Going into summer season there may therefore be slightly better product tanker demand than expected before, and we have already started to see some more supporting arb. and rate developments at times in recent weeks. The counter to this argument is the tariff threat which ultimately is likely to weigh on demand if followed through, which is the main downside risk for the market this year, other than conflict resolution which does not appear imminent...

Fleet growth YTD has been limited, only 0.3% as of the beginning of March. There is more to come, but mostly in the second half of the year, and mostly for product tankers. Total scheduled gross deliveries this year equal 2.9% of the fleet, which is not scary as demand may grow by as much or more, overall. Net fleet growth should end lower, with some phase-out both in the form of scrapping and some lower utilisation for older vessels and the shadow fleet. Crude tanker fleet growth may effectively end up at zero or less also this year, but for products the picture is a bit more challenging, especially in the second half of the year which makes for a gradually softening rate outlook. 

The next two years scheduled gross fleet growth rises to about 5%, which likely means a gradually softer outlook for rates, unless oil demand and supply growth surprise to the upside.

However, ordering has come to a near complete stop, with only 1m dwt confirmed ordered so far. Although there is some more to come, the current sentiment suggests the total tally for this year may end up significantly below the 28 and 45m dwt ordered the last two years, and potentially also well below the historical average of nearly 16m dwt. 

Meanwhile, scrapping has picked up. Although it is not a lot, the 0.6m dwt that has been scrapped so far already surpasses both of last years, and there are reports of quite a few more ships sold for scrap.

Two weeks ago, we wrote the following: *The fundamentals look good for the next couple of months, so we do not expect a major spot market correction within that period. 
However, the spot market might be close to reaching a ceiling, as the Capesize/Kamsarmax ratio is above 2, which, since 2018, has meant further upside is limited. That said, we expect the Kamsarmax spot market to improve in the next month or two as the second ECSAM grain wave should kick in.*

Notwithstanding the last weeks' market softness, year-to-date spot market highs within the next month seem likely. Imported iron ore consumption in China has kept rising. VLOCs will be "out" of the market for a while still. We think C3 looks tight, and even though C5 activity was very low last week the market drop has not been significant. Activity on C5 has picked up this week.

content.content:
In our previous report published in January, we wrote the following

*The fundamental outlook for 2025 remains bearish in our view. There are no clear signs yet that China's recent stimulus announcements are translating into higher credit growth. Next month’s release of the January lending numbers will be important in this respect, as that is when lending figures are the highest. Should that figure be at record high one can perhaps start counting down to when a recovery will take hold, but in any case, there is always a lag until it impacts dry bulk markets. Manufacturing activity in the World ex-China remains dull, with all PMIs hovering around 50 and most countries’ readings below 50. These readings are likely to remain around 50 at best as long as China's growth is low, the dollar remains strong and interest rates remain relatively high.* 

Link to the January report: https://fearnpulse.com/drybulk-report/fearnleys-dry-bulk-market-outlook-january-2025. 

China's total social financing numbers came in at an all-time high of 7 trillion Yuan in January. The growth rate we calculate remains negative, so one needs to see a few more months of strong financing data before the growth rate turns up - which in turn would paint a more bullish picture for dry bulk markets going forward. Given the 9 to 15-month lag before increasing or decreasing financing growth impacts dry bulk markets, it is still unlikely that stimulus measures will have any significant effect this year, however. 
Nonetheless, China's steel and iron ore markets are not performing badly so far this year. Blast furnace output and imported iron ore consumption are both higher than the same period last year, the iron ore price has climbed steadily the last months, and steel prices have remained stable. However, inventories of iron ore in ports and at steel mills are higher than in the same period last year by about 20 million tons. 
Notwithstanding a relatively good start to the year demand-wise, growth for the full year is likely to be low at best, considering that the mentioned stimulus measures are not yet going strongly. A few weeks ago, it was also reported by several reliable sources that there will be steel output curbs at some point this year, seeing as the steel industry has struggled with low or negative profitability the last year. 
The big downside risk from China's demand this year is not iron ore, though; it is coal. Since the middle of 2021, inventories have been built massively, from 100 million tons to 700 million tons, as energy security became a strong priority. Increased domestic production and record import levels drove the inventory accumulation, but that now seems to be at an end. Coal imports are already negative year on year (- 4% through February), and there have been recurring reports over the last weeks that some importers will stop purchasing on a spot basis within the next months. These reports are not confirmed, but it does not seem entirely unlikely, considering the fundamental picture. 

In the rest of the World, excluding China, fundamentals are not strong either. The weakest spot remains Europe, where the manufacturing sector has been in recession since the middle of 2022. The push towards greener sources of power has caused the demand for coal to drop and electricity prices to rise, rendering the manufacturing sector less competitive. Other developed countries like Japan, Korea, and Taiwan have also seen the demand for dry bulk imports decline since 2021/22. 
There is unlikely to be any significant cyclical upturn in developed economies dry bulk imports until interest rates are cut and inflation is under control. The former depends on the US, both in terms of the interest rate levels there but also in terms of the dollar exchange rate. A strong dollar makes it harder for countries ex-US to loosen monetary policy, and also reflects a scarcity of dollars, which means trade financing can be harder to obtain. The year-on-year change of a broad USD index has therefore correlated tightly with the year-on-year change of dry bulk shipment volumes the last 10 years in that a stronger dollar means weaker global demand and vice versa. 
Emerging economies (LATAM, Africa, SEA, ME, India) usually see dry bulk demand increase every year, but the weakness in China plus developed economies could mean growth will be hampered in emerging economies this year. In Q4 last year, India's growth slowed abruptly, for example. 
So, as outlined in our previous report, we find it hard to see what factors will cause demand to grow strongly this year. **Summing it all up, we think the demand picture looks weaker than in 2023, and we therefore assume in our earnings estimates that this year will end up averaging lower than that year.** 

**It might all turn through the course of 2026, however.** China's stimulus measures, further global interest rate cuts, a potentially weaker USD exchange rate, lower fleet growth, and cycle duration analysis suggest that markets will improve in 2026 and 2027. We think the cycle will bottom in Q4 this year at the earliest and Q2 2026 at the latest. 

**The political landscape is at its most uncertain in decades.** In general, we see the ongoing conflicts as having a small direct impact on the dry bulk markets. The secondary effects could be more significant. Below are some thoughts on each major ongoing "issue". 

- Trump's tariff policies: Small direct impact on dry bulk markets as the volumes in question are not significant. The negative secondary effect is that the broader macroeconomic situation could worsen further (stock markets are certainly not appreciating Trump's policies). The positive secondary effect could be a weaker dollar (the USD seems to be weakening each time tariffs hit the news), which usually is positive for dry bulk demand growth. Positives could thus come from the negatives, as a potential US economic downturn could lead to lower rates and a weaker Dollar, which would allow the rest of the World to cut interest rates further. 
- The war in Ukraine: A continuation of the standstill means Russia's coal exports are likely to decline further due to sanctions and constraints to railway capacity. In the event of peace, Russia's coal exports are likely to rise (the development of sanctions would still be unknown, but the railway capacity would increase), and there would be added commodity demand for the rebuilding of Ukraine. If the war escalates further, the consequences are unknown. 
- Israel vs Iran and Proxies: As it stands, the transits through the Suez Canal will continue to be lower than usual. This has been a positive factor for the markets, but probably not as positive as many had thought it could be. Europe's demand has been weak the last year and a half, and exports from the Black Sea, Med, and North Atlantic to the Middle East or India became more costly, which impacted volumes negatively. So, a potential full reopening of the canal would not necessarily be bearish for the dry bulk markets. A potential escalation of hostilities in the Middle East would risk a spike in the oil price and a consequent worsening of global economic growth. The dry bulk volumes in the Middle East are too small to make a direct impact on the markets. 
- US penalization of Chinese-built ships: It is still uncertain whether the proposed regulations will be implemented. Should it happen, the market balance per se would not be affected, but it would be very disruptive from an operational perspective. Non-Chinese built vessels could benefit, and Chinese built vessels could be at a disadvantage. In the end, after a period of adjustment, it would end up being a tax on the US consumer which in turn is negative for global economic growth.

*Next year, we do not see much potential for growth in iron ore import demand. Port inventories in China are close to the highest level in the last 10 years, with high-grade inventories making up most of it. Imported iron ore consumption in China is 3.2% lower than in the same period last year, so even if the stimulus measures work immediately there is a gap to 2023 levels that needs to recover. 
Manufacturing in the world, excluding China, seems too weak to expect much growth, with recent layoff announcements in the German industry as one clear signal. PMI readings are below 50 in over half of the countries included in the surveys by Markit.*

Through February, China's iron ore imports are lower than the same period last year. Imported iron ore consumption has been higher on a year-on-year basis since late November, but the higher inventories weigh on import demand. However, the January- February imports were also affected by supply issues in Australia and more rain in Brazil than last year. We expect the year-on-year import growth rate to rise in the coming months.

The charts shown below still paints a bearish picture for fundamentals this year. 

Top left chart:

Comment from our late January report:

*China’s credit growth is a smoothed average change of the monthly total social financing numbers, a figure that includes all financing to the “real economy” i.e. excluding interbank financing. This curve is shifted 12 months forward, as it leads the Baltic Dry Index year on year by roughly that time period. Through the displayed period, there was only one major deviation between the two series, in the middle of 2019. As the credit growth rate continued to fall through the second half of last year, it suggests that the Baltic Dry Index year on year change will remain negative through 2025. The monthly total social financing numbers for January will be released in a few weeks, and will be a very important indication as to whether all the recent stimulus announcements from Chinese officials is starting to translate into increased credit growth.* 

Monthly total social financing came in at all-time highs in January, which shows that the stimulus measures have started to work. However, high monthly financing needs to continue in the coming months for credit growth to turn upwards. In turn, that would suggest a more positive dry bulk market outlook for 2026.  

Top right chart:

Comment from our late January report:

*The China Economic Growth Index is an average of key economic data, which, in our opinion, gives a more accurate measure of China’s growth rates than GDP. The average growth rate of that index since 2020 has been a mere 1.2%, and last year, the index was negative at -2.1%. These figures are far below the reported GDP numbers. 
The index has correlated tightly with total dry bulk shipment volume growth (all countries and commodities) over the last 15 years. However, last year there was a deviation, as inventory building in China drove import demand rather than underlying fundamentals. This may be a cause for concern as the last year there was such a deviation was in 2014.*

The macro economic data releases needed to construct the index have yet to be released for January and February. China's import growth has started the year on a negative note, with both coal and iron ore imports lower than the same period last year.  

Middle left chart:

The USDCNY year-on-year change continues to predict China's dry bulk import growth with high accuracy. The USDCNY suggests China's import growth will be around 0% this year.

Middle right chart:

The energy price leads have lost correlation with the Baltic Dry Index year-on-year change the last months. Going forward, energy prices suggest macro economic weakness until a potential bottom in Q2 2026. 

Bottom left chart:

Comment from our late January report:

*The chart shows total iron ore inventories in Chinese ports and at Chinese steel mills, divided by daily imported iron ore consumption. This ratio is now at the highest point since early 2022. Either consumption must rise or inventories have to fall for the ratio to go to a level where one could turn bullish on market fundamentals.*

Since then, the inventory/consumption ratio has improved, as consumption has risen and inventories have been drawn. Further improvement is needed for the outlook to turn bullish, in our opinion. 

Bottom right chart:

The chart shows the US dollar index year-on-year change vs dry bulk shipment volume growth. A rising US dollar is negative for dry bulk demand growth, as it reflects that global financial conditions are tighter, and it makes imports more expensive for several countries. A rising US dollar also makes it harder for countries to loosen their monetary policy.

content.content:
The new year began with renewed interest in LNG vessel sales. The first two months have been active with rumors and movements; two vessels have found new owners, while one has been sent to the breakers. Notably, a substantial number of vessels are currently under consideration, indicating a robust pipeline of potential transactions for owners seeking to divest older tonnage. Based on current market dynamics, it is projected that an additional three to five vessel sales may be finalized shortly.

One trend among market participants is an increased focus on strategic timing for tonnage acquisition, largely attributed to the ongoing and forecast soft chartering market, particularly for older vessels. The lack of chartering opportunities is applying downward pressure on price expectations, leading to careful consideration of market entry points for potential buyers.

The market outlook remains cautiously optimistic, though. Activity in recent months suggests a healthy demand for vessels despite the challenges. The expected sale of more vessels in the near future supports this optimism. Stakeholders must stay vigilant and adaptable to navigate the complexities of market timings and price expectations in order to capitalize on emerging opportunities.

The newbuilding market in general has started the year with a lack of inertia, in stark contrast to the container sector's continued activity. Across most segments, a "wait-and-see" stance prevails, with shipyards, owners, and charterers all showing caution. This uncertainty has widened the gap in pricing between yards, reflecting their varying levels of slot availability and risk appetite. Aside from notable orders from Celsius at SHI and Hanwha Shipping at their own facility, both order books and inquiry pipelines remain notably subdued.

The flurry of activity seen since inauguration of the 47th president of the United States has had its effect on interest rates, as key benchmarks have trended lower. The implications of a potential increase in trade barriers and a more uncertain geopolitical environment is challenging the fundamental outlook on global growth, which the credit markets rapidly translate into lower interest rates.

A number of central banks have already commenced interest rate cuts (US, Eurozone), and while still citing inflation as the "guiding star" it feels as if growth prospects may become a central theme in the near-term. Of course, in the case of slower growth we can only hope that inflation tails off too, as market pundits have begun to whisper about stagflation scenarios. While our last comment included Mr. Powell's wait-and-see attitude, the sentiment seems to be more action than inaction these days and as such it would not be a surprise if we see a further slide interest rates.

content.content:
Rates have recovered nearly as expected so far this year, and with the backdrop of more sanctions coupled with more crude oil volumes coming, further upside should materialise in coming months. 

The geopolitical landscape is highly uncertain, with new and often contradictory statements and headlines each day. What seems relatively certain is increased sanctions pressure on Iran. Tariffs could spark some more trade diversion, where longer sailing distances may offset negative economic impact. Any conflict resolution still seems some way off, but is a downside risk for tanker demand if and when diversions are (partly) unwound. Another risk, as ever, is macroeconomic. 

For now, tanker market fundamentals should tighten further through the spring and summer, mostly for the bigger crude tankers, while the outlook for smaller segments is more normalised.

Volumes YTD have been lower than during the same period last year, driven partly by better OPEC+ compliance and partly by underwhelming Americas production amid some preliminary outages. Crucially, however, crude tanker demand has been boosted by longer sailing distances as Eastern buyers seek more compliant barrels in the Atlantic basin.
More oil to come - which seems to be needed

There should be more in coming months too, with expected production increases in the Americas, most prominently in Brazil and Guyana. Five new FPSOs are scheduled to come online this year, with a combined capacity of about 1 mbpd. One of them has already arrived in Brazil, and two others have been delivered ex. yard, so should be on schedule to start production within the next couple of quarters. 

After slumping by nearly 0.5 mbpd in Q1, the EIA forecasts an increase in Americas production of 0.75 mbpd in Q2, and another 0.8 mbpd in Q3. Most of that is likely to be exported by sea, and contribute to to both higher volumes and longer average sailing distances - mostly benefiting the biggest tankers.

The oil market balance YTD has appeared much tighter than expected. The forward curve has remained backwardated, and global inventories have drawn meaningfully. Partly, that is due to some production outages at the beginning of the year, but also partly due to stronger demand. At most, in its October report, the IEA predicted a 1.2 mbpd oversupplied market this year, while in the most recent report this has dropped to 0.5 mbpd as demand has been revised up by 200 kbpd and supply down by 500 kbpd. 

At this point, it will not take a lot of downside in supply from Iran, Venezuela or Russia amid tightened sanctions, before there is a need for the OPEC+ to unwind cuts. However, with oil prices coming off again lately, there is reason to suspect another delay to the cut unwind schedule beyond April.

Speaking of sanctions, with the latest rounds from the EU and OFAC, a vast portion of the fleet is now sanctioned, and interestingly the latest round also included sanctions on the main export terminals in Iran and Chinese traders - which could up the pressure further. It looks like this has quite the effect: Loadings on OFAC listed tankers have plunged in February to date, as have discharges from these vessels - with further potential downside going forward after a waiver period for oil loaded on these tankers end imminently. This has also corresponded with a build-up of floating storage and oil in transit. 

In turn, refinery run rates of Chinese independent refiners have declined substantially YTD, only for the slack to be taken up by the state-onwed refiners (who source oil from compliant sources). Chinese refinery runs overall have risen marginally over the last two months, and crude inventories have drawn, by about 2 mbpd in February according to Argus. This means more volumes and demand to come still for the compliant fleet - after some near-term refinery turnarounds.

The full effects on loadings from Russia, Iran and Venezuela are yet to be seen. January loadings in Iran were very high, but the run-rate in February is substantially lower as shipping cost has risen on lower shipping availability. This, coupled with slim discounts for Iranian oil currently means compliant crude oil is more competitive landed in China. Preliminary January and February numbers suggest a total 600 kbpd decline in loadings from these countries vs. the same period last year, led lower by Russian exports which are down 400 kbpd. Some more downside may be likely going forward as sanctions put pressure on Iran, Russia struggles with infrastructure, and Venezuela concessions end.  

After the most recent round of sanctions, 12% of the total tanker fleet is on the OFAC and EU's black lists, 10% on the OFAC's which is the one that really matters. In utilisation adjusted terms, the market impact is about half of that, which is still significant. There is more to target, though, if relevant authorities want to, as less than half of the total shadow fleet has thus far been sanctioned. Overall, the now OFAC listed fleet carried 37% of exports from Russia, Iran and Venezuela last year, 49% of crude.

Another pointer to a relatively strong oil market YTD is refinery margins which have recovered a bit YTD and hold near historical averages. This is still a far cry from the highs of the last few years, and run estimates for this year still point to lower growth than in recent years - meaning lower product tanker volume additions. As more of the expected upside for runs this year is also closer to end-user demand, tonne-mile growth will likely be relatively low.

With refinery margins having held better than feared on decent demand and some other factors like low natural gas inventories in Europe and continued Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, there are also expectations that maintenance may not be as extensive this spring. Overall, refinery runs are expected to increase by 0.6 mbpd this year, following a 0.5 mbpd increase last year and well below 2023's 1.1 mbpd. 

Lower volume growth, higher fleet growth, and more normalised crack spreads all point to more normalised earnings for product tankers  this year. Sure, there will be volatility, but we expect the floor and ceiling to be lower than over the last couple of years.

content.content: This year's scheduled gross delivery number is expected to rise to 3%, from only 1% last year. For crude tankers the gross figure is still a low 1.7% while products is quite high at 6.1%. Given sanctions and new regulations, we expect that net fleet growth for the crude tanker fleet will effectively be negative this year, and that products may end up closer to 3-4% - although mostly in the second half of the year. Hence, the outlook in coming months is still very low, and coupled with demand that is set to pick up should bode for unseasonably strong rate development going forward.

With nearly 16% of the tanker fleet already having passed the 20 year mark, an orderbook to fleet ratio of 13.4% is hardly scary. More so, with 10% of the fleet being sanctioned by the OFAC, much of which is at risk of never returning to the 'normal' fleet, there is ultimately a need for more orders to materialise beyond 2027. 

Sure, if sanctions on Iran and/or Russia are lifted, some of the OFAC listed vessel may come back, but as shown below a vast majority, especially for the Iran linked vessels, is getting very old - on average built in 2003. 27% of the Iran linked OFAC listed tankers are already 25+ years old, and 76% are 20 or older. For Russia, the average built is 2007, with 5% being 25+ years old and 40% being 20+. Hence there is a risk that some of these may come back to the broader market - especially going into domestic shipping companies.

So far this year ordering activity has come to a near complete halt, partly due to all the geopolitical uncertainty, but partly also due to lower rates the last half year and softening secondhand values. For most segments it is currently relatively cheaper to buy secondhand than ordering, plus you still get decent TC rates for tonnage on the water. We do not expect to see any significant run-up in ordering interest until rates and values pick up meaningfully. 

Meanwhile, phase-out has picked up, and already nearly as much has been confirmed scrapped as the last two years, with more also reportedly on the way to the scrap yards. We do not expect a major scrapping drive this year, but some more than in the past few years due to the growing portion of the fleet which is becoming near-obsolete. If there is a way to work around payment/sanction issues, we would expect that quite a few of the older OFAC listed vessels may be scrapped going forward - and for sake of saving environmental risks, there should be given waivers for this...

content.content:
The recent sanction news boosted what had already emerged as a return of some Atlantic-Asia flow, which has contributed to lift rates. Depending on enforcement of sanctions, the tanker market outlook is now firmer than just a month ago, with upside risk to our forecast. 

Oil pricing has to a greater extent reflected the recent sanction developments, and with a wide open Atlantic-East arbitrage owners have arguably left some money on the table during the most recent rate slump. At the time of writing, the momentum has firmly shifted up again. 

Due to the wind-down period for ongoing voyages and a time-lag in crude sourcing impact, it is still too early to judge the effect that sanctions will have on the market, and the decline in rates following the initial boost is therefore not necessarily anything to go by.

There has so far been a more meaningful impact on the oil market. Chinese and Indian buyers have scrambled to replace Russian barrels beyond February deliveries. This has led spot premiums for Middle Eastern crude oil to soar, and opened a wide Atlantic - East arbitrage. We expect to see a much higher Atlantic - East cargo count in March than in 2H'24 - reversing the tonne-mile trend and absorbing a vessel overhang. 

Good thing, then, for oil buyers and tanker owners that there is expectations of plenty of crude oil supply growth this year - mostly from the Atlantic basin, and an increased likelihood that the OPEC+ may unwind some cuts.

content.title: WTI-Dubai, adj. for 2-1 month fwd. spread

content.content:
Already toward the end of last year Asian buyers increasingly turned their eyes to the West, and fixing for the first two months of this year shows increased Atlantic-East cargoes vs. the last few months of 2024. More is expected to come, both as seasonal demand in the West dips, to free up more export barrels, and as these Asian buyers have sped up the chase for compliant barrels. 

With that, VLCCs rates have recovered and look set to gain more going forward. In January the average MEG-Far East rate, adjusted for the fleet's average speed/consumption, ended at about $38k/d, slightly shy our $40k/d forecast. With that, VLCCs have regained pole position - earning the highest TCEs across tanker segments, in line with expectations of relative normalisation. Going forward, there may be upside risk to our forecast curve, especially for crude tankers, if sanctions are enforced and complied with.

The oil supply expectations for this year have been reduced somewhat in recent months, on lower activity in the U.S. and underwhelming growth in Latin America in 2024. At the same time, oil demand estimates have been revised higher, and with that, the glut of oil that was expected for this year all of a sudden does not look too bad after all. 

Just four months ago, the IEA predicted a 1.2 mbpd oversupplied market this year, whilst the latest estimate is 0.7 mbpd. Add in some further production hickups, pressure on Iran, Russia and Venezuela from sanctions, and all of a sudden there may be a need for the OPEC+ to unwind cuts after all. The forward curves have remained backwardated into this year, even steepening, which suggests the market is a lot tighter than forecast. There is thus some reason to expect that President Trump may get what he wants, as the consensus currently seems to be that the OPEC+ will follow through with the gradual cut easing from April as planned.

content.content:
Another deciding factor for the rate trajectory this year is when the four new FPSOs in Brazil and one in Guyana comes online. Three of these are believed to have already sailed from yards in the East which should correspond with the below supply growth expectations from the EIA. This may mean a solid volume boost through the summer, benefiting mostly the largest crude tankers, which also potentially means an atypical seasonal rate pattern this year. 

Canada is another question mark. The EIA expects nearly 300 kbpd of production growth this year, mostly in the second half. Much of that will likely go toward filling the remaining capacity of the TransMountain Pipeline, and the delta will likely be headed for Asia. There is realistically little good reason for there to be U.S. Tariffs on Canadian oil, considering that nearly two thirds of U.S. crude oil imports come from Canada - a vital source of heavy crude for blending. Crude quality matters, and if the U.S. would have to replace these imports from elsewhere, it could wreak havoc with the global oil market - let alone the impact of some Canadian production probably having to be shut in as other export options are rare. More likely, if tariffs are in fact implemented, U.S. refinery profitability will soften and/or gasoline prices will rise. Setting tariffs aside, Canada's increasing production should contribute to tanker demand growth this and next year, supporting Afras out of Vancouver and partly VLs through STS in PAL.

Russia's response to the recent sanctions may also set the pace for the market going forward. Amid some confusion so far, there are some price points which suggest that exports will largely continue to flow - and contribute to tightening the (compliant) Aframax market. 

Russia's Eastern exports are on paper those which will be affected the most, as the now-sanctioned vessels covered nearly two thirds of last year's liftings. For the Baltic and Black Sea only 23% and 34% of last year's liftings were covered by these vessels. Rates have also responded the most in the East, with some exorbitant Kozmino numbers reported. That will lure in new unsanctioned tonnage, which in turn may leave a gap for Russian Western exports. We have seen a number of SnP transactions for 15+ years old Aframaxes at 10-20% higher than last done prices, which suggests a replacement process has already begun. 

The Urals price has also responded, reportedly declining to about the G7 price cap - which may at least through a transition period also be necessary for Russia be able to uphold exports at decent levels. Last year, total Russian exports declined by 220 kbpd from the preceding year, mostly for products after Ukrainian refinery attacks, and there may be some downside risk this year too. According to Bloomberg, Ukrainian drones have struck pumping stations to Ust-Luga, where loadings in January have declined by about 300 kbpd from last year. 

For the broader OFAC listed fleet, it is worth reiterating that 80% of its discharges last year were into areas that have explicitly said these ships are no longer welcome. As long as this 'ban' is upheld, and the U.S. enforces sanctions, the impact on the tanker market should be significant. In turn, the lower oil prices are, the more likely it is that the U.S. will be hawkish on Russia, Iran and Venezuela.

Other than reversal of geopolitically linked trade diversion, the biggest downside risk for the tanker market this year is on the oil demand side. Current crack spreads in Asia are not great with some run cuts being suggested, and there is diverging macro data from key countries in the region. 

On the one hand, housing data in China have improved somewhat in recent months and prospective stimulus has added to some potential for optimism, while at the same time January industrial PMIs were back in contractionary territory for the first time in three months. A stronger U.S. Dollar certainly does not boost buying interest, all else equal, neither does tariff threats. 

Oil demand has surprised to the upside in the West recently, and Trump's proposed SPR refill may add to that going forward. From a tanker demand perspective, that may eat into potential for West-East trade. For now, oil pricing works against storage builds, and rather the sanctioned barrel replacement is the name of the game.

content.content: Refinery margins keeping some arbs alive, for now...

Refinery margins globally have come down to more normalised levels through the last six months, although some pockets of strength remain offering some trade opportunities - particularly for diesel in the West. A potential loss of the third and fourth biggest refineries in Russia may underpin these in the near term, but otherwise, barring new disruptions, this year may continue to show more normalised profitability. 

The weakness in Asian margins recently has led to frontloading of maintenance and some economic run cuts. Chinese independent refiners lose competitiveness when sanctioned barrels are no longer as easily available, and run cuts are likely - although much of this downside is expected to be compensated by state-owned refiners. 

The price and refining landscape suggests lower product tanker demand growth this year, and generally less arbitrages and trade opportunities available - factors which have contributed to some of the extraordinary rate strength in recent years.
Low-ish fleet growth for the foreseeable future

The orderbook to fleet has hardly grown over the last few months, with the recent dip in sentiment and secondhand values taking its toll on newbuild interest. Orders will return in time, but for now there may be a breather. 

For context, the 12.9% orderbook to fleet stands against 9.5% of the fleet currently on the OFAC's black list and 15.9% of the fleet already being 20+ years old. Another 4.3% of the fleet turns 20 this year, and 3.6% next year. Assuming that the vast majority of these are semi-obsolete and will in one form or another be increasingly phased out, more ordering is needed - especially if tanker demand continues to grow like it most likely will. 

We expect the slower ordering pace to persist near-term - at least unless or until secondhand values rise meaningfully or newbuild prices come down. The latter does not seem very likely in the near term due to yards' very comfortable order backlogs.

Although gross fleet growth picks up this year, deliveries are scheduled to remain low through the first half with only one third of the year's deliveries pencilled in. Total scheduled deliveries amount to 3% vs. the fleet, up from only 1% last year, but mostly tilted toward product tankers at 6.1%, vs. crude at 1.7%. 

Given the extensive sanctions and new regulations, net fleet growth for crude is likely to effectively be well below zero, whilst for products there may still be growth of some 3-4%.
Values may be about to find support again

Values have generally corrected a bit to the downside in recent months, on softer TC rates. The biggest downside has been seen for the segments which outperformed the most over the past two years, namely Afra and MRs - and the older end of the asset curve has seen the biggest slide. 

The latter has reversed over the last two weeks, with a renewed bid from players seeking to replenish the Russia trading fleet. If sanctions are upheld, and more importantly enforced, there may be more to come here too. 

For modern assets there is still a relatively wide bid/ask spread and as a result few transactions. That said, the rout may have stopped. At current TC rates, which seem to have found a floor, most recent value estimates should on paper be well supported. With upside risk to TC rates re. our forecast, especially for crude tankers, there may even be some upside potential.

In our previous report published in December, we wrote the following: 

*Our market viewpoints always start by analyzing shipment volume growth against supply growth, as the other factors are more uncertain. Since Q4 last year, our view has been that shipment volume growth would drop below supply growth during the first half of 2025, so downside risk would escalate during the second half of 2025. We still seem on track for that development, which is a little worrying considering where earnings are now. On the other hand, as shipment volume growth remains positive it could mean that markets will rebound strongly after the Chinese New Year next year if sailing distances, congestion, and sailing speeds go in owners favor.*

The part about “worrisome” is so far playing out, with Pacific earnings around all-time lows for all segments. Record high coal inventories in China and a much slower-than-usual grain harvest in South America could mean the weakness will persist for a few more weeks after the Chinese New Year. A positive point is that China’s iron ore consumption is higher than last year, but it remains below 2023 levels and inventories in ports and steel mills are higher than last year.  

The fundamental outlook for 2025 remains bearish in our view. There are no clear signs yet that China's recent stimulus announcements are translating into higher credit growth. Next month’s release of the January lending numbers will be important in this respect, as that is when lending figures are the highest. Should that figure be at record high one can perhaps start counting down to when a recovery will take hold, but in any case, there is always a lag until it impacts dry bulk markets. Manufacturing activity in the World ex-China remains dull, with all PMIs hovering around 50 and most countries’ readings below 50. These readings are likely to remain around 50 at best as long as China's growth is low, the dollar remains strong and interest rates remain relatively high. 

As it is hard to find factors suggesting strong demand growth in any country or region this year, earnings are likely to average lower than in 2023, as in that year China's demand improved strongly. We expect the cycle to bottom at some point between Q4 this year and Q2 2026 and are therefore tentatively bullish for 2H 2026 and 2027. The below earnings forecasts reflects these views.

content.content:
The charts shown below paints a bearish picture for fundamentals going forward. 

Top left chart:

China’s credit growth is a smoothed average change of the monthly total social financing numbers, a figure that includes all financing to the “real economy” i.e. excluding interbank financing. This curve is shifted 12 months forward, as it leads the Baltic Dry Index year on year by roughly that time period. Through the displayed period, there was only one major deviation between the two series, in the middle of 2019. As the credit growth rate continued to fall through the second half of last year, it suggests that the Baltic Dry Index year on year change will remain negative through 2025. The monthly total social financing numbers for January will be released in a few weeks, and will be a very important indication as to whether all the recent stimulus announcements from Chinese officials is starting to translate into increased credit growth. 

Top right chart:

The China Economic Growth Index is an average of key economic data, which in our opinion gives a more accurate measure of China’s growth rates rather than GDP. The average growth rate of that index since 2020 has been a mere 1.2%, and last year the index was negative at -2.1%. These figures are far below the reported GDP numbers. 
The index have correlated tightly with total dry bulk shipment volume growth (all countries and commodities) the last 15 years. However, last year there was a deviation, as inventory building in China drove import demand rather than underlying fundamentals. Maybe a cause for concern as the previous year there was such a deviation was in 2014. 

Middle left chart:

We have covered this chart in previous reports. Here is the text from our November report:

*China’s currency trades under a so-called ‘managed float’, which means the central bank is heavily involved in trying to keep it trading around a desired level. This process sometimes obviously involves buying Yuan against the USD, and vice versa. The USDCNY is therefore an important part of the domestic liquidity situation. Recent stimulus measures in China will naturally involve expanding the domestic money supply to fund infrastructure projects as well as trying to revive the property sector. That, along with weaker domestic economic growth rates means there should be heavy downward pressure on the Yuan.

To counteract this downward pressure, the central bank has to buy increasing amounts of Yuan to keep the currency stable, with the flipside of this being that it nullifies other liquidity-increasing factors. That is why there is a very high correlation between the 9-month lead of the year-on-year change of the USDCNY and China’s year-on-year growth of dry bulk imports. The chart displaying this relationship is shown in the middle left below. Over the last year, the Yuan has strengthened relative to the USD, which strongly suggests China’s dry bulk import growth will continue to fall over the coming 9 months. In our view, China’s government has to allow the Yuan to weaken considerably going forward for the stimulus measures to succeed.*
Since the November update, the correlation continues to hold, as China’s import growth trends down. The USDCNY year on year change have increased a bit, but is not yet indicative of higher import growth over the next 9 months.* 

Middle right chart:

The chart shows the preceding 18 months change of coal, oil and natural gas prices, respectively (so, prices now compared to July 2023). These curves are shifted 18 months forward, as the change in energy prices are important drivers of economic growth. The higher the curves are, the cheaper energy prices are relative to 18 months ago, and vice versa. The Baltic Dry Index year on year change has a quite good correlation with these curves. However, the last months the correlation has been lost, as the Baltic Dry Index year on year change have turned negative, even though the energy price change leads suggested it would remain positive through the first half of 2025. That should be slightly encouraging for owners, as the energy price leads suggest global economic growth will continue to weaken until the middle of 2026, at least. 

Bottom left chart:

The chart shows total iron ore inventories in Chinese ports and at Chinese steel mills, divided by daily imported iron ore consumption. This ratio is now at the highest point since early 2022. Either consumption must rise, or inventories have to fall for the ratio to go to a level where one could turn bullish on market fundamentals.

Bottom right chart:

Daily imported iron ore consumption in China, and the year on year change. Consumption remains below the peak levels of 2022 and 2023, but at least the year on year change have started to turn positive. The post CNY seasonal upturn will be interesting to watch over the next two months.

content.content: After more than three years of near total complacency, the Biden administration has recently taken significant steps toward stopping sanctioned oil flows. The significant new sanctions and response from relevant authorities in receiving countries boosts the tanker market outlook, which may now tilt toward a bull case for this year. With soaring FFA rates and more enquiries for TCs, asset values may again climb too. The main question and decider for how much of a boost the market may receive is how stringently these sanctions will be enforced - history shows where there are sanctions, there are also loopholes.

With a significant portion of the fleet now being sanctioned, Russia and Iran may have to reduce exports and/or renew the shadow fleet - both of which will contribute to tightening the 'normal' tanker market. This was already (slowly) strengthening, especially for the biggest vessels, and now the outlook has become much stronger also for Suez- and Aframaxes. For product tankers there is less impact, other than trickle-down from the bigger siblings. 

The equally important factor of the last week's sanctions news is India and Shandong's tough stance on OFAC vessels. This should (and has already started to) lead the buyers of Iranian and Russian oil to divert purchases to other sources. Over recent weeks the spot premiums for Middle Eastern crudes has jumped and there has also been increased Asian buing from West Africa, the USG and the North Sea. That may now accelerate, unless the OPEC+ reverses cuts earlier than currently planned. 

The little evidence so far suggests that OFAC sanctions are relatively effective as vessels previously placed on the list have become much less active, and in some cases idled entirely. Unless there are sanction waivers, or complete disregard by key market players, the last week's sanction news is is likely to have a meaningful impact on the tanker market given the scale of the clampdown. This shifts the market outlook toward a bull-case for this year.

The latest batch of OFAC sanctions includes183 vessels, of which 129 are (relevant) tankers: 4 VLCCs, 24 Suez, 75 Afra/LR2, 2 LR1s and 23 MR/Handy, which are on average built in 2008. The total OFAC list now includes nearly 400 (relevant) tankers: 91 VLCCs, 66 Suez, 145 Afra/LR2, 18 Pmax/LR1 and 68 MR/Handy. This equates to just below 10% of the total tanker fleet, split between nearly 12% of the crude tanker fleet and slightly more than 4% of product tankers. 20% of the ice class Aframax fleet is now sanctioned, and another about 30% will definitely not do Russian business, which may also givethe Russians some challenges this winter. 

The newly added vessels have on average lifted 1.6 mbpd over the last year, 94% from Russia (26% of Russian oil exports) and 84% crude oil. Nearly 500 kbpd has been lifted into Shandong. About half of the flow has gone to other countries than China, most prominently India and Turkey. Thus, three quarters of the flow has gone to regions that will have to adhere by U.S. sanctions going forward. 

The vessels on the total OFAC list lifted 3.3 mbpd last year, 88% of which was crude oil. This equates to 4.8% of total seaborne oil, and 4.1% of tonne-miles. Due to the inefficient nature of shadow flows, however, these vessels performed 7.6% of total tonne-days. About one third of the total volume was carried into Shandong, and a full 80% went into areas which now cannot accommodate OFAC vessels after the recent Shandong ban and Indian stance.

Of the vessels on the OFAC list, we find 135 which are current laden, most of which with Russian and Irianian crude. This may cause some further increase in floating storage going forward, as these may find a harder time discharging despite a wind-down period until 12 March - quite a few are observed stopping the last few days. There has already been some increase in floating storage of Iranian crude in recent weeks and months after a drawdown until around the time of the U.S. Election, which points to buyers shying away. 

Furthermore, and crucially, two of the largest Russian insurance companies, Ingosstrakh Insurance Company and Alfastrakhovanie Group, have also been sanctioned. These have been the predominant providers of insurance for the Russian shadow fleet, which could also pose some difficulties for Russian exports unless the price falls below the G7 price cap.  

The US also blacklisted Chinese state-owned operator Shandong United Energy Pipeline Transportation for providing servives to Sovcomflot, which could be part of the reason why the Shandong Port Group has announced it will no longer accept OFAC listed tankers. Shandong United Energy Pipeline Transportation accounts for half the crude pipeline capacity from Yantai Port.

The sweeping sanctions, and equally the response from importing countries (India) and ports (China), suggests there will be growing difficulties for Iran and Russia to find shipping and buyers, and that there is downside risk to sanctioned flows going forward. How much will depend on how stringently these sanctions are enforced and how much Russia and Iran are willing to lower prices and accept higher freight costs. 

So far into the new year, the oil market appears to be much tighter than the IEA's significantly oversupplied expectation, with soaring flat prices, steepening backwardation, and higher refinery margins. Some of the strengthening oil price even before the sanctions news was due to lower than expected non-OPEC+ production recently, and better than expected (or, feared) demand, the latter partly due to a cold winter. 

There is probably downside risk to Russian exports also this year, after last year's 200 kbpd y/y decline. Similarly, Iranian exports have declined by about 300 kbpd in recent months from the 2024 average, and there is further downside risk if Shandong upholds the stance on OFAC listed tankers. 

To offset this, especially if oil prices strengthen further, there may be some pressure from the U.S. and China on Saudi Arabia and the OPEC+ to unwind cuts as planned, or before. Otherwise, there may be some risk to oil demand due to a fragile macroeconomic backdrop. 

The latter risk, along with strong expected non-OPEC+ supply and ample OPEC+ spare capacity, is also one reason why there may be a limit to how far the oil price can rise, likely not beyond last year's trade range of $70-90/bbl. However, while the risk before this was more likely to the low end of the range or even lower, that has now changed. 

An intriguing question is whether these new sanctions were coordinated with the incoming Trump administration. While it puts increased pressure on Putin to come to the negotiation table, it also gives Trump some difficult choices amid higher energy costs - contrary to his campaign trail promises. Drill-baby-drill might just not cut it, as production recently has been somewhat underwhelming amid low activity.

- Lower prices sufficiently to lure back buyers - below the G7 price cap in the case of Russia. 
- Replace the now OFAC-listed tankers in the shadow fleet. 
- Provide alternative insurance. 
- Shift more exports to products vs. crude - provided that there is sufficient refinery capacity, which there may not be considering power outages in Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. 
- Start negotiating with Trump. In the case of Russia there are reports that war expenditures are increasingly funded by corporate debt, which has soared, even at very high interest rates, which is unsustainable and adds further pressure on Putin's efforts.

- Essentially, divert purchases to other sources unless Iran and Russia find loopholes or compliant ways of supplying oil. High non-OPEC+ production growth this year should thus be welcome. 
- Draw on inventories (mainly China), although if energy security is a worry (see steepening backwardation) that is likely not a preferred option.  
- Literally call-on-OPEC 
- There may be some pressure on Chinese independent refiners to reduce runs on lower profitability amid more expensive alternative feedstock.

- Sit back and enjoy Biden's departing 'gift' which can be used as a negotiation card against Russia. 
- Drill baby drill, although that is likely insufficient to offset any major supply losses from Iran and Russia. 
- Incentivise Saudi Arabia and the rest of the OPEC+ to follow through on its planned production cut unwind from April, or before. 
- Be willing to turn a blind eye to sanction evasion, to make sure of ample supply and tolerable energy prices. 

A combination of the latter two may be the more likely in a scenario where oil prices continue to rise.

The year 2024 began with high anticipation, following the most profitable year of Very Large Gas Carrier (VLGC) earnings in history. However, this year presented a different picture, with freight rates and earnings hitting the lower end of the scale, especially in the last six months. Nevertheless, the year-to-date average ended at $50,500 per day, just below the 2022 total.

In response to the high earnings of the past two years, newbuilding activity for VLGCs continued throughout the year, with 47 orders placed, 12 more than the previous record year in 2023. This surge in demand from both established owners and newcomers led to a further increase in VLGC newbuilding prices, with the current price of an LPG dual-fuel, ammonia-capable vessel reaching approximately $120 million. Yard capacity remains tight in both Korea and China, with strong ordering activity from other segments, particularly LNG and tankers, driving prices up. Consequently, we expect newbuilding prices to remain elevated throughout the coming year.

Global seaborne LPG grew by 5.4 million tonnes in 2024, to 143.9 million tonnes, resulting in a 3.87% growth. Of these volumes, 101 million tonnes was lifted on VLGCs, giving a total market share of 71.2%. This growth is attributed to increasing exports from the United States, which rose by 5%. Of the U.S. exports, 32.8% went to China, which imported 33.7 million tonnes, up 5% from 2023. Chinese demand remains a key driver for the LPG trade, boosted by the continuous expansion of PDH plants in the country. 

The Middle East exported 39.7 million tonnes, just 1 million tonnes up, resulting in a 3.3% growth. The leading providers of volumes in the region were Qatar, the UAE, and Iran. Increased exports are expected from the region in 2025 and 2026 due to new natural gas plants in Qatar and Saudi Arabia. This increase in volumes will be beneficial in terms of the coming fleet growth.

**The quarterly TCE average concluded at $45,888 per day**, the second lowest quarterly result year-to-date. It is a 64% decrease from Q4 2023, and a 57% decline from Q4 2022. It is no secret that this years winter-season did not bring with it the usual periodical spikes in earnings. 

**BLPG1 - $35,675
BLPG2 - $58,264
BLPG3 - $43,723**

All throughout 2024 the market has been affected by an oversupply of ships. We believe this oversupply to be the lagged effect from the 39 newbuildings delivered in 2023 (in addition to the 21 delivered this year).

**U.S. Gulf/U.S. East Coast**
October: 95 in total/27 being spot fixtures
November: 101 in total/31 being spot fixtures
December: 103 in total, 29 being spot fixtures

**Middle East Gulf**
October: 74 in total/15 being spot fixtures
November: 73 in total/16 being spot fixtures
December: 70 in total/19 being spot fixtures

The monthly average number of liftings continue to grow, while the monthly average of spot liftings is decreasing.

Throughout the year, there was a deviating correlation between the arbitrage window from West to East and the BLPG-3 (Houston-Chiba) freight rate. In general, there was an increased buying interest for product, causing fewer spot fixtures out of the U.S. Gulf. This is further explained as a larger share of the fleet was controlled by traders rather than owners. This caused the market to see less spot shipping activity, further adding to fleet availability and contributing to lower freight rates. Additionally, maintenance and disruptions at export terminals in the U.S. had ripple effects on export availability.

The opening of transits in the Panama Canal also contributed to increasing fleet capacity, as voyages could be completed in a shorter period due to shorter sailing distances through Panama instead of around the Cape of Good Hope.

The sailing pattern of the VLGC fleet is a major variable in terms of fleet capacity and availability. In 2023, when the Panama Canal was highly congested with record-high auction costs and harsh transit restrictions, a majority of the fleet chose the longer route around the Cape of Good Hope instead of the canal. We also saw an increase in the utilization of the Suez Canal before it was deemed unsafe territory. As water levels in the Panama Canal resurged, restrictions were retracted, and we saw a continuous increase in VLGC transits again. A significant portion of ships sailing in ballast back to the West still choose the longer route instead of the canal. This is both due to the instability of transiting the canal, as well as the option for Middle Eastern and African cargoes. This unpredictable variation in waypoint transits creates uncertainty in terms of future fleet capacity.

The U.S. continues to increase its production and exports, with expectations of further growth. Terminal capacity has been a bottleneck, which we expect to resolve towards the end of 2025, with several terminals increasing their capacities through expansions. Some projects will be finalized in 2025, and others in 2026. The strong demand for U.S. LPG was further evident in the increased terminal fees, which spiked to their highest in September at 34 cents per gallon. On a yearly average, terminal fees were 81.5% higher in 2024 than in 2023.

In Q4 only 3 newbuildings were delivered, one each month. This brings the total newbuildings delivered in 2024 to 21, precisely as expected. The fleet now comprises of 400 vessels with an average age of just below 10 years. Approximately 50% of the existing fleet is now fitted with a dual-fuel engine, or a scrubber, which we see is something that becomes more and more important in terms of operation. 15% of the fleet is now older than 20 years, accumulating 59 vessels. In the last 10 years we have only seen 12 VLGCs being scrapped so the scrapping potential is big. With operational requirements as well as age restrictions becoming more transparent, if not scrapped, these vessels will likely enter into dedicated trades in the near future. This could ease the impact of the 70+ vessels coming in 26 & 27.

The orderbook-fleet ratio is now at 25% with 98 vessels on order. Out of the newbuilds, 59 are of type Panamaxes, so that they will be able to sail through the old Panama Locks, to mitigate with the congestion issues. 55 are of the type “VLACs”, Very Large Ammonia Carriers. We do believe in the development of large scale transportation of ammonia, likely on VLACs, however, this will not be until after 2030. In addition to more production being required, further investment in infrastructure for loading and discharging is needed. As per now, there are no ammonia terminals that can accommodate VLACs, due to their large size and intake. For these vessels to trade in ammonia, we also need to see more long-term demand. As these vessels will start delivering in 2026, they will likely enter the market as regular VLGCs, lifting LPG. We therefore do not differentiate them in the overview of the orderbook delivery.

The incremental ammonia volumes that will come online, will likely be captured by the MGCs, where the orderbook-fleet ratio is at 44%, and all vessels of this segment can lift ammonia. They are also the segment with the widest infrastructure network, as well as experience, in the commodity. 30% of all seaborne ammonia is also currently lifted by Handysize Gas Carriers, which will likely cover an additional part of future supplied volumes.

75 vessels are due for their five-year special survey in 2025, equivalent to deducting six vessels from the market. Additionally, only 12 newbuildings will be delivered. However, during 2026 and 2027, another 76 vessels will be delivered, which might disrupt the fleet balance further, causing an oversupply of tonnage.

“Water levels in the Panama Canal have returned to normal after expected rainfall, and all restrictions imposed in 2023 have been retracted. Daily transit capacity is back to full, at 36 transits per day. To mitigate continued congestion troubles, the canal imposed a Long Term Slot Allocation system (LoTSA), which entered into force on January 1, 2025. This system entails slot packages, pre-paid in an auction conducted in September and October 2024, where just below 200 slots were up for auction, spread across 2025. This will create smoother sailing for the purchasers of these slots; however, it will reduce availability for normal traffic in the canal, with almost half of the daily transits in the Neo-panamax locks being reserved.

Expected growth in production and export from both the U.S. and the Middle East will be crucial when looking beyond 2025, as the fleet will continue to expand.

*Please note that during Q4, we switched data source, causing some irregularities and changes in numbers related to trade flows etc.. The trends remain the same, however, this has changed some historical values.*

Spot charter rates have experienced a consistent decline throughout the year. The typical post-winter drop characterized the first quarter, while the second quarter remained flat at relatively low rates compared to previous years. The end of the second quarter into the beginning of the third quarter was initially seen as the first signs of the winter market, as LNG was drawn East by the opening of the inter-basin arbitrage, which, despite long availability lists, concentrated tonnage in the Pacific basin. However, this brief uptick, which rebalanced within a few weeks, remains the only indication of a 2024/2025 "winter market", despite relatively high cargo values and a cold start to the winter in Europe.

While this situation may appear surprising, especially given the long distances resulting from the avoidance of both the Suez and Panama canals, the fundamentals show a market with an ample supply of ships. The fleet has grown by approximately 60 newbuilds, with seven vessels sent for demolition. This growth, coupled with minimal growth in LNG volumes and no opportunities for floating cargoes, has led to an oversupply from previous years, now reflected in availability lists and rates. The willingness for disponent owners to sublet tonnage has provided charterers with numerous options, but resulted in further downward pressure on rates. The year has been marked by a lot of spot activity, with the number of spot fixtures increasing by more than 70% year-on-year, while the number of term fixtures has decreased.

On the volume side, ENI's Congo FLNG and New Fortress Energy's Fast LNG Altamira have each loaded six cargoes, some of which were partial. Although commissioning cargoes were expected from Corpus Christi Stage 3 and Plaquemines towards the end of the year, this has been postponed to early 2025. Despite limited volumes from new projects, there have been fewer outages, and production during the summer months has been higher than in 2023. However, it is evident that the increase in tonne-miles is primarily due to the distances rather than the volume of cargo.

Ordering activity this year has been robust, primarily driven by the final orders of vessels for the Qatar North Field Expansion Phase 2. However, speculative ordering has slowed due to the muted market and persistently high newbuild prices. The orderbook remains substantial, representing 46% of the trading fleet, with 321 vessels scheduled for delivery between 2025 and 2031. Shipyards are now largely booked until the end of 2027, with potential fleet growth possible from 2028 onwards. While seven vessels being sold for demolition is not substantial given the muted market, there was still a strong signal when four vessels aged 24 years were recently sold for demolition when LNGCs historically have been scrapped at 35-40 years.
Source: JKM from S&P Global Platts

Charter rates continued their descent through Q4, bringing the 2024 average spot charter rates to the lowest in our records for two-strokes, and the lowest since 2016 for TFDEs and steamers. The two-stroke yearly average was $55,000 per day, in stark contrast to $125,000 in 2023 and $155,000 in 2022. November, which is typically the peak of the spot market, saw two-stroke spot charter rates in the low $20,000s, a mere 12% of the levels in the same month in 2023. The spread between spot rates in the East and West has been close to zero in the last few weeks, but earlier in Q4, there was a slight premium in the East, as a closed arbitrage and high numbers of inter-Atlantic cargoes have kept vessels in the West.

One-year charter rates saw some slight improvements mid-year, as focus on covering winter demand increased. However, this did not last, and from the end of Q3, one-year rates have dropped significantly. This is due to the market being flooded with available ships, and broad expectation that this trend will continue well into 2025. Currently, a two-stroke can be secured for a year at less than $40,000 per day.

For longer-term charters (three years and up), there have been no rate increases throughout the year. With more project delays and the impact of newbuilds hitting the market at a fast pace, the longer-term outlook has been reflected in the rates. While sentiment matters, it is mainly the lower interest rates and slight reductions in newbuild prices that have driven the long-term ten-year rates down. Longer-term rates, which provide coverage into 2028, are still at a significant premium to shorter-term rates, which mainly provide coverage for a period expected to be oversupplied. Currently, we quote a three-year deal at $65,000, a five-year deal at $82,000, and a seven-year deal at $91,000 per day.

Availability has been higher than in previous years for the majority of 2024, with a good mix of ship technologies. While most of the two-stroke availability has been from subletters, who either went long during the unprecedented times in previous years or are still waiting for delayed term volumes, there is increasing availability of steamers from independent owners, which have redelivered from their long-term charters.

In Q4, fixing activity increased compared to Q3, resulting in more than 360 spot fixtures throughout the year, an increase of nearly 80% from last year's approximate 200 spot fixtures. Despite the significant rise in the number of spot fixtures, the number of spot fixed days only increased by 34%, indicating shorter spot periods (defined as anything under 90 days). While the timing for charterers to secure term tonnage has been favorable, interest has been limited. Consequently, the number of multi-month fixtures decreased by 17% year-on-year, and the number of 1-3 year deals declined by nearly 30%. However, Q4 did see some activity in 1-year deals, with six fixtures concluded. Notably, five out of these six were for two-strokes, and on average, 55% of 1-year deals for 2024 were for two-strokes.

The share of short-term fixtures involving sublets was 73% in Q4, slightly down from the Q1-Q3 average of 82%. Availability clearly remains predominantly with the subletters rather than independent owners. Most availability from independent owners has been in the form of small steamers, which have proven difficult to charter out.

A new record was reached for LNG loadings in Q4, with 107 MT LNG loaded. This is up nearly 2 MT from Q4 the year before, and is mainly driven by December where a record high 38 MT were loaded. It would be great news if this increase was due to commissioning of new projects, but it is rather driven by high production levels at existing plants. The total loaded volumes in 2024 ended at 414 MT, up 2 MT from the year before.

United States was the largest exporter in 2024, with 87 MT and more than 5 MT more than the runner-up, Australia.  Qatar exported slightly less than the year before, with a 0.7 MT reduction, while both Australia and and the United States reached record production levels. The top three importers remain the same; China, Japan and South Korea. China's imports reached 76 MT, which is significantly up from the previous two years, but still more than 3 MT less than the 2021 benchmark, which remains the record.  In terms of year-on-year increases in LNG imports, India is in second place after China, and both have close to 5 MT in year-on-year increases. At the other end of the scale, Spain and United Kingdom significantly decreased imports, with 5 MT and 7 MT reductions respectively. If looking at percentage increases, instead of absolute ones, Egypt has grown the most, by far, with 37% year on year increases. This is a result of lower domestic production and pipeline imports from the Middle East, turning the country to a net LNG importer during summer months (it is usually the case that Egypt stops exporting LNG during summer) and tendering for numerous cargoes and FSRUs. 

A cold start to the European winter resulted in high storage withdrawals, and an increase in European LNG imports. Storage levels ended the year at 73% full, 14% lower than the year before, and 5% lower than the 5-year average. The majority of US LNG has thus gone to Europe, with the yearly average at 51% of the cargoes, and the Q4 level at 54%. This is significantly up from Q3, which was the first quarter in some time in which more than 50% of US cargoes went East, and a sustained open inter-basin arbitrage was observed. While the Suez canal is not used by LNGCs, the destination of Middle Eastern cargoes remains interesting. Around 13% of Qatar cargoes went to Europe in 2024, down from 17% in 2023, countering some of the potential effect of the longer voyages via Cape of Good Hope. However, Q4  increased to 13%, from only 10% in Q3 when prices were higher in Asia. 

Despite the increase in inter-basin trade towards the end of the year, distances remain long due to the slim-to-no use of either of the canals. Due to the long distances, tonne-miles have been high throughout the entire year, at higher levels than the previous year for every month except November, when both production and distances dropped. With record high production levels in December, tonne-miles then reached new records, but despite this, fleet utilization is still lower than  has been seen in December in previous years. This is explained by the rapid fleet growth, which has increased the fleet capacity more than enough to absorb the tonne-mile growth. However, despite what the rates may show, the long distances have kept tonne-miles high enough that on average, the fleet utilization in 2024 was marginally higher than previous years. It is therefore clear that the oversupply from previous years, which was not really reflected in the charter rates due to cargo values and the focus on energy security, has now made an impact on the market - it is this overhanging oversupply in addition to the 2024 fleet additions that has driven rates down. 

Average speeds have actually been slightly higher than in 2023, which compensates for the higher tonne-miles. However, speeds are still well below what they were in for example 2021, and once again an indication of shipping oversupply, where plenty more shipping capacity could be available by speeding up.

The fleet experienced a record growth of 63 ships in 2024. The delivery ramp-up throughout the year was significant, with 10 deliveries in Q1 increasing to 22 in Q4. With seven vessels sold for demolition and one heading to layup, the "trading" LNGC fleet now stands at 687. We use the term "trading" because we observe 10-15 old steamers idling, many of which are likely to head to layup or a scrap yard next.

In 2024, 84 orders were placed, an increase of four from the previous year. More than 60% of these orders were for the Qatar North Field Expansion, and only four speculative orders were placed due to high prices and a muted market.

Two-strokes now constitute 39% of the fleet, while steamers make up 31%. More than half of the fleet is younger than 9 years old, making the fleet relatively young on average, despite the presence of 21 vessels older than 30 years and 105 vessels older than 20 years.

The first "new" Chinese yard delivered its first LNGC, with Al Shelila delivered to ADNOC from Jiangnan in November. This marks the yard's first large-scale LNGC, with seven more in the orderbook. Dalian is also scheduled to deliver its first large-scale LNGCs in the second half of 2025. Hudong-Zhonghua is the only yard that has taken orders for delivery in 2030 and beyond, currently having 33 vessels on order for the Qatar North Field Expansion (three already delivered), with deliveries extending well into 2031.

In the coming year, the newbuild deliveries scheduled amount to 93 vessels, although nine of these are for Arctic LNG-2, where several were pushed to 2025 as deliveries in 2024 did not occur. It is highly unlikely that these vessels will hit the market in 2025 either, so 84 newbuild deliveries may be a more realistic expectation. Twenty-six vessels in the orderbook are available/charter-free, with deliveries in 2025 (two), 2026 (12), and 2027 (12).
