The outlook for 2025 does not appear promising for disponent owners with excess length and independent owners with redelivering tonnage. While volume growth is expected from several projects in North America, as well as some volumes from Senegal and Australia, the majority of these volumes are expected towards the end of the year. Consequently, the 80-90 LNGC deliveries scheduled for next year will exacerbate the current oversupply until volume growth provides relief. Therefore, the fleet should be more than capable of handling inter-basin trade, floating cargoes, and closed canals, leading to another year of low charter rates.

If current project schedules hold, the market should see some tightening towards the end of the year, but it is important to note that "some tightening" is far from tight. The orderbook is substantial enough to accommodate both distance and volume growth well into 2027. However, by 2028, more newbuilds will be needed due to significant growth in US volumes, increasing US to Asia trade, and fleet replacement resulting from increased scrapping activity over the coming years. 

One might have expected the muted 2024 market to have led to more vessels being laid up and scrapped. Although not officially in layup, we note that around 15 LNGCs have exhibited slow speeds and limited draft developments over the past months. With further redeliveries expected in 2025 and a continued low charter market, we anticipate this trend to become more pronounced. While conservative owners may initially opt for layup, we believe the oldest steamers, nearing their 25-year drydock and smaller than 140k cbm, have limited life left as trading LNGCs. This will be an intriguing topic to follow throughout the year!
Source: Supply/demand forecasts from S&P Global Platts

Last year ended on a weak note which usually means January ends up being even weaker. So far that seems to be the case. 
However, there are several pointers toward a rebound starting around the middle of February. 
There is currently a record number of VLOCs sailing toward Brazil, which is a good indication that a Capesize rally will materialize. The previous four times the count was similar to now were in late August last year, early September 2023, and late August 2022. However, most of the vessels are still positioned in the Pacific or Indian Ocean, so it will take time before the vessels have loaded and freed up space for Capes. 
Further, the iron ore price leads shown below indicate a firming market from late Feb and through March.

The market has started the year on a very weak note in the Pacific. The P3A index was lower than now only during the first half of 2020, since the index's inception in 2018. We do not see any imminent signs of improvement there, as the tonnage list keeps creeping up, and as China will be slow until after their New Year celebrations. 
As a result of the weakness in the Pacific, and the upcoming Brazilian Soybean export season, the count of vessels sailing toward Brazil is increasing rapidly. This is the start of what will likely be a spot market upturn in February.

When reflecting on the year 2024 from an LNG Sale and Purchase (SNP) perspective, key aspects such as transaction volumes, fluctuations in asset values, challenges with KYC compliance, and the implementation of trading restrictions have shaped the landscape. Despite these complexities, we remain among the fortunate, navigating an industry that continues to adapt and thrive amidst shifting global dynamics.

2024 was a year of stark contrasts—a whirlwind of geopolitical tensions, devastating humanitarian crises, and glimmers of hope for a brighter future.

The ongoing conflict in Ukraine continued to cast a long shadow, with profound humanitarian consequences and destabilizing effects on the global stage. As we look to 2025, there is hope that world leaders will find pathways to de-escalation and peace.

In the Middle East, the shocking outbreak of violence underscored the fragility of peace, leaving a trail of destruction and loss while raising fears of a broader regional escalation.

Meanwhile, extreme weather events intensified by climate change wreaked havoc across the globe. Floods in India, wildfires in Canada, and droughts in Africa served as stark reminders of the urgent need for collective climate action. Each of us has a role to play in mitigating these impacts and driving positive change.

Deepening political and social divides within and between nations fueled unrest and hindered collaboration on critical global challenges, further emphasizing the need for unity in addressing shared issues.

Yet, amid these challenges, there were sparks of hope and progress:

Progress on climate action was achieved despite the difficulties. The COP28 summit in Azerbaijan saw renewed commitments to reduce emissions and invest in renewable energy and technology. The pressing question remains whether world leaders and industries will honor these commitments—and how these actions will shape the global landscape, including sectors like shipping, in the years to come.

Technological breakthroughs in artificial intelligence, medicine, and space exploration offered a glimpse of a brighter future, laying the groundwork for even greater advances in 2025.

In the face of adversity, communities around the globe displayed extraordinary resilience and solidarity. From ordinary citizens to local leaders, people stepped forward to help those in need, serving as a powerful reminder of our shared humanity.

As 2024 comes to a close, the world stands at a crossroads. The challenges ahead are significant, but so too is the potential for transformative change. Addressing global issues requires:

- Strengthened international cooperation and a renewed commitment to multilateralism.
- Prioritizing conflict prevention and resolution while addressing the root causes of violence.
- Accelerating climate action to secure a sustainable future.
- Upholding fundamental human rights and fostering a more just and equitable world.

While 2024 was marked by turbulence and uncertainty, it also highlighted the enduring power of hope, resilience, and the human spirit. As we navigate the complexities of the 21st century, let us strive together to build a more peaceful, sustainable, and just world for all.

From all of us in Fearnley LNG we thank you for the support in 2024 and look forward to continuing our good working relationship in 2025. We wish you all a Happy New Year in the coming days, and let's make 2025 a year to remember.
No significant changes in the New building sector since our last report. The only real question at this point in time is if someone will take a punt and secure some of the final 2027 slots or not.

Since our last update, the U.S. presidential election has concluded, ushering in a new leader expected to implement a series of policies and initiatives in the White House. These forthcoming changes are anticipated to significantly impact financial markets after the January inauguration.

Meanwhile, Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell has highlighted the difficulty of predicting future developments at this early stage. He noted, "There’s nothing to model right now — it’s such an early stage," further stating, "We don’t guess, we don’t speculate, and we don’t assume." This cautious stance reflects the prevailing uncertainty regarding the economic and market outlook.
So on that note, all we can do is have a wait-and-see attitude for a little longer.

The year comes to a close at unseasonably low levels, although has on average been in line with our expectations. While sentiment is currently dire, next year looks much more promising for crude tankers, especially VLCCs. The outlook for product tankers is subdued which should realign earnings between the tanker segments. We adjust our forecasts for 2025-26 correspondingly. 

In a base case scenario for next year, we expect strong crude tanker tonne-mile growth (up toward 5%) on strong Atlantic crude oil production growth. Gross fleet growth of just 1.6%, may give zero net fleet growth. Due to a likely softer start to the year than previously expected, given current weakness, we lower our forecast for the full year slightly. Still, much stronger volume growth than last year, plus potential Iran sanctions in the mix means the outlook remains very strong. 

Product tanker tonne-miles are in a base case 'only' expected to grow by 1-2% on normalised refinery margins and slower throughput growth. The latter should also be located closer to end-user demand growth. Meanwhile, the product tanker delivery schedule gives 5.7% gross fleet growth - or closer to 3% effective fleet growth. We lower our forecasts as risks stack more to the down- than upside. 

Various scenarios could tilt earnings development, thus we outline a base, bear and bull case for next year. Due to increasing fleet growth the following year we expect a slightly softer rate trajectory.

Base case: strong production growth from Non-OPEC+ and some from OPEC+ producers should boost tonne-mile demand meaningfully vs. this year's sluggish growth, although there may be slight downside risk to the IEA's current non-OPEC+ expectations. More stimulus in China may pave the way for a demand recovery - and an oversupplied oil market should lead to inventory builds there too, to fill increasing storage capacity. Oversupply and contango may also tilt market balances toward the favour of bigger vessels and mean normalising rate relations between the segments. 

Bull case: Non-OPEC+ producers may live up to strong growth expectations and a harder clamp-down on Iran by the Trump administration may give more volumes to the normal market, potentially boosted further through the OPEC+ reversing some cuts to offset any Iranian supply losses - especially if (Chinese) oil demand surpasses current estimates. 

Bear case: Non-OPEC+ production growth may come in well below expectations along with further OPEC+ cuts if demand also surprises to the downside. This could leave less volume upside, and may continue to constrain West-East movement. 

For 2026 we also lower our forecasts due to higher fleet growth for most segments, and potentially lower volume growth. There are scenarios to be made for both up- and downside, in line with the 2025 scenarios.

content.title: Crude tanker tonne-miles vs. crude oil production growth
Oil supply and demand by basin

content.content: Softer market development than expected recently

Crude tanker volumes rose month over month in November, but was still slightly below the same time last year. Products caught back up after slumping in October due to refinery maintenance. In December to date volumes have continued to rise in both markets due to some outages and maintenance ending and some production increases. 

Volumes overall have been flattish YTD vs. the same period last year, also if Iranian volumes are excluded. There has, however, been a meaningful decline in Atlantic-East volumes in the second vs. first half of the year, due to an insufficient arbitrage - partly caused by the Red Sea 'closure'. The latter has also caused less migration of tonnage West-East and left the Atlantic basin artificially oversupplied. 

A bigger volume boost can be expected into the first quarter of next year. Q1 volumes for crude tankers have been higher than the historical norm during the last two years, as Atlantic producers are bigger seaborne export drivers than in the past. Due to seasonally lower demand in the region through the first few months of the year, a relatively greater portion of crude oil production can be exported. Next year, production hikes may come on top of that, although more of the increased production is expected toward the summer.

Seasonality may at the moment be working against long-haul crude oil shipments, with oil restrictive pricing in recent months. Higher natural gas prices in Europe due to shorter supplies and more rapid inventory draws than in previous years, and reliance on intermittent renewable energy, have also led to strengthening demand (as observed through rising gasoil crack spreads), all else equal contributing to narrower West-East arbitrages. On the other hand, less crude especially going USG-East has left more going Transatlantic, which has boosted Suez- and Aframax rates. 

Given the expectations of an oversupplied oil market into the first half of next year, however, we expect this dynamic to change. We should get an oil price forward curve contango which incentivises longer-haul shipping. There has at times even been some market chatter about potential for floating storage, which on paper could be supported if IEA balances are correct - showing 1.2 mbpd oversupply in Q2, although that is not the most realistic scenario. 

The tanker demand outlook for 2025 is in any case very promising, starting with a catch-up trade in Q1 with western refineries slowing purchases ahead of spring maintenance, and continuing into late spring and early summer when new (offshore) production projects come onstream in the Americas and North Sea.

Our November global VLCC cargo count was about 240, which is ten more than the average of June-Oct (when TD3c averaged WS 52), and closer to the Mar-May average (when TD3c averaged WS 67). The Nov’23 count was 250, but then rates were also about $25k/d higher than this year. Hence, there is 'something missing' here - partly explained by charterer's well proven 'below radar' tactics and partly by an overhang of vessels from the weaker months earlier. The Atlantic cargo count is also lagging. Weaker Chinese demand should not have affected overall cargo counts, but should not be overlooked as part of the impact on market psychology. 

December fixture counts indicate another volume slowdown for VLCCs, to the benefit of smaller vessels, but a volume ramp-up into January both through higher exports and more Chinese buying of non-sanctioned barrels should lift sentiment and rates going forward.

content.title: Monthly VLCC cargo count by load area

content.content: Oil market balances pointing toward more (crude) tanker demand

The oil market has YTD been fairly balanced, where weaker demand growth has been met with lower than initially expected supply growth. The OPEC+ has on average produced 900 kbpd less than last year, which offsets much of the 1.5 mbpd non-OPEC+ growth. On an exit to exit basis, global oil supply is flat now vs. Q4'23 - and for the 'normal market' even lower as Iran's supply growth has been 2-300 kbpd.  

Next year, the IEA expects a significantly oversupplied oil market, with a near 1 mbpd surplus despite demand growth increasing from 0.9 mbpd this year to 1.1 mbpd next year. Non-OPEC+ is expected to lift production by another 1.5 mbpd, but a big difference from last year is that some catch-up by lagging OPEC+ producers may lead the group's output up by 0.5 mbpd y/y. Hence, Q4'25 production is expected to be more than 2 mbpd higher than now. 

The double whammy of higher overall production and oversupply/contango should lend much greater support to tanker demand than this year, although the IEA's non-OPEC+ supply growth predictions may be a bit optimistic (and includes quite a bit of U.S. NGL). 

Going into 2026 supply growth expectations are somewhat lower than for next year, unless demand growth picks up sufficiently so that the OPEC+ can materially unwind cuts.

Refinery runs have risen more than  500 kbpd less than expected this year, as margins have normalised. Next year, capacity additions are likely to be lower than the last two years, and the IEA expects 'only' about 600 kbpd of run growth. Much of the expected run growth is also nearer end-user demand growth, which potentially means shorter average sailing distances, capping tonne-mile growth further. Unless there is a sharp increase in refinery margins, the demand side looks less supportive for product tankers next year than over the last two years.

content.title: Atlantic MR rates vs. NWE diesel crack spread

content.content:
China apparent oil demand in September and October was about 500 kbpd higher vs. the low this summer. With that, apparent demand for the full year is flat vs. the same period last year. Interestingly, diesel demand rebounded – some 400 kbpd higher than in July/August – remember when all those stories about heavy trucks switching to LNG came out? Industrial PMIs are back into expansionary territory, which is a better explanation for the diesel demand recovery - and the slump during the summer (although lower LNG prices back then probably had some impact too). Similarly, all those stories about gasoline demand having peaked because of EVs? Gasoline demand YTD is still 3.5% higher than the same period last year as the total car fleet keeps growing rapidly and PHEVs have a significant (and growing) share of the NEV market. 

Both refinery runs and crude oil imports slid, and were about 1 mbpd lower than the same time last year. However, both have risen again in November (crude oil imports back to y/y growth) and there are indications of further upside in December. Refinery margins have increased by about 20% in November vs. October, and strengthen further into December. Continued and possibly increased stimulus should help boost demand, although the full effect might take a few quarters to develop. 

Reduced tax rebates on product exports from December may negatively impact runs and imports going forward – but should at the same time improve refining economics for other countries in the region to offset any negative impact from China (margins elsewhere in Asia have also risen lately). That could mean a slightly different VLCC market dynamic, where more cargoes are freed up to non-Chinese charterers - assuming that demand in the rest of Asia remains stagnant,  or increases - the IEA predicts Asian (ex. China) demand growth of about 400 kbpd next year.

content.title: China apparent main oil products demand

content.content:
There are two things which may meaningfully move the needle for the Chinese impact on the tanker market next year: whether it will continue to import as much from Iran and whether it will draw or build inventories. 

There have been plenty of reports about independent refineries starting to diversify crude sourcing away from Iran recently. The most recent cited prices for Iranian crude are much less discounted vs. non-sanctioned crude (only $2-3/bbl) than has been the case in the past - which begs the question, is it worth the risk with a more hawkish incoming U.S. government? Chinese buyers are now more actively purchased spot cargoes in West Africa and the Middle East recently, which could be a sign of a shift - as is increasing floating storage of Iranian oil. 

This year, China 'only' built 33 mb of storage capacity, and with lower crude oil imports inventories have developed fairly sideways (or drawn slightly when including diesel and gasoline inventories which have drawn quite a bit). Next year, planned inventory capacity expansion is 125 mb, nearly as much as the last three years combined. That, an expected contango in forward curves and possibly lower oil prices given the large oil supply increase next year should incentivise bigger inventory builds next year - which could be a good kicker on the upside for crude demand.
Increasing, but still relatively low fleet growth outlook

Deliveries are set to pick up from the second half of next year, from historical lows which are scheduled to hold for another six months. The pick-up is 'worse' for product tankers, starting the second half of 2025 vs. crude which really only picks up from 2H'26. 

The 1.6% scheduled crude tanker deliveries next year will likely be (more than) absorbed by inefficiencies amid new regulations which essentially means (another) year with net negative real carrying capacity. For products the scheduled 5.7% is so high that real carrying capacity should still expand by around 3%, which is not dramatic in a historical context, but may still exceed demand growth for which expectations are relatively low. 

The orderbook to fleet has reached 12.8% as of the beginning of December. Although this is nearly 3x vs. the low early last year, it remains low vs. the historical average of 20%. For further context, by the end of this year 12.1% of the fleet will be at or above the historical average scrap age. Much of this is already semi-phased out in lower utilisation in the shadow fleet. Still, another 3.5% of the fleet turns the same age next year and 2.5% the year after. This likely means continued low fleet growth also in coming years - and that further newbuild orders may be needed towar the end of the decade. For now it seems the order influx has nearly come to a halt, with much fewer orders in recent months and less interest among owners - partly also because yards are sold out well into 2028.

content.title: 20+ years old share of the fleet

content.content: Where can we be wrong? The known unknowns

Beyond non-OPEC+ production growth, there are two obvious factors which pose the biggest risks to the outlook: the macroeconomic development and what the new U.S. administration will do vs. Iran. 

The macroeconomic risk is by nature difficult to predict, but it is worth highlighting that global debt to GDP figures are historically high, and there are some pointers to resurgent inflation in certain areas. 

The incoming Trump administration is expected to be much more hawkish on Iran, which all else equal should limit Iran's ability to evade sanctions and could hamper crude oil exports. These have increased by about 200 kbpd this year and 300 kbpd last year. This has covered much of China's crude oil import growth, and left a drag on the 'normal' tanker market. Already, Iranian officials who have previously expressed a desire to increase production further have rather started talking about 'maintaining' current levels. 

Furthermore, Chinese independent refiners who have previously bought Iranian crude have shifted interest toward other sources in the Middle East and West Africa. This is partly because the U.S. OFAC has in recent months blacklisted more shadow vessels, some Chinese banks are cautious about financing, ports do not want to accommodate shadow vessels, and the discount for Iranian crude is much narrower than it has been in the past. Following this we also see some more shadow vessels being idle, and floating storage of Iranian crude is on the rise after being drawn in recent months ahead of Trump's inauguration. 

It is therefore likely that Iranian exports will decline slightly next year due to increasing U.S. pressure, but the downside may be limited vs. the last time Trump was in office as trade mechanisms have become more established, largely avoiding the U.S. Dollar. That said, the VLCCs that have been added to the OFAC list see about half the utilisation of the rest of the shadow fleet, which again sees half the utilisation of the normal market - which does suggest that sanctions have some impact. Some shadow vessels have been circulated for scrapping too, but not found any takers for fear of seconddary sanctions. 

If President Trump can use Iranian oil as a bargaining chip in trade discussions with China, there could be further downside risk for Iranaian volumes - which may need to be offset by other OPEC+ producers. The latter may be one of the reasons why the group keeps kicking the can re. the cut reversals which there really is no room for given current oil market ecpectations.

content.title: Shadow fleet share of overall fleet

content.content:
Russia's impact on the market may be another one to watch, in context of Trump's promise to end the Ukraine conflict. We believe there is a rather long way to finding a solution, but recent developments in the Middle East with a weakening Axis of Resistance could be a slight step forward. Still, Russia's support for tanker tonne-miles has declined this year, with falling exports (down 200 kbpd y/y) and a bigger share going on the shadow fleet (the proper one - Iran/Venezuela linked). Russian origin tonne-miles now make up slightly more than 9% of global tonne-miles, which is down from nearly 11% at the peak last year, but still well above the 4-5% it used to be. There is a reported 10-year 500 kbpd supply agreement between Reliance and Rosneft (about one third of India's import from Russia) - which suggests at least part of the trade flow shifts will be sticky in any case. 

Further sanctions from the EU recently on the fleet carrying Russian oil in breach of the G7 price cap could also have some impact going forward, especially as some of the older ones in this fleet might find it hard to come back into the normal market under normal circumstances. 

Hence, downside risk from a potential solution to the Russia/Ukraine conflict is more limited than it has been. For the biggest crude tankers it could even help contribute to supporting the West-East arbitrage.

content.title: Shadow fleet share of Russia's crude oil exports

content.content:
The Red Sea is another risk if the Houthis becomes the last piece of the Axis of Resistance to fold. Given the increased income from 'safe passage payments' and domestic support the Houthis have gained from this campaign it is likely that they will resist pressure to give up anytime soon, however. 

Crude volumes through the Red Sea have declined by 1.7 mbpd this year, while COGH passage has only increased by 0.7 mbpd. With that, tonne-miles have declined by about 1%, but the impact on the crude tanker market has likely been more negative, with less migration West-East leaving a surplus of ships in the Atlantic. 

Product volumes have declined by 2.7 mbpd, while COGH diversion has increased by 2 mbpd which gives a tonne-mile increase of close to 5%. Thus, this segment carries the biggest negative risk from any changes.

content.content:
Total shipment volume growth has fallen from 4.6% in June to 4.0% at the end of November, which is still higher than the supply growth of 3.0%. Despite fundamentals being positive by this measure, markets have fallen as growth in West of Suez shipments has dropped from 6% in July to 2.5% in November, and there is no congestion in loading or discharge ports. Further, vessel sailing speeds remain low but have trended upward since the beginning of August. 

Our market viewpoints always start by analyzing shipment volume growth against supply growth, as the other factors are more uncertain. Since Q4 last year, our view has been that shipment volume growth would drop below supply growth during the first half of 2025, so downside risk would escalate during the second half of 2025. We still seem on track for that development, which is a little worrying considering where earnings are now. On the other hand, as shipment volume growth remains positive it could mean that markets will rebound strongly after the Chinese New Year next year if sailing distances, congestion, and sailing speeds go in owners favor. 

Nonetheless, the outlook remains bearish, and we do not think that will change before Q4 2025 at the earliest, and Q2 2026 at the latest.

Basis the correlation between earnings and asset values since 2010, we believe the following adjustments have to be made in order to bring the relationship back to normal. 

Handysize: 1-year time charter rates either have to rise above 15.000 USD pd, or the 10-year-old value has to fall to around 17 million USD. 
Supramax: 1-year time charter rates either have to rise to the high-teens USD pd, or the 10-year-old value has to fall to around 20 million USD.

content.content:
In our previous monthly update from early November, we went through our viewpoints on China's stimulus measures. 

Quote:

*China’s currency trades under a so-called ‘managed float’, which means the central bank is heavily involved in trying to keep it trading around a desired level. This process sometimes obviously involves buying Yuan against the USD, and vice versa. The USDCNY is therefore an important part of the domestic liquidity situation. Recent stimulus measures in China will naturally involve expanding the domestic money supply to fund infrastructure projects as well as trying to revive the property sector. That, along with weaker domestic economic growth rates means there should be heavy downward pressure on the Yuan.

To counteract this downward pressure, the central bank has to buy increasing amounts of Yuan to keep the currency stable, with the flipside of this being that it nullifies other liquidity-increasing factors. That is why there is a very high correlation between the 9-month lead of the year-on-year change of the USDCNY and China’s year-on-year growth of dry bulk imports. The chart displaying this relationship is shown in the middle left below. Over the last year, the Yuan has strengthened relative to the USD, which strongly suggests China’s dry bulk import growth will continue to fall over the coming 9 months.

In our view, China’s government has to allow the Yuan to weaken considerably going forward for the stimulus measures to succeed. The other thing to watch in this regard is obviously the actual financing growth domestically. Reserve requirement and interest rate cuts have not led to higher financing growth this year, which in our view goes back to the still too-strong currency. Seasonally, monthly financing is always the highest during Q1, especially in January. It will therefore be very interesting to see how high (or low) those numbers are at the beginning of next year.*

Unquote

One month later, China's credit growth rate has dropped further, and the USDCNY is not suggesting that import growth will pick up within the next 9 months. 
Steel industry experts in China remain skeptical of the outlook for demand in 2025. A recent report from Platts outlined the situation well, which reads that the issuance of local government special bonds is up 81% on the same period last year. However, despite this massive increase in bond issuance, infrastructure investment increased by just 4.3% through January-October vs the same period in 2023. The reason for the low growth is that most of the bonds have been used to pay down or swap local government debt, rather than funding new projects. The consensus for next year is that flat steel products demand will be relatively good as infrastructure related to clean energy will continue to expand, whereas long steel products will remain under pressure primarily due to prevailing weakness in the property sector. 

In the World ex-China, manufacturing is not showing much strength. JP Morgans's latest Manufacturing PMI report had the global reading at 50, stabilizing after four months of contraction. More than half of the World's countries included in the report had a reading below 50, with the Eurozone in particular being weak. 

The below charts paint a bearish picture going forward. 

The top left chart shows the total dry bulk imports of Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and Europe, which have remained at average monthly import volumes of 65 million tons since the start of 2023, compared to 75 million tons in 2021 and 2022. No upturn has materialized this year despite the global economy being on an upswing, which is highly unusual. 

The top right chart shows an index we make tracking China's economic growth. The index is composed of property market data, fixed asset investments, power generation, and freight volumes handled in ports. This index is highly correlated to the year-on-year growth of total dry bulk demand growth. This year, the index has been negative whereas dry bulk demand growth has grown by about 4%. The last time there was such a mismatch between these two data series was in 2014. 

The middle left chart shows China's bulk commodity import growth vs the year-on-year change of the USDCNY. We explained this dynamic in our previous monthly report. The USDCNY year-on-year lead suggests China's import growth will continue to fall over the next 9 months. 

The middle right chart displays the year-on-year change of the Baltic Dry Index against the 18-month change of coal, gas, and oil prices (so comparing December 2024 prices to June 2023 prices). When energy prices have cheapened compared to the previous 18 months, it usually boosts economic growth and in turn leads to a positive year-on-year change in the Baltic Dry Index. The converse is also true. The 18-month change in energy prices usually leads by about 18 months, and the suggestion going forward is that the economic cycle will peak in the middle of 2025. 

The bottom left chart shows China's dry bulk import growth against OECDs index of cyclical changes in economic growth for the G-20 countries in aggregate. China's bulk commodity import growth is shifted 1 year forward in order to display that it leads the economic cycle. This year's falling import growth suggests the economic cycle could weaken through next year. 

The bottom right chart shows China's daily imported iron ore consumption. Average consumption has been 2.81 million tons per day in 2024, against 2.91 million tons per day in 2023. This is a drop of 3.2% year-on-year. 

All the above considered, it is very hard to be anything else than bearish for market prospects in 2025.

content.content:
The significant changes to charter rates seem to have given tailwinds to the sale of vessels. Several vessels have changed hands and we see an increasing number of owners evaluating the options before them. Is layup in anticipation of a market recovery the right choice or should they say "goodbye" to their hard-working ladies and hand them over to the undertaker (aka recycling buyers)?

We would argue that laying up a vessel in today's LNGC market presents more complex challenges compared to previous downturns. Factors such as increasing cargo sizes, heightened scrutiny on emissions, and the declining tradeability of smaller, less efficient, and older vessels are all significant obstacles for owners to navigate.

Not only do Owners have to think about the costs associated with entering layup, but also the cost and time of reactivation when (not if) the winds of fortune change. The ability to make it to the market in time if the vessel has to go to drydock to obtain updated class status and ability to trade - and will charterers be willing to accept vessels not having sailed for an extended period.
These considerations, combined with asset prices coming under scrutiny, will pose for interesting discussions in the months to come. 

However, despite the challenges facing Owners with aging tonnage, there is an appetite to buy vessels and we expect to see more vessels change hands before the end of the year.

Shipyards are seeing few to no inquiries in the LNGC space at the moment, spending time and resources on developing and improving designs. There are still a few slots left in 2027, where yards are willing to negotiate. For mid-2028 and onwards they keep their current price ask.

As interest rates have become an increasingly larger element in Owner's calculations - coming from a world of free money - it is interesting to look at what the market is saying about the future. The 10-year/2-year spread (aka yield curve spread) is currently hovering around 0, suggesting a flattish interest rate environment in the range of 4.2%. This is slightly below the current SOFR which stands at appx 4.5%; hence expectations of a continued softening.
The inverted yield curve is no longer to be seen - and hopefully, the policy makers are able to avoid any recessions (which historically have been predicted well by the yield curve).

content.content:
Since our last report in late September, we have not changed our outlook for the Capesize/Newcastlemax segment. We expect next year’s BCI5TC average to be somewhere in the mid-teens. 

We have pointed to lower iron ore consumption in China and high iron ore port inventories in China as risk factors, and the last few months' developments in demand growth show that these factors have started to weigh on the market. Ton-time growth is markedly down, as shown in the Trade Flows section of this report. 
We expect 2026 to be higher, and to what degree will depend on the eventual success of China’s stimulus measures. The next 6 to 9 months’ development in lending growth, the USDCNY currency pair, and inventory changes of iron ore and steel will be the key factors to watch in this regard. 

Regarding the outlook for the Kamsarmax, Ultramax, and Handysize segments, we still see macroeconomic risks building, and expect this to weigh on the markets until perhaps the middle of 2026. That said, the weakness in the Kamsarmax segment in particular came earlier than what we had thought a few months ago. A much weaker autumn grain season in the Atlantic has been the primary factor behind the market drop, along with the prevailing supply issues in seaborne coal markets. 

Like in the Capesize segment, there has been a significant drop in ton-time growth for the Kamsarmax, Ultramax, and Handysize segments. That, along with the mentioned macroeconomic risks and high deliveries in the Ultramax and Handysize segments leads us to think these markets could average in the low teens next year rather than the mid-teens, as we previously expected. Fundamentals could start improving again in 2026, led by stimulus efforts in China, and probably supported by global rate cuts, along with lower supply growth than 2025. 

So, in terms of our “bearish timeline” we don’t change the viewpoint, but it could be that 2025 will be lower on average than 2026. 
Regarding asset values, there is a wide gap down to earnings, so we expect corrections across the board going forward. Given our fundamental outlook, we see asset values bottoming between Q4 2025 and Q2 2026.

content.content:
China’s currency trades under a so-called ‘managed float’, which means the central bank is heavily involved in trying to keep it trading around a desired level. This process sometimes obviously involves buying Yuan against the USD, and vice versa. The USDCNY is therefore an important part of the domestic liquidity situation. Recent stimulus measures in China will naturally involve expanding the domestic money supply to fund infrastructure projects as well as trying to revive the property sector. That, along with weaker domestic economic growth rates means there should be heavy downward pressure on the Yuan. 

To counteract this downward pressure, the central bank has to buy increasing amounts of Yuan to keep the currency stable, with the flipside of this being that it nullifies other liquidity-increasing factors. That is why there is a very high correlation between the 9-month lead of the year-on-year change of the USDCNY and China’s year-on-year growth of dry bulk imports. The chart displaying this relationship is shown in the middle left below. Over the last year, the Yuan has strengthened relative to the USD, which strongly suggests China’s dry bulk import growth will continue to fall over the coming 9 months. 

In our view, China’s government has to allow the Yuan to weaken considerably going forward for the stimulus measures to succeed. The other thing to watch in this regard is obviously the actual financing growth domestically. Reserve requirement and interest rate cuts have not led to higher financing growth this year, which in our view goes back to the still too-strong currency. Seasonally, monthly financing is always the highest during Q1, especially in January. It will therefore be very interesting to see how high (or low) those numbers are at the beginning of next year. 

Before we see a combination of a weaker currency and increasing domestic financing growth, we cannot definitely say that China’s stimulus measures will work. In any case, there is always a lag before better financing conditions impact dry bulk markets, so there is not enough time in our view to fix fundamentals for 2025 already. Imported iron ore consumption is lower by about 4% year on year, so to start with, that must make up lost ground just to bring it back to the same levels as in 2023. Further, iron ore port inventories are at similar heights to late 2021/early 2022 and early 2018. We think stocks will be drawn closer to historical averages going forward like it was following those periods. Negative iron ore import growth to China next year therefore looks highly likely, in our view. 

China’s bulk commodity import growth in turn is an important driver of the global macroeconomic cycle. This is displayed on the bottom left chart, which plots OECDs economic indicator for the G-20 countries in aggregate vs the 1-year lead of China’s bulk commodity imports. China’s weakening import growth is strongly suggesting the macroeconomic cycle is close to a peak and about to head downwards. This will, in turn, impact World ex-China dry bulk demand, and is a major reason for our bearish outlook for the markets next year. In terms of manufacturing, the global picture is already quite weak, with countries/regions with PMI readings below 50 outnumbering those with a reading above 50. Many analysts had expected a bit more strength from the Eurozone, US,  Japan, and Korea this year than what has been the case, but it seems like the overhang from the massive manufacturing boom in 2021/22 is too heavy for a recovery to materialize. Recently, several emerging markets' manufacturing activity has also weakened, probably as a result of the slowdown in China along with the lack of upturn in developed economies. In our view, global interest rates need to be cut significantly for a manufacturing recovery to happen. It seems like that process has started, but there is still a way to go, and these things take time before it impact the real economy. 

With this backdrop, it is hard to see where a recovery in dry bulk demand growth shall come from the next year. China’s iron ore demand looks weak, developed economies' manufacturing is unlikely to recover, and emerging markets' growth is likely to be lower than this year because of that. Coal supply issues are likely to prevail, with Indonesia still the only major exporter that seems capable of adding significant volumes. Minor bulk growth will of course be impacted by a weaker macroeconomic backdrop, which leaves grains as the only potential bright spot next year. That could cause some spot market spikes for the Kamsarmax, Ultramax, and Handysize segments, but any eventual strength there is not enough to counter-act weakness in the other commodity groups.

content.content:
So, what is missing? Although it is 'only' the end of October, the anticipated winter market has so far underwhelmed, somewhat in line with softer oil demand growth. Still, it is not entirely clear why, as tanker demand has increased more than rates would suggest. 

The latest leg down for oil prices could on the delta help - after all there is no cure for low oil prices like low oil prices. 

Although the Q4 average will now most likely end up well below earlier estimates, we believe it is too early to write of the winter market and 2025 just yet. It does take some time before increased volumes work through any excess position lists, further supply increases are expected, and remember that wall of Non-OPEC+ crude oil supply coming next year.
Recent development - 'Lies, damn lies, and statistics'

Rates have risen slightly over the last month, although not as much as expected. Looking at the statistics, Mark Twain could be excused for  having difficulties in understanding figures in the tanker market too. 

Preliminary volume and tonne-mile estimates for October indicate a solid increase in tanker demand, especially for crude tankers, and as fleet growth remains negligible we are surprised that rates have not reacted more to the upside. That said, it may take some time before any oversupply that has built over the seasonally slower period can be fully absorbed. The Libya outage probably delayed this process vs. the normal season. 

Libya's comeback meaningfully boosted Suez- and Aframax volumes and this was also where the biggest rate gains were posted. We would have expected this comeback to give a greater West-East arb. to also further boost demand for the biggest tankers, but this has only partially happened. There are now, however, some more indications of a saturated crude oil market in the Atlantic which all else equal should tilt pricing toward the favour of more long-haul shipments. 

Product tanker volumes have taken a hit as low refinery margins have led to run cuts. Similarly, amid these lower margins the necessary arbitrages have not been there to boost freight, although the U.S. hurricanes did spark some (short-term) life. 

After the very strong start to the year, rates have overall declined sufficiently lately so that our base case forecast for the full year is increasingly likely, as a market average - rates YTD are on a dwt. weigthed average 6% above that base case.

For the biggest vessels we have seen MEG volumes ramp up more or less as expected, apart from the smaller portion of Saudi Arabian exports which has shifted from the MEG to the Red Sea. There should be slight further seasonal upside in coming months, and going into next year a gradually increased production quota (300 kbpd) for the UAE and possibly broader OPEC+ cut reversal at a later stage. 

Atlantic-East movement, however, has been slower due to a lacking West-East arb. With Libya now back and relatively higher inventories in Europe than other regions we would expect this trend to turn going forward. There are indications that the Atlantic basin is near saturated for some crude oil grades (coupled with more products coming inbound), which either means more U.S. inventory builds (no need for it in theory with shale now being the real SPR) or more flows to other regions. With refinery margins in the East having improved somewhat lately and increased Chinese crude oil import quotas into next year, we believe that directionally, West-East trade flow will increase.  

Another thing to note, re. China, is that the the non-Chinese controlled portion of MEG-China fixtures has declined substantially over the last two months, which has most likely contributed to add pressure on rates for the few open market cargoes that have been there. This may continue, and change the dynamic against non-Chinese owners in the MEG, although could open up more opportunities to push for better rates elsewhere.

The West-East arbitrage has improved slightly in recent weeks, after having been closed much of the last few months, although is still not quite wide enough to spark a significant boost to long-haul activity. Preliminary November counts suggest a slight tick up in Atlantic VLCC loadings, even from the North Sea. 

For now, slightly lower than expected production in the Americas, slightly better demand in the U.S. and slightly lower than expected demand in the East seem to prevent a full reopening of the West-East arb. The crude forward curves remain backwardated, and even the recent oil price sell-off has hardly changed the shape of the forward curve - as inventories keep drawing. The expected growing surplus of crude into next year should change this and boost big parcel and long-haul economics.

Next year, the IEA expects non-OPEC+ supply growth of 1.5 mbpd, with 1.3 mbpd of that originating from the Americas. While we think the IEA may still be too optimistic on the U.S. at 400 kbpd, there should still be plentiful additions for a solid crude tanker demand push. 

The EIA expects most of next year's production increase to come in Q2 and Q3, which could smoothen the seasonal pattern somewhat vs. normal. The IEA expects the supply push to come already from Q1, so some discrepancy where the biggest difference lies in U.S. output. 

Both agencies, however, suggest a 500+ kbpd production increase for non-OPEC+ over the remaining couple of months this year.

What may be the difference between a good and a great year for owners next year is the OPEC+. If the group does follow through with a gradual 2.2 mbpd unwind of cuts next year risk is well on the upside vs. our forecast. We should get the answer in early November, but with the latest sell-off for oil prices, further delay appears likely and 'sources' suggest a month's or more) delay will take place. Waiting one more month also gives the group the appearance of not interfering with the U.S. election. However, waiting one month puts a prospective cut reversal into the seasonally weaker Q1 - which seems unlikely. 

As indicated below, there is probably not an oil market balance which supports an unwind next year, although lower oil prices (which are likely to follow any supply hike) usually stimulates demand.

content.content:
Similarly, Chinese oil demand holds some of the key to the tanker market development. Over the last few months demand has disappointed vs. market expectations, although September data showed some improvement and YTD demand remains up 0.8% vs. last year with jet fuel and naphtha leading the way. 

Apparent oil demand increased by 3.2% m/m in September, although was 4.9% lower than the same month last year. Notably, the biggest gainer m/m was diesel. The main reason for recent diesel demand weakness may be more a function of low industrial activity than the widely cited switch from diesel to gas fuelled trucks. The LNG/CNG market share of the total truck fleet is miniscule. Regardless, current lower diesel prices and higher gas price may lead to a switch back.. 

It will be interesting to see in coming months whether recent (and expected) government stimulus will have an effect - a slight increase in Chinese crack spreads (gasoil is now back to 'normal'), and some indications of increased industrial activity (more pollution etc.) could be positive signs. October manufacturing PMIs were back in expansionary territory for the first time since April. Increased crude oil imports quotas for next year should be utilised and underpin tanker demand.

content.title: Still implied crude oil stock builds

content.content: For product tankers the demand outlook is not as benign as for crude. Lately, volumes have been negatively impacted by low margins and run cuts, and looking into next year, run estimates have been significantly lowered. Next year, 'only' 250 kbpd of capacity additions are expected, from 1.1 mbpd this year. With most additions being closer to where end-user demand is also likely to grow the most, there may not be a whole lot of distance delta for tonne-miles either. From a capacity addition standpoint, 2026 looks better, although by then fleet growth will have picked up meaningdully.

content.content:
Refinery margins globally have normalised, after solid volatility to the upside the last two years. This signals slightly weaker oil demand growth and has led to extended maintenance and run cuts recently. 

Margins in the West have hardly moved the last few weeks, but in China there has been some improvement for gasoil again. The latter is more in line with what we hear about trucks potentially switching back to diesel and some anecdotal evidence of an industrial recovery amid increased government stimulus. It is too early to tell still, but if sustained this could hold some key for increased crude oil flows into Asia.

Partly underlining this is also inventories, where products have built while crude oil has drawn recently. While overall OECD stocks have developed relatively sideways YTD, crude oil stocks have declined marginally, and products have built by 40 mb. 

Another interesting split, European inventories have built relatively more than most other regions globally. This may suggest less of a demand pull from other Atlantic crude exporters going forward than has been the case until now. There is an abnormally large amount of seaborne diesel/gasoil incoming, which may dampen European fuel demand. This is something to watch re. the West-East arbitrage, and we may expect to see more NSea-East loadings to come. 

Looking at OECD inventories vs. the 5-year average, one might argue that oil prices should be higher. This could, however, just be a reflection of the expected oversupply next year.

content.title: OECD inventories vs. 5-year avg. and Brent

content.content:
Global oil supply excluding Iran has disappointed vs. forecasts this year, although both the IEA and EIA expect more to come in the final two months of the year (EIA has non-OPEC+ growing by 0.7 mbpd). Especially U.S. production growth has been lower than earlier estimated - but here again there are expectations of a ~200 kbpd increase near-term. 

Looking into the next couple of years a larger share of oil production growth is expected to come from Latin America vs. the northern part of the Americas which should lend greater support to tanker tonne-miles vs. this year. Re. the IEA's forecasts below, U.S. Supply growth estimates may still be too high, but that still leaves around 1.5 mbpd of global supply upside even if the OPEC+ leaves production unchanged. It is not until 2027 that oil supply growth could become so small that it should be a greater worry for tanker demand vs. increasing fleet growth (although 2026 may see a gradually softening market balance).

Fleet growth YTD has been very low, despite virtually no scrapping. Deliveries are scheduled to increase next year, especially for product tankers, albeit nothing dramatic when looking at the overall picture and factoring in fleet inefficiencies amid new regulations. 

With the softening sentiment in recent weeks and months, it appears that the YTD newbuild ordering drive has lost steam. The run-rate in Q4 to date is by far the slowest since rates took off in 2022. Still, there has been enough of an order intake so that 2026 and 2027 supply growth likely means softer tanker rate development, but still not 'off the cliff' as ageing tonnage will be offsetting.

The vast portion of the fleet which is closer to historical average scrap age is likely to limit rate downside and actual fleet growth in coming years. 

Sure, the vast majority of vessels already around historical scrap age has been absorbed by the shadow markets. Interestingly, the U.S. OFAC  has blacklisted a number of tankers recently, most of which were already on our shadow lists. The VLCCs which have already been blacklisted for a while, have on average ‘only’ lifted 1.7 cargoes each YTD. The 13 newly sanctioned VLCCs (and other non-OFAC listed VLCCs on our shadow lists) had on average lifted 3 or more. If the latter 13 will experience a similar drop in utilization, that equates to a ‘phase-out’ of almost six VLCCs. At 0.7% of the VLCC fleet, that is not huge, but still nearly equals the total seven VLCCs scheduled for delivery this and next year… More importantly, watch out for potential further OFAC updates – if these become more widespread, it could have greater market implications.

Seasonal factors like increased Guinean bauxite shipments and Australian iron ore and coal shipments are in play for the next two months. So, it looks like there will be another rally before year-end. However, each spot market peak has been lower than the previous one since December last year, as China's fundamentals have worsened and the Kamsarmax market has dropped. We do not think there will be much change to this situation in the near-term, so it is likely that the next spot market peak will be lower than the one in late September.

content.content:
After experiencing exceptionally high earning levels for 24 months, the VLGC market has entered a downward trend once again. The seasonal low of the summer period has reoccurred, with all three months of the third quarter showing signs of this decline.

**The quarterly TCE average concluded at $39,191 per day**, marking the lowest quarterly result year-to-date. This figure represents a 65% decrease from Q3 2023, but only a 7% decline from Q3 2022. 

In terms of the total year-to-date average TCE, it now resides at $51,615 p.d.

Except for the month of July, the West (BLPG3) traded at a theoretical premium to the East (BLPG1).  *See graph for an overview of the three different index routes.*

BLPG1 - $30,150, BLPG2 - $51,192, BLPG3 - $36,230. 

Entering into the fourth quarter of the year, U.S. propane inventories are currently at high levels after summer piling, coincidentally with peak demand season starting. However, the current shipping market is long and the level of volatility remains *extremely high*.

**U.S. Gulf/U.S. East Coast**
July: 85 in total/22 being spot fixtures
August: 101 in total/28 being spot fixtures
September: 91 in total, 20 being spot fixtures

**Middle East Gulf**
July: 80 in total/28 being spot fixtures
August: 80 in total/20 being spot fixtures
September: 70 in total/19 being spot fixtures

**The VLGC earnings level is normally highly correlated to the arbitrage window from the West to the East.** However, as the graph clearly illustrates, this has not been the case in recent months. The graph specifically compares the Houston-Chiba index (BLPG3) with the arbitrage. Several factors have contributed to this situation.

During the summer, the U.S. export market experienced disruptions due to maintenance activities as well as hurricane Beryl, which led to delays in loadings. Such incidents usually create a ripple effect, impacting the period following the occurrence. This resulted in fewer spot fixtures from the region and generally higher FOB activity. Consequently, shipping activity was lower than desired, and the impact of an expanded fleet became evident in the position lists, causing a long shipping market.

Due to the changing availability and restrictions at the Panama Canal, there has been a significant shift in the sailing patterns of VLGCs over the past 12 months. These patterns have become a crucial variable in terms of fleet capacity and availability.

The notable change of more vessels opting to sail around the Cape of Good Hope, rather than risk the Panama Canal with its unpredictable conditions, increased significantly around this time last year. This trend persisted throughout the year, but it is only now in Q3 that we have observed a reversal.

There are still no ships sailing through the Suez Canal due to the security situation in the Red Sea. However, as the Panama Canal has returned to normal water levels and full operational capacity, we are seeing more VLGCs utilizing the canal once again. Q4 tends to be the most trafficked quarter for the Panama Canal, and this is typically when congestion reaches its peak.

For volumes lifted on VLGCs, the **United States** remains the dominating party, who **increased their exports by 4.9% quarter-on-quarter**. Year-on-year, the U.S. has exported 2 million tonnes more this year, with a total of 38.4 million tonnes so far in 2024. This is equivalent to a growth of 6%. Quarter-on-quarter, they displayed an 8% increase in exports.

The Middle East is expected to increase their production and exports levels in 2025 & 2026, mainly from Qatar & the United Arab Emirates.

All top five importing countries increased their imports in Q3 2024 compared to Q3 2023. China, being the main driver, has imported 25.5 million tonnes so far this year, which is an increase of 1 million tonnes from the same period last year. China's strong import demand is likely to continue further, as the new PDH capacity additions added in 2024 & 2025 will result in a 64% growth from 2022 levels.

The U.S. still remains the market leader in exports, with 53% of all VLGC liftings. The nation has exported just over 40 million tonnes LPG so far in 2024, which is 10 million tonnes below the 2023 total (on VLGCs only). After a summer of stock building, inventories have rebounded towards the top of the 5-year period, and at the end of September, the stock holds 97.8 million barrels.

As the data displays, the U.S. has been consistent in production and consequently exports provided to the market. There are three terminals (Targa, Enterprise & Nederland) that are undergoing expansion projects to increase their export capacity (of both LPG & ethane). These projects will first finalize in 2025 & 2026, and can be understood as a testament to the underlying sentiment for further production and export growth from the region.

**The total fleet now comprises of 398 VLGCs**, where 16 are used for storage/semi-storage. 18 newbuildings have been delivered YTD, where only 3 of these were in Q3. For the last quarter of the year, another 3 newbuildings are scheduled for delivery. 

In the last 10 years, only 12 VLGCs have been scrapped. However, 13% of the fleet is now older than 20 years, and 9% above 25 years - which would indicate that the scrapping candidates are increasing extensively. However, due to the general positive health of the market, we do not see any incentives for scrapping of these vessel to have an uptake. Unless, the environmental regulations should force a harder hand on the operational requirements, or imposed age restrictions from ports and/or charterers.

**The orderbook-fleet ratio is at 25% with 99 vessels on order.** Until 2026, there will be little fleet growth, with only 12 newbuilds scheduled for 2025. Contrary to this, 2026 and 2027 combined will end with 74 newbuilds planned for delivery. This will result in a total fleet growth of 18% in 2 years.

To accommodate the fleet expansion, export volumes must increase accordingly. The significant fleet expansion in 2023 was initially viewed by many market players as a potential tipping point that could destabilize the market. However, the high production and export levels from the U.S. allowed the market to absorb these vessels seamlessly, rendering the fleet expansion relatively unnoticed. Nevertheless, the subdued seasonality observed in Q3 highlighted the impact of the 39 additional vessels introduced last year.

It is therefore uncertain whether another substantial influx of vessels can be absorbed similarly. To achieve a more balanced market, export volumes must rise. There is already positive sentiment from the U.S., with several terminals expanding their capacity. However, the production levels forecasted by the EIA will be crucial. Their projections, to be published next quarter, will provide valuable insights into the expected export levels from the U.S. for 2025 and 2026. 

All of the vessels in the orderbook are LPG dual-fuel, except for seven. Currently, there are 53 "VLACs" on order, capable of carrying ammonia as cargo at 98% capacity. These vessels are scheduled for delivery in the second half of 2026. However, we anticipate that these vessels will initially enter the market as "regular" VLGCs, transporting LPG as cargo for the foreseeable future. The ammonia production and export market requires substantial growth in both volumes and infrastructure before any trading on VLACs becomes likely.

The anticipated incremental Clean Ammonia Capacity to come before the next decade will not require these vessels for the trade. It will likely be absorbed by the Midsize Gas Carriers (MGCs), which is the segment that currently lifts most of seaborne ammonia. The MGC orderbook-fleet ratio is at 41% now.

In total, there has been 45 newbuilding orders placed in 2024, this is 10 more than the total in 2023 - with 3 more months of the year to go. This is a historical high, especially given the position of the current newbuilding prices. Al throughout the year, they have remained stable around the are of $115-125 million, depending on whether ammonia capable and the different fuel alternatives. 

In terms of yard capacity, the situation continues to tighten, with limited availability left in 2027. There are now 10 VLGC orders scheduled with delivery in 2028.
*LPG is categorized under "others", but their total share is around 5%.*

After the transit restrictions were imposed in Q4 last year, the fluctuations of the three main waypoints for VLGCs increased. The water levels in the Panama Canal have returned to normal, and the daily transit capacity is back to full at 36 transits per day. The Canal Authority has become acutely aware of its vulnerability during peak seasons and is planning to find a long-term solution to its capacity challenges, although this seems distant at the moment. During Q3, they introduced the LoTSA (Long Term Slot Allocation), which involves packages of slots for 12 months, sold in an auction. Some larger LPG and LNG players took advantage of this, though half of the packages remained unsold at the end of the auction.

We still see many ballasting vessels choosing the Cape of Good Hope route, but it remains to be seen whether this percentage will increase again when the projected congestion hits the Panama Canal during the final quarter of the year.

As we soon will be entering 2025, a year where the fleet will grow very little compared to 2023 and 2024, with only 12 newbuilds scheduled for delivery. There are also about 80 VLGCs that are scheduled for their special survey dry-dock in '25 & '26. This will create a deficit in the available fleet. Chinese demand is expected to remain strong, and we will see conclusions of expansion projects at U.S. terminals. Increased production and export volumes are needed to catch up with the coming fleet growth, which we will see after next year and onwards.
