Panamax / Kamsarmax - India Coal Imports Seasonality vs 2024

content.content:
The headline market fundamentals remain firmly positive, and the market is higher than in the same period last year, but only just so. 

- The weaknesses in the Panamax / Kamsarmax segment are suppressing this segment.
- The prices of industrial metals are not suggesting imminent improvement (nor imminent weakening). 
- Direction-wise, seasonality has been followed closely all year, although levels have been lower than what that suggested in the last two months. Seasonality suggests this week and the next could be an uptrend, before another downturn until mid/late November.

This has been another quarter with modest changes in the charter rates. Q3 started with some slight increases, and a wide premium for vessels available in the West versus the East. The gap narrowed almost immediately and even inverted, with two-stroke spot rates in the East at a premium to the West by the beginning of August, driven by a rebalancing of vessels and softening demand in the Atlantic. The peak in levels at the start of the quarter currently serve as the yearly charter rate peak, as rates have fallen since and the seasonal winter market is not yet in sight. The fundamentals are the main market driver, and while distances are long and tonne-miles high, the fleet is more than capable of doing the transport work, which has reflected in the rates. The list of open available steamers has been long throughout the quarter, but availability of modern tonnage has also been high. 

The JKM LNG price has been in the range 11.7 to 14.4 $/MMBtu throughout the quarter, relatively stable around the 13$/MMBtu mark towards the end of the quarter. This is similar to Q3 levels in 2023, but significantly lower than in the two years prior. Current prices are high enough that there has been some demand destruction in price sensitive areas. 

34 orders were placed in Q3; double the number placed in Q2. 24 of these are the Q-max orders at Hudong-Zhonghua for the Qatar expansion, eight are for ADNOC, and the last two are additional orders for Cosco at Dalian. 16 LNGCs have been delivered in Q3, meaning several orders have been pushed to Q4. To reach the originally-planned number of deliveries in 2024, 29 LNGCs will need to be delivered in the last quarter of the year. That would be 10 more than the historical record in Q1, 2018. Five of the remaining deliveries for this year were originally tagged to the Arctic LNG-2 project, so these are currently unlikely to be delivered to the project, but also unlikely to become trading vessels in the LNG fleet. 

A shadow fleet has emerged for the first time in LNG, following other segments which have practiced sanctioned trade for years. So far, six cargoes have been lifted from the sanctioned Arctic LNG-2 project, and none have reached international markets. The operation of these vessels has been far from conventional, as two vessels have transited the Northern Sea Route without any ice class, two vessels completed open-sea ship-to-ship transfers and one recently crossed the Red Sea and the Bab el Mandeb strait. India has announced that they are not willing to take sanctioned cargoes, and with current relatively low LNG prices, most are not willing to risk sanctions for a slightly cheaper cargo. Most of the LNG from Arctic LNG-2 is currently stored in the two 360kcbm FSUs located in Murmansk and Kamchatka, and it remains to be seen if the cargoes can find an import market.
Source: JKM for S&P Global Platts

Spot charter rates in the Atlantic were increasing at the start of the quarter, as the open inter-basin arbitrage drove a lot of tonnage East, making it harder to find suitable tonnage in the Atlantic. With a rebalancing of vessels, rates in the Pacific soon caught, reaching a peak in the beginning of August when rate reductions where already coming in the Atlantic. Since then, rates in both basins have fallen and are historically low this close to Q4. The quarterly average spot charter rate for a two-stroke was $73k per day, marking the lowest levels since 2020 when COVID-19 impacted the LNG and LNG shipping market. While July levels were not too far off levels in the past three years, and actually slightly higher than in 2022, it is the absent surge in August and September which has produced this low quarterly average. 

Term charter rates have also been on a downward trend throughout the quarter, although no big changes. Longer term rates are reducing mainly due to reduced finance cost, but also due to 20+ speculative orders and an orderbook that will see deliveries arrive before volumes. Current forecasts indicate a rebalancing/tightening in the second half of the decade, which has been clear for a while. Therefore, a lot of the reduction has been taken out already, and we do not see significant softening from current levels unless there is further softening in financing cost or newbuild prices. 

On the shorter-term, the one-year rate has also seen a drop despite the slight increases in Q2 as the focus on winter fixing increased slightly. While owners are keen to fix multi-month to a year, to avoid idling in the shoulder months in an oversupplied 2025, charterers are likely thinking that winter coverage can be secured relatively cheap in the spot market.

While spot activity in July was very high, activity has since dropped to much lower levels than seen earlier in the year. The high levels in July do, however, bring spot fixture counts almost in line with the very active Q1 and Q2 this year, and significantly higher than previous years' Q3 levels (the highest since 2020). Activity usually drops in Q3, as was also clear in August and September this year, and this has typically been due the lack of available ships going into winter; however, this year it can instead be explained by a lack of requirements, and the list of available ships has been more than sufficient. 

Spot fixtures have on average been much shorter than in recent years: the Q3 spot fixture count is up by 71% YoY, but the number of fixed days is only up by 38%. On longer term charters, both multi-month and short-term up to 3 years, activity is significantly lower than previous years. Three one-year charters were concluded in Q3, so less than half those seen in Q3 last year, and the same as in 2022. In the 3-5 year range, only one fixture was concluded, and hence the focus on securing term tonnage for coming winters has eased. 

80% of short-term fixtures were sublets, and while the wave of redeliveries which has already started could change that, the majority of redeliveries are 138k steamers which are increasingly difficult to charter out. Nonetheless, the share of short-term fixtures done for steamers increased from 9% in Q2, to 24% in Q3. Of these, 60% (12 fixtures) were 138k vessels, and the majority of duration less than 30 days.

content.title: Short term fixtures by sublet vs independent owners

content.content:
100 MT of LNG was loaded in Q3, up 2 MT from Q2, and 4 MT from Q3 last year. There haven't been any commissioning cargoes from new projects this quarter, except for Fast LNG Altamira loading its first "full" cargo on the very last day of the quarter. Plaquemines has received a partial cool down cargo from Hammerfest, and commissioning cargoes from this project, as well as from Corpus Christi Stage 3, are expected in Q4. This, in combination with the usual seasonal uptick in volumes as summer maintenance ends, should bring levels higher in the coming weeks. In fact, volumes did increase throughout the quarter, and monthly levels in September were almost 1.3 MT higher than in July. 

The United States was the biggest exporter in Q2, with 1 MT more than Qatar, and 1.2 MT more than Australia. On the import side, China is leading, followed by Japan and South Korea as per usual. India has been very active this quarter, importing 13% more than in Q3 last year.

European storage levels are at 94% full, and since they were relatively full at the start of the summer season, refill needs have been limited. Europe only imported 19 MT in Q3, which is 21% less than in Q3 last year, and 30% lower than the year before. It is also 5 MT lower than in Q2. High renewable and nuclear output, as well as pipeline imports, have reduced European LNG demand. Asia has in turn imported 6 MT more than in Q3 last year, and 2.4 more than in Q2. The increase is largely driven by Japan, which has imported more than 2.2 MT more than in Q2 due to extended hot weather. 

There has been some increase in LNGC transits via the Panama Canal, due to low European demand and an open inter-basin arbitrage. However, levels are still much lower than last year despite US to Asia flows being 33% higher for Q3. Red Sea transits are still avoided (Suez transits have mainly been to discharge in Aqaba and Ain Sukhna), so combined with limited Panama Canal use, the activity around Cape of Good Hope remains high. LNG fleet distances are therefore high, which has been driving tonne-miles higher than previous years. Tonne-time on the other hand, is relatively similar to last year despite the long distances, driven by slightly higher speeds. 

The open arbitrage has resulted in 9 MT of US LNG heading to Asia in Q3, which is 43% and the highest levels seen since 2021. The trend for Qatar cargoes has continued, with only 10% heading to Europe (compared to an historical average of 20%).

There are currently 672 LNGCs live on the water (counting three already delivered in Q4 as well), five in layup and 338 on order. The orderbook-to-fleet ratio is thus 50%, and with some slow-down in ordering, this ratio seems to be on a downward turn. 

The fleet grew by 16 vessels in Q3, which leaves another 26 to be delivered in the remainder of Q4 if planned delivery years remain on track. However, nine of these outstanding deliveries were originally for Arctic LNG-2/Novatek, so 21 is likely a more realistic number for Q4 (including three already delivered). 34 orders were placed, of which the majority were for the Qatar expansion project. 

While the fleet keeps growing at a fast pace, the number of vessels leaving the fleet is limited. Only one vessel was sold for scrap: the 126k cbm, 1979 built Coral Energy, owned by Sinokor.

That leaves 16 ships that are older than 30 years old, 93 which are older than 20. In addition to the numerous steamers redelivered to owners so far this year, another 21 are scheduled to redeliver in Q4 according to our records, of which 80% are 138k cbm or smaller. 

2025 is still the year where the most deliveries are expected, currently 88 scheduled deliveries. 2026 is also fully booked with 84 scheduled deliveries, and only very limited slots could be made available in 2027. 24 ships in the orderbook are charter-free, of which the majority deliver in 2026 and 2027. 71% of the orderbook is being built in South Korea, and 28% in China.

content.title: Fleet evolution (considering current orderbook and phase-out at 25 years)

content.content:
We still believe fleet utilization will be higher this winter than it has been throughout the summer, due to seasonally higher production levels. While long distances have kept fleet utilization relatively high throughout the year, the significantly reduced focus on energy security, with lower LNG prices and limited contango opportunities, have kept sublet willingness high and availability lists long. We don't think utilization levels in the last three years should be representative for rate forecasts, as the theoretical utilization of the fleet is currently higher than it was at the same in the previous three years, yet rates in previous years have been on a steep climb towards the winter peak, unlike this year. As the Suez Canal is likely to remain unused, this winter market comes down to the inter-basin arbitrage and the weather. Our calculations do however show that even with a sustained open arbitrage, the rapid fleet growth ensures that the fleet is capable of the additional transport work, and without help from the cargo market it should not cause rate jumps anywhere near to those seen in the last few years. 

In addition to the seasonally higher production levels, some commissioning cargoes are expected from Plaquemines and Corpus Christi Stage 3. However, the fleet continues to grow significantly faster than the LNG supply. With recent delays, most capacity scheduled for commissioning in 2025 is coming towards the end of the year. This means that we should prepare for another summer season with high fleet availability, and decreasing utilization of the oldest vessels. We expect the oversupply to continue well into 2027, but a tightening trend is expected from 2026 given current project plans and vessel deliveries. There is likely need for more LNGC newbuilding by 2028, but that depends on the pace of fleet phase-out. Seeing as almost 70 LNGCs are celebrating their 25th birthday in the remainder of the decade (in addition to the 30 that are already older), the total fleet capacity is very dependent on the age of which we see vessels leaving the trading fleet. While the historical age limit has been high, we do see a changing trend with environmental regulations, parcel sizes, and terminal age restrictions, and believe tradability beyond 25 years is limited.

Environmental regulations are an increasing part of discussions, with the EU ETS already in force and FuelEU Maritime just months away. The FuelEU Maritime will affect LNGCs trading to Europe already from January, 2025, and some of the most modern vessels will be affected by 2034.

There has been a clear slow-down in project FIDs, both in the United States due to the pause in approvals, but also in the rest of the world. While more FIDs are expected, we do not see any significant upside to the currently planned (FIDd) volumes this decade. That should bring LNG liquefaction capacity to about 660 by 2030 (of which historically 85% is actually produced), which is well in line with several LNG demand forecasts.

This week or the next is usually a seasonal peak, and we think this will be the case again. The fundamentals in China are weaker than last year, and eventually, it is likely to impact the Capesize market. Further, the ratio between Capesize and Panamax is extremely high. Finally, the 60-day and 30-day volatility is around the lowest levels seen in the last years, which is often followed by a big move.

Shipment volume growth is well above supply growth, which should mean a positive year-on-year change in spot and period rates. The below charts display these correlations. content.content: https://pbrkapp.blob.core.windows.net/report/b3a016e9-1153-4f09-a3e0-33cc30fcc2b6/PANAMAX KAMSARMAX SPOT MARKET YOY VS MARKET BALANCE.png

Spot earnings year-on-year remain positive, but only just so, despite positive fundamentals. Like the Panamax market, the weakness in the North Atlantic is the main explanation for it we think. It is doubtful whether there will be much change to the market in the next months. The US grains season is underway but has yet to impact the market in a significant way. 
Seasonality turns a bit more negative in November and December.

We do not make any changes to the outlook in this report, but highlight the following key takes: 

- The change in sentiment in the oil market should not meaningfully change the outlook for the biggest tankers which means a seasonal upturn should be imminent. Energy agency balances still point to supportive fundamental drivers next year - and the softer price picture has improved freight economics. Fleet growth for the biggest tankers is and will remain very low over the next year. 

- The product tanker outlook is weaker with softer (normalised) refinery margins and revised refinery run estimates, possibly with shorter average sailing distances to come. This stacks against increasing fleet growth, and we see downside risk to our rate forecasts for next year. 

- Reports saying that Saudi Arabia is ready to give up oil price support in favour of gaining market share would be a meaningful net positive for rates into the winter and next year.

After a very strong start to the year, sentiment is now more measured. While we earlier leaned toward a bull-case rate trajectory, we are now closer to the base case again for the remainder of the year, unless the OPEC+ delivers on its cut unwind. 

For the same reason as we were a bit cautious about the rate outlook for this year, namely macro worries after a long up-cycle, we could see some downside risk for next year, especially for the smaller tanker segments which may see a more rapid normalisation of earnings vs. VLCCs than we had expected. We will, however, await further indications in coming months before contemplating any rate forecast changes. Continued trade disruption and most recent energy agency forecasts still support a positive overall market outlook. 

So far in September, 'everything' looks to be moving along a 'normal' trajectory for this time of the year, with VLCC rates having gained some traction, and the smaller segments lagging a bit still. That said, while VLCC rates came in spot on our $30k/d forecast in August, they have lagged in September, only recovering a few $k/d vs. our $45k/d forecast. With further volumes expected to come toward year-end, both seasonal and absolute, and hardly any deliveries, at least for the bigger vessels, rates should strengthen significantly.

A big positive for tanker rates if true: According to the FT Saudi Arabia may follow through on the gradual 2.2 mbpd OPEC+ cut unwind from December, thus foregoing price support. This is a scenario we have for some time highlighted, which becomes all the more likely. Saudi Arabia has lost significant market share to the Americas and Iran, and next year, the IEA expects non-OPEC+ production growth of 1.8 mbpd – vs. oil demand growth of ‘only’ 0.9 mbpd. Hence, risk was already on the downside for oil prices. Further OPEC+ cuts to shore up prices could challenge sustainable production capacity and threaten OPEC+ unity (most other members would rather prefer increasing output). Several members have overproduced in recent years, and Iran's production has doubled, and thus the alleged shift in strategy can be seen as both trying to hurt U.S. shale producers and punish OPEC+ ‘cheaters’. Further, this could curtail Iran's (oil) income, which has partly contributed to proxy wars and increased Middle East instability. An added benefit is that lower oil prices should stimulate higher demand. 

As a reminder, current OPEC+ cuts are threefold: an ‘official’ group cut of 2 mbpd until the end of 2025, a 1.66 mbpd voluntary cut by certain members until the end of 2025, and the voluntary 2.2 mbpd cut which will now likely be gradually unwound.  

For the tanker market, this is an obvious positive. This may limit some non-OPEC+ production growth next year, as the WTI forward curve is already below U.S. shale producers' average breakeven to drill new wells. However, the magnitude of the proposed OPEC+ reversal is the bigger story, and if followed through this gives upside risk vs. our rate estimates next year – mostly for VLCCs.

content.title: Saudi Arabia and OPEC lost significant market share

content.content:
Volumes YTD have been flat for crude tankers and slightly higher for product tankers. Seasonally, with lower domestic demand in key producing areas, volumes normally increase by close to 3 mbpd between August and December, with three quarters of this tilted toward crude tankers. 

On paper, there is no room for higher OPEC+ production, as non-OPEC+ continues to grow (although YTD the additions from the latter group has been much smaller than forecast by key energy agencies). Before any OPEC+ addotions, the IEA expects global oil production to rise by 1.2 mbpd between a low-point in September and year-end. 

One question mark, especially for Aframaxes is Libya, where the most recent headlines point to progress. If and when Libyan production does come back, it is not just a (direct) positive for Afras in the Med, but also crude tankers more broadly (indirect) as it should again help push relative pricing to accommodate an open USG-East arb..

Tonne mile-demand has risen slightly more than volumes YTD, by 1.7%, with the biggest growth by far posted by LR2s, while Aframax has declined slightly. In August, tonne-mile gains were again led by LR2s, but VLCC and Suezmax demand growth had also picked up meaningfully vs. the same month last year.

Fleet growth has been minimal YTD, and well below demand growth. This should have led to stronger rate development, and the recent strengthening for VLCC rates is really 'only' a catch-up trade. With no real crude tanker fleet growth through year-end, this is a good starting point for rates to recover more strongly - once sentiment turns and owners reclaim the driving seat.

The oil market sentiment has turned less optimistic recently, with lower oil prices, softer refinery margins, weaker macro data, especially from China, and the OPEC+ delaying its production cut reversal by two months. 

The IEA's balances indicate a significant oversupply next year with demand growth of 'only' 0.9 mbpd vs. supply growth of 1.9 mbpd. It is interesting to note that the EIA forecasts a fairly balanced market, though with much more optimistic demand forecasts (+1.5 mbpd). Both include expectations for very strong non-OPEC production growth (IEA at 1.8 mbpd and EIA at 1.6 mbpd), which appears quite optimistic - especially at current oil prices.

content.title: Slightly backwardated but flattening forward curve
Reflecting ongoing stock draws which will turn to builds
Big divergence in energy agency market balance forecasts

content.content:
Although both agencies have reported strong non-OPEC+ production growth this year (IEA at 0.9 mbpd and EIA at 0.7 mbpd), mostly from the Americas, crude oil exports growth has been very slim. YTD exports from North America have risen by about 110 kbpd from the same period last year, and Latin American growth has been about 90 kbpd. 

OECD inventories in the Americas have risen by about 0.2 mbpd whilst refinery runs have risen by about 300 kbpd, making up the majority of the difference.  Local absorbtion might help explain the low tanker volume and tonne-mile demand growth YTD compared to expectations at the beginning of the year. Next year, however, this is should change, with the IEA forecasting 1.8 mbpd of non-OPEC+ production growth, most of which is expected from the Americas, and on top of that refinery runs in the region are expected to decline by 300 kbpd.

content.title: North America seaborne crude oil exports
Latin America seaborne crude oil exports

content.content:
Beyond a building oversupply of crude oil into next year, the IEA's estimates point to a wider geographical mismatch between oil production and demand growth. The combination of the two should stimulate more long-haul trade, with an expectation that it should lead the oil price forward curves to flip into contango, and the WTI-Dubai spread to widen, all else equal, to provide a wide open West-East arbitrage.  

Even in a scenario where the energy agencies are much too optimistic about non-OPEC+ supply growth, where the latter only about matches (IEA) demand growth (0.9 mbpd), that alone could give crude tanker tonne-mile growth of around 4% (for reference the IEA's forecasts could imply VLCC tonne-mile demand growth of nearly twice that..). Hence, while the oil market sentiment has turned recently, there are still reasons to be optimistic about crude tanker, and especially VLCC demand next year.

content.title: Oil demand and supply growth by area

content.content:
Chinese oil demand remains a worry. August oil demand improved slightly m/m, but remained lower y/y. That said, jet fuel (+14.2%), naphtha (+9%) and gasoline (+5.3% - so much for the EV story, where we actually see that BEV takes increasing market share of the EV statistics which are therefore somewhat misleading...) demand remain well above last year, while fuel oil (-11.9%) and diesel (-3.9%) contribute to the downside, mainly due to slower industrial output. Overall, products demand YTD is up 1.6% vs. the same period last year. Inventories built meaningfully in August, due to a sharp increase in imports while refinery runs only rose marginally. 

Going forward, increased stimulus from the PBOC announced recently should help shore up some recovery for activity, at least sufficiently so that crude oil imports should remain relatively high. Lower oil prices tend to help.

content.title: China available crude oil vs. refinery runs

content.content:
The relative price picture for crude has weakened markedly, and led to improving long-haul freight economics. All else equal, higher Americas crude oil production, lower refinery runs, and an oil market balance which tilts toward oversupply should in coming months keep an open arbitrage. This can be a deciding factor for how strong the winter market for VLCCs becomes. 

One thing to note, too, is that crude oil priced in Chinese Renminbi is among the very cheapest it has been in a few years. Any further weakness in oil pricing could thus be a positive driver for (crude) tanker demand.

content.title: Brent/WTI-Dubai spread, adjusted for 2-1 month forward spread

content.content:
With weakening refinery margins globally runs have broadly been cut. The IEA's recent y/y growth forecast of 0.4 mbpd for this year is down from more than 1 mbpd at the beginning of the year. Next year's estimate has been lowered to 0.7 mbpd from 1 mbpd initially. 

Much of the upcoming growth is expected to come in China, where new refineries more than offset some closures of older, inefficient refineries. The remaining refinery capacity growth is mostly located closer to where demand growth will also be, meaning product tanker sailing distances might overall shorten going forward. Thus, product tanker tonne-mile growth could come in below 2% next year. 

Runs in the Americas are expected to decline slightly next year, which should all else equal leave more crude oil available for exports - on top of already strong production growth. 

Beyond lower tonne-mile demand growth for product tankers, lower (read: normalised) refinery margins also likely means less supportive arbitrages and less room for high freight. This may thus mean a quicker normalisation of product tanker rates than we had earlier assumed - and therefore downside risk to our 2025 rate forecasts.
Low to balanced fleet growth outlook

Fleet growth YTD has been scarce at 0.5%. The crude tanker fleet has grown by 0.2% and products by 1.4%. These figures could nearly double by year-end - still low overall numbers. The next two years, however, growth increases, especially for product tankers which is a key reason why we expect a continued levelling of the playing field earnings wise between the segments going forward. 

The orderbook to fleet at the beginning of September stood at 10.9% vs. the fleet, which is still not huge in a historical context, but getting to the point where it, including expected coming orders near-term, may limit some rate upside in coming years. 

Should rates soften in a potentially weaker demand environment, however, there is a vast number of phase-out candidates which should limit downside risk vs. earlier down-cycles. Hence, the fleet growth outlook in coming years is fairly balanced, and rate development to a larger extent hinges on the demand side.

The ageing part of the fleet will at some point become an issue, particularly for charterers adhering to stringent maximum age restrictions. By 2026, nearly a quarter of the fleet will be made up of 20+ years old vessels, which means much slimmer pickings. 

At some point this will also lead to increased phase-out, either directly or through the form of lower utilisation for the oldest vessels. For the large portion of the fleet which is already above the historical average phase-out age, most are engaged in sanctioned trades. Among these, most would strive to even achieve 50% utilisation vs. the normal fleet - hence is already 'half way phased out'. This largely explains why we have a fairly tight tanker market balance today, despite fleet growth of 10.6% on paper between 2019 and now vs. tonne-mile growth of 'only' 5.3% over the same period. 

Although Iran's president has recently expressed a desire to restart JCPOA talks, it does not appear like any resolution is imminent, considering recent Middle East turmoil and the progress in enrichment of uranium in Iran's nuclear development. Therefore, the oldest part of the fleet which would otherwise have been obsolete, is likely to continue trading, albeit at very low utilisation.

content.content:
Nothing is quite straight forward in the current volatile geopolitical landscape - not to mention macroeconomically, where there are still risks. 

The main downside scenarios, beyond any macro turmoil, relate to normalisation of trade after the last few years' trade disruptions. We do not deem any resolution either in the Russia/Ukraine or Middle East conflicts as very likely, although there are continuously some (premature) news headlines suggesting otherwise. 

If Trump is elected, he has stated he will quickly end these conflicts, and force an agreement with Iran. The two former scenarios would be sharply negative for the segments which have benefited the most from disruptions. The Russia/Ukraine conflict has caused about 6% upside for overall tanker tonne-miles, slighlty more for MRs and nearly 15% for Afra/LR2. The risk to the latter two segments adds to downside risk from a weaker demand growth picture and higher fleet growth already. 

Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries and slightly lower crude oil production has led Russian exports lower, and tonne-mile support for tankers similarly slightly lower in recent months. However, Urals now trade well below the G7 price cap again, which begs the question whether more owners will return to this trade.

content.content:
Red Sea evasion has mostly supported product tankers, which again face the biggest downside risk if any resolution is found. We estimate a total tonne-mile increase of about 3% from this situation, and about double that figure for product tankers. 

YTD, crude tanker transits through the Red Sea have declined by 1.6 mbpd while about 0.8 mbpd has found its way around the COGH. Corresponding figures for product tankers are -2.7 mbpd and 2 mbpd, respectively. Some of the uplift in product tanker tonne-miles has been mitigated by VLCCs and Suezmaxes cleaning up in recent months. While VLCC rates have increased sufficiently so that this switching effect should ebb, it might still make sense to clean up Suezmaxes at current rates.. While this has not at all been the major driver to the downside for product tanker rates over the last few months, an unwind could be at least some help for product tanker rates.

content.content:
The perhaps biggest risk to the upside for the tanker market, other than a full OPEC+ comeback, is if Iran sanctions are lifted. Iran's successful crude oil exports, rising about 1 mbpd in recent years has plagued the 'normal' crude tanker market. This has absorbed a lot of the increase in Chinese crude oil demand in recent years and taken potential market share from OPEC+ peers. 

Furthermore, it has supported continued artificial employment for older tonnage which in many cases should have been phased out in most normal market condictions historically. Although this massive part of the fleet is already halfway phased out, a lifting of sanctions on Iran would most likely lead a large portion of this fleet to finally be scrapped. For the parts of this fleet that might continue trading, that would require extensive dockings etc. to regain 'normal' trading status and approvals - a cumbersome process. 

Hence, a prospective lifting of Iran sanctions, although currently seeming far fetched, is a bull case for the tanker market, both from a supply and demand perspective.
YTD status - demand vs. supply vs. rate development by segment

While a very theoretical exercise, the below compares tonne-mile demand vs. supply growth for the various segments, and compares with the YTD rate development, to see whether the latter is ahead of or behind the curve..

VLCC tonne-miles YTD have risen by 1.2%, while fleet growth has been zero. Meanwhile, rates YTD have been more than $6k/d lower than over the same period last year - a catch-up should be in the cards... 

Next year, depending on various scenarios, tonne-mile demand is expected to rise considerably more, potentially well above 5% is the IEA's oil demand and supply forecasts turn out to be correct, while gross fleet growth is expected at a 'whopping' 0.6%. Only one more vessel is scheduled to deliver this year.

Suezmax tonne-miles YTD have risen by 2.1%, while fleet growth has been 0.3%. Meanwhile, rates have been more than $8k/d lower than over the same period last year, so here too a catch-up appears likely. 

Only two more deliveries are scheduled through year-end, but next year gross Suezmax deliveries may pick up to 4.6% fleet growth, which should give fairly balanced market development due to spillover demand from the favourable geographical setup for oil demand vs. supply which mostly favours the biggest vessels.

Afra/LR2 tonne-miles YTD have risen by 2.7%, while fleet growth has been 1.5%. Meanwhile, rates YTD have been about $2k/d lower than over the same period last year - so fairly in line though a strong end to the year should still be expected... 

Through the remainder of this year another 1.4% is scheduled for delivery, and next year overall Afra/LR2 gross fleet growth is scheduled to be 5%. We believe it will be a tall ask for demand to reach similar heights. Hence rates are expected to soften vs. this year - getting closer to but still well above the historical average.

MR/Handy tonne-miles YTD have risen by 2.9%, while fleet growth has been 1.2%. Meanwhile, rates have been nearly $6k/d higher than over the same period last year, perhaps a bit much although a weaker end to the year than last year's now appears increasingly likely. 

There is another 1.1% of scheduled deliveries through year-end, and next year scheduled MR deliveries stack up to 5.1% gross growth. As tonne-mile demand should be well below that, we expect a softer rate environment, although still well above historical averages.

We make a few changes to our outlook from our previous report. On Capesize, we change from a lower market next year and a more bearish 2026, to a more bearish 2025 and a recovery in 2026. 
We expect China’s iron ore import growth to be negative next year, as credit growth is weak, iron ore and steel demand is down 3.5% from last year, and iron ore port inventories are around the highest level seen in the last 10 years. We do not expect fresh stimulus measures to take effect before Q4 2025 at the earliest

2025:

-	Continued weak steel and iron ore market fundamentals in China.
-	Iron ore inventory drawing, due to prevailing negative steel mills margins. 
-	Negative growth in China’s iron ore imports. 
-	The weak steel market fundamentals also pose a risk for coal imports, and Bauxite import growth.

2026:

-	Iron ore inventories in China could be at low levels. 
-	Rebound in China’s steel and iron ore market fundamentals, due to stimulus measures being added through 2025. 
-	Ramp-up of Simandou iron ore shipments, which could displace some domestic Chinese iron ore. 
-	Lower fleet growth than 2025. 
-	Global macro could be a negative factor. We expect a US recession in 2026. 

Regarding Kamsarmax, Ultramax, and Handysize, we keep our viewpoints as per last. We expect earnings to average at similar levels to this year, although downside risks could increase from the middle of the year onwards. The picture looks mixed to us. 

2025: 

-	Weakness in China could be a bearish factor, as still weak steel market fundamentals could mean coal imports will be lower than in 2024. 
-	Several global money supply indicators point strongly upward for 2025, meaning several commodity prices could increase significantly. In such an environment, it is rare to see a bearish year for the mid and small-sized segments. The price of industrial metals is the key factor to watch in this regard. 
-	Supply of coal remains a problem. This year, only Indonesia managed to add volume in significant quantities. Russia’s volumes are down by almost 20%, and the other major exporters do not have the capacity to increase exports by much. 
-	The upside potential mainly lies in developed economies' imports. 
-	India’s and South East Asia’s imports are likely to continue growing. 

2026:

-	Weakness due to a cyclical downturn in economic growth. This will likely affect all countries and regions.

Basis the correlation between earnings and asset values since 2010, we believe the following adjustments have to be made in order to bring the relationship back to normal. 

Handysize: 1-year time charter rates either have to rise above 15.000 USD pd, or the 10-year-old value has to fall to around 17 million USD. 
Supramax: 1-year time charter rates either have to rise to around 19.000 USD pd, or the 10-year-old value has to fall to about 20 million USD. 
Kamsarmax: 1-year time charter rates either have to rise above 20.000 USD pd, or the 10-year-old value has to fall to 23-24 million USD. 
Capesize: 1-year time charter rates either have to rise towards 25.000 USD pd, or the 10-year-old value has to fall below 40 million USD. 

In our previous report from late August, we wrote the following:

*In our reports before the summer, we outlined the view that 1-year time charter rates will make year-to-date highs for all segments during the second half of this year. This looks less likely currently, especially for Capes given the steep drop in steel and iron ore prices. However, seasonal factors like increased grain exports from the US and Canada and higher coal demand in Asia could result in year-to-date highs for the Kamsarmax, Ultramax, and Handysize segments. 

In any case, we believe it could be hard to support valuations at current levels, as we see downside market risks building from late 2025 and through 2026.  
Should our forward viewpoints prove correct, the next question arising is whether the prevailing regime of expensive asset values relative to earnings will continue. For example, if average earnings in 2026 end up being similar to 2023, will values be supported at 2023 levels, or will they go lower? 
The key factors in this regard are yard capacity and interest rates. Come 2026, will yard capacity be more available than now? And, how much will interest rates in the US be cut in the event of an economic downturn/recession?*

Some cracks have started to appear in asset values. We have lowered our assessments of 10-year-old values for all segments. We have also lowered our assessments of modern Kamsarmaxes. Should earnings remain around similar levels for the next six months, more downside can be expected in Kamsarmax, Ultramax and Handysize values. The Capesize market is high enough currently to support valuations close to current levels.

content.content:
In our previous report, we outlined that the macro economic upcycle is well and alive, but that risks are building from late 2025 and through 2026. We make no change to our viewpoints in this regard. 
The most important macro economic developments the last months have been the interest rate cut in the United States, and the stimulus announcement in China. How might this impact the dry bulk markets?

Starting with the US interest rate cut, we see this as both bullish and bearish. Bullish because interest rate cuts could cause the dollar to weaken, which should support commodity prices and dry bulk demand. The below chart shows that there is often a very tight correlation between a weaker dollar exchange rate and higher dry bulk shipment volume growth. The Federal Funds rate is at about 4.8%, but the 2-year treasury yield is at 3.5%, which strongly suggests that the Federal Funds rate will be cut by at least another 1.0%. Many economists expect the Fed to cut by another 0.5% in their next meeting in December. 
The flip side of this is that these rate cuts are giving a strong warning that the US is headed for a recession. The spread between the 2-year treasury yield and the federal funds rate is as wide now as it was in 2008 and 2000. A few quarters after this, the unemployment rate increased significantly, and stock markets performed badly during these periods. 
So, we do think the rate cuts in the US will be supportive for dry bulk markets until the middle of next year. We do however think a recession will happen, with this impacting dry bulk markets negatively in late 2025 and through 2026.  

What about the stimulus announcements in China then? The first thing to consider in this regard is that all the measures done by the Chinese authorities are supposed to lead to an increase in lending growth. For over two years, monetary policy in China has been eased by reserve requirement ratio and interest rate cuts. However, credit growth has been weak throughout the whole period, with the measures only preventing credit contraction rather than being stimulative. 
Below, the two upper charts show that reserve requirement ratios have been cut continuously since the middle of 2021, so the year-on-year change in the reserve requirement ratios has been negative since then. Still, credit growth has been much lower through this latest stimulus period than it was during the three previous stimulus periods in 2019/20, 2015/16, and 2019/10. This is a reflection of the lack of credit demand in China. Households are not leveraging up as the property sector is collapsing, and there have been reports in the last months that government entities are struggling to find infrastructure projects to invest in, despite funds being allocated. This could mean that China’s economy is so mature that a zero interest rate policy along with increased central government spending (QE) is needed to get a real stimulus going…

Regarding China’s import demand, the USDCNY year-on-year change has been a very accurate leading indicator of import growth in the last 10 years. That indicator is pointing to negative import growth early next year, which seems supported by other factors like falling steel and iron ore consumption, higher iron ore inventories, and weak credit growth. In turn, negative import growth to China could be a significant downside risk to the global economy, as represented by the chart showing the OECD economic indicator against China’s bulk commodity import growth with a lead of 1 year. 

In terms of the growth outlook for each major country/region, we expect the following:

**China:** 

Negative import growth in 2025, possibly a recovery in 2026, depending on stimulus measures done (or not done) next year. 

**Developed economies:**

Most likely higher imports over the next year, but a cyclical downturn again from late 2025 and through 2026. 

**India and Southeast Asia:** 

Continued import growth in 2025. Possibly zero or negative import growth in 2026, depending on how weak the next global economic downturn will be. 

**South America, Africa, and the Middle East:**

Cyclical weakness from late 2025 and through most of 2026. 

Should these assessments be correct, the Capesize market is likely to average lower next year. The Kamsarmax, Ultramax, and Handysize segments could average around the same levels as this year, although downside risks are likely to increase from mid-2025 onwards.  In 2026 weakness will likely persist, though the Capesize segment might recover before the smaller sizes.

Steel market fundamentals in China are bearish, with domestic production down by 3.5% on the same period last year. This is primarily due to prevailing weakness in the property sector. However, infrastructure spending growth has also fallen, and some weaknesses have emerged recently in the automobile sector. 
Due to the weaker domestic demand, China's steel product exports are set to reach an all-time high this year. This leads to increased discontent amongst trading partners, with many having raised or threatening to raise tariffs on Chinese products. 

Steel prices have lost correlation to a couple of macro indicators displayed in the below charts. The global economy is in an upcycle this year, as shown by the high value of the OECD diffusion index. The steel rebar price is negative year on year, however. 
China's credit growth remains low despite having had accommodative monetary policy for over two years. Further stimulus measures were recently announced, and it remains to be seen whether those measures will be enough to turn around the steel market.

content.content:
In our previous report from early July, we gave the following summary and outlook:

*Year-to-date, the Baltic Dry Index has averaged 59% higher than the same period last year, so far in line with our general view that 2024 would be an "upcycle" year and that a 50% or more increase is normal to see during such years. The upturn has primarily been driven by the Capesize segment, with the BCI5TC up 92% year on year. The Panamax 5TC, Supramax 10TC and Handysize 7TC are up by 35%, 33.5%, and 25%, respectively. We believe the year-on-year percentage increases will rise further during the coming two months for all segments, as we expect a much stronger summer than last year. 

Next year, we see several downside risks emerging from the second half of the year onward, likely translating into slightly lower earnings averages in 2025 than in 2024. Weakness could primarily be felt in the Capesize segment, as China's import demand is the primary bearish factor we see. 
We expect a more bearish year in 2026, but only if the indicators we rely on for our view of a weaker 2025 continues to worsen over the coming quarters. Regarding asset values, we expect little change over the next year. Prices are too high to expect much upside, notwithstanding our bullish view on earnings, whereas downside should be limited by the tight yard capacity and upwards pressure on newbuilding prices. 

All in all, we maintain our general view of a bullish 2024, a slightly lower market in 2025, and a more bearish 2026.*

**We make no major changes to our outlook.** Recent comments from steel companies in China along with weak data seem to almost confirm that China's coal and iron ore import demand will be lower next year than this year. The Capesize market is therefore likely to average lower next year, although factors like World ex-China demand, Bauxite imports to China, and escalating tensions in the Middle East (more vessels avoiding the Suez Canal) could provide support. 
For the Kamsarmax, Ultramax, and Handysize segments, lower coal imports to China will weigh on the market next year, although India and Southeast Asian imports are likely to grow, and there could still be a cyclical upturn in developed economies' (Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and Europe) imports. However, macroeconomic indicators are starting to point more clearly towards a late 2025  and 2026 downturn, as we have expected for a while. 

The earnings estimates we gave before this year are likely a bit too high, with the main reason for this being the lack of any cyclical upturn in developed economies' imports. 
We therefore lower our estimates slightly for 2024 and 2025, and keep our 2026 estimates unchanged.

Basis the correlation between earnings and asset values since 2010, we believe the following adjustments have to be made in order to bring the relationship back to normal. 

Handysize: 1 year time charter rates either have to rise above 15.000 USD pd, or the 10-year-old value has to fall to around 17 million USD. 
Supramax: 1 year time charter rates either have to rise to around 19.000 USD pd, or the 10-year-old value has to fall to about 20 million USD. 
Kamsarmax: 1 year time charter rates either have to rise above 20.000 USD pd, or the 10-year-old value has to fall to 23-24 million USD. 
Capesize: 1 year time charter rates either have to rise towards 25.000 USD pd, or the 10-year-old value has to fall below 40 million USD. 

In our reports before the summer, we outlined the view that 1-year time charter rates will make year-to-date highs for all segments during the second half of this year. This looks less likely currently, especially for Capes given the steep drop in steel and iron ore prices. However, seasonal factors like increased grain exports from the US and Canada and higher coal demand in Asia could result in year-to-date highs for the Kamsarmax, Ultramax, and Handysize segments. 

In any case, we believe it could be hard to support valuations at current levels, as we see downside market risks building from late 2025 and through 2026.  
Should our forward viewpoints prove correct, the next question arising is whether the prevailing regime of expensive asset values relative to earnings will continue. For example, if average earnings in 2026 end up being similar to 2023, will values be supported at 2023 levels, or will they go lower? 
The key factors in this regard are yard capacity and interest rates. Come 2026, will yard capacity be more available than now? And, how much will interest rates in the US be cut in the event of an economic downturn/recession?

*Growth rates have fallen in the last months*

Shipment volume growth remains firmly above supply growth. However, growth declined from slightly under 5.0% earlier this year to 3.9% in July. Most of the decline in growth is due to China, where import growth declined from nearly 9% in January to slightly over 3.0% in August. We expect China’s import growth to continue falling over the coming months (more detail in the macro section of this report). However, total shipment volume growth could remain above supply growth, as we expect continued import growth in the World ex-China. Notwithstanding weaker shipment volume growth, the distance side of the equation is contributing positively, with higher volumes in the Atlantic along with the deviations from the issues in the Suez Canal. The total ton-time growth of the fleet is therefore considerably higher than shipment volume growth, at about 8.0%. There could be a further increase in sailing distances should the Israel vs Iran Proxies War escalate further, as it could lead to a further reduction in ships sailing through the Suez Canal. In July, there were 326 dry bulk vessel transits of the Suez Canal, compared to 515 transits in July 2023.
 
Below is a summary of trade flow statistics through July. Per commodity group, the main weakness is seen in coal trades, where export growth is flat compared to last year. However, there are big differences in growth rates depending on which country one looks at. China, India, and Southeast Asia’s import growth has been very high this year, whereas Europe, Japan, and Korea’s import growth has been negative. On the export side, strong growth in Indonesian and Colombian volumes has been offset by a contraction in Russian and South African volumes. The other major commodity groups, iron ore, minor bulks, and grains, are all growing above the rate of supply growth.

content.content:
*The upcycle is well and alive, but risks are building from 2H 2025 and 2026*

The global economy remains in expansion mode, as displayed by various OECD indices, and clearly visible from dry bulk demand growth numbers. However, the upturn is not completely synchronized. Manufacturing activity in the Eurozone remains in contraction, whereas in the US, Japan, and Korea it remains barely in expansionary territory. There are some indications from liquidity factors like interest rates and currencies that there will be a more pronounced cyclical upturn over the next year in these regions. However, there were also indications of this through the end of last year and before the summer of this year, but the upturn has so far not materialized. Total dry bulk imports to Europe, Japan, Korea, and Taiwan ended at about 900 million tons last year, whereas in previous upcycle years imports have usually ended at a bit over 1 billion tons. Should a cyclical upturn materialize, it might therefore cause further upside for the Ultramax and Kamsarmax markets, and provide support for the Capesize market. 

We write “support” regarding the Capesize market because we find it highly likely that China’s iron ore and coal import growth will be negative next year. Imported iron ore consumption at Chinese steel mills is about 3% lower than in the same period last year, yet iron ore imports are 3.6% higher, due to inventory building in ports. With steel mills' margins deeply negative (99% of mills are currently losing money) and stimulus measures unsuccessful in reviving the property sector, the outlook is for 2025 to be a year of inventory drawing and probably negative growth in steel demand. 

China’s bulk commodity import growth is an important driver of the macro-economic cycle. This is displayed in the mid-left chart below, which plots OECDs economic indicator for the G-20 countries in aggregate vs China’s bulk commodity import growth rate shifted one year forward. China’s import growth points to an economic cycle peak between Q4 2024 and Q1 2025, with a continued slowdown into the autumn of 2025. With negative Chinese import growth likely going forward, one can expect the economic cycle to continue to weaken until the end of 2025 and the beginning of 2026. 

Another macroeconomic indicator pointing toward weakness from late 2025 onwards is the change in energy prices. The preceding 18 months' change in the price of coal, oil, and gas is going less and less negative each month, indicating that the global economy's boost from the decline in energy prices since Q2 2022 is fading. Should the price of coal, gas, and oil rise from current levels, it will point to weak economic growth in 2026, as the price changes often leads by about 18 months (mid-right chart below). In turn, that could mean that an eventual cyclical manufacturing upturn in developed economies will be short-lived, and it might start weakening again from Q3 2025 onwards. There are also several recession warning signs from the yield curve in the United States, some weakening labor market data, and an upcoming Presidential election. On the latter point, it is worth noting that economic and stock market performance often is weakest during the first or second year of a Presidential term.

Otherwise, economic growth in India and Southeast Asia is strong and is likely to continue growing unless the next economic downturn evolves into a major global recession. Will the next downturn be major? Record high stock market valuations in the US, the Chinese property sector, escalating military tensions in the Middle East and Russia/Ukraine are all factors that could mean it will be. On the other hand, interest rate levels are high, which means a downturn could be cushioned by slamming rates back down to zero percent. For dry bulk markets, the key point is that we expect shipment volume growth to go negative at some point during the second half of 2025 and remain there through most or all of 2026. 

In terms of the growth outlook for each major country/region, we expect the following:

**China:** 

Negative import growth in 2025, possibly a recovery in 2026, depending on stimulus measures done (or not done) next year. 

**Developed economies:**

Most likely higher imports over the next year, but a cyclical downturn again from late 2025 and through 2026. 

**India and Southeast Asia:** 

Continued import growth in 2025. Possibly zero or negative import growth in 2026, depending on how weak the next global economic downturn will be. 

**South America, Africa, and the Middle East:**

Cyclical weakness from late 2025 and through most of 2026. 

Should these assessments be correct, the Capesize market is likely to average lower next year. The Kamsarmax, Ultramax, and Handysize segments could average around the same levels as this year, although downside risks are likely to increase from mid-2025 onwards.  In 2026 weakness will likely persist, though the Capesize segment might recover before the smaller sizes.

content.content:
•	Weaker earnings recently are mostly caused by seasonality, but also some slightly weaker oil market developments
•	Energy agency forecasts and continued geopolitical disruption suggest a (sharply) firming rate trajectory into the winter and 2025
•	There are some macroeconomic and geopolitical threats to the outlook

Rates have softened in recent weeks and months, in line with the normal seasonal pattern. There are some underlying causes for this too, especially as Chinese crude oil buying interest has weakened over the last few months and the oil market sentiment appears overall softer. 

Recent macro worries with the reversal of the JPY carry trade after the BOJ's rate hike underscores the risks for the economy and in turn for the tanker market. Still, most recent oil energy forecasts - updated after the recent macro scare, point to solid upside potential for volumes through year-end, which will build on YTD tonne-mile demand gains. This, in turn, should give normal seasonality to the upside into the winter.

Overall tankers volumes have been just about flat YTD vs. the same period last year, with crude volumes down 1.7% and products up 1.5%. Typically we see the trough in July with gradual increases from here until year-end, and this year should be no different. 

Tanker tonne-mile demand has increased by 1.7% YTD, with growth 'saved' by Red Sea evasion which has contributed to an estimated 3% overall tonne-mile growth - skewed toward product tankers. We believe that demand growth potential is now higher for crude tankers going forward as most supporting factors for products (Russia/Ukraine, Red Sea and refinery expansions) have already to a large extent played out - not that these supporting factors will dissapear, but perhaps not contribute further to the upside..

VLCC earnings through the first seven months of the year have been about $10k/d lower than the same period last year, and in August to date also remain somewhat below. That is despite only one VLCC being delivered (vs. two converte to FSOs), and tonne-miles increasing by 0.6%. Hence, on paper current and recent VLCC rates are arguably too low. Last year earnings bottomed in September, but this year we believe the inflection point should come slightly earlier given this current 'underpricing'. 

For Suezmaxes, the decline in earnings has been about similar, despite tonne-miles increasing by 2.3% and zero fleet growth, suggesting that here too earnings lag fundamentals.

The earnings decline is similar also for Aframaxes, following a 3.1% dip in tonne-miles, whereas LR2s have fared much better with earnings up by nearly $15k/d y/y  following a 9.7% YTD increase in tonne-miles. Looking at these two combined, which is more appropriate given the switching flexibility, we see fleet growth YTD of 1.5% vs. tonne-mile growth of 3.2% - which also rhymes with the overall increase in earnings between them. 

For MRs tonne-mile demand of 3.2% has also outpaced fleet growth of 0.9% which corresponds with a $3k/day increase in earnings.

Global inventories have drawn recently, matching a relatively steeply backwardated forward curve. The oil market narrative, however, has tilted slightly more bearish recently, although recent energy agency updates did not materially revise demand growth estimates other than for China. Still, even the revised China estimates point to 3-400 kbpd upside for demand through year-end. 

In the IEA's most recent update, this was more than offset by lower production estimates, especially for the U.S. Hence, the projected deficit for the third quarter has grown, but still there is an implied oversupply in 2025 for OPEC+ to overcome before being able to materially reverse cuts. That said, if the recent slowdown and even slight decline in U.S. crude oil production continues, and demand surprises to the upside, there may be some more room. 

Through the remainder of this year, the IEA forecasts nearly 500 kbpd of supply growth, mainly from the Atlantic Basin. That comes on top of increased exports after seasonal domestic demand in key export areas reach a peak this month. Next year's supply growth from non-OPEC+ is estimated at 1.5 mbpd, with 0.6 mbpd of that coming from the U.S. and most of the rest from Guyana, Canada and Brazil.

The geographical mismatch between global oil supply and demand growth is set to grow further, which should facilitate for increased West-East trade going forward. The IEA's latest estimates do show a narrowing of the supply/demand gap with slightly lower supply growth in the West (0.8 mbpd) and slightly lower demand estimates in the East (0.9 mbpd) this year vs. previous expectations - although the gap widens further next year (Western supply growth of 1.7 mbpd and Eastern demand growth of 0.8 mbpd). 

In line with this recent slight softening of Eastern and slight strengthening of Western demand, the the Atlantic-East arb. has developed unfavourably for long-haul tanker demand recently. The Middle East turmoil and Red Sea 'closure' has possibly also contributed to some risk premium in Brent and WTI prices.

content.title: Oil supply vs. demand growth by region

content.content:
China’s apparent oil demand figures were again slightly lower y/y in June, but YTD remain 3.8% higher vs. the same period last year. Refinery runs are down 1.5% and crude oil imports down 2.3%. There has thus been an implied stock build of nearly 1 mbpd YTD vs. 750 kbpd last year. 

It is worth noting that apparent demand has developed most strongly for jet fuel, naphta and gasoline - all linked to consumption which mirrors strong services PMIs, whereas fuel oil, bitumen and diesel demand has declined - in line with softer manufacturing PMIs. 

Argus estimates that for China’s GDP growth to hit targets this year, oil demand should recover by at least 400 kbpd through the remainder of the year. With ample import quotas, crude oil imports could increase, probably depending on price (and/or government stimulus).

content.title: China crude oil availability vs. crude runs

content.content:
Refinery margins have generally weakened from earlier this year and the last few years, although remain somewhat above historical averages. New capacity coming on and somewhat sluggish global demand has taken its toll and as seasonal demand will soon start to fade it remains to be seen how profitability will keep up - which may pose some risk to product tanker volumes and the ability to accommodate high rates. 

One thing to note is that Chinese margins have recovered somewhat recently, which together with a stronger CNY (oil priced in CNY has rarely been cheaper over the last three years) and expectations for new export quotas could lead to increased crude oil buying appetite going forward.

In both hemispheres there has recently been more talk about refinery run cuts due to weaker margins. The IEA's most recent run growth estimates were revised down 150 kbpd for this year, with a significantly lower 3Q estimate. Next year's estimate was also revised 180 kbpd lower. This still suggests growth of 840 kbpd, although a good portion of that may have already come, and 'only' 600 kbpd next year. This may be considered a slight disappointment for product tanker owners. 

The recent softening of product tanker rates is in large part explained by the combination of lower refinerry runs, less room for high freight rates amid lower margins and small arbs, and VLCCs and Suezmaxes cleaning up - although the effect of the latter is likely to ebb going forward.

As normal with strong rates the orderbook has continued to increase recently, and is most recently up to 10.7% vs. the fleet. There is still a number of reported and rumoured orders which will most likely add another couple of percentage points to the orderbook to fleet ratio. A 15% orderbook to fleet ratio would be considered normal or what is required, while the historical average is closer to 20%. 

Regardless, fleet growth for this and next year will remain historically low, following a 22-year low for deliveries last year. From 1.2% gross fleet growth this year and 2.7% next year we expect that inefficiencies for older vessels and operational constraints from new regulations will ensure that real fleet growth is closer to zero.

content.title: Orderbook to fleet, current vs. historical

content.content:
That said, there appears to be some rebalancing in the cards over the next year and a half, where fleet growth will be the lowest for VLCCs and Suezmaxes and highest for Afra/LR2s and MRs, which means that the outperformance of the latter two over the past few years will likely subside. Overall, gross product tanker fleet growth is scheduled to pick up to 5.5% next year, vs. 1.6% for crude tankers.  

From 2026 onwards fleet growth may become more meaningful, which means the market outlook becomes more vulnerable to change in demand.

Ordering YTD has risen to an annualised pace which has only been surpassed a few year historically, while scrapping remains minimal. The 27m dwt which has already been ordered is nearly on par with last year's full year count of 28m. However, to accommodate for continued demand growth and the wall of phase-out candidates coming from the early 2000s newbuilding boom, ordering of such magnitude may be needed - not only now, but also going forward as eventually the oldest vessels will become obsolete, even from the shadow markets... 

Only two vessels have been confirmed scrapped this year, and while a handful more have been converted, on-paper phase-out has been minimal.

Already by 2026 nearly half the tanker fleet will be 15+ years old. While not relevant for phase-out, it does at least pose a challenge for those charterers who adhere to a strict 15 years age limit, and suggests these restrictions may be eased going forward. 

More relevant is the 20-25% of the fleet which will be 20+ years old in two years. Again, this does imply that average scrap age may to rise from the 10-year average of 21-22 years old for the biggest and 25+ years old for the smaller segments. Otherwise, the orderbook as is today would be insufficient to accomodate for demand growth and phase-out. We do, however, expect to see scrapping tick gently up from the most recent levels within a few years, and that gradual phase-out in the form of lower utilisation for older vessels will continue.
