content.content:
A solid quarter earnings-wise, with not much unregular market activity. YTD average TCE resides at $57,000 p.d.

The earnings level remained quite stable, with the lowest rates seen in mid-April, in the mid-30s range.  **The average daily Time Charter Equivalent for the VLGCs ended at $61,900 p.d.**, with the following per Baltic index: BLPG1 - $51,858, BLPG2 - $74,650, BLPG3 - $59,216. Total average resulting in a 16% decrease from Q2-2023, however, 24% above Q2-2022. The month of May performed with the highest earnings of $71,000 p.d.

We reiterate our solid forecast for the year in the $60k p.d. range, and expect 2H to bring the rates up even further, due to seasonal demand as well as a tight shipping market.

**U.S. Gulf/U.S. East Coast**
April: 86 in total/34 being spot
May: 87 in total/32 being spot
June: 91 in total, 27 being spot

**Middle East Gulf**
April: 81 in total/24 being spot
May: 86 in total/27 being spot
June: 76 in total/23 being spot

Due to the changing availability and restrictions at the Panama Canal, we have seen a big change in the sailing patterns of VLGCs in the last 8 months. The share of vessels going in ballast back to the U.S. Gulf/U.S. East Coast from the East, who choose to sail around the Cape of Good Hope have increased extensively since the beginning of the year. In June, over half of the vessels, 55% to be exact, chose the longer route rather than sail through the Panama Canal  - even though the availability at the canal has increased back to "normal levels".

For volumes lifted on VLGCs, the **United States** remains the dominating party, who **increased their exports by 4.9% quarter-on-quarter**. There was a slight increase in volumes from Qatar and the UAE, while Iran and Saudi Arabia rather saw some decreases.

Amid China importing 27% more in Q1 y/y, their imports in Q2 was down 2.5%. On a total YTD basis, China is up 14%. 
South Korea imported 50% more than they did in Q2-2023. These increases coming mainly with origin in the U.S. and Saudi Arabia.

The U.S. still remains the market leader in exports, with 53% of all VLGC liftings. The nation has exported over 26 million tonnes LPG in the 1H of 2024, which is 53% of its 2023 total exports (on VLGCs only). The inventory levels dropped extensively in Q1 due to increased domestic demand, however, in Q2 they have rebounded and the summer build-up has started. At the end of June, the stock holds 75.8 million barrels.

As the data displays, the U.S. has been consistent in production and consequently exports provided to the market. There are two different terminals (Nederland & Beaumont) that are undergoing expansion projects to increase their export capacity (of both LPG & ethane). These projects will first finalize in 2025 & 2026.

**The total fleet now comprises of 395 VLGCs**, where 16 are used for storage/semi-storage. 16 newbuildings have been delivered YTD, where 5 of these were in Q2. Another 5 are expected in the second half of the year. 

In the last 10 years, only 12 VLGCs have been scrapped. However, 13% of the fleet is now older than 20 years, and 9% above 25 years - which would indicate that the scrapping candidates are increasing extensively. However, due to the general positive health of the market, we do not see any incentives for scrapping of these vessel to have an uptake. Unless, the environmental regulations should force a harder hand on the operational requirements, or imposed age restrictions from ports and/or charterers.

**The orderbook-fleet ratio is at 23% with another 91 vessels on order.** There will be a slow fleet growth in the next 18 months, with only 12 newbuilds scheduled for 2025. However, combined in 2026 and 2027, 65 newbuilds are planned for delivery. This will result in a total fleet growth of 15%. 

All of the vessels in the orderbook are LPG dual-fuel, except for 7. There is currently 45 "VLACs" on order, which are capable of carrying ammonia as a cargo, at 98% capacity. These vessels will start to be delivered in 2H-2026, however, we anticipate that these vessels will enter the market as "regular" VLGCs, lifting LPG as a cargo.

The anticipated incremental Clean Ammonia Capacity to come before the next decade will not require these vessels for the trade. It will likely be absorbed by the Midsize Gas Carriers (MGCs), which is the segment that currently lifts most of seaborne ammonia. The MGC orderbook-fleet ratio is at 35%.

In the first half of 2024, 35 newbuilding orders have been placed, which is the equivalent to the total orders placed in 2023. This further demonstrates the increased interest in the VLGC sector from an investment perspective. We have seen many new owners entering the market with newbuilding orders the last 18 months. 

In terms of yard capacity, the situation remains tight, with limited availability left in 2H 2027. 7 newbuilding orders are already inked for delivery in 2028. 

Newbuilding prices have continued on an upward trajectory, with the current price-tag of around **$120 million for a DF VLGC, with no additional ammonia specs.**

After the transit restrictions was imposed in Q4 last year, the fluctuations of the three main waypoints for VLGCs, have increased. The water levels in the Panama Canal is soon “back to normal” after expected rainfall, and almost all restrictions have been retracted. Daily transit capacity is soon back to full, at 36 transits per day.

The share of laden transits around the COGH have increased by 115% from the 2023 average of 12.6 to YTD average of 29.3. This due to the major uncertainty that the Panama canal has brought upon the market. 

Going into the second half of the year, where Q4 tendsto be the most trafficked quarter of the year, the Panama Canal will still be facing the same challenges as in previous years. The orderbook for both LNG and containerships is huge, we therefore expect waiting days to hit new highs, and auction cost will likely follow suit. This will further increase the utilization of the longer route around COGH, pushing tonne-miles further. 

With only 12 newbuilds scheduled for delivery in 2025, **we believe the transit inefficiencies will contribute to a tight shipping market going forward.**

Q2 has seen the flattest spot charter rates in several years, with limited movement until the very end of the quarter. Despite long distances as a result of essentially no use of either of the canals, the availability lists have stayed long. The recent open arbitrage between East and West has further contributed to longer distances, and a significant drainage of tonnage in the West with a surge in vessels available in the East. As a result, the spot market has disconnected between the basins, and while Atlantic rates are on an upward trend, the East is lagging behind with plenty of ships to choose from. 

There have been both planned maintenance and unplanned outages, and production levels have thus remained a little below full capacity. There has been no commissioning of new liquefaction projects, except one cargo from Congo LNG. With 12 newbuild deliveries, there has been plenty of shipping capacity to support the long distances. Gas prices have climbed steadily upwards throughout the quarter, from single digit pricing at the start of the quarter, to JKM being in the 12-13 $/mmBtu range over the last few weeks. 

27 newbuild orders have been placed in Q2, dominated by phase 2 of ordering for the Qatar expansion projects. 

Finally, there have been some positive news on liquefaction project FIDs, with Ruwais LNG reaching FID end of June, adding 9.6 MT of capacity from 2027. Additionally, the 3.3 MTPA Cedar FLNG reached FID, and the FLNG for Genting's 1.2 MTPA FLNG has officially started construction at Wison New Energies. All eyes remain on the US pause in approving projects, and how the process will change as a result of the pause. 

On the topic of geopolitics, a new raft of sanctions against Russia have been adopted by the EU. This package prohibits the reload and ship-to-ship transfer of Russian LNG in European terminals. This will largely affect volumes from Yamal, which are loaded on to non-Ice Class ships mostly in Zeebrugge, Fluxys and Montoir. No sanctions have been adopted on European imports of Russian LNG, as long the import terminal is connected to the European grid.

Q2 spot charter rates were on average the lowest seen since 2020. Rates have remained at a relatively flat floor for the majority of the quarter, but some small jumps have been seen in the Atlantic towards the end of the quarter, while remaining flat in the East. This is a result of an open arbitrage for USG cargoes to head East, which has lead to an abundance of available ships in the Pacific, while some struggle to find a ship in the Atlantic. With EU storage levels around the same as this time last year, and with muted industrial demand, LNG demand has been subdued, although recent heat waves in Asia have drawn volume East. Current EU storage levels are at almost 80% full, well on track to reach the target of 90% by November. The current difference in spot charter rates in East and West is about 30k $/day. Prompt availability has dwindled significantly from the highs seen at the start of the quarter, and close to all prompt availability is found in the Pacific. Egypt's recent tender for around 20 cargoes was also feared to demand a lot of chartering in, but for now seems to have been awarded largely to traders with existing large fleets. 

Multi-month to 1-year periods have firmed up throughout the quarter, as players seek to cover winter demand. However, with nearly 50 newbuild deliveries for the remainder of the year, and likely just a few commissioning cargoes added to the global LNG supply, some also believe there should be plenty of vessels to choose from going into winter. 

Long-term charter rates have continued their descent, as the market prices in the anticipated softer market in the next couple of years and that the large orderbook is delivering well in advance of the liquefaction project start-ups. Longer term charters are still priced at a premium to shorter term, as market tightening is expected in the second half of the decade. 

With a slow-down in both the newbuild price and interest rate hikes, the 10-year rate for a newbuild has remained relatively flat throughout the quarter, although liquidity in this sector of the market is low and very few deals of this length have been recorded.

Although charter rates have not caused much excitement, the first half of the year has been far from boring, with more than 170 spot fixtures concluded or on subjects. In 2023, we recorded a total number of spot fixtures of just over 200, so this year has seen significantly more activity. 2024 so far is well above the fixing activity at the same stage in 2022 and 2023, and in line with 2021 fixing levels. Multi-month fixtures in H1 are recorded at just above 30; the highest levels seen in years. 78% of short-term fixtures (< 3 years) so far this year have been sublets, a slight decrease 85% in Q1.

Comparing with Q2 previous years, multi-month and the rest of short-term (up to 3 years) fixture counts are close to the last two years' levels. The spot activity count is up compared to Q2 in 2022 and 2023 but the number of fixed days are a little behind, indicating shorter charter periods. 

The number of 1-year deals stands at 7 for Q2; about the same as in Q2 last year. Only one of these deals was for a 2-stroke vessel (14%), whereas in Q1 four out of five 1-year deals were for 2-strokes. All the 1-year deals done so far this year (12, which is the same as in H1 last year), have been sublets. There have not been any 3-5 year deals so far this year. 

Note that the graphs below do not include deals still on subjects, and total numbers are likely to increase slightly.

content.title: Short term fixtures by sublet vs independent owners

content.content:
98 MT of LNG was loaded in Q2, which is slightly lower than the two previous years. The quarter has been characterized by both planned maintenance and unplanned outages, which have kept traded levels a little low. The United States remains the top exporter, and 21% of LNG loaded in Q2 came from there, closely followed by Australia (19.5%) and Qatar (18.8%). The top three importers are unchanged, with China importing 18 MT; more than 3 MT more than Japan and 8 MT more than South Korea. 

LNGC transits via the Suez Canal remain at a minimum; two voyages to reach Aqaba in Jordan, so not crossing the Bab el Mandeb strait, as well as one steamer, Asya Energy, which did a full Red Sea transit in June. Panama Canal use is also limited, and less than 3% of voyages from the United States to Asia utilized the Panama Canal in Q2. Therefore, voyages are long, and while traded LNG levels are lower than previous years, the long distances have pushed tonne-miles to historical highs. Naturally, this has increased the fleet utilization from last years' levels, but the extensive and early fleet additions have ensured that there is more than enough tonnage to handle the tonne-miles. Fleet utilization, calculated as actual tonne-miles performed divided by a theoretical tonne-mile capacity, is lower so far this year than it was in 2021, when increased US-to-Asia voyages stretched the fleet and caused high speeds and much quicker tonne-mile growth than fleet growth. As speeds have been slightly higher than last year's very low levels, tonne-time growth has been much lower than tonne-miles. 

In Q2, 50% of US LNG went to Europe, down from 68% in Q1. This has in turn resulted in a 10% increase in US-to-Asia trade, as well as to the Caribbean and South America. In Q2, 16% of Qatar LNG went to Europe, lower than the 23% in Q2 last year, but up versus the 12% seen in Q1 this year. All voyages from Qatar to Europe have taken the long voyage via Cape of Good Hope.

Looking at the first half of the year, Argentina, the United Kingdom and Greece have reduced imports the most in year-on-year percentage change, with reductions by 68%, 58%, and 54%. For the UK, this has meant a reduction in the number of cargoes from 149 throughout 2023, to only 63 in 1H 2024. As for increased imports, Philippines, the Virgin Islands, Vietnam, Jordan and Egypt have all imported cargoes this year, and did not import any in 2023. Looking at the largest increases in number of cargoes imported, China and India dominate at the top, with 58 and 49 more cargoes than in 1H 2023. This is a 12% and a 31% growth in imports, respectively. 

EU storage levels are high again this year, as the draw-down during winter was limited due to warm weather. Current levels of around 77% full suggest the EU is well on track for 90% full by November. Russian pipeline gas is still flowing through the Ukraine Gas Transit and Turkstream, at even higher levels than in 2023. However, the transit contract for Russian pipeline gas via the Ukraine Gas Transit expires at the end of the year, and Ukraine will not extend the contract. This means that some landlocked countries in Europe will need to secure capacity from other countries.

The fleet grew by 12 ships in Q2; a total of 22 so far this year. That brings the total fleet to 650 live vessels, with seven remaining in layup. 27 orders were placed in Q2, of which almost all were for the Qatar expansion project. The orderbook currently stands at 349 vessels (including the eight ordered by ADNOC, which were technically ordered in Q3), which gives an orderbook-to-fleet ratio of almost 54%. 

35% of the orderbook are for the Qatar Expansion, with 122 vessels, while 23 vessels remain charter-free. The orderbook now extends all the way into 2031, with the furthest deliveries being the Q-max vessels ordered at Hudong-Zhonghua. Some vessel deliveries are also being brought forward into 2024, as yards make space for the huge delivery numbers scheduled for the coming years.

Only one conventional LNGC has been sold for scrap so far this year, the 1994-built YK Sovereign (in addition, the small-scale 1996-built Surya Aki). The steamers therefore still hold a large share of the fleet, with 33% (including STRH and STaGE).  However, the 2-strokes have now taken over as the major component, with 229 live vessels and a 35% share. 

On average, the LNGC fleet is young, with more than half of the vessels less than 10 years old. However, a total of 17 vessels are older than 30 years old, and as many as 94 are older than 20. 150 LNGCs are smaller than 140k cbm, which in today's market is an increasingly unattractive size. 

Activity in the secondhand market has been high, with 15 secondhand sales registered so far this year. While some sales have been for 2-strokes (JP Morgan vessels sold to Venture Global), the majority of sales candidates are for older, redelivering steamers. The number of sales candidates is expected to continue to increase, as a wave of redelivering steamers are expected for the remainder of the year and next year.

content.title: Live fleet by size range and age

content.content:
While a closed Suez and an open arbitrage has increased tonne-miles significantly, the effect on rates has been limited. This is driven by the fact that fundamentals again drive the market, and not the cargo values as has been seen previous years. There are enough ships in the fleet to do the transport work, and quick deliveries have countered the effect of higher tonne-miles. However, low production levels have compensated for longer distances to some extent, and higher production levels are expected as we approach winter. Seasonally, this happens every year as maintenance periods end, and this year some commissioning cargoes are also expected from Plaqumines, Greater Tortue and Fast LNG. Higher production levels will further increase tonne-miles, and stretch the fleet, likely resulting in the seasonal winter peak in the spot charter rates. With plenty of capacity to speed up, the fleet is, at least theoretically, capable of handling this winters' trade flows even with a sustained open arbitrage. However, cold weather, outages and geopolitical tension are all factors which can reduce the effect of the fundamentals, and increase the risk of being short shipping. 

Oversupply of ships is expected in the next few years, as vessels deliver quicker and earlier than liquefaction project volumes. While tightening is expected already next year as projects come online (considering current start-up plans), a tightening does not mean tight. As can be seen on the below graph, the ships per mtpa of liquefaction are increasing significantly over 2024 and 2025. While this looks dramatic, more ships are needed per new ton of liquefaction, as long-haul US volumes come online. Focus remains on the US pause in non-FTA approvals, which largely affects liquefaction, and shipping demand, towards the end of the decade. The latest news is that a federal judge in Louisiana has ordered an end to the pause, stating that the policy is unlawful. What this means for US non-approved projects remains to be seen. Nonetheless, the pause has lasted for almost half a year, and has likely already had a delaying effect on some projects. We do however still expect more liquefaction project FIDs, both from the United States and other regions, and more LNGCs will be needed in 2028+, to cover demand from new projects and fleet replacement. However, this demand is likely well within current yard capacity.

Year-to-date, the Baltic Dry Index have averaged 59% higher than the same period last year, so far in line with our general view that 2024 would be an "upcycle" year and that a 50% or more increase is normal to see during such years. The upturn has primarily been driven by the Capesize segment, with the BCI5TC up 92% year on year. The Panamax 5TC, Supramax 10TC and the Handysize 7TC are up by 35%, 33.5% and 25%, respectively. We believe the year on year percentage increases will rise further during the coming two months for all segments, as we expect a much stronger summer than last year. 

Next year, we see several downside risks emerging from the second half of the year onward, likely translating into slightly lower earnings averages in 2025 than in 2024. Weakness could primarily be felt in the Capesize segment, as China's import demand is the primary bearish factor we see. 
We expect a more bearish year in 2026, but only if the indicators we rely on for our view of a weaker 2025 continues to worsen over the coming quarters. Regarding asset values, we expect little change over the next year. Prices are too high to expect much upside, notwithstanding our bullish view on earnings, whereas downside should be limited by the tight yard capacity and upwards pressure on newbuilding prices. 

All in all, we maintain our general view of a bullish 2024, a slightly lower market in 2025, and a more bearish 2026.

content.content:
Shipment volume growth remains firmly above supply growth. Positive growth has been seen for all commodity groups. Coal shipment volume growth turned positive over the last month, with all the major exporting countries seeing rising year on year growth rates the last month. Demand is still lacking in developed economies, however. Europe, Japan and Korea's imports are lower by 27%, 7% and 5% year on year, respectively. A slight recovery in demand can be expected if the manufacturing recovery continues, and otherwise it will all depend on other energy sources, with weather as always being important in this regard. 
China's imports are higher by nearly 9% year on year, which we doubt can be sustained through the remainder of this year seeing as the steel sector is weaker than last year. Further, thermal power generation fell year on year in May, as heavy rainfalls in the country has caused Hydropower generation to surge. This latter point is a major reason why the Panamax and Supramax markets have dropped in the Pacific the last weeks. 

Iron ore exports are up 4.8% year on year, with all the major exporters contributing positively. Brazil's export growth continues at around 10%, whereas India's exports are up by nearly 20%. 
China is driving most of the demand growth, with the country's imports up over 5% through June. However, consumption of imported iron ore in China is down by 3.5% year on year, meaning the import growth has been held up by inventory building. This raises a risk for next year's import demand, as stimulus efforts continues to be unsuccessful in reviving the property sector. Falling Chinese import growth could cause the global economic cycle to turn downwards through next year, as displayed in more detail in the macro section of this report. 
World ex-China iron ore imports continues to recover, with imports up by 4.4% year on year. This is driven by the global recovery in manufacturing, as seen from improving manufacturing PMIs in almost all regions. Still, it seems like the recovery is in its early innings, meaning more upside can be expected for the World ex-China's import growth over the coming year.  

Grain exports are up 5.3% year on year, driven by a near doubling in Argentina's grain exports. Brazil's exports are lower than last year, however. Going forward, the IGC expects higher Black Sea grains exports than last season, and also higher exports from the US in the autumn. 

Minor bulks exports are up by 5.4% year on year, supported by the global economic recovery as well as continued growth in Bauxite exports. The 5% or more growth rate can be expected to be maintained over the next year, as we expect the economic cycle to be strong until then. 

On the distance side, the Suez Canal issues along with higher exports in the Atlantic gives further support to fundamentals. Ton-time growth was up by 7% year on year through May, compared to total shipment volume growth of 5.4% through June.

content.content:
Most macro economic indicators continues to improve, though some pockets of weakness remains - especially in the Eurozone. As per the latest reports from S&P Global, a recovery in the region is expected later this summer or early autumn, however. The region's bulk commodity imports have increased noticeably from the bottom, although it remains far below previous cycle peaks like 2021 or 2018. Should import demand return to previous cycle peak levels, it is likely to result in further upside for the dry bulk markets, as the Atlantic basin has under performed relative to the Pacific - which is not common. Although an upturn in demand can be expected going forward, a return to previous cycle peak levels is hard to expect. A costly was in Ukraine, strikes amongst farmers, increased car imports from China, the "green shift", lingering inflation and high interest rates are factors that weigh heavily on growth in dry bulk related sectors. 
In other developed markets like Japan and Korea, manufacturing PMIs indicated a return to expansion in June. South Korea's manufacturing orders increased at the fastest pace since February 2022 (the beginning of the previous downcycle) whereas Japan's manufacturing output rose for the first time in over a year. Like Europe, these markets are a zero growth region, but the cycles are important for dry bulk markets nonetheless. Last year, Japan imported nearly 400 million tons of dry bulk commodities, South Korea imported 260 million tons, and the Eurozone imported nearly 400 million tons. All of South East Asia imported slightly more than Japan and Europe (for the first time), and this region is going to be a long-term driver of demand, but the importance of developed economies is huge still. 
Regarding South East Asia, Vietnam's new manufacturing orders surged to a near record high in June, which along with a notable increased in Thailand's activity brought the ASEAN manufacturing PMI to new cycle heights. China and India's manufacturing PMIs also remains in expansion, though in the case of China this does not accurately represent the conditions relevant to dry bulk, as the steel and iron ore sector is in contraction compared to last year. 
On that note, the lower left chart displays the importance of China's bulk commodity imports for the global economic cycle. The OECD G-20 economic indicator lags China's imports growth by roughly one year, which suggest that the global upturn end next year as China's import growth have dropped from 15% to 5% over the past 9 months. A further drop in import growth is likely in our view, as imported iron ore consumption is 3.5% lower than last year, but iron ore imports are up by 5.5%. The resultant inventory building, weak credit growth, a failing property sector recovery and high iron ore imports the second half of last year strongly suggest growth could fall to 0% or below that by the end of this year. If that happens, the leading indication for the OECD G-20 economic indicator will be similar to what it was entering 2022 or 2019, and thus pose a significant downside risk for dry bulk markets and the global economy from the second half of 2025 onward. 
Along with that, there are early signs that US liquidity conditions will tighten from mid 2025, and that the boost given to the global economy from dropping inflation rates will be over from the start of 2025. A resurgence in inflation might even become a problem next year, as several commodity prices have risen significantly the last 9 months. In the asset value section of this report, it is displayed that the price of gold often leads the rest of the commodity space, and on that basis it seems likely that oil prices could rise significantly over the next year. The lower right chart shows how oil prices could lead the ups and downs of the Baltic Dry Index. The indication is already of weakening momentum from mid 2025, and if oil prices stays around current levels the next 6 months the lead will suggest a negative year on year Baltic Dry Index in 2026. 

To summarize how we see the cycle developing, expect further upside until the middle of 2025, after which downside risks will start to increase.

content.content: Summary and recent tanker market development

Rates YTD have been less volatile than the last two years, but have rather hovered around strong levels. The highest YTD rate average is seen for LR2s, with TC1 TCE of around $56k/d. VLCC, Suezmax and Aframax earnings have been around $46-47k/d whilst MRs have seen continued relative strength at $37k/d. 

Seasonality has already kicked in for the biggest vessels, and we expect some contagion also to the smaller vessel sizes in the near term. A few months down the line, however, there is a set-up to support a very strong end to the year with expected volume increases on top of continued trade diversion among a geopolitical scene that does not appear to change anytime soon. 

We still believe that rates will realign to something closer to the norm across the segments over the next two years, with fleet growth picking up for the segments which have enjoyed the relatively strongest earnings, and oil demand/supply fundamentals also likely leading to bigger demand gains for the larger vessels. There is upside risk to our forecasts going forward the longer geopolitical upheaval persists, but we also note macroeconomic risks to the downside..

Overall tanker volumes YTD have declined marginally vs. the same period last year, with crude oil slightly lower and products slightly higher. The recent decline in crude oil volumes is nothing out of the ordinary and some more downside can be expected near-term due to continued OPEC+ cuts and seasonal demand in exporting areas. Similarly, we could see slight downside also for products in the coming few months. 

We expect a sharper recovery especially for crude volumes from September onwards due to easing seasonal demand and increasing production in key areas. The IEA expects that non-OPEC+ production may rise by more than 1 mbpd by year-end, a large portion of which may need to find a home in the East - if not stored in the West.. There are, however, some indications that OPEC+ production may not rise as much as energy agencies predict - especially in the U.S., which means the OPEC+ may be able to unwind some cuts like recently outlined.

LR rates have softened recently, after a few brief but significant spikes in recent months. Our tracking suggests that the switching of LR2s from the dirty back into the clean trade has stopped, as rate premiums have now eased. However, a number of VLCCs and Suezmaxes have cleaned up to take CPP cargoes from the Middle East and India to the West - making up as much as a 2-3% product tanker fleet growth equivalent in dwt terms, albeit short-term.

The Red Sea situation has not changed much recently, despite renewed headlines at times suggesting progress in ceasefire talks. If anything, the Houthis' attacks appear to have become more accurate, posing a greater threat to those still opting to transit. Therefore, there has not been a substantial change in transit volumes and COGH diversion, other than the cleaning up of larger vessels for improved economies of scale. 

Through May, crude oil volumes transiting the Bab-el-Mandeb strait were 1.6 mbpd lower than the 2023 average, and products 2.6 mbd lower (-61% and -68%). Meanwhile, crude oil going around the COGH increased by 1 mbpd and products by 2 mbpd (+19% and +246%). Preliminary numbers suggest this has led to an overall 3% increase in tanker tonne-miles, heavily skewed toward product tankers.

The oil market this year looks fairly balanced - according to the IEA it will on average be 0.3 mbpd undersupplied with draws tilted toward the second and third quarters. This is fairly in line with the Brent forward curve backwardation which has steepened again recently. Going into the first half of next year, however, the IEA's balances imply oversupply of 0.75 mbpd, without any OPEC+ cut reversal. That means little room for the group to actually unwind cuts, although we suspect the IEA's balances include a bit too pessimistic demand forecasts and a bit too optimistic non-OPEC+ production expectations.

content.title: Oil supply and demand, implied balance

content.content:
Chinese apparent oil demand declined in May vs. previous months and the same month last year. Still, YTD it remains up 6.4% vs. the same period last year (down from a growth rate of 8.8% until April). Refinery runs were also slightly lower, and the YTD average is now down -0.9% y/y over last year. Crude oil imports, meanwhile, grew slightly over preceding months, although were also lower than the same month last year. All told, this points to a weaker picture for oil demand in China – which begs the question whether this is a temporary setback or a levelling out from the strong growth seen over the last year and a half. Refinery margins did spike briefly going into June, but have since receded… 

Some of this decline is seasonal, especially for refinery runs, and a demand recovery may be expected going forward. The IEA expects some 300 kbpd of demand growth from China until year-end, which should support continued strong crude oil import demand.

content.title: China apparent main oil products demand
China available crude oil vs. refinery runs

content.content:
While there is also contradictory travel activity data, the EIA's weekly implied main products demand estimates show an underwhelming start to the driving season. Should this apparent weakness persist, there is greater potential for a (even bigger) crude oil export push going forward. This is not a base case, but something to ponder going into the second half of the year. 

The U.S. oil rig count has been steadily dropping for some time, but has been offset by continued productivity gains in key basins so that production has tracked sideways in recent months. Expectations are that these productivity gains will continue, with the EIA forecasting about 400 kbpd higher production by year-end, about 100 kbpd lower than the IEA's forecast. However, there are also less optimistic voices, suggesting production has already topped out for now and may remain flattish for some time to come...

In its recent Oil 2024 report the IEA outlined oil market expectations until 2030, predicting peak oil demand in 2029. The report has received widespread pushback on its too optimistic assumptions about alternative energy sources and electrification, among other things. Even with that, the agency predicts 3.4 mbpd oil demand growth between 2023 and 2029, with strong growth in Asia and Africa partly offset by declining demand in North America and Europe. 

The IEA also predicts strong supply gains from Non-OPEC (2.9 mbpd), processing gains (0.1 mbpd), Biofuels (0.6 mbpd) NGLs (1.1 mbpd) over the 2023-30 period. This may also prove optimistic, especially given the implied growing oversupply this leaves for the oil market over the period. Still, it does imply continued strong potential for West-East crude oil trade to come and therefore solid tonne-mile demand growth especially for the biggest vessels.

Refinery margins have overall weakened again recently, and are now relatively in line with historical averages. Some of this may be due to higher refinery runs after maintenance, but at the same time demand should be rising in tandem. Thus, margins have not displayed the same signs of strength as the crude oil price curves. There has at times this year been suggestions that we may see run cuts or reduced ramp-up, and therefore there is some risk to the downside for product tanker volumes vs. earlier estimates. For now, however, most recent energy agency refinery run estimates have remained unchanged.

According to the IEA's estimates, the refinery capacity vs. demand changes over the next few years may reverse some of the East-West trade growth trend from recent years, which has been a driver of product tanker demand. Volumes will increase according to these estimates, which is the more important part of the tonne-mile equation, but there may not be a big distance driver as more intra-regional trade may be a result.

YTD tanker deliveries have been few and far between. Only 3m dwt has been delivered, and although the delivery pace will pick up from here it will still be marginal with 4.5m dwt scheduled before year-end. That makes up to a total gross fleet growth for the year of 1.2% - hardly a lot, and although next year's growth picks up, 2.7% gross will not be a lot either. Still, for the segments which have fared the best the last couple of years fleet growth is set to pick up more, which may even the battlefield somewhat. 

Whilst crude tanker fleet growth looks set to remain very low, products pick up in coming years toward something closer to historical averages. Recently too, there has been some rebalancing between the segments, with the Suezmaxes and VLCCs cleaning up to lift CPP cargoes proving the fluidity of the tanker fleet and that it is all inter-connected.

The orderbook to fleet ratio has grown to 8.6%. There are more orders which have been reported or rumoured but not yet materialized, which will likely push the overall orderbook to fleet toward 10%. Still, that is low in a historical context and insufficient to enable fleet renewal as will eventually be needed. 

That is not to say that we expect any meaningful scrapping in the relatively near term due to strong earnings and outlook, but eventually time will take its toll on the oldest part of the fleet, mostly in the form of lower utilisation.

In just two years, around 20-25% of the different fleets will be 20+ years old, and much more difficult to trade. Even if we do not see a pick-up in scrapping we expect that lower utilisation for this ageing part of the fleet will offset much of the overall deliveries the next few years. This means there is little effective fleet growth to accommodate for demand growth - which there likely will be. Hence, we believe that more ordering will be needed, especially for the segments in which orderbooks are still low.

content.content:
Owners look to have taken the latter point to heart, with 19.5m dwt ordered so far this year which is on an annualised pace to reach more than 40m dwt for the full year - well above last year's 28m dwt. 

If, however, 18+ years old vessels continue to see about 30% lower utilisation than normal for younger vessels, demand grows in line with the historical trend, and there is NO scrapping, closer to 35m dwt needs to be ordered and delivered each year going forward to balance the tanker market.

In our previous report last week, we wrote the following:

Year-to-date, the Baltic Dry Index have averaged 55% higher than the same period last year, so far in line with our general view that 2024 would be an "upcycle" year and that a 50% or more increase is normal to see during such years. The upturn has primarily been driven by the Capesize segment, with the BCI5TC up 93% year on year. The Panamax 5TC, Supramax 10TC and the Handysize 7TC are up by 30%, 26.5% and 20%, respectively. We believe the year on year percentage increases will rise further during the coming three months for all segments, as we expect a much stronger summer than last year. We base that viewpoint on leading indicators like industrial metals prices, iron ore prices, steel prices and the OECD diffusion index. Additionally, fundamental data is more firmly positive than last year, as total ton-time growth averaged 1.9% the first four months of 2023 versus 6.4% in 2024. With all this considered, it is very hard to expect anything else than strong fundamentals for the remainder of 2024, and higher earnings averages during the second half of the year than the first. 
Next year, we see several downside risks emerging from the second half of the year onward, likely translating into slightly lower earnings averages in 2025 than in 2024. We expect a more bearish year in 2026, but only if the indicators we rely on for our view of a weaker 2025 continues to worsen over the coming quarters. Regarding asset values, we expect little change over the next year. Prices are too high to expect much upside, notwithstanding our bullish view on earnings, whereas downside should be limited by the tight yard capacity and upwards pressure on newbuilding prices. 

All in all, we maintain our general view of a bullish 2024, a slightly lower market in 2025, and a more bearish 2026.

We reiterate our viewpoints given in our previous report, namely that there is likely to be little change to second hand values the next year to year and a half. Continued upwards pressure on newbuilding prices, long lead time on delivery and solid market earnings is likely to prevent prices from falling. However, price levels are too high to expect much, if any, upside going forward either. For Kamsarmaxes down to Handysizes, current prices puts required earnings in the high teens, and that is with the assumption that one is able to eventually sell the vessel at the current curve. 

The below charts shows 1 year time charter rates and spot market earnings against asset values. We believe the following adjustments have to be made to either earnings or values in order to bring the spread between earnings and values closer to historical levels (for Japanese tonnage):

Handysize: 1 year time charter rates either have to rise above 15.000 USD pd, or the 10 year old value have to fall to around 17 million USD. 
Supramax: 1 year time charter rates either have to rise to around 19.000 USD pd, or the 10 year old value have to fall below 20 million USD. 
Kamsarmax: 1 year time charter rates either have to rise above 20.000 USD pd, or the 10 year old value have to fall to 23-24 million USD. 
For Capesizes, we assess the spread between earnings and asset values as fair basis historical correlations. 

We believe 1 year time charter rates will make year-to-date highs for all segments during the second half of this year. This will serve to close the spreads somewhat for the small and mid-sized segments, and leave the potential for a bit further upside in Capesize values.

content.content:
As gone through in our monthly reports over the past 6 months, the global economy has entered an upcycle. Various indices published by the OECD and S&P Global confirms this, and as usual during economic upcycles, stock markets, commodity prices and dry bulk markets are significantly higher than the previous year. Notwithstanding this, there is not the same broad-based strength this year as for example through 2021 or 2017. Manufacturing growth in Europe is still largely absent, probably due to the ongoing war in Ukraine and lingering inflation problems. The Netherlands manufacturing PMI did return to growth at the latest reading in April, however. 
Further, the manufacturing recovery in the United States lost some momentum in April, with the PMI barely remaining in expansionary territory. That the cyclical upswing in Europe and the US remain relatively weak compared to in Asia and emerging markets is probably why the dry bulk market in the North Atlantic have been relatively lower than other regions so far this year. The high market levels seen in the Pacific this year usually causes the North Atlantic markets to spike above Pacific levels for a few weeks, but there has been no such squeezes this year. 
Though the cyclical upswing is stronger in Asia than in Europe and the US, factors like China's property sector and a very weak Japanese Yen are weighing on growth in that region. China's steel and iron ore sector is weaker than last year as infrastructure and manufacturing growth cannot counter-act weakness in the property sector. In April, the country's total social financing growth went negative for the first time in at least twenty years, despite a host of stimulus measures undertaken by the government since mid 2022. 
This most likely means that China's year on year dry bulk import growth will continue to trend downwards, and perhaps even go negative by the end of this year. The bottom left chart displays that China's dry bulk import growth leads the global economic cycle by about one year, so if China's import growth turns negative by the end of this year it would strongly indicate that the economic cycle and therefore the dry bulk market cycle will start turning downwards from Q3 2025 onwards. 
The bottom right chart also points towards a similar development. The preceding 18 months change of energy prices usually leads the economic cycle by 18 months, and this tells us that the positive boost the global economy has got from dropping inflation rates will last until mid-2025, but start to wane after that. As shown in the asset values and period rates section of this report, oil prices usually lags gold prices by about 1 year. Should this correlation continue to hold, oil prices will go up significantly over the next year, which in turn would be a bearish indication for late 2025 and all of 2026. 
Before that period, fundamentals should be strong, however. It is likely that earnings will average higher during the second half of this year than the first, as pointed to by the economic growth index lead shown on the top right, the OECD diffusion index on the top left, as well as market seasonality.

Tanker market strength continues, with rates overall holding at quite firm levels going into what is normally a seasonally slower period. Apart from LR strength in the East, building on Red Sea evasion, rates across tanker segments are slightly more aligned than over the past couple of years. 

We believe the rest of the year and onwards will bring further normalisation, with the biggest vessels benefiting from a potentially stronger demand set-up and lower fleet growth than for smaller sizes. 

In the near term we expect rather flattish rate development going into what is normally a seasonally weaker period. Oil production increases and low fleet growth may offset some of the 'normal' seasonally softer factors through the summer, although some softer patches cannot be ruled out.

Rates strengthened again in May. For VLCCs this was driven by a tick up in cargo counts (likely due to timing) and correspondingly shorter position lists. The MEG-Far East average VLCC TCE in May to date has been $53k/day, up from $42k/d in April and slightly above our $50k/d bull case forecast for May. With a softening trend over the last week the full month average may end up closer to our forecast. 

Per our bull case forecast curve we expect rates to remain at strong levels through the next month or two before potentially dipping into what is normally the weakest months of the year. However, risk could be on the upside toward the end of the summer when seasonal demand in oil producing countries tails off and exports may  increase.

With a strong(er) macroeconomic backdrop and increased geopolitical tension YTD rates have held firm, and we expect further strength - akin to our bull case scenario. There could also be upside risk also to our bull case, both through the remainder of this year and next year if both the economy (and by extension oil demand) and geopolitical events do not subside. 

With very low expected fleet growth this and the next two years, the main downside risks to the outlook remain on the demand side. The macroeconomic development could be fragile with historically high debt levels globally and some patches of weakness, although the development so far has surprised positively. Reversal of trade diversion due to geopolitical conflicts may also negatively affect tonne-miles, although for now conflict resolition does not seem imminent.

Overall tanker volumes have developed sideways to slightly lower lately, in line with a normal seasonal trend. Although crude oil production is expected to rise going forward, higher domestic consumption in key production areas through the summer means volumes are likely to trend sideways in coming months. 

The exception to this may be if the OPEC+ decides to reverse some cuts into the second half of the year. The broad consensus expectation, however, is that the group will stay put. Some signs in the physical market of sufficient supply supports this, and while energy agencies forecast a shortage of crude oil in the second half of this year next year looks more balanced.

Tonne-miles, meanwhile, have risen YTD. Through the first four months, preliminary data shows 3% higher tonne-miles vs. the same period last year. This increase is largely driven by Red Sea evasion as overall tanker volumes over the same period were 1% lower y/y. 

In the second half of the year, after peak summer oil demand ebbs, seaborne volumes are again slated to rise, and as West-East trade is by then likely to be the primary driver, tonne-mile demand should rise further. This is mostly expected to boost the larger tanker segments. 

For now, however, the West-East arbitrage has narrowed despite the signs of a weaker physical oil market in the Atlantic basin. The latter is something to keep an eye on as further weakness and a following re-opening of the West-East arbitrage to a greater extent could spur some life into the VLCC market..

content.title: Relative pricing, WTI and Brent vs. Dubai, adj. for fwd. curve

content.content: Red Sea volumes remain significantly lower, and a larger portion of what used to go through has found its way around Africa. Through April, crude oil volumes transiting the Bab-el-Mandeb strait had declined by nearly 1.6 mbpd while products had declined by nearly 2.6 mbpd vs. the 2023 average. At the same time, crude oil passing the Cape of Good Hope had increased by 1 mbpd and products by 2 mbpd. Hence, still it is not a one-for-one shift, with some more oil trading locally, but the overall tonne-mile effect remains meaningful.

content.title: Cape of Good Hope passage by product

content.content: Volumes have largely moved sideways, in line with a seasonal pattern so far this year, but oil market balances point to upside going forward. Both oil demand and supply are expected to rise materially in coming months, and further next year. A tighter oil market going forward is priced in, with a backwardated oil price forward curve (although diesel is in contango..) and refinery margins which remain above historical averages (although have softened somewhat lately).

content.title: Brent 7-1 months forward spread vs. oil market balance

content.content:
In its most recent monthly report, the IEA's implied balance points to a slightly tighter market than previously expected through the remainder of the year. Global oil supply is expected to rise by 0.6, 1.0 and 0.3 mbpd Q/Q in Q2, Q3 and Q4, respectively. Most all of that is driven by non-OPEC+, but still there would be room for the OPEC+ to lift production in the second half. That does not seem to be the market's expectation, however. Given the prevailing market narrative, that would likely give quite a bit softer oil prices (which in itself should be able to stimulate some demand upside...), but a bigger problem, perhaps, for the OPEC+ is that next year's balances imply an oversupplied market - even if the group does not reverse cuts. 

Non-OPEC+ production is expected to increase by 1.4 mbpd y/y both this and next year. The U.S. is still expected to contribute the most, with 640 kbpd this year and 580 kbpd next year, although this is a lower market share than in previous years with Brazil, Canada and Guyana taking up a growing share.

OECD inventories declined to a 20-year low in March, contrary to preliminary data in last month’s report which pointed to a bigger build. Preliminary April data point to a build. With a growing surplus of crude oil in the Atlantic basin due to stagnant demand and growing supply, there could be room for further inventory builds going forward. However, economics currently do not support that, and hence there could rather be room for more West-East trade. 

Implied Chinese crude oil balances still point to steady crude oil inventory builds, although various satelite tracking services point to stock draws earlier this year. Some of the difference may be explained by building oil products inventories.

Refinery margins have largely softened recently, indicating somewhat weaker underlying demand. Especially diesel/gasoil margins have come off, to something closer to historical averages, with the forward curve also flipping into contango. Earlier this year there was a bigger discrepancy between Western and Eastern refinery margins, but these have levelled slightly in recent weeks, which could give less East-West trade opportunities.

Overall, as margins remain somewhat above the historical averages and new refineries come onstream, refinery runs are expected to reach new all-time-highs this year - 1 mbpd higher than last year. Next year too, runs are expected to rise, by 0.7 mbpd. 

While this bodes well for product tanker demand, one thing to consider is the impact of the start-up of the Dangote refinery in Nigeria and the elusive Dos Boccas in Mexico (when or if). Once fully operational, these are likely to alleviate some of the Atlantic basin gasoil/diesel shortages. 

In 2021 and 2022 Europe (ex. Turkey) imported about 650 kbpd of gasoil/diesel from Russia. In 2023 the replacement of Russian barrels came in the form of a 300 kbpd decline in overall imports (lower demand), and about 100 kbpd higher imports from each of the Middle East, Asia (mainly India) and North America. As the Dangote and Dos Bocas refineries combined are likely to produce more gasoil/diesel than Europe has recently imported from the Middle East and Asia, this leg of the last year's tonne-mile increase may at some point reverse.

The orderbook to fleet remains on the low side, although keeps creeping up. There is still a long way to go before the ratio hits figures which would historically be associated with (too) high fleet growth.
Regardless, fleet growth between 2024-26 will be low, and although there remains open capacity for 2027 deliveries at yards, this is not likely to become a very high fleet growth year either.

content.title: Historical deliveries and orderbook by segment

content.content: The highest relative fleet growth in coming years is expected for the smaller segments - perhaps the flipside of relatively stronger earnings the past years. VLCC deliveries this and next year are few and far between, and although the delivery tallies rise in 2026 and 2027, these years may also be relatively low in a historical context.

content.content:
Ordering has picked up this year, although the pace has slowed somewhat most recently. That is, for confirmed orders at least, as there still remains a number of reported or rumoured orders which could lift the tally further in coming months. Still, that may be needed, considering the outlook for continued demand growth, limited deliveries in coming years and an already quite tight tanker market balance. 

Meanwhile, only three vessels have been scrapped year to date, one Suez, one Afra and one Handy, following just slightly more than a handful of vessels last year. As earnings remain strong, and the outlook is mainly a positive one, we do not expect to see a whole lot of scrapping, other than the odd vessel here or there, also going forward.

Last week, we suggested that the market downtrend that began in mid-March could reverse within the next month. 
Still, we had expected the turnaround to come a bit later than what has been the case (late May/early June). 

The reason for expecting the turnaround to come in late May or early June was basis usual lead times fundamental improvements in China has on the market. That the market reacted quicker than usual to improvements in China shows that underlying fundamentals are very firm. 

Still, given that the market upturn is a bit "ahead of schedule" there could be a cool-off into June.

However, the market has continued to push upwards, and more so in the Pacific than the Atlantic, which is slightly surprising given the high share of the fleet positioned East of Suez combined with the seasonal lull in coal demand.
